Piedmont Park’s lawn buzzed with youngsters cartwheeling and family picnics, all in the name of the autumnal season’s return. The City of Piedmont has celebrated the fall equinox by hosting the Harvest Festival for 26 years, and the accompanying Piedmont Jazz Festival has been part of it for 23 years. articles.text: Part 2 in a series The Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage each election cycle so voters may learn more about each City Council candidate and make well-informed decisions on election day. In the weeks leading up to the November 5 election, we will continue to publish a regular Q&A segment where candidates will answer questions about their backgrounds, qualifications and policies with a 200-word limit for each response. City Council dates. Two open seats and four candiWeek 2 Question: What specific issues would you address if elected and how will you address them? Conna McCarthy, Incumbent My priorities are determined by listening to the needs and interests of our residents and then working collaboratively with Councilmembers and City staff to implement priority projects. As a Councilmember for the past four years, I know public safety is a primary concern. We must continue to maintain high level police and fire services. To that end, Council prioritized funding the Dispatch Center Relocation Project. I prioritize “effective government” by supporting policies and structures that provide for the delivery of high quality city services. I also prioritize fiscal stability through oversight that supports Piedmont’s continuing financial health with efficient staffing, responsible budgeting and long range forecasting. I will continue to address Piedmont’s aging infrastructure by maintaining or improving municipal buildings and facilities for public use and enjoyment. I prioritize environmental stewardship to help the reduction of Piedmont’s carbon footprint. I support consensus driven policies for sustainability and energy conservation. And I prioritize consistent, predictable and inclusive civic engagement. I support community conversations challenging us to define our vision of Piedmont for present and future generations, and to determine how we will act upon that shared vision. Lorrel Plimier, Candidate One of my main priorities for Piedmont is community engagement. This means providing numerous, diverse avenues for public conversation and partnering with the community organizations and groups that make Piedmont special; it also means hosting regular town halls for people to voice their concerns, provide their ideas for creating new solutions, and working together. A second priority of mine is Public Safety. This means prioritizing fully funded and staffed Police and Fire Departments; it means strategically assessing and maintaining the city’s buildings, streetlights, crosswalks, and bike routes; and it means addressing our aging infrastructure, mitigating hazards, and maintaining our disaster preparedness efforts. Finally, I will prioritize the city’s continued focus on climate, housing, and our schools. This means supporting climate action in Piedmont that considers climate impact in all city decisions. It

Religion Corner Exploring the Greatest of All Time By Pastor Jim Hopkins Greatness is a topic much discussed and debated in our society. Basketball fans argue about the GOAT of their sport. Is it Jabaar? Is it Jordan? Is it James? Is it Curry? Their perspectives vary based on many factors but the fact that the matter is very subjective and ultimately insoluble does not prevent voices from rising or tempers from flaring. The slogan of one of 2024’s presidential candidates was “Make America Great Again.” It is a slogan with a long history and one that is guaranteed to cause emotion-laden responses. The slogan itself needs to be explored. What is greatness? How is America defined? To what historical moment or period does “again” refer to. Jesus was no stranger to debates about greatness. He was queried about which commandment was the greatest. His disciples seemed to vie against each other to be called the greatest and, on at least one occasion, enlisted their mother to jump into the argument. One such episode is recorded in The Gospel of Mark 9:33-37. Jesus asked the Twelve, upon returning to their headquarters in Capernaum, what they had been arguing about while walking home. They did not answer for they were ashamed to admit that they had been fighting about who was the greatest. (Then, as now, just because such topics are certain to generate more heat than light, doesn’t mean we can stay away from them.) Jesus called the group together and said, Whoever wants to be first must be least of all and the servant of all. To drive his point home Jesus brought a little child into the circle, embraced him and said, Whoever welcomes one of these children in my name welcomes me; and whoever welcomes me isn’t actually welcoming me but rather the one who sent me. There is more than one way to interpret Jesus’ words and actions. Yet, I hear him saying “The debate about who is the greatest of all time may be an interesting discussion but it can’t be satisfactorily answered and it gets to be very irritating. What I can say with a great degree of certainty is that there is no greater call than to seek the best for our children.” In other words, he declares that the greatest work of all time is working for the well-being of children. There are many in our country who would likely profess to agree See Religion Corner on page 29 JOAN HARE, Wildwood Avenue My favorite is Rocky Road. articles.text: Can you host a Ukrainian family from October 1 until the end of school year in the summer of 2025? The father lives in Piedmont now and is awaiting the arrival of his wife and two sons, ages 10 and 2, in September. The family, separated by the conflict in Ukraine, is hoping to reunite and start anew in the USA. They need 2 bedrooms and 1 bathroom; any housing arrangement would be appreciated. They are wonderful people, the father is employed and seeking IT opportunities. They can drive and help with shopping, running errands, household repairs, and gardening. For more information and references, call Piedmont resident Maxim Sulimov at 510-457-5635. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: On Wednesday, September 18, the Jewish Community of Piedmont, in partnership with PJ Library, welcomed award-winning musician and educator Eliana Light for a family concert in Piedmont Park. Joining her on drums was Bay Area native Gabriel Lehrman. A lively crowd of more than 90 people, including 35 families, joined the celebration. A native of North Carolina, Eliana is currently on her “Elul Tour,” bringing people together in song all across the country. In these challenging times, music has the power to open our hearts and help us find joy in connection with one another. This was powerfully demonstrated on Wednesday evening as the community ate, sang and danced together behind the beautiful Exedra Plaza. “It was an honor to bring such a renowned talent like Eliana to our community,” said organizer Donna Friedman Meir. “It filled my heart to see the park filled with families singing and dancing together, celebrating our Jewish heritage at a challenging time for our community. As always, our goal is to bring people together for joy, meaning and connection, and Wednesday night’s picnic in the park most definitely achieved that.” Music also has the power to teach. Eliana’s songs for kids aim to be Schoolhouse Rock with a Jewish twist. Her concert focused on songs all about the fall holidays. like “Happy Birthday World’, highlighting how Rosh Hashanah as the birthday of the world and “Tap Your Heart,” a family-friendly Ashamnu, a traditional Jewish prayer of repentance recited every Yom Kippur. The Piedmont family concert is one of five Bay Area stops on Eliana’s Elul Tour Eliana also writes soulful, memorable, meaningful Jewish music and melodies for adults. Join her this weekend for the other events noted above. Links to more information at elianalight.com/elul “It was wonderful to feel the warm embrace of the Jewish community of Piedmont and Oakland, and to laugh and sing along with this amazing community,” she said. “May this be a year of light and hope for all.”
articles.title: Jewish community of Piedmont brings music to Piedmont Park

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is currently having a drive for residents to sign up for AC Alert Notifications in observation of National Preparedness Month. Residents who register for alerts by October 15 will be entered into a raffle for a chance to win a $100 gift card. AC Alert is an opt-in system utilized by Piedmont and Alameda County safety officials to offer instructions by phone, text message and email to residents on what to do in the event of emergencies such as earthquakes and wildfires. The alert system can be used by officials to share information regarding evacuation orders and warnings, shelter-in-place instructions and where to find shelters and services during an emergency. The alerts may also be used by county officials to share information on road closures, red flag warnings and significant weather forecasts. The fire department described the AC Alert system as “the single most important step every resident should take to be prepared for a disaster.” Piedmont residents who wish to receive the AC Alerts and who would like to enter the raffle are encouraged by the fire department to visit ACAlert.org where they can add their home, work and children’s school addresses to their alert locations. The PFD said safety officials target alerts to the geographic areas that are impacted by the event. Once a resident receives a confirmation that they’ve enrolled in the alert system, they should send an email with proof of registration to prepared@piedmont. ca.gov by October 15 in order to enter the raffle. National Preparedness Month is an annual campaign that seeks to impart the importance of being prepared for unforeseen disasters. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The City of Piedmont recently hired Andrew Kaplowitz as the new Americorps Climate Fellow. Under the direction of Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun, Kaplowitz will be responsible for implementing the City’s Climate Action Plan and engaging with the public on related issues. He will also be responsible for Piedmont’s annual Greenhouse Gas Inventory later this year, which tracks the level of carbon emissions being emitted by the city each year. Kaplowitz started at his new position on Monday, September 9. “Piedmont is a great and welcoming community, and I look forward to continuing to promote that concept of community as we understand the environmental issues that the city faces,” said Kaplowitz. Kaplowitz takes over the position after the departure of Alyssa Romea, the previous Climate Fellow, whose 11-month contract ended in July. Originally from New York City, he was born in 2002, and grew up on the city’s Upper West Side where he attended Anderson Elementary School and graduated from Millennium High School. During high school Kaplowitz was inspired to enter the field of environmental policy after the national climate walkouts that gripped the nation’s schools in the late 2010s. “That was really my first motivator for why I wanted to pursue this field,” he explained. Kaplowitz attended the University of Michigan, where he received a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Studies earlier this year. He then entered the Sustainability Service Corps, an Americorps fellowship program that delivers professional development to emerging climate protection leaders. He was contacted about a position in Piedmont, and said, “Of all the sites that could have called me, Piedmont was the first.” Kaplowitz remembers being Staff photo Andrew Kaplowitz is the City of Piedmont’s new Americorps Climate Fellow. impressed by Piedmont the first time he saw it. “First of all, Piedmont is really beautiful,” he laughed. He gets a good look at the city every morning when he commutes via public transit from his apartment in Berkeley. He also notices several kids taking the bus to school every morning – another reminder in his mind of the community’s character. “It makes me really happy to see these kids take the bus because I would do the same thing in middle school. I know a lot of parents opt to drive their kids to school, but I think there’s a lot of environmental benefits to taking the bus and a lot of independence that can come from that,” he said. Now that he’s on the job, Kaplowitz is excited to get to work helping the city reduce carbon emissions and educating the public. Specifically, he looks forward to executing Piedmont’s initiatives for electrifying residential gas appliances and encouraging public transportation. Andrew Kaplowitz, Piedmont’s Climate Fellow, may be contacted at akaplowitz@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City welcomes Andrew Kaplowitz as new Climate Fellow

articles.text: As the weather suddenly shifts cooler, it brings our minds to the reality that fall is just around the corner. While we must be ready to say goodbye to summer, it means many of our favorite fall events are fast approaching. This year, like the last eleven, means the Piedmont Center for the Arts Artisanal Beer Fest. This year’s event takes place on Friday, October 18, from 5:30-7:30 p.m. at the PCA, 801 Magnolia Ave. at Bonita. As in years past, the preparation for the popular event began earlier this summer with invitations to craft brewers from Piedmont and the greater Bay Area. Most beers take weeks, if not months to create, so brewers need to begin their creations long before. The forecast for the variety of beers presented this year is excellent. The number of brewers who will be attending exceeds the last two years. With several brewers planning to present more than one entry, the selection and variety of beers to be tasted will increase. The list of brewers is made up of many who have participated in years past along with the addition of experienced brewers who are entering their first festival. The festival is meant to support and enjoy local home brewers’ efforts, and as in the past, the top beers selected by the judges will be announced during the event, This year’s judges will be Dave Larson, owner of Piedmont Grocery, City council members Conna McCarthy and Jennifer Long, Piedmont Recreation Commissioner Dick Carter, and Piedmont Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosevich. This year’s event will also include a “Peoples’ Choice” scoring to parallel the judges’ efforts. In addition to sampling many beers, the festival also features a German Oktoberfest meal outside on the lawn in front of the Center. A meal of grilled bratwurst and German mustard, red cabbage, and potato salad will be provided by long time supporter Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery. Adding to the picnic atmosphere will be music provided by a trio of Piedmont High musicians. Tickets for beer tastings are $15, which includes a keepsake Center for the Arts Beer Glass. The Oktoberfest meal is also $15. More information can be found by visiting the PCA website at www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org Tickets will be sold at the door but advanced ticketing is recommended and can be accessed by visiting https:// tinyurl.com/3cx2pzrj

articles.text: On September 21, the Piedmont community came together for the Wish, Wonder, and Wine fundraising event, hosted at the Piedmont Community Church. The event brought together camp supporters for a delightful evening of fine food by Chef Robert Dorsey, delicious wine from David Shaeffer and Dana Murray, exciting auction items, and some heartfelt moments. This vibrant evening was dedicated to supporting Camp Augusta, an organization that creates transformative experiences for youth as well as family fun, exploration, and bonding at family camps. Guests enjoyed an array of heavy hors d’oeuvres while mingling with fellow camp enthusiasts. The atmosphere buzzed with excitement as attendees bid on an impressive selection of items during both the silent and live auctions. A special Camp Augusta “playstation” element was built into the live auction with props and costumes. True to Camp Augusta’s values of “Wish, Wonder and Surprise,” a “balloon pop” game allowed guests to buy a mystery balloon, then pop it to reveal a prize. The event was filled with laughter and camaraderie as people shared a commitment to enriching the lives of young people and families. On a busy weekend, friends of Camp Augusta who couldn’t attend showed their support by donating, which along with the successful auction raised $20,000. That amount was matched by an anonymous generous donor. Thanks to the community, the Wish, Wonder, and Wine event not only raised funds but also strengthened community bonds, making it a night to remember for everyone involved. Becky Spies pops a balloon. Photos by Joshua Posamentier Ayyana Chakravartula, Cindy Hinman, and Mike Ero enjoy the live auction skits. Appetizers by Robert Dorsey Camp Augusta Auctioneer Jude Martin Kristin Quinn and Garrett Gonzales win a prize.

articles.title: PMS Medieval Faire

articles.text: The annual 7th Grade Medieval Faire at Piedmont Middle School started in the patio where Brenneman Manor did the magnificent and magical Maypole dance for everyone. Shortly after, the Vilkova Manor danced to Dancing Queen by Abba on the red carpet as King Sai and Queen Quinn made their way to their thrones. The trumpeters played a Royal Fanfare for the King and Queen. Then it was time for the Scherman Manor to perform the skit, “Don’t Put Your Whole Hand in the Pot,” by Erasmus. The skit explained to the other manors how to properly eat a feast of juice, cheese and cookies using proper Medieval etiquette. Afterwards, the Brenneman Manor performed the traditional circle dance, rotating between different dances, solo dances, and formations - a truly hypnotizing performance fit for a King and Queen. Next the Pirate Dance was performed by the Kelly Manor, an incredible and truly accurate dance of a medieval battlefield, the swords clanging against the opponents, both enemies fighting in unison and synchronizing. The fallen lay dead on the ground - true entertainment for the nobility. It was the fights their bards sang of in legends. After all the groups finished their dances and everyone had eaten properly, King Sai said with a smile, “To all who attend this feast, the queen and I thank you once again for the beautiful performances you have all put together, and again for coming to this feast. In the courts we have prepared games and booths for all of you to enjoy as a sign of our gratitude.” Everyone clapped for the generosity of the king and queen. With that, the feast was over, and everyone left to go play games.
articles.title: A Medieval gathering at Middle School

articles.text: As we call this year’s seventh graders back for the annual medieval faire and take a trip back in time, an important part of this tradition is the roles being played and royalty. There are seven core classes in seventh grade, from which two lucky people were picked out of a hat to be king and queen. This year’s king and queen, Sai Gonzalez and Quinn Kan-Miller, learned that having this special role is not all crowns and pretty dresses. The king and queen have to write a speech, thanking everyone for being there, and they lead the banquet. But the king and queen aren’t the only roles portrayed in the faire. Each core class has a lord and lady. They also have to speak at the banquet. Sometimes it isn’t more than three cheers for the king and queen, and a couple of hip-hip-hoorays from the class manor. Roles also include not only royalty, but roles in skits. This year’s skit, Erasmus’s Rules, was performed by Mr. Scherman’s class. It gave a light-hearted review on manners, and how to be a good guest. The talented actors had to wipe grease on each other, shove each other, and even pretend they were picking their noses, which was the highlight of the performance. Other classes did performances for the king and queen including a dance by Ms. Vilkova’s class and a performance that included sword fighting, done by Ms. Kelly’s class.
articles.title: Roles & Royalty

articles.text: The Medieval Faire had lots of interesting games. One of the games was a corn hole game in which you faced an opponent and had to get as many bean bags as you could in the hole or on the game board. Some other games included the “Donut on a String,” which required contestants to put their hands behind their backs and eat as much of a donut on a string as possible. One other food-related game was the “Diet of Worms,” in which students had to find three gummy worms on a plate of whipped cream without using their hands. That one got a little messy! Another fun activity at the faire was “Soak A Bloke,” where a teacher would go into stocks and students would throw a wet sponge at them, trying to hit their faces. In addition, there were stilts, and some students decided to take their chances and try to walk with them; it was not as easy as it looked! Finally, the “Marriage Booth” was incredibly popular. Students could marry another student and get a fake certificate of marriage and get a ring pop in return. Overall, the students had a great time playing the various games.
articles.title: Games for all

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, September 25, 2024 PMS Medieval Faire A Medieval gathering at Middle School By Julien Lintner-Calvo The annual 7th Grade Medieval Faire at Piedmont Middle School started in the patio where Brenneman Manor did the magnificent and magical Maypole dance for everyone. Shortly after, the Vilkova Manor danced to Dancing Queen by Abba on the red carpet as King Sai and Queen Quinn made their way to their thrones. The trumpeters played a Royal Fanfare for the King and Queen. Then it was time for the Scherman Manor to perform the skit, “Don’t Put Your Whole Hand in the Pot,” by Erasmus. The skit explained to the other manors how to properly eat a feast of juice, cheese and cookies using proper Medieval etiquette. Afterwards, the Brenneman Manor performed the traditional circle dance, rotating between different dances, solo dances, and formations - a truly hypnotizing performance fit for a King and Queen. Next the Pirate Dance was performed by the Kelly Manor, an incredible and truly accurate dance of a medieval battlefield, the swords clanging against the opponents, both enemies fighting in unison and synchronizing. The fallen lay dead on the ground - true entertainment for the nobility. It was the fights their bards sang of in legends. After all the groups finished their dances and everyone had eaten properly, King Sai said with a smile, “To all who attend this feast, the queen and I thank you once again for the beautiful performances you have all put together, and again for coming to this feast. In the courts we have prepared games and booths for all of you to enjoy as a sign of our gratitude.” Everyone clapped for the generosity of the king and queen. With that, the feast was over, and everyone left to go play games. Brenneman Manor performs the Maypole Dance. Photos by Anne Smith and Picture Happy Photos Roles & Royalty By Lila Levinsohn As we call this year’s seventh graders back for the annual medieval faire and take a trip back in time, an important part of this tradition is the roles being played and royalty. There are seven core classes in seventh grade, from which two lucky people were picked out of a hat to be king and queen. This year’s king and queen, Sai Gonzalez and Quinn Kan-Miller, learned that having this special role is not all crowns and pretty dresses. The king and queen have to write a speech, thanking everyone for being there, and they lead the banquet. But the king and queen aren’t the only roles portrayed in the faire. Each core class has a lord and lady. They also have to speak at the banquet. Sometimes it isn’t more than three cheers for the king and queen, and a couple of hip-hip-hoorays from the class manor. Roles also include not only royalty, but roles in skits. This year’s skit, Erasmus’s Rules, was performed by Mr. Scherman’s class. It gave a light-hearted review on manners, and how to be a good guest. The talented actors had to wipe grease on each other, shove each other, and even pretend they were picking their noses, which was the highlight of the performance. Other classes did performances for the king and queen including a dance by Ms. Vilkova’s class and a performance that included sword fighting, done by Ms. Kelly’s class. King Sai Gonzalez and Queen Quinn Kan-Miller, pose with the Maypole dance going on in the background. Blacksmith Forrest Poole (left) and peasant William Rivera help Rob Ashton find a jester’s innate ability to walk on stilts. Paolo Dimas (left), Henley Azad, and Sasha Lindgardt at the marriage booth Ben Brasfield (left), Jude Oldrin, and Abby Gregovich work the guillotine at the Medieval Fair. Games for all By Sawyer Hepner The Medieval Faire had lots of interesting games. One of the games was a corn hole game in which you faced an opponent and had to get as many bean bags as you could in the hole or on the game board. Some other games included the “Donut on a String,” which required contestants to put their hands behind their backs and eat as much of a donut on a string as possible. One other food-related game was the “Diet of Worms,” in which students had to find three gummy worms on a plate of whipped cream without using their hands. That one got a little messy! Another fun activity at the faire was “Soak A Bloke,” where a teacher would go into stocks and students would throw a wet sponge at them, trying to hit their faces. In addition, there were stilts, and some students decided to take their chances and try to walk with them; it was not as easy as it looked! Finally, the “Marriage Booth” was incredibly popular. Students could marry another student and get a fake certificate of marriage and get a ring pop in return. Overall, the students had a great time playing the various games. articles.text: This year’s edible food contest recorded 165 total entries of food grown by Piedmont residents within the Piedmont City borders. Thirty-seven categories of homegrown edible foods and culinary products from fruit butter to vegan baked goods, and curds to hot sauce received multiple entries and were judged by respected members of the Piedmont community. Kudrat Kontilis’ Pasta sauce won first place in the Sauce category. Photos by Sophie Hess The Biggest Zucchini category was won by the De Young Family. The Bill Drum Award, named for the co-founder of the harvest festival of the event. honors the person winning the most blue ribbons. As a team Dorinna Mendoza and Jamie Austin were awarded a $60 gift certificate from Ace Garden Center. The Sweepstakes Award goes to the family entered in the most categories. The Marinelly Family with 22 separate entries, won the 2024 title and a Village Market $40 gift certificate. Thanks to Edible Contest volunteers Lilla Wells, Alex Slatoff, Carolyn George and Susan Hill. Carolyn Pan’s apple pie won in the “Other Pie” category. Key Lime bars by Carolyn Pan were popular – and earned her a first place.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team brought home the firstplace trophy of the 2024 Napa Tournament by going undefeated through four games on Friday and Saturday, September 20-21. Playing in the B bracket, Piedmont opened with a 13-10 win over San Rafael and closed the first day with a 17-1 pounding of Justin Siena. articles.text: Staff Photos Tommy Ashton rushed for 157 yards and two touchdowns against Encinal. Piedmont High’s football team improved its record to 3-1 now approaching the midway mark of the season. They celebrated Homecoming with a one-sided 49-14 win over against Encinal at Witter Field on Friday, September 20. It marked the team’s third dominant win in a row. They now have outscored their opponents 126-35 in the past three weeks. Although Piedmont ended the first quarter with a narrow 7-0 lead, they extended the gap to 21-0 in the second quarter before Encinal got its first touchdown. The Jets didn’t score again until the early minutes of the fourth quarter. “We came out flat in the first half. We weren’t tackling well and gave up a long third-down twice. It’s great we won, but it felt like we were losing even when we were up 21-7. Encinal was excited and feeling good going into the half. That’s not how we need to play ball, but it’s good to know we played well in the second half,” said coach Jordan Seiden. Seiden carried a similar tone after Piedmont’s previous 35-0 win over Mt. Eden, when the Highlanders didn’t score until the second quarter. Despite the big win over Encinal, Seiden feels Piedmont need to put games away faster, knowing stronger competition is on the horizon. “Our new saying is, ‘You can’t play with your food.’ You get into games in our league against Hayward, Irvington, and Washington, and you can’t let them hang around. We’re not going to be able to play against playoff teams like that. If you turn the ball over, not having the offensive line in sync, that’s a recipe for trouble. I want to see what it looks like when we put four full quarters together,” Seiden said. Piedmont goes into its bye week and next suits up next against Dougherty Valley, which is 2-2 as a Division 1 North Coast Section School. The Wildcats are coming off a 20-12 win over Kennedy, which competes in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Mission Division against the Highlanders. Game Recap Piedmont led 7-0 after the first quarter and extended the gap to 21-7 by halftime. The Highlanders then put up 21 points to double their score in the third quarter, then added one more touchdown in the fourth. It was a huge game from Tommy Ashton at running back, recording 157 rushing yards on 13 carries for two touchdowns, averaging a gaudy 12.1 yards per carry. Encinal had the opening possession and drove down to the Highlanders’ 20-yard line before a field goal attempt went wide left. Piedmont then scored on just three plays, capping off with a long 53 yard run by quarterback Markos Lagios on a read-option keeper with 2:15 left in the first quarter. On the following kickoff, Piedmont recovered a chip kick botched by Encinal’s return team at the Jets’ 26. However, Encinal intercepted a pass on the first play but punted after three plays, including tackles for loss by Xavier Anderson and Jordan Xavier Anderson filled the stat sheet with a rushing touchdown, kickoff return touchdown, nine tackles, a QB sack, and tackle for loss.

articles.text: Piedmont lost 20-0 to defending WACC champion Alameda. Piedmont’s flag football team traveled to Alameda High’s Thompson Field on Thursday, September 19 to take on the defending Western Alameda County Conference champions, losing 20-0. Despite the score, PHS had some bright moments on defense. “They are the defending champions., but we’re continuing to make progress,” said coach Beth Black. “We saw our defense locked in and them playing as a team. Instead of getting down on themselves, they are recognizing specific areas to improve.” Miya Fujimoto returning to action after recovering from an ankle injury sustained in a preseason game. She lined up both offensively and defensively after playing on offense only last season. “It’s nice to have Miya back. It’s great having her play both sides of the ball; she didn’t play defense last year. We can see her abilities translate to the defensive side,” Black said. PHS looks ahead to a pair of games against WACC competition this week, traveling to Hayward tomorrow, September 26, before taking on Berkeley on Monday, Staff Photos Dorothy Nemeth reels in a reception. September 30. Hayward is 2-0, but the Yellowjackets are 2-8, including a 33-6 loss to Alameda. Game Recap Piedmont trailed 13-0 by halftime and allowed one more touchdown in the second half. After a three-and-out, Alameda scored on a six-play drive with 17:28 left in the half. During the series, Piedmont’s Lily Colbert recorded a sack on 1st-and-Goal at the 11 yard line. However, Alameda scored on a third-down pass. On Piedmont’s ensuing possession, Dorothy Nemeth had a Miya Fujimoto is making an impact on both offense and defense. 15-yard reception to nearly convert a first-down, but Piedmont punted after being a few yards short. Alameda scored on its next drive, including converting a 3rd-and-21 situation, followed by a 40-yard touchdown pass— making it 13-0 with 11:54 before halftime. Piedmont’s offense couldn’t muster a first down conversion in the opening 24 minutes, but held Alameda without another score in the remaining minutes of the first half. Making their mark was Ella Yasar and Dahlia Osman recording pass defenses, while Fujimoto had a five-yard tackle for loss. Alameda scored the game’s final touchdown in its first possession of the second half, scoring after nearly six minutes on a 10 play drive. articles.text: Staff Photos Samantha Huynh, part of Piedmont’s No. 1 doubles team, won matches against Castro Valley and Lick-Wilmerding. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team won two of its last three matches in successive days. The Highlanders shut out Arroyo 7-0 at home on Tuesday, September 17, and lost 6-1 to Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco the next day. They blanked Castro Valley 7-0 on the Trojans’ home court on Thursday, September 19. The Highlanders won all of its singles matches against both Castro Valley and Arroyo for the first match of the league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference’ Foothill Division. “We won all 14 sets against Castro Valley and Arroyo teams and most of them were pretty one sided. We played the top of our lineup against CV and we lost a total of 17 games in the seven matches against Arroyo,” coach Jim Landes said. PHS has two matches at home at the Corey Reich Tennis Center this week. They host Division 2 North Coast Section opponent Marin Academy today, September 25, then bring in WACC foe Alameda tomorrow, September 26. Shutting out Castro Valley At si n g le s , C a r ol i n a Romanczuk double-bageled her opponent in a 6-0, 6-0 sweep at the No. 1 spot. Kate Jumper played at No. 2, winning 7-5, 6-2. Arianna Kortum won 6-4, 6-2 at No. 3, while Faith Chin won 6-2, 6-1 at No. 4. At doubles, Samantha Huynh and Maddie Tran and played as the No. 1 pairing, winning 6-1, 6-1. At No. 2 was Inara Mehta and Abigail Call, winning 6-1, 7-5. Alina Shahid and Ella Thompson won 6-4, 7-5 at No. 3. 6-1 to Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont lost its four singles matches and two of three matches at doubles. PHS’ only win on the afternoon came at No. 1 doubles, where Emma Eisemon and Huynh won in three sets including a very close 10-point tiebreaker for the third set, 4-6, 6-2, 10-8. “Our new number one doubles team, Emma E and Sam, lost an up and down first set, much like the match against University. They found their rhythm and won a quick second set. Things tightened up in the ten point tiebreaker, but their experience and solid tactics prevailed 10-8,” assistant coach Corey Reich described. At singles, Romanczuk lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 1, Jumper fell 6-2, 6-0 at No. 2, Kortum lost 7-5, 6-0 at No. 3, while Chin lost 6-3, 6-0 at No. 4. Maddie Tran was paired at No. 1 doubles with Samantha Huynh for the win against Castro Valley. At doubles, Tran and Emma Chan lost 6-3, 6-3 at the No. 2 spot. Mehta and Amelia Addington had a three-set loss at No. 3, where the third-set tiebreaker went an extra point. Their final score was 7-5, 2-6, 11-9. 7-0 over Arroyo In singles, Kortum appeared in the No. 1 spot, winning 6-2, 6-2. Chin played No. 2, winning in a 6-0, 6-0 shutout. Lila Rosen appeared at No. 3, winning 6-4, 6-2. Hallie Burden rounded things out at No. 4, winning 6-1, 6-1. The doubles duo of Chan and Mehta at No. 1 won 6-2, 6-0. Shahid and Amelia Addington won 6-0, 6-3 at the No. 2 spot, while Chiara Silvo and Thompson won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 3. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-6 overall, 1-0 league) hosts Marin Academy today, September 25, at 3:30 p.m. PHS then hosts Alameda tomorrow, September 26, at the same time. Kate Jumper at No. 1 singles won against Castro Valley.

articles.text: Piedmont’s JV football team claimed a dominant 41-0 win against Encinal. Hong, George Saunders Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team claimed its second straight dominant win with a 41-0 shutout against Encinal on Friday, September 20 at Witter Field. It comes after Piedmont’s 49-12 win over Mt. Eden the previous week. The JV Scots have outscored their opponents 84-12 in the last two weeks. Piedmont’s captains for Friday’s game included freshmen Max Fujimoto and Mateo Long, along with sophomores Owen Curran and Colby Hong. Hong becomes the first twotime captain of the season and is currently leading the team in tackles and interceptions. Also returning to the quarterback spot was freshman Jimmy Lagios after recovering from an injury. The Scots came out slow in the first quarter after tossing an interception on the first drive of the game. The Jets drove to Piedmont’s red zone on its ensuing possession, but the PHS defense forced a turnover on downs. Lagios got things rolling on the next drive, connecting with receiver Diego Hurwitz for a 30-yard touchdown. It was the first of three touchdowns for Hurwitz, giving him eight total scores on the season. On Encinal’s next offensive series, Fujimoto blocked a punt, resulting in a scoop and score by Hong to make to 14-0. articles.text: Kids’ event at Mills College campus and pool The Oakland Triathlon Club will hold its second annual “Youth Splash and Dash” at Mills College on November 2, offering youngsters aged 6 to 15 a chance to take an invigorating athletic swim followed by a hearty run. The Splash and Dash event will begin with the swim segment in the 10 lane Trefethen Aquatic Center pool before students run through the heart of the Mills College Campus. Participants between the ages of 6 and 10 will complete a 100-yard swim followed by a 1k run, while older participants between the ages of 11 and 15 will complete a 200-yard swim followed by a 2k run. “As a triathlete and parent, I’ve loved seeing my own kids’ excitement when I compete,” said Triathlon Club President Deepak Gupta “I loved having their first experience of multisport at last year’s Splash & Dash feel celebratory and approachable. The OTC Youth Splash & Dash demonstrates OTC’s trademark community and camaraderie, and we are excited to share that with Oakland’s youth again this year.” Parents can register their kids on the event website: splashanddash.oaklandtriclub. org. The event is intended as an introduction to multisport and will not have official timing or prizes. “The Youth Splash and Dash is more than a race – it’s a community celebration,” explained the Triathlon Club’s press release. “Families, friends, and fellow community members will be there to cheer on these young athletes as they conquer the course.” All children participating will receive an Oakland Triathlon Club swim cap, a goodie bag and a USA Triathlon finisher medal to honor their accomplishment. The Oakland Triathlon Club’s event is the first USA Triathlon-sanctioned Splash and Dash event in Northern California. The club’s event is now one of several that make up the 2024 Northern California Youth Series. “I love the USAT Splash and Dash format, as it embraces everything I love about the joy of multisport, and gives me a way to invite my own kiddo into the sport without any pressure,” said Oakland Triathlon Club Race Director Betsy Block. “Last year’s event was a celebration of joy of being active, and I’m so excited to see this event grow.” The club’s second annual “Youth Splash and Dash” is sponsored by Transports, Talamel, B3 Coach, and ACE California Law. Additional sponsors include Zone3, Gentico and Zen Strength & Conditioning.
articles.title: Triathlon Club to host Splash & Dash event on Nov. 2

articles.text: Piedmont High junior Lucas Smolko traveled to New Mexico over the Labor Day weekend from Saturday, August 31 through Sunday, September 2, winning the United States Tennis Association Level 4 Northern New Mexico Masters tennis tournament in the Boys’ 16 and under singles event. Playing in Albuquerque’s heat and high elevation against some tough competition, Smolko made it look easy with an opening 6-2, 6-1 victory over Hugh Sheffield of Texas. He advanced to the quarterfinals with a near shutout of Ayden Thielsen of Arizona, 6-0, 6-1. In the semifinals, Smolko battled to a three set win over Zachary Tan of Washington by scores of 6-4, 5-7, 10-6. He went on to capture the title with another three-set marathon win in the finals, 6-3, 6-7 (7-2),10-5 over Ethan Valdez of Texas. Smolko is set to be a threeyear starter on Piedmont High’s tennis team next spring. He has competed every year as the No. 1 singles starter. We named him our 2023 Freshman of the Year and was our honorable mention for 2024 Sophomore of the Year. Piedmont High junior Lucas Smolko won the USTA Level 4 Northern New Mexico Masters 16 and under tournament. In the spring of 2024, Smolko won the WACC Individual Tournament singles title with a 6-2, 6-2 win over Bishop O’Dowd’s top player. He went on to reach the Div. 2 North Coast Section Individual semifinals. Staff Photos Lucas Smolko played as Piedmont’s No. 1 singles player and is the defending WACC Individual Tournament champion.
articles.title: PHS junior Lucas Smolko wins Northern New Mexico Masters tennis tournament

articles.text: Piedmont’s girl’s water polo team battled to a 5-3 win against American in Fremont on Monday, September 23 to bring its record to 6-8 “This was a tight, hard fought game. Our girls just didn’t quit and played a clean game with just two exclusions compared to American’s nine fouls,” said coach Georgia Lewis. ”They began to catch up with American in the fourth quarter. Our girls scored two hard fought goals with less than a minute to go.” Piedmont also competed in the Napa Tournament at Vintage HS on Saturday, September 21, where they lost 16-4 to Righetti in the opener and fell 11-5 to Monterey later. Our players didn’t back down but kept up the pressure in the fourth quarter Sydney Olsen sends in a shot. Photos by Lynne Wright Abigail Jacoby had a goal and two assists in a victory over American. and came back, scoring four goals to Castro Valley’s one. We were building momentum, but ran out of time. It is exciting to watch the team work together and pull hard for each other.” PHS next competes at Foothill in Pleasanton on Monday, September 30 then takes on San Leandro at the Pirates’ home pool the next day, October 1. 5-3 over American Both teams stayed deadlocked 1-1 through the first quarter and were scoreless in the second to keep the tie. I PHS broke through with two goals with just 42 seconds and nine seconds left in the game. articles.text: Mary Zimmerman returns to Berkeley Repertory Theatre to direct the West Coast premiere of The Matchbox Magic Flute on October 18. The Matchbox Magic Flute is Zimmerman’s adaptation of Mozart’s iconic opera The Magic Flute and uses only 10 singers and five musicians. The adaption reimagines Mozart’s beloved opera by using big music in a small space with a few talented artists and actors. “Berkeley Rep is my theatrical home away from home,” said Zimmerman. “It was the first theatre ever to produce a run of a show of mine outside of Chicago, and it remains my favorite place to come. I love the theatre, the entire staff, the audiences, and the surrounding city, hills, and Bay. The whole cast is really excited to spend time here with our crazy little music-hall Flute.” The cast of The Matchbox Magic Flute includes Marlene Fernandez, Emilie Lynn, Russell Mernagh, Lauren Molina, Tina Muñoz-Pandya, Reese Parish, Shawn Pfautsch, Emily Rohm, Billy Rude, and Monica West. The play runs through December 8. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/the-matchbox-magic-flute/. Photo by Liz Lauren From the Goodman Theatre production of The Matchbox Magic Flute ®
articles.title: Berkeley Rep premieres The Matchbox Magic Flute on Oct. 18

articles.text: The cast of The Prom at Berkeley Playhouse Berkeley Playhouse launches its 2024-25 season with The Prom, with performances now through October 13. The Prom tells the story of four Broadway actors and actresses who visit small-town Indiana to champion a local high school student’s right to bring her girlfriend to the prom. The play, based on a book by Bob Martin, was originally performed on Broadway in 2018 and was later made into a movie featuring Meryl Streep and Nicole Kidman. The Berkeley Playhouse production is co-directed and co-choreographed by Megan McGrath and Christina Lazo, with music directed by Daniel Alley. Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley said she was thrilled to select The Prom as the theater’s season opener. “This musical is bursting with so much heart and humor, plus it’s full of laughter and fantastic dancing,” said Dooley. “It’s the perfect show to open our new season for its beautiful messages of acceptance, joy, friendship, and love for all.” “There have been instances over the years across the country of parents pulling their students from high school productions and local theaters canceling their shows due to the material,” said co-director Lazo. “We have to do this show and keep doing shows like this. I can’t wait for audiences to see the sparkle and the beauty of the world within The Prom.” The play features Arri Toshiko Glenn as Emma Nolan, Aleshani Altan as Alyssa Greene, Taylor Bartolucci as Dee Dee Allen, DC Scarpelli as Barry Glickman, and Mary Kalita as Angie Dickenson. To purchase to tickets and for showtimes, visit https://tickets. berkeleyplayhouse.org/
articles.title: The Prom at Berkeley Playhouse through Oct. 13

articles.text: Back to Back, a concert starring Jay Krohnengold and Amy Dondy, with Larry Dunlap on piano, will be performed at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, September 28 at 4 p.m. With decades of performing in the worlds of cabaret, traditional and immersive theater, and the concert stage, actors and vocalists Jay Krohnengold and Amy Dondy have joined forces to present a program spanning decades of songs from the worlds of musical theater and jazz. Focusing on composers and lyricists Stephen Sondheim, Alan and Marilyn Bergman, Kurt Weill and Oscar Hammerstein, to name a few, their show explores the intricacies, and the highs and lows, of life and love. articles.text: Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) by Kara Walker The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) new, commissioned piece by Stockton-bor n ar tist Kara Walker, entitled Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine), will be on view through May 2026. Walker is a contemporary painter, silhouettist, printmaker, installation artist, filmmaker, and professor who explores race, gender, sexuality, violence, and identity in her work. She is best known for her room-size tableaux of black cut-paper silhouettes. Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) is a colossal version of her trademark artworks, and marks Walker’s most ambitious large-scale public project to date. It is the first time the museum commissioned an artist to create a site-specific installation for the Roberts Family Gallery. Walker’s new artwork follows other major exhibitions at the museum including Diego Rivera’s massive world-renown mural, Pan American Unity. The commission of Fortuna and the Immortality Garden was organized by Eungie Joo, SFMOMA’s curator and head of contemporary art, who worked with the artists many times over the last 27 years. “Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) emerges out of the abject loneliness of the COVID-19 pandemic and the ominous depopulation of our once thriving downtown San Francisco,” Joo said. articles.text: Monette’s artwork focuses on Hurricane Katrina aftermath The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) will present Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive by Jessica Monette. The exhibition features motifs borrowed from aerial surveys of Hurricane Katrina’s impact, as well as commercial building materials such as house paint, plaster and thin-set mortar taken from wrecked houses. Thus the restaurant is a feast for the appetite as well as a feast for the eyes. The owner is a young enthusiastic man named Fardad Khayami. I thought it best that he select the cuisine. He described the brioche as “360 degrees of lamination.” If you think that French pastry is the best, think again. Begin your meal with the brioche. Next came a tomato salad. To ensure quality, Fardad gets up early every morning and shops at the Farmer’s market for the best produce. Our main course was the “catch of the day,” in this case bronzino, which had been pan seared so that the skin was crisp and the flesh of the fish was tender and juicy. It was served skin side up, which is not usual. When you turned the fish over, a surprise awaited you. The fish had been served over two different sauces. The branzino could be enjoyed in three different ways… The fish alone, or with a green sauce or with a white sauce. For a side dish, Fardad recommended that we get the roasted carrots. When they arrived, I thought they had been roasted and slightly charred on the outside. What looked to be charred to perfection was actually a sauce made of roasted herbs. After a dinner like this, a good dessert is required. The dessert cart arrived, and I wished that I could have had every one of the desserts. My wife and I selected the strawberry tart. It was a once-in-a-lifetime experience, which I hope to experience again. Service was friendly to say the least. After we paid the bill, we received a personal note from everyone who served us. The prices are not exorbitant for the quality that you get. But it is not a restaurant for those on a frugal budget. How much would you pay for the experience of a lifetime? After you finish dinner, go for a walk at the beach. You will have no problem thinking good thoughts. College? Retirement? Find out how to prepare for both. articles.text: Tickets now on sale for Piedmont performances in Oct., Nov. Festival Opera’s 33rd season will continue into autumn with two more Sunday afternoon artist recitals at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series began on September 22, with Lucky in Love presenting mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and Piedmont favorite, pianist Jeffrey LaDeur, founder of San Francisco International Piano Festival The series continues on Sunday, October 27, at 4 p.m. with Nothing to Fear featuring contralto Sara Couden and pianist Derek Tam. The final recital will be on Sunday, November 17 at 4 p.m. with Muses and Musings of an Impresario - a birthday celebration with special guest artists to be announced - showcasing Festival Opera General Director and baritone Zachary Gordin as well as pianist Daniel Lockert. Earlier in the company’s season, Festival Opera presented two annual Opera in the Park concerts at Orinda Community Park and Walnut Creek Civic Park, featuring beloved community park programs of grand opera and Broadway musical highlights. For the mainstage production at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin and guest stage director Céline Ricci presented a double bill of two one-act operas regarding love and betrayal: Francis Poulenc’s riveting mid-1950s monodrama La Voix humaine based on iconoclast Jean Cocteau’s play of the same name and Baroque masterpiece Dido and Aeneas by Henry Purcell, based on Virgil’s epic work, the Aeneid. Sunday, Oct. 27 at 4 p.m. Nothing to Fear Contralto Sara Couden commented, “What do art, song and Halloween have in common? Well…monsters. Beasts without and within, love gone horribly wrong, generalized anxiety and existential crises, conversations with death… the world of classical music is rife with horrors, and I am excited to introduce as many of them as possible to the audience this October. I will be working with the fabulous and multi-talented pianist Derek Tam and presenting works by a list of composers including Schubert, Strauss, Wieck and Weill as well as modern composers Jordan Rutter-Covatto, Erika Oba and Chris Castro. Don’t worry, there’s nothing to fear… but fear (love/ death/the beast within) itself.” Sunday, Nov. 17 at 4 p.m. Muses and Musings of an Impresario Baritone Zachary Gordin said, “I am honored to collaborate with this group of Bay Area treasures on this recital series and most especially to rekindle my work with the incomparable Daniel Lockert in a recital of repertoire and anecdotes that will tell a story of my journey and muses in this life of music. Songs of composers so very dear to me [will be featured]: Schumann, Mahler, Reynaldo Hahn and Jake Heggie mixed with a splash of early music and American Songbook classics.” Surprise guests are to be announced, and a birthday celebration reception including wine, bubbly and treats will follow the program. Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin will be showcased in Muses and Musings of an Impresario in a concert in Piedmont on Sunday, November 17. Contralto Sara Couden will be featured at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in Nothing to Fear on Sunday, October 27. Festival Opera was founded in 1991 by Dr. Theodore Weis who twenty years earlier had helped create the Arizona Opera Company in Tucson. Past Festival Opera leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp and Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony. It is currently led by Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera is committed to presenting emerging and local artists in compelling and socially relevant productions of both new and classic repertoire. Festival Opera proudly gives emerging artists a venue to hone their craft in leading roles with the guidance and collaboration of established professionals - providing a vital launching pad for their professional future. Festival alums have gone on to perform in major opera houses and symphony halls around the globe. Tickets for the Festival Opera Artist Recital Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are $40 per person for each concert, or individuals may purchase all programs for the discounted price of $95. To purchase tickets online, visit https://www.festivalopera. org/artist-recital-series

articles.text: Thursday, September 26, 7:00 p.m. Chamber Music Society of SF This favorite chamber group returns after a two-year absence to present a thrilling program of string quartets by Brahms and Haydn, brilliantly performed by Natasha Makhijani and Jory Fankuchen, violins; Clio Tilton, viola; and Samsun van Loon, cello. Advance tickets at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/1010711163297 by sliding scale donation. Sept. 27 –October 8 (weekends) Michelle Tholen Original Art Between the above dates, PCA’s walls will be covered with original art by local East Bay artist Michelle Tholen. Inspired by restrained color and order, she is challenged to create pop using a color combination that is refined and yet suggests more. In a Modern minimalist style reminiscent of Rothko, the artist paints in acrylic on canvas. Please join Michelle for an artist reception celebrating her new work on Friday, September 27, 5-7 PM. Enjoy bites and beverages, with music by classical pianist Ellen Walker. Saturday, September 28, 4:00 p.m. Cabaret Afternoon with Jay & Amy An unusual afternoon of vocal and piano music will be presented by Jay Krohnengold and Amy Dondy, to explore the highs and lows of life and love through the works of Sondheim, the Bergmans, Kurt Weill, and Oscar Hammerstein, They will be joined by noted East Bay jazz pianist Larry Dunlap. Tickets at the door, or in advance at https:// bpt.me/6391110. Sunday, September 29, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert In the first of four chamber concerts this season, Berkeley Symphony presents Advocates & Influencers, a program including an 1846 piano trio by Clara Schumann, her “greatest, most mature four-movement work;” a more modern piano & strings concerto by Caroline Shaw, and Joaquin Turina’s unusual Spanish-themed piano quartet from 1931. This exciting program will be performed by Emanuela Nikiforova and Sarah Elert, violins; Darcy Rindt, viola; Stephanie Wu, cello; and Kymry Esainko, piano. Individual ($45) or series tickets ($128) are available at https:// www.berkeleysymphony.org or by phone at (510) 841-2800. Sunday, October 13, 4:00 p.m. Japanese Internment Camps: Life, Art & Music The first of three events in a new series created and presented by PCA will include Karen Korematsu, daughter of Fred Korematsu, who was arrested and convicted for not responding to military orders to report for transfer to an internment camp in 1942. He appealed the conviction all the way up to the US Supreme Court, but it was upheld. Karen will detail his story and that of their family during the Camp years, will answer questions from the audience wil, and will interact with you during a reception. The second event in the series, November 2, will feature Wendy Tokuda, the former News anchor at KPIX, and Kimi Hill, grandaughter of Chiura Obata, an artist who continued to paint while in the camps. The series will finish November 23 with a screening of Alternative Facts: the Lies Behind Exec. Order 9066, the instrument that created the whole controversial sequence! Event and Full Series tickets are now available at https://bpt.me/6449591. Friday, October 18, 5:30 – 7:30 p.m. 12th Annual Artisanal Brewing Competition PCA’s annual beer festival once again takes center stage, offering tastes of multiple home-brewed beers from local home brewers in a souvenir beer glass along with a traditional German Oktoberfest meal donated by Piedmont Grocery. Served on the front lawn at the Center, the meal includes grilled bratwurst, German potato salad, and warm red cabbage. The beers will be rated by a panel of judges, with several prizes to be awarded. A trio of PHS musicians will provide music on the front lawn. Beer glasses and food tickets are available at the door.

articles.text: The Piedmont Chamber Orchestra (PCO, now in its seventh year, will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 16 at 4 p.m. The program, titled Remembrances, Recollections, and Reflections, includes popular gems by Ravel, Fauré, Honegger, Sibelius, and Schubert, plus Serendipity, a spirited recent work by Bay Area composer John Beeman which he re-orchestrated especially for PCO. The orchestra’s concerts have become a favorite of local music lovers, who have filled Piedmont Center for the Arts at each performance. The orchestra is composed of current and former professional musicians as well as highly skilled amateurs from Piedmont and surrounding areas. It is led by music director Martha Stoddard and assistant conductor Andrew O’Donnell. The concert is free to the public. A post-concert reception with the musicians will follow. Piedmont’s hometown orchestra, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra.

Festival Opera proudly gives emerging artists a venue to hone their craft in leading roles with the guidance and collaboration of established professionals - providing a vital launching pad for their professional future. Festival alums have gone on to perform in major opera houses and symphony halls around the globe. Tickets for the Festival Opera Artist Recital Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are $40 per person for each concert, or individuals may purchase all programs for the discounted price of $95. The Piedmont Chamber Orchestra (PCO, now in its seventh year, will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 16 at 4 p.m. The program, titled Remembrances, Recollections, and Reflections, includes popular gems by Ravel, Fauré, Honegger, Sibelius, and Schubert, plus Serendipity, a spirited recent work by Bay Area composer John Beeman which he re-orchestrated especially for PCO. The orchestra’s concerts have become a favorite of local music lovers, who have filled Piedmont Center for the Arts at each performance. The orchestra is composed of current and former professional musicians as well as highly skilled amateurs from Piedmont and surrounding areas. It is led by music director Martha Stoddard and assistant conductor Andrew O’Donnell. The concert is free to the public. McConaughey (in the library with a candlestick) is Baker Dill, a deeply tanned fishing boat captain, and a hard drinking denizen of a tropical island named Plymouth. He’s clearly damaged, lives in a converted metal ship container, modified with door and windows, and walks naked to the edge of a cliff each morning and jumps into the ocean. His ex-wife, Karen, portrayed by Hathaway, shows up one morning on the dock and makes Baker an offer he at first refuses. Has something to do with her current abusive, psyIf you’re willing to plumb the realms of suspending your disbelief, try the delightfully over-thetop movie. The premise is reminiscent of the 1924 short story by Richard Cornell, titled The Most Dangerous Game. Its plot is pretty straightforward: Idle rich people wanting excitement devise a game where people are hunted instead of animals, with, of course, unexpected consequences. The film opens with a few moments of exposition where Alex Le Domas (Mark O’Brien) and his bride-to-be, Grace (Samara Weaving), are discussing a post-ceremony ritual that has been a tradition in his staggeringly rich family for generations. Before she can become fully and officially a member of the Le Domas clan, she must play a game: pick a card and whatever its face instructs, that is what you must do. Alex explains to a skeptical Grace that the card could be, benignly, Old Maid or likely a board game such as checkers. So, the agreeable bride and mildly apprehensive groom get married and prior to the honeymoon, like immediately, the family and the newlyweds congregate in a large trophy room where the game will be executed. Grace sits at the head of a long table and the large extended family, granted a bit weird, to include a worried Alex, gather around to watch. Grace picks a card from a covered box and holds it for all Samara Weaving in Ready or Not to see. It says, Hide-and-Seek. No worries. A kids’ game. But the look on Alex’s face is now beyond worried. What follows after the card is drawn amounts to one long reveal. Grace, still innocent of what awaits her, still wearing her wedding gown, climbs awkwardly into a large dumbwaiter to wait, assuming it’s only a matter of time until she’s found and the game is over. Back to the honeymoon. But she soon learns that this is not a game of Hide-and-Seek but Hide-and-Hunt. From the moment of that realization, Grace reaches deep inside to overcome panic, a reactionary klutziness, desperate to find even a shred of resourcefulness. She soon rips apart her wedding dress so she can run, slips into a pair of Converse red tennis shoes, and begins to play the game. Sure it’s outrageous, but outrageously riveting, due in great part to the excellent portrayal of Grace by Weaving. She is as convincingly vulnerable as she is strong. This film is hardcore B-moviemaking with often tongue-in-cheek comedic vignettes that unrelentingly bump into one another. Fans who love a dangerous game will be massively entertained. Ready or Not. Directed by Matt Bettinelli-Opin and Tyler Gillett. Starring Samara Weaving, Mark O’Brien and Henry Czerny. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Streaming on Fandango/prime/apple tv. The first movement is a lyrical and jovial conversation amongst friends, followed by a lusciously serene and meditative second movement. The stillness is gently re-energized by a cheeky dancing third movement and the work is capped with a fiery finale. Brahms' c minor String Quartet is the first of only three extraordinary string quartets that the perfectionist composer would publish in his lifetime. The work opens with a turbulent first movement, oscillating between surging lines of tension and extreme lyricism. The drama takes a breath in the tenderness of the second movement Romanze. The third movement is shrouded in mystery and the roiling fourth movement brings the quartet to a heart-racing finish. articles.text: Spirited Away is an extraordinary, award-wining (Oscar, Golden Bear, Annie Award) animated feature film by Hayao Miyazaki. It is a compelling fairytale-adventure that will captivate its young audience. The narrative opens with Chihiro (Daveigh Chase), a young girl, 10, sitting in the backseat of the family car. Her arms are crossed, her attitude is petulant; she’s clearly not happy. The family – mother (Lauren Holly) and father (Michael Chiklis) – have decided to move to the countryside. Chihiro is already missing her friends. As it turns out they take a wrong turn, enter a tunnel, and discover they are in what appears to be an abandoned amusement park. Spotting a restaurant, they go in and her parents begin to eat. Chihiro wanders away and soon runs into a boy her own age, Haku (Jason Marsden), who takes her on a tour of the park. When she returns to the restaurant she discovers that her parents have been transformed into pigs. She learns that this shocking change was brought about by a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette) who runs a bathhouse for tired spirits. articles.text: The Piedmont Post is presenting one month of reviews of films by celebrated Japanese animation director, Hayao Miyazaki. As a writer, director, and animator he is one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, and worldwide. His award-wining animated films have been embraced by audiences that have found his beautifully detailed hand-drawn visuals and thematic storytelling compelling. As well, his protagonists are often strong young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors and writers. This week’s reviews are: Kiki’s Delivery Service (1989) and Spirited Away (2001).
articles.title: presents: A month of Hayao Miyazaki films

articles.text: Kiki’s Delivery Service, adapted by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, from a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s animé and prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home to complete her magic training in another town. She takes her talking cat Jiji, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, Kiki’s Delivery Service is also a wonderful adventure, but it is also a personal crossroads for Kiki, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. The tale is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Voiced by Kirsten Dunst, Debbie Reynolds and Matthew Lawrence. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated G, Released 1989. Now streaming on Fandango/apple tv/ MAX/YouTube. articles.text: PIedmont couple supported many arts organizations Piedmont resident John Nady, credited with revolutionizing live concerts with his invention of the wireless microphone, died on August 2, 2024. Born on February 13, 1945, he came into the world at the end of World War II as his family attempted to flee war ravaged Hungary. This was a precarious time to be born, struggling to stay alive amidst exploding bombs, little to eat, and an uncertain future. In his early life, John was nourished on chalk and beer…the only source of nutrition available. acle baby. The Nady family eventually made their way to San Francisco in 1951 and began their new life with next to nothing. John, the youngest of 3 siblings, excelled in academics, sports, and music, but perhaps his most endearing traits were his irreverent sense of humor and burgeoning creativity. He attended St. Ignatius College Prep in San Francisco, graduating at just 16 years old. He later graduated from the prestigious California Institute of Technology (Cal Tech) where he studied nuclear physics, ultimately receiving a degree in Electronics Engineering. He then received a Masters degree from the University of California at Berkeley. From an early age, John was exceptionally innovative and a brilliant problem solver. After several post graduate engineering positions, he was ready for a new challenge. He’d become an accomplished rock guitarist (playing local gigs at night), and his love of music, along with his electronics expertise, planted the early seeds of a new mission—to untangle the hardwired world of live entertainment. He made the risky decision to devote himself full time to music—and to the pursuit of the first commercially viable wireless guitar system. With few resources, but his entrepreneurial spirit in full gear, John became the first to tackle the complex issue of noise reduction in wireless microphones. In the early 1970’s, after eight years of painstaking research & development and one particular “Aha moment”, John succeeded in developing and patenting a circuitry known as audio companding. As a result, the first Nady Wireless was spawned…the accomplishment for which John became best known and which soon revolutionized the way live music was performed worldwide. To this day, Nady technology sets the industry standard for clear, natural sound. And for John’s pioneering work in establishing wireless in the live entertainment industry, he is widely regarded as the “Father of the Wireless Microphone”. John established his company, Nady Systems, Inc, in 1976 in the kitchen of his small Berkeley, California home. Soon after, he began marketing to the music/ pro audio industry. In 1981, Nady outfitted the Rolling Stones with wireless for their upcoming tour. When Mick Jagger appeared on the cover of Time Magazine with a Nady wireless mic tucked in his pants, people were instantly awestruck…not just by the image, but because the potential for the technology was suddenly recognized. top performing acts were using Nady wireless. In addition to the Stones, Nady introduced the concept to many of the biggest name headliners at that time including Madonna, Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi, Aerosmith, Styx, and Neil Young. Now everyone wanted a wireless microphone or guitar and the freedom it offered. In 1987, Nady Systems took off like a rocket with the introduction of the legendary and very affordable – 101/201 Wireless Series, opening up the world of wireless to virtually everyone. After this, Nady microphones became widely used not just for stage performance, but in schools, churches, broadcasting and numerous public speaking applications. Nady distribution continued to grow, and in 1996, Nady Systems was recognized by the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences with an Emmy for “Outstanding Technical Achievement” in pioneering wireless microphone technology. This prestigious award acknowledged Nady’s groundbreaking contributions to the field. Never one to rest on his laurels, however, John was not content to remain simply “the wireless leader”. Over the years, Nady Systems diversified into related fields, establishing itself as a broad-based pro audio/communications company, introducing numerous professional audio products. The list is long and included amplifiers, speakers, hardwired microphones and a vast array of other popular gear distributed throughout the U.S. and internationally. Aside from Nady Systems, in 1986 John embarked on yet another venture – the establishment of a multi venue concert promotion company, California Concerts, along with his wife, Toby. It eventually included three of the largest nightclubs in the Bay Area – The Omni in Oakland, The Stone in San Francisco, and One Step Beyond in Santa Clara. The company also promoted live shows in larger venues throughout California. John and Toby worked closely together in business and also shared a deep commitment to supporting many charitable causes, including Children’s Hospital of Oakland, Bread & Roses, Living Jazz, the Salvation Army, Oakland Symphony and a host of others. They believed their home in Piedmont was meant to be shared, and they welcomed requests to host fundraising events. John loved life and he approached it with zestful energy and a sense of purpose. His family is what he loved most of all, and his commitment to family never wavered even during the most challenging of times. His drive and enthusiasm were hard to resist and fueled many family adventures over the years. John was a force of nature. Uniquely gifted and talented, he dreamt big and more often than not, saw his dreams through to fruition. His curiosity was endless; his knowledge of history, science, sports, current events and politics was daunting. He had a keen intellect along with a quirky, offbeat sense of humor. And while he was known to be opinionated, he was acutely prinJohn Nady, inventor of the wireless microphone shown with an early wireless prototype. John Nady displays the Emmy Award he received in 1996 for “Outstanding Technical Achievement” in pioneering wireless microphone technology. cipled, never hesitating to explain his positions. John will be deeply missed by family, friends and his many contacts in the music community. He is survived by his wife, Toby Garten Nady; children, Matthew and Samantha Nady; sister, Elizabeth Moore; sister-in-law, Karen Nady; brother-in-law, Allan Basbaum; and nieces and nephews Stephanie Moore DiMarco, Jennifer Moore Riebli, Andras Nady, Katherine Basbaum, and Jesse Basbaum. He was preceded in death by his parents, Hermine and Ivan Nady, and his older brother, Louie Nady. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Medecins Sans Frontieres / Doctors Without Borders. A private celebration of life will be held in the coming weeks. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of 37 walkers and two K-9 best friends last Wednesday. It was cloudy so the group headed to Sunnyside Avenue. This was an early Piedmont street with some history and there are interesting things to see along the way. The walkers went down Magnolia to Nova Drive where it becomes Wildwood Avenue. They discovered one of Piedmont’s many hidden paths which connects Nova and the lower portion of Fairview Avenue. The land between lower and upper Fairview was originally a right-of-way for the early 20th Century Key System 12 Line. It went from today’s Jerome and Fairview Avenues to Grand Avenue and to downtown Oakland. Early homeowners wanted to easily get to the Key System trains, and pathways were drawn into neighborhood master plans to accommodate them. The group went down to Grand Avenue and walked up Sunnyside. They stopped to talk about the house at 228 Sunnyside, the home of Daryl Rush, a contractor and decorative metalwork artist. The house was built in 1879 and has a waving brick wall surrounding it. They continued on to see early Piedmont homes built in 1893 and 1896. At the end of the street they saw 110 Sunnyside the former home of Lieutenant Egbert Beach and his parents. Beach was killed in 1918 during action in World War I, the first officer from California killed in the war. Later that year the Lake Avenue School was renamed in his honor and is now Beach School. The walkers returned on Lake Avenue and through the dog run on Linda Avenue, emerging at the Oakland Avenue bridge. Some of Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society research was also shared. The Oakland Avenue Bridge was the historic entrance to Piedmont. Albert Farr designed it in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont. Farr used the same Spanish design that he had used in the Piedmont City Hall and the Bonita Avenue School, which later became Havens School. The bridge replaced an old wood trestle that was built in 1890 for the cable cars that served the area in its early years. The bridge was built in 1911 by Engineer John Buck Leonard of Union City, Michigan, who was a pioneering bridge engineer, architect, and early advocate for reinforced concrete. There are architectural motifs such as steep walls and overhangs which were once used to prevent entry into medieval fortresses. This seemed appropriate then and now for Piedmont. It is a concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue with a 160-foot arch span and retaining wall supported approaches in a closed spandrel concrete deck arch design. The largest span is 159 feet, and the total length is 343 feet, slightly longer than a football field. The relatively new lampposts, lights, and now the guardrails make the Oakland Avenue bridge a lovely entrance to the city, and the guardrails make the bridge safer for pedestrians. The group went on Oakland Avenue to Arbor Drive and the upper portion of Fairview, where the Key System 12 Line once ran. Then it was back to Oakland Avenue for a short walk to the upper portion of San Carlos Avenue and a return to the Exedra via Magnolia.
