Walkers explore the length of St. James Dr. By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group was up for a longer walk last week on a lovely morning with a strong turnout of 50 walkers and one K-9 best friend. St. James Drive is a long, flat street and easy to walk. Going all the way to its end at Park Boulevard would let the walkers see a very little visited street with Piedmont homes, Cavendish Lane. There were places along the way to turn back for anyone not wanting to go this far. The group went up Crocker Avenues to Hampton Road and the beginning of St. James Drive. Two white columns mark one of the entrances to St. James Woods, a very large real estate development begun in the 1920s. The neighborhood was governed by the St. James Wood Homes Association founded in 1926 and represents over 185 homes in Piedmont and Oakland. The CC&Rs have some restrictions on what homeowners can do with their property. However, the last annual meeting and website posting was in 2012. Phil Witte, who lives on St. James Drive, said the association is no longer active. The columns are missing lanterns on their tops. The neighborhood once wanted the City to put replicas of the originals on them, but neither the residents nor the City wanted to pay for them, so it never happened. The walkers also noted the distinctive four brown tiles that are inlayed in each section of all the concrete sidewalks that were part of this neighborhood. St. James is seven tenths of a mile long to its end at Park Blvd. At St. James’ end just past Trestle Glen Road is Cavendish Lane, a narrow street that looks like an alley. It is in Oakland, but there are four homes with Piedmont addresses at its end. The street was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a construction project on a Trestle Glen home below. The hillside and road slipped away, and the Piedmont families were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont made temporary fixes, but permanent repairs by Oakland did not begin until 2019, two years later due to inaction by the City of Oakland. After walking a few hundred feet the group saw the repaired roadway, a retaining wall, and the hillside below with rusting concrete rebar on top of it. A hard-to-read Piedmont Public Works notice, dated August 2021, was taped on the wall and said all construction work was to be stopped because of violations of City ordinances. It seemed that nothing had been done to the hillside since the walkers’ visit last year. The group retraces their steps back to the middle of town, It had been a four-mile walk, longer than usual. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. First Monday Reading Group discusses Heaven and Earth By Dick Carter A group of 22 book lovers showed up on September 9 for the First Monday Reading Group’s discussion of The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store by James McBride, released in 2023 to favorable reviews. The novel starts in 1972 in Pottstown, Pennsylvania, where an excavation operation for a new housing complex discovers a skeleton in the bottom of a well. Some items are found near the body, including a mezuza, which leads a policeman to question the town’s only Jewish resident. However, the investigation is hampered when the crime scene is washed away by Hurricane Agnes. The story then goes back to the 1920s and 30s and details the lives of the town’s residents in what was mostly the Black and Jewish Chicken Hill neighborhood. Two of the Jewish residents, husband and wife Moshe and Chona Ludlow, own a local theater with a dance hall and The Heaven & Earth Grocery Store. Nate Timblin, one of the town’s Black residents who works for the Ludlows, asks them to hide a deaf young Black boy, Dodo, from the authorities who are trying to institutionalize him in a notorious mental asylum. The actions of the town physician, who is a member of the Ku Klux Klan and has sexual desires for Chona, lead to Dodo being sent to the asylum. The Black and Jewish townspeople mobilize to help the boy. The book provided a lot of enjoyment for the readers; McBride is a wonderful storyteller. It was “a large book with more than a touch of Charles Dickens” said one reader. There are multiple layers to the story. The themes of communities working and living together, the importance of families, and how people are treated all resonated with the readers. McBride took his time developing the characters and provided details that most readers enjoyed. However for other readers felt the characters were stereotypes or caricatures. The stereotypes had some truth to them and these readers could relate to them. This was especially true for readers who had personal experiences with the setting, or the Jewish, Black, and disabled communities. McBride seemed to be poking fun at everyone. The readers were emotionally touched by the harsh treatment of Dodo and his severely handicapped asylum friend, Monkey Pants. Readers could feel for the characters who didn’t have a lot of love in their lives. The group also liked the strong women who drove the story’s action. Pleasure was taken by the justice rendered to the bad guys and the story’s mostly happy ending. Objections from the were that more than a half of the book was a “slog” with too many characters and too many details. The book needed a better editor, they felt, and an important story was being treated in a slapstick manner. Some other interesting, related elements emerged from the discussion too. The characters had a distrust of the area’s government and its ability to perform basic functions. This may have contributed to the development of the Mafia. The readers had previously selected Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell for their October book and North Woods by Danile Mason for November. After hearing reviews presented by Laura Goldman of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected Leadership: In Turbulent Times by Doris Kearns Goodwin for their December read. The group’s next discussion will be on October 7 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join and there is no fee. In fact, all the architectural styles we have been discussing are built of certain materials that have long been developed, along with the building forms, to define the different styles. There are many overlapping and intertwined considerations in the selection of building materials, including aesthetics, cost, durability, and structural qualities. But maybe local availability was, and still is, the driving force. The ancient Egyptians didn’t build extensively with wood because they didn’t have much of it. They used stone and formed bricks from the desert instead. Here in the western U.S. our abundant supply of lumber naturally became the first, most economical selection. The development over the years of accepted, preferred aesthetics has led to newer manufactured processes and materials that imitate the original materials that were first used with and have become associated with design styles. Stucco for example, the most common exterior building material in California, looks in its more roughly textured finishes, like the plastered adobe walls on the Spanish styles of architecture, or, with its more finished (flatter) textures, like the plastered masonry of many other architectural styles. The most apparent exterior materials of any building are those of the walls and roof. Beyond these however, the aesthetic of a building is strongly influenced by minor visible material choices like flashing, trim, gutters, railings and flues. On good buildings these “punctuation points” of design clearly have been considered to fit with and complement the dominant material selections. In addition to aesthetic considerations, material selection always is a balancing act between quality and cost. More durable, longer-lasting materials generally cost more initially. Factoring in the true building-life costs, however, mitigates the differences. If, for example more expensive copper flashing and gutters are used, they are probably going to last the life of the building, whereas less expensive gutters of less durable materials will have to be replaced after a certain number of years. On good buildings these “punctuation points” of design clearly have been considered to fit with and complement the dominant material selections. articles.text: Dear MacMama: I see there is a new iPhone out. I have an iPhone 12, should I upgrade? There seem to be so many choices, can you explain? –Lizzy, Piedmont Dear Lizzy: Every year around the middle of September, Apple comes out with a new iPhone. Soon to follow that is a new operating system for the iPhone and iPads. And every year the speed gets better the camera gets better, and hopefully the battery gets better although that hasn’t always been the case. If you are a person who likes to travel and uses your iPhone to take pictures then I would say absolutely, it’s a great idea to upgrade to the new iPhone 16. Of course there are actually four versions of the iPhone 16. There’s the iPhone 16, the 16 Plus, the 16 Pro and the 16 Pro Max. The features between the models and their respective larger versions are not very different, but there are notable differences between the iPhone 16 models and the more expensive and feature-rich Pro models. These are all available for order and will be in stock as of Sept. 20. iPhone 16 and 16 Plus: The iPhone 16 has a 6.1-inch display and is the smallest iPhone 16 available. The 16 Plus model has a 6.7 inch display. These iPhones have an aluminum case with a color infused glass back and come in five colors including ultramarine, teal, pink, white and black. The cameras on these models are what Apple calls the Advanced dual-camera system 48MP Fusion 12MP Ultra Wide. They have optical zoom capability at .5, 1x and 2x. This is a much more advanced camera than your iPhone 12 has, but not as advanced as the pro models of the iPhone 16. The iPhone 16 comes in three storage capacity choices; 128 GB for $799, 256 GB for $899 or 512 GB for $1099. The iPhone 16 plus has the same storage capacity choices and is $100 more expensive for each iPhone 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max The Pro models are slightly bigger. The iPhone 16 Pro has a 6.3 inch display, while the 16 Pro Max has a 6.9 inch display. These models have a titanium case with textured matt glass back. They come in four colors; desert titanium, natural titanium, white and black. It’s with the camera on the pro models that we start to see some of the major differences of the pro models to the less expensive iPhone 16 models. In these phones, Apple has included what they call the Pro camera system with 48MP Fusion and 48MP with Ultra Wide and Telephoto capability. The zoom factor is also more impressive with .5, 1x, 2x and 5x. Although you can certainly take macro photos with the iPhone 6, the pro models give you a 48 megapixel experience with macro. That means if you want to take a close-up of a flower or an insect or a beautiful stone, you will get a much higher resolution with the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro models also offer Dolby Vision up to 4K at 120 fps, so if you’d like to make videos, you could shoot a movie in a pretty high resolution. I have seen some amazing videos created by professional filmmakers with just their iPhone 15. So if photography is something you’re interested in then it might be worth investing in one of the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro comes in for storage capacity, choices; 128 GB for $999, 256 GB for $1099, 512 GB for $1299, and one terabyte for $1499. The pro max version comes in only three capacity choices; 256 GB for $1199, 512 GB for $1399 and one terabyte for $1599. Another thing that the prom models have that the base model does not have is what they call ProMotion technology which according to Apple, “ …is a new technology that delivers refresh rates of up to 120Hz for fluid scrolling, greater responsiveness and smoother motion content.” I have only listed a few of the features of these phones, but in real life, most people will be just fine with the iPhone 16. It comes in brighter colors and is slightly more affordable. And the iPhone 16 is the smallest of the new models. But if you travel, and photography is important to you as well as watching movies or video content on your phone, then the iPhone Pro models might be the way to go. Since these are new models, we don’t know if there are any bugs or issues with the hardware. That’s why it’s always prudent to buy AppleCare, or AppleCare plus which includes theft and loss. There are lots of ways to buy these phones, you can buy them directly from Apple, or you can buy them from your cell service provider. Sometimes the cell provider has better deals. You can certainly trade in your iPhone 12, and probably get close to $100 for it from Apple. But you should also check with your cell provider to see if they have promotions. data is very easy if you have backed up your current phone to iCloud. If you haven’t, it’s a good idea to do it before you get a new phone. Your new iPhone can be set up from your iCloud back up or directly from your older phone by having them next to each other. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com

Soon to follow that is a new operating system for the iPhone and iPads. And every year the speed gets better the camera gets better, and hopefully the battery gets better although that hasn’t always been the case. If you are a person who likes to travel and uses your iPhone to take pictures then I would say absolutely, it’s a great idea to upgrade to the new iPhone 16. Of course there are actually four versions of the iPhone 16. There’s the iPhone 16, the 16 Plus, the 16 Pro and the 16 Pro Max. The features between the models and their respective larger versions are not very different, but there are notable differences between the iPhone 16 models and the more expensive and feature-rich Pro models. These are all available for order and will be in stock as of Sept. 20. iPhone 16 and 16 Plus: The iPhone 16 has a 6.1-inch display and is the smallest iPhone 16 available. The 16 Plus model has a 6.7 inch display. These iPhones have an aluminum case with a color infused glass back and come in five colors including ultramarine, teal, pink, white and black. The cameras on these models are what Apple calls the Advanced dual-camera system 48MP Fusion 12MP Ultra Wide. They have optical zoom capability at .5, 1x and 2x. This is a much more advanced camera than your iPhone 12 has, but not as advanced as the pro models of the iPhone 16. The iPhone 16 comes in three storage capacity choices; 128 GB for $799, 256 GB for $899 or 512 GB for $1099. The iPhone 16 plus has the same storage capacity choices and is $100 more expensive for each iPhone 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max The Pro models are slightly bigger. The iPhone 16 Pro has a 6.3 inch display, while the 16 Pro Max has a 6.9 inch display. These models have a titanium case with textured matt glass back. They come in four colors; desert titanium, natural titanium, white and black. It’s with the camera on the pro models that we start to see some of the major differences of the pro models to the less expensive iPhone 16 models. In these phones, Apple has included what they call the Pro camera system with 48MP Fusion and 48MP with Ultra Wide and Telephoto capability. The zoom factor is also more impressive with .5, 1x, 2x and 5x. Although you can certainly take macro photos with the iPhone 6, the pro models give you a 48 megapixel experience with macro. That means if you want to take a close-up of a flower or an insect or a beautiful stone, you will get a much higher resolution with the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro models also offer Dolby Vision up to 4K at 120 fps, so if you’d like to make videos, you could shoot a movie in a pretty high resolution. I have seen some amazing videos created by professional filmmakers with just their iPhone 15. So if photography is something you’re interested in then it might be worth investing in one of the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro comes in for storage capacity, choices; 128 GB for $999, 256 GB for $1099, 512 GB for $1299, and one terabyte for $1499. The pro max version comes in only three capacity choices; 256 GB for $1199, 512 GB for $1399 and one terabyte for $1599. Another thing that the prom models have that the base model does not have is what they call ProMotion technology which according to Apple, “ …is a new technology that delivers refresh rates of up to 120Hz for fluid scrolling, greater responsiveness and smoother motion content.” I have only listed a few of the features of these phones, but in real life, most people will be just fine with the iPhone 16. It comes in brighter colors and is slightly more affordable. And the iPhone 16 is the smallest of the new models. But if you travel, and photography is important to you as well as watching movies or video content on your phone, then the iPhone Pro models might be the way to go. Since these are new models, we don’t know if there are any bugs or issues with the hardware. That’s why it’s always prudent to buy AppleCare, or AppleCare plus which includes theft and loss. There are lots of ways to buy these phones, you can buy them directly from Apple, or you can buy them from your cell service provider. Sometimes the cell provider has better deals. You can certainly trade in your iPhone 12, and probably get close to $100 for it from Apple. But you should also check with your cell provider to see if they have promotions. By the way, transferring your data is very easy if you have backed up your current phone to iCloud. If you haven’t, it’s a good idea to do it before you get a new phone. Your new iPhone can be set up from your iCloud back up or directly from your older phone by having them next to each other. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com

MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I was drawn to run for school board because of my interest in making Piedmont School District a place where every kid gets Roma Continued from page 20 cant is that the father of the child, Fermin (Jorge Antonio Guerrero), an obsessed kung foo neophyte, and a coward. When he hears of Cleo’s condition he immediately abandons her in a movie theater where she sits and waits for him to return with ice cream. The second male to leave is Antonio, a hospital doctor, who says he is going on a business trip to Quebec. In reality he takes his mistress to a resort on the coast. Sofia, growing ever distraught, maintains a lie to protect the children who begin to sense their father’s prolonged absence means more than they are being told. And so the audience is drawn into the very ordinary experiences of this family. Days pass. Months pass. Cleo grows larger. Still Antonio does not return. At first I was a bit distracted by the repeated wide screen shots. I wanted to move closer to Cleo, to observe the look in her eyes, the set of her mouth, see her protective hand placed on her expanding stomach. But Cuaron seems to insist that distance is a great education. As a STEM tutor, long-term substitute math teacher, a member of the Superintendent’s Advisory Committee and the Middle School Site Council, and as a former co-president of ALPS and adviser to the High School Math Club, I know firsthand what’s working well for our students and what isn’t. Every Piedmont student is unique – each has different interests, gifts, and goals, which often change as they grow. I believe our district must meet each student where they are, and challenge them accordingly as much and as soon as they’re ready. I’m very optimistic about teaching and curriculum, and the district is developing some promising approaches. I’m also focused on results. Ultimately what matters is the quality of outcomes for our students. To provide a great education, with well-designed curriculum and excellent instruction, PUSD must be a great place to work. Our district’s administration and faculty are all top-notch, but we need to retain and attract high-performing teachers and staff. I support cost-effective policies which result in better academic outcomes, emotionally and physically healthy kids, and improved employee satisfaction. MAX ROMAN, Candidate As a product of Piedmont’s schools (and the child of a longtime school district employee), I have a deep appreciation for our community’s commitment to its students and their education. I recognize that our schools face several challenges, including declining enrollment, a shortage of teachers, and the work to fund all of the programs that make Piedmont schools the special places that they are. I believe that every child deserves access to a high-quality education, regardless of their background or zip code. I will use my experience, both in business and with nonprofits (having served on multiple boards including the Piedmont Education Foundation) to ensure positive academic outcomes for all children in the district, make sure that all students and families are welcomed into the Piedmont community and made to feel that they belong, and to provide pragmatic, results-based decision making at the district level. essential. He once said about this technique, “I was interested to observe those moments at a distance without judgment.” But then, perhaps, it is an acknowledgement that the deeply personal narrative he is sharing is told through his prism of memory. Gradually the camera does move closer. The pace begins to accelerate and Cuaron engages us, culminating in several scenes that are heartbreaking and breathtaking in their stark loveliness. Later, there is a long wide angle shot of two of the children wading out in the ocean, going too far, suddenly in trouble, and Cleo, who cannot swim, walking deliberately through the waves, on the precipice of being overcome, unwavering in her attempt to rescue them. It’s a wrenchingly beautiful moment, the connection between her and the children touchingly inviolable. Roma repeatedly asks the question: what is the relationship between the moviegoer and the story? What are our expectations? To select a film, sit in a theater, which is where Roma should be seen (not on a small screen of any kind), is aspirational. We want to be pulled into a narrative that in some way touches us, that exists somewhere on the spectrum of emotions. Cuaron’s movie asks a great deal of us. Wait. Watch. Allow the vignettes – and Roma is constructed of a series of tightly crafted moments – to build, allow them to be slowly fitted together. And then relish the final scenes that are so wonderfully human, each a revelation. As an aside, Roma was nominated for Best Picture and Best Foreign Language Picture, Best Director, Best Actress and Best Supporting Actress, Best Original Screenplay, and Cinematography. articles.text: the decision-making required around material selection can be overwhelming. The process often has just begun with the actual selection of a material or product. The next decision may be size, then the choice of an available texture (the tactile surface) and then the colors. Most of the time selections are made from manufacturers’ standards, but often for a premium they can be custom made to the architects’ unique specifications. And finally, in the case of materials like masonry or brick, the laying pattern and coursing has to be decided. Editor’s Note: Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Roof materials are often prominent, especially with steeply sloped roofs like this beautifully designed Julia Morgan house. James Green, Candidate Politics in our country over the last few years has become divisive, contentious, and – at times – dangerous. Over the last three decades serving in the Federal Government and working on public policy in the Bay Area, Washington DC, and overseas, I have been fortunate enough to work with national leaders like Secretary Madeleine Albright and Governor Gary Locke. What I learned was how to listen, how to disagree without being disagreeable, how to lead when times get tough. In essence, what our system of representative democracy should do: elect leaders to improve people’s lives, better the environment, and care for those in need. And to show that Piedmont can be a leading example in politics, as it already is in many other areas. articles.text: The state of California has been expanding a Transitional Kindergarten (TK) program since 2022 and which will add an extra grade of school for four year olds by 2025. Architect Ector Mojica from Quattrocchi Kwok Architects (QKA) advised Piedmont’s School Board of its options to accommodate the new students during an August 14 school board meeting. There are 79 students in four TK classes in Piedmont this year; students that turned four by June 2 were eligible. Next year the eligibility will open up to any kids that turn four by September 1. For the 2025–26 school year, the District anticipates needing at least one more classroom to accommodate the new students. “Our administrators see kids coming and they don’t know where we are going to put them,” explained PUSD CBO Ruth Alahydoian. Mojica showed the board three options (A,B, & C) for each site. Potential facility changes included low-cost ways (option As) to shuffle classroom assignments around. At Havens the option A was to put a TK class in room 117 and migrate classrooms to keep grades together. Some options create TK and K combo classes, and some options involve some construction. The architect went over specific changes at each site, including one that would remove the Wildwood Schoolmates portable and build a new learning space. Mojica and board member Hilary Cooper talked about avoiding critique from the Division of the State Architect’s (DSA) office. The district incurred costly change requests from the DSA on the STEAM and Theater construction at PHS. This was an informative item for the board to further proactive discussion. The concluding sentiment on the item was to avoid new costs, new construction and to send the options to teachers at each site. “I think there’s a bit of facility fatigue in town,” said Vice President Lindsay Thomasson. “I’m personally of the thought that we need to take a deep breath on facilities and have a break.” No date has been set for this item to return to the board.
articles.title: School board explores options for TK

articles.text: Historic record sales by this year’s Beach Dads The aroma of hot pancakes and sausages mingled with jazz music at the 19th Annual Beach Dads Pancake Breakfast at Beach School on Sunday morning, September 8. Families attended the long-running event to eat pancakes, socialize with neighbors and raise money for the Beach Parents Organization. Volunteers with the Beach Dads served up plates of buttermilk, blueberry, chocolate chip and oatmeal pancakes plus sausages, bacon, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee to eager customers. A five-piece jazz band of student musicians from all over the East Bay entertained breakfast-goers with a series of instrumentals, providing a nice ambiance. “It is an amazing turnout. We are rocking and rolling this year,” said Michael Wilhelm, this year’s “Padre Grande” (Beach Dads Club president). “The line just keeps growing. It seems like we’re going to run out of everything at this rate.” This year’s pancake breakfast was a riveting success for the school. They sold roughly 650 tickets and served over 1,650 pancakes, making this their highest-grossing year. Raising the ticket price a bit compared to previous years certainly helped. As is tradition, previous Beach Dads president Michael Gross greeted guests at the event in the club’s giant pancake costume. The pancake suit is customarily worn by last year’s president and is typically a hit with parents and children alike. This year was no different. articles.text: I am certain that I am not alone in thinking about, worrying about and praying about the November 2024 elections, particularly the 2024 presidential election. Traditionally, Labor Day is the starting point for the most intense political awareness and involvement. Thus, I offer a few thoughts as we prepare to vote. 1. The right to vote must not be disrespected or neglected. In the long history of humanity, the right to vote for our leaders, laws and policies is a relatively new, hard-earned and very vulnerable right. Many of our foremothers and forefathers made great sacrifices in order that their children and grandchildren could vote. For that we praise them. Yet, praising them without thoughtfully exercising the right to vote is meaningless. 2. Our votes should be a reflection of our values. While we do not all share the same values, it is incumbent on each of us to vote in a way that expresses our goals for our communities, our vision for our country and our hopes for our world. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Matt Simons, Lead reporter Sophie Hess, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. RELIGION CORNER Every vote counts By Pastor Jim Hopkins I am certain that I am not alone in thinking about, worrying about and praying about the November 2024 elections, particularly the 2024 presidential election. Traditionally, Labor Day is the starting point for the most intense political awareness and involvement. Thus, I offer a few thoughts as we prepare to vote. 1. The right to vote must not be disrespected or neglected. In the long history of humanity, the right to vote for our leaders, laws and policies is a relatively new, hard-earned and very vulnerable right. Many of our foremothers and forefathers made great sacrifices in order that their children and grandchildren could vote. For that we praise them. Yet, praising them without thoughtfully exercising the right to vote is meaningless. 2. Our votes should be a reflection of our values. While we do not all share the same values, it is incumbent on each of us to vote in a way that expresses our goals for our communities, our vision for our country and our hopes for our world. Most of us would say that the well-being of the next generations is a high value for us. I would urge us to vote accordingly. 3. Freedom of conscience matters. One reason that faith leaders should, refrain from, or at least be very cautious about instructing their communities how to vote is our belief that freedom of conscience always matters and that, like voting, it is a sacred right. 4. Self-interest matters. It would be naïve to suggest that our own well-being should not matter when it comes to casting our ballots. However, self-interest need not be narrow or selfish. I firmly believe that there is such a thing as enlightened self-interest, the understanding that when you thrive, it is much more likely that I will thrive, the belief that when you are better-off, it is much more likely that I will be better off. 5. We can love our neighbors with our votes. articles.text: As a child, Lucas Romero’s parents took him for a tour of his local fire station. He remembers fondly the way he marched through the halls, took pictures of riding on the fire engine and pretended to spray a hose on imaginary fires around him. It’s a memory that he considers dear, especially now that he’s the one giving the tours. “I would say it’s come full circle,” he laughed. Firefighter Paramedic Lucas Romero, 27, is one of the newest recruits to the Piedmont Fire Department. Hired in January 2024, Romero brings with him experience as an EMT in San Joaquin County. He also brings a cheerful personality which has allowed him to mesh well with the other members of the department. Lucas Romero was born in 1997 in Tracy, and soon after his birth his family moved to Manteca. He attended Neil Hafley Elementary School and then graduated from East Union High School in 2015. After graduation, Romero briefly attended Delta College in Stockton before deciding that a career in academia wasn’t the best fit. In 2018, Romero decided he wanted to change careers. “I was climbing a pole for my job, and it was pouring rain. I saw an ambulance drive by with its lights flashing, and I remember thinking how cool that job would be,” recalled Romero. “That’s Lucas Romero was pinned by his girlfriend Kylee Killion at a Piedmont City Council meeting on July 15. That same year, Romero began working part-time as a reserve with the Manteca Fire Department and earned an EMT license from Abrams College in Modesto. In 2020, he joined American Medical Response in San Joaquin County as an EMT, where he worked a busy schedule encompassing several cities. “We covered Stockton, Lodi, Tracy, and many others,” he explained. “It was good experience, especially for what I do now.” Romero heard about the Piedmont Fire Department and after taking a written exam for the Firefighter Candidate Testing Center, Romero met Piedmont Fire Lieutenant Brian Gidney, who was handing out job flyers at the testing site. Romero applied in September 2023 and was given a conditional offer by the end of the month. Romero’s first impressions of Piedmont were like “a breath of fresh air,” and he said that the city has been extremely welcoming. “Some cities, they don’t care for their fire department, and some fire departments don’t care for their new hires. That’s not the case here.” Additionally, Romero said that the Piedmont Fire Department is different than any job he has had in the past, especially concerning its morale and quality of service. “You’ve got guys who take firefighting seriously. Captain Fitzpatrick’s huge on working out. We have a mandatory 90-minute workout every day. In Piedmont, you have to be ready for the job and do it well. And it’s all for the citizens,” he said. Romero was officially hired by the department in January, and on Monday, July 15, after five months of training at Las Positas College’s East Bay Regional Fire Academy in Livermore, Romero was sworn in at City Hall during a regularly scheduled City Council meeting. articles.text: Message to community from former School Board candidate Victoria Rosenbaum: Thank you to all my supporters who encouraged me to run for a PUSD Board seat in the upcoming election. I have a great interest in the continued excellence of PUSD, and as an educator, parent, and resident of this wonderful city, I know that I would add an important perspective to the issues facing our schools. However, after much consideration, I have decided that this is not the right time for me to serve on the PUSD School Board. Unfortunately, I have been informed by the City Clerk that it is not possible to remove my name from the ballot. In light of that fact, I am endorsing the candidacies of Susy Struble, Michael Malione and Max Roman and am encouraging others to support them, too. They each have unique strengths, perspectives, and a strong desire to promote PUSD’s mission, and I believe PUSD will continue to thrive with them at the helm. Thank you for your understanding and support. 2024 September 21, 2024 9 AM - 12 PM 800 MAGNOLIA AVE. PIEDMONT, CA RSVP: coffeecarscops@piedmont.ca.gov

articles.text: Treasure Island Museum is co-hosting an expert speaker event entitled “Resilience – Planning for Sea Level Rise in San Francisco Bay.” The event is open to the public and will be held at the Ferry Building in San Francisco this Friday, September 13, at 2 p.m. The event is co-sponsored by Treasure Island Museum and the Port of San Francisco and includes topics on climate action and sustainability, including how the museum’s redevelopment addresses climate change and sea level rise. The speakers include Allison Brooks, Executive Director of Bay Area Regional Collaborative, , Bay Conservation and Development Commission Director Dana Brechwald, and Save The Bay Political Director Allison Chan. The event’s host is Treasure Island Museum Board Member Rebecca Schnier, a Piedmont resident. The panel discussion will be moderated by San Francisco Chronicle urban design writer John King. Resilience is from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. at the San Francisco Ferry Building in the Port Commission Hearing Room, 2nd Floor. Admission is free, but advance reservations are encouraged. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/resilienceplanning-for-sea-level-rise-in-sanfrancisco-bay to reserve a spot. Treasure Island Museum is co-sponsor of a panel discussion on September 12 concerning a likely sea level rise in San Francisco Bay. articles.text: Tonight’s school board meeting, September 11, will take place at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall and is available remotely via Zoom. us/j/83434877218. One item seeking board review and action is a financial update report for Piedmont School District to be given by the district’s Business Manager Ruth Alahydoian. Wildwood parents should be interested to hear the a State of the School presentation delivered by its Principal Melissa Daymond. Her presentation will detail changes at Wildwood, including the hiring of six staff members. The Wildwood report will also talk about attendance and chronic absenteeism from last year, compared to other schools in Piedmont. Alahydoain’s unaudited Actuals report will update the community on budget adjustments, for example revenues increased by $2,157,025 since the Adopted Budget in June 2023, and expenditures increased by $1,377,414. Alahydoain will address changes and future insights. Also of interest from the Unaudited Actuals report is the State Schools Facilities Fund (Fund 35) which were used for Witter Field renovations. The ending balance is $5,766,000 and the facilities projects completed this summer, new roofs and HVAC systems, will also be paid from this balance.

articles.text: Life is filled with transitions, whether we like it or not. From childhood to adulthood, starting a new job, or even moving to a new city, transitions happen to all of us. And let’s be honest—they’re rarely easy. It doesn’t matter how old you are or what stage of life you’re in; change brings uncertainty, and uncertainty often brings stress. But if there’s one thing we know for sure, it’s that transitions are inevitable. For some, transitions come a little easier. But for most of us, change can feel overwhelming. What if, instead of dreading transitions, we embraced them as opportunities? What if we saw transitions not as disruptions, but as invitations to grow? The key to navigating transitions with ease lies in adopting a creative mindset—a way of thinking that transforms the way we approach change. Embrace the creative mindset The creative mindset is about seeing the world through a lens of possibilities. When we shift our perspective, transitions stop seeming so scary. Instead of focusing on the fear of the unknown, we start to recognize the exciting potential that comes with change. It’s the difference between saying, “This is going to be hard,” and asking, “What can I learn from this?” One of the most powerful aspects of a creative mindset is that it allows us to anticipate transitions. Rather than being blindsided, we can recognize when changes are on the horizon and prepare ourselves to ride the wave. Instead of resisting, we can embrace the shift, knowing we have the tools to navigate it. How to foster a creative mindset If the creative mindset is the key to making transitions smoother, how do we cultivate it? One of the most effective ways is by learning to view the world as malleable—not fixed or binary. Life is rarely a matter of “right” or “wrong”; it’s filled with nuance and complexity. To practice this kind of thinking, start with small, low-stakes decisions. Let’s say you’re deciding what to have for dinner. Instead of defaulting to your usual pizza or Thai, make a list of all the possibilities. Could you try a new recipe? Explore a different cuisine? The goal here isn’t necessarily to pick the perfect option but to open yourself up to variety. Another exercise is to seek out ways that your perspective can be both right and wrong at the same time. This is not about doubting yourself but about exploring multiple dimensions to every situation. When you do this, you build mental flexibility, which makes it easier to handle transitions because you become more comfortable with uncertainty and open to new solutions. Navigating change with confidence Transitions are never easy, but they don’t have to be paralyzing. we can reframe the way we see change—from something to fear to something full of possibilities. The next time you find yourself on the brink of a transition, whether big or small, try leaning into the creative process. You’ll find that when you start thinking in terms of possibility, change becomes less of a wave to fear and more of an adventure to embrace. T is for Transition, but it’s also for Transformation. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in the 3Cs: Creativity, Communication and Connection. https://ninameehan. com/

articles.text: Nearly 700 students from Piedmont and the East Bay in grades 7-12 are now participating in youth robotics programs organized by Piedmont Makers. Robotics has become the largest non-sports activity in Piedmont, after Scouting, and Piedmont Makers continues to use robotics to inspire youth to be innovators and creative problem solvers in S.T.E.A.M. Over 200 parent coaches and student mentors from across the community have volunteered to lead teams. Piedmont Makers has also hired Alya Hameed as a FIRST LEGO League Program Manager. Over the summer, Hameed worked tirelessly to coordinate with families and coaches to form over 100 teams while securing the equipment for the season, which began in August. Participants are from 20 other cities in the East Bay, including Oakland, Lafayette, Orinda, Berkeley, and Alameda, with Piedmont students accounting for 58% of participants. This December, Piedmont Makers will host its largest-ever robotics tournament at Piedmont Middle School, transforming it into “Piedmont Makersville” for two days of innovative projects, robotics competitions and Maker fun. FLL Challenge teams (grades 4-8) will compete for the Champion’s Award, given to the team excelling in robot performance, robot design, innovation project and core values. The weekend will also feature the FLL Explore Expo, a showcase FIRST Lego League Explore team Robo Friends watch the season reveal video for “Submerged.” Standing room only in the Ross Engineering Lab as the FTC game is revealed. A FLL Challenge team assembles the mission models at their first practice. FLL Challenge team “The Robo Sapiens” get to work assembling ocean-themed mission models on their robot practice table for this year’s “Submerged” theme. Team Cheerios gets a “head” start on the FLL Challenge season during their robot drive test. of projects from the youngest roboticists and will be open to the community to attend. Teams have already kicked off their seasons, inspired by this year’s theme of ocean exploration. For the youngest students (grades K-3) in the FIRST LEGO League Explore division, practices have combined ocean activities with LEGO building and programming. Their season will culminate in December with the Explore Expo where all the teams will present their final oceanthemed LEGO models and poster projects. FLL Challenge teams (grades 4-8) build autonomous robots with LEGO Spike kits to solve 15 different LEGO missions on a tabletop field. They also need to research a problem tied to this season’s Ocean theme and propose a solution that they present to a panel of adult judges as part of the Innovation Project. “It’s a great way to practice your creativity!” said 7th grader Ryan Morrison. A record 37 teams are competing at the Challenge level this season, which represents 50% year-over-year growth. Their season kicked off at the beginning of August and teams are now building and brainstorming the best strategies to solve the season’s challenges. Teams will next meet in a robot scrimmage in October and project scrimmage in November before the Community Tournament in December. This past Saturday morning, September 7, FIRST Tech Challenge teams (grades 7-12) gathered in the Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High to watch the reveal of this season’s “Into the Deep” challenge. Piedmont’s FTC division has grown to eight teams this year with over 60 kids participating, Coached by parents and mentored by FIRST Robotics Challenge team members, each

pages.text: 10 Wednesday, September 11, 2024 Chalk Art Continued from page 1 artists of all levels and any age to try their hand at creating with colored chalks provided by Flax Art & Design in Oakland. “It’s fun, but you don’t have to be good at art to participate. Everybody does it,” said Ella Fleischer, 17, who has attended the event for nearly 10 years. “I was always a really big art kid, and I definitely saw my style develop since my early years in the festival,” laughed Caitlin Boothby, 17. “Now, I get competitive with some of the older artists who attend.” Most pieces on the blacktop were group efforts, and it was common to see two or three people working on a square together. Some groups make their squares a family affair. Raul Jorcino, co-founder of the Chalk Art Festival, re-created a drawing from the popular children’s book Goodnight Moon (1947) with the help of his son Tómas, 18. The duo divided their chalk square into a series of grids and faithfully re-drew the scene piece by piece to make sure every detail was included. “I think every kid will recognize the art here because many like to read this book at night. It’s a classic,” said Raul Jorcino. All the while, children ran around the perimeter of the squares, shouting and playing games. The mood was upbeat and convivial, and many artists took time to walk around and appreciate one another’s work when they were finished. As is custom, the chalk art drawings will remain on the blacktop until they fade away naturally or are washed away by rain. In the meantime, they will serve as a colorful addition to the school for Beach kids to run by, play on and admire for weeks to come. The blacktop at Beach Elementary was divided into roughly 100 squares for the Chalk Art Festival. Nearly every square housed a unique chalk drawing from the community. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont High School boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan resigned earlier this summer. He is one of the most successful soccer coaches in school history. He is shown after his team won the 2022 North Coast Section championship. During the summer, Piedmont High boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan, originally from England, announced a big change in his life. He has elected to step away from coaching the high school game. Still coaching at the club level at 24-7 UK Soccer Academy, Sullivan decided he wanted to spend more time with one-year old son. After eight years at the school, Sullivan becomes one of Piedmont’s most successful soccer coach in school history. “It was a tough decision,” he said. “With the family, the plan was to get back to the UK before the 2024 season and I wouldn’t be able to coach. But, for now, we’re staying in the U.S. Hopefully now I’ll be able to catch some games without being a coach. It was a great eight years. There was never a season where we didn’t give it everything as a school,” Sullivan said. Sullivan revived Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer program, achieving several honors. His teams finished on top of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division in 2019, 2021, and 2022, earning the a promotion to the Foothill Division. But his greatest accomplishment was leading the team to back-to-back Division 4 North Coast Section titles in 2022 and 2023. The first title came in a 1-0 win over No. 2 University as the No. 1 seed at Witter Field. The second was another 1-nil win over No. 2 University, this time coming as the tournament’s Cinderella story as a No. 8 seed. Piedmont now plays in Division 3 after a promotion in 2023. The 2022 NCS title was the boys’ team’s s first section title in school history. The second NCS championship was a surprise. Piedmont was the No. 8 seed that year. “I’ve been asked this a few times and I always answer the same – one title isn’t more special than the other. We had fantastic players the first year we won it, then were underdogs the next year against some really good teams. The boys really did take the mantra of having a tough, hardworking identity. “The 2023 team if anything was more surprising to people on our team and perhaps the larger soccer world in the Bay Area. People recognized Piedmont as a serious team. I’d go as far to say the 2023 probably had a greater impact on the school.” 2019 marked the school’s first league championship in 10 years. That February night when Piedmont claimed the WACC banner appeared to be the turning point of the program. Sullivan signed on as head coach in the winter of 2016-17, replacing Rory O’Connor. In four years as head coach, O’Conner had one NCS win and finished with a positive winning percentage just one time. PHS went 9-2-9 (W-T-L) in Sullivan’s first year and 7-2-13 in his second year when still developing a system change – Todd Sullivan concludes his time at Piedmont with 87 wins and 155 total matches as head coach.
articles.title: PHS boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan resigns after 8 successful years

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team gained its first win of the season under the lights of Witter Field on Friday, September 6, claiming a dominant 42-21 win over the visiting Middletown Mustangs. It was a mighty response to Piedmont’s season-opener loss to Salesian the previous week. “It was just great to see. This game was a little personal, just to bounce back. We’ve gone through a lot of turmoil the past few weeks and it felt like we got the nucleus back together. This was a big one for us,” coach Jordan Seiden said. Senior quarterback Markos Lagios finished the day with four rushing touchdowns, while running back Tommy Ashton had a pair of scores. “Tommy and Sam [Shelby] did all the work to get us down the field. The touchdowns are really all three of us doing our job; it was a team win, everyone did their job. A shoutout to our offensive line, they did a great job and are improving every week,” Lagios said. “We knew our opening two games were going to be tough. We didn’t take care of business last week, but we came in tonight after a really good week of practice. The energy coming out of the locker room was there, we really set the tone early and kept it flowing throughout the game,” Ashton mentioned. Tommy Ashton had two touchdowns against Middletown as a running back and seven tackles as a linebacker. Staff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios (4) ran for four touchdowns against Middletown. He celebrates with Sam Shelby (2) and Nick King (77). Although he didn’t finish with any touchdowns, receiver Sam Shelby recorded seven receptions for 118 yards, averaging 16.85 yards per catch. “We played really well as a team today. We were super cohesive and coherent to everything. We knew it was a must-win and we came in with a mentality to just leave everything out there on the field,” Shelby said. Middletown actually had control of the game through much of the first half, holding a 15-14 lead with eight minutes left in the second quarter. But Piedmont’s defense held the Mustangs scoreless until 1:23 left in the fourth when the game was already far out of reach. Ashton, who doubles up as a middle linebacker, was a big part of the defensive performance. He made sure to praise fellow linebackers Cash Elmquist and Xavier Anderson. “We knew going into the second half that we had to bring intensity; defense wins games. My fellow linebacker, Cash Elmquist, he’s the brains of the operation. I work off of him and he led us to that defensive stop. Also, Xavier Anderson was great out there,” Ashton said. The Highlanders now continues its non-league schedule when hosting Mt. Eden of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division on Friday, September 13. PHS received a promotion to the Mission Division after winning the Shoreline last year, which included a 46-7 win over Mt. Eden. Game Recap After Middletown went up on the opening possession with a near four-minute drive, Piedmont drove from its own 26 to the Mustangs’ 21 on three consecutive screen passes to Shelby. Then, Cash Panico took a reception 20 yards to the Middletown one, leading to Ashton punching it into the end zone with six minutes left in the first. Piedmont’s defense then forced a turnover on downs on 4th-andGoal from its 10 yard line. On the ensuing possession, Shelby had a 24-yard reception followed by a 34 yard reception where he switched the field on his run after the catch, similar to DeSean Jackson with Cal in 2007. On 1st-and-10 from the Middletown 14, Lagios took a quarterback keeper to the house, making it 14-8 with 40 seconds left in the first. Middletown went back up 15-14 with 8:02 left in the first half, but that was the turning point. Piedmont then scored on a 13-play, seven minute series that included a fourth-down conversion on a fake punt. Driving down to the two, Lagios got it into the end zone for his second score— making it 21-15 with 1:51 left. In the third, Xavier Anderson took the opening kickoff all the way to the Mustang’s 25. articles.text: Each team listed five doubles Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team traveled to Mountain View for this year’s Golden State Classic, a fivematch doubles only tournament on Friday and Saturday, September 6-7. The Highlanders faced Los Gatos, Homestead, and Leigh on the opening day and played Foothill and Gunn on Saturday. “We had a great weekend down on the peninsula. We lost all three matches on Friday but we had two very close matches against Homestead and Leigh. Los Gatos was a very strong team that defeated Miramonte in their next match. We finished very strong, sweeping Gunn High School,” coach Jim Landes said. Final stats for the loss to Leigh were not provided. 5-0 over Gunn Carolina Romanczuk and Emma Eisemon paired as Piedmont’s No. 1 team and beat Gunn High of Palo Alto, 6-3, 4-6, 10-7. articles.text: Head Coach Stefan Bill honored at community event In a heartwarming display of appreciation and admiration, the Piedmont Swim Team, a yearround youth swimming organization, honored their head coach, Stefan Bill, for his remarkable decade of dedication and leadership. The celebration, during the team’s annual awards banquet, was held at the Community Hall and was a testament to Coach Bill’s profound impact on the team and the community. Coach Bill, who hails from Switzerland and initially made his mark in the UK before joining PST in 2014, has been a transformative leader for the team. Under his guidance, the team has seen its membership swell from approximately 60 swimmers to nearly 200 and with a notable increase in high-level competition participation. “Once we got him, I knew things were really going to change,” said Assistant Coach Colby Price, reflecting on Bill’s influence. The profound impact of Coach Bill was echoed by many. Piedmont Swim Team parent Amy Aubrecht praised him for exceeding expectations in making a difference in the lives of the swimmers. “I don’t know what life or career goals you had for yourself, but if making a difference in the lives of your swimmers is anywhere on that list, you have achieved it 100 fold,” she remarked. Current and former swimmers also shared their gratitude. Piedmont High School grad Parker Long recalled meeting Coach Bill as a child and immediately recognizing his expertise. “It was clear that he knew what he was talking about,” Long said. Similarly, alum Brian Wu expressed his appreciation, “Thank you for taking a chance on our team to build it from the ground up.” The celebration took a special turn when PST parent volunteers raised over $5,000 for the team’s financial aid fund in Coach Bill’s PST Head Coach Stefan Bill and star swimmer Josie Oesterer Photos by Clayton J. Mitchell Piedmont Community Hall was packed for Piedmont Swim Team’s celebration of Stefan Bill’s 10th year as head coach. Stefan Bill responds to a standing ovation. Head Coach Stefan Bill gets emotional watching video messages from the team’s swimmers and coaches. honor. The event featured surprise video messages from past and current swimmers, as well as fellow coaches, further underscoring the depth of his impact. Piedmont Swim Team Alum Simon Lins, the team’s only member to qualify for the national meet and who now swims for the University of Virginia, was visibly moved. “Words can’t describe the amount of impact you’ve had on me and the rest of the Piedmont community,” he said. “I know I wouldn’t be the same man I am today without you.” Another alum, Ryan Stokes, praised Bill’s mastery, noting, “It’s really amazing to see how far Piedmont Swim Team has come in the past ten years with Stefan as the head coach.” The evening was capped by a heartfelt video message from PST Assistant Coach Rob Moreside, who expressed gratitude for rekindling his own passion for coaching, and a standing ovation from the entire room. It was clear that Coach Stefan Bill’s decade of dedication has left an indelible mark on the Piedmont Swim Team and the community, solidifying his legacy as a cherished community figure. Stefan Bill is overcome with emotion as he is applauded with a standing ovation by family and friends and members of the Piedmont Swim Team.
articles.title: Swim Team celebrates decade of excellence

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s young team is still looking for its first win after five matches. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team continues pushing through its difficult pre-league schedule looking for its first victory of the season. They suffered a 3-1 loss to Skyline on the road in Oakland on Wednesday, September 4, lost 3-0 at Campolindo in Moraga the next day, and lost 3-1 to San Rafael at home in Binks Rawlings Gym on Monday, September 9. Final stats for the losses to Campolindo and San Rafael were not provided. “We just haven’t done well with adversity. We seemed timid being in a gym that’s hot like Skyline’s and a crowd that’s aggressive. I’ll be saying this all season long, but we’re young and we need to grow into ourselves before we start being really successful,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Against Skyline, Piedmont won the second set 25-15 to tie the match at 1-1. However, PHS couldn’t execute at the same consistency in the final two sets of the match, falling 25-18, 25-16 to close. “We couldn’t get under the short-serves. We need to keep focusing on the fundamentals. I want us to be aggressive at the net, but we haven’t been able to transition the ball to swing on the net. If our errors outweigh our successes, of course we’re going to lose. But you can see glimpses of success, it’s finding a way to maintain that when we have it going,” Cardenas said. Piedmont looks has two matches left in its pre-league schedule against Berean Christian on Thursday and Oakland High next Tuesday before taking on Alameda on September 25. 3-1 to Skyline Skyline won in four sets by scores of 25-16, 15-25, 25-18, 25-16. In Piedmont’s winning second set, they jumped out to a quick 4-0 lead when Skyline called a timeout to regroup. From there, PHS scored the next three to lead 7-0 before Skyline gained its first point. The Titans battled back to a 16-12 deficit, but PHS scored eight of the next nine points with a pair of aces by Skye Prata and another ace by Kalindi Kim to gain set-point at 24-13. Piedmont gained set-point on a Skyline offensive error. But from there, Piedmont struggled on its serve-receive and subsequently creating chances on Jules DeYoung led the way for Piedmont against Skyline with eight kills and a block. Fiona Olson had five kills against Skyline.
articles.title: PHS volleyball team still seeking first win

articles.text: Piedmont’s JV football team suffered its first loss of the season on Friday, September 6 at Witter Field, falling 27-14 to the visiting Middletown Mustangs after committing four turnovers on the afternoon. PHS tied Salesian the previous week in its season-opener. This week’s captains were sophomore Henry Brennan, and freshmen Jimmy Lagios, Joaquin Fierro, and George Saunders. Brennan was called up to varsity last week against Salesian. The Highlanders received the opening kickoff but threw an interception on the third play of the game. Middletown drove toward the goal line, and although the PHS’ defense got three straight stops inside the five-yard line, the Mustangs punched the ball across on the fourth down. Piedmont’s offense came out looking to change the momentum. Starting at their own 45 yard line, Lagios tossed a screen pass to receiver Diego Hurwitz on the first play, taking it 55yards to the end zone for a 7-7 tie. After multiple trades of possession, Piedmont defensive back Owen Curran intercepted a Mustangs pass on a deep pass down the sideline. Unfortunately, the Highlanders couldn’t capitalize and both sides went into halftime knotted up at 7-7. Middletown opened with possession in the third quarter, but Piedmont’s defense forced a punt. On the ensuing possession, Lagios and Hurwitz connected for another big play to get the Highlanders into the red zone. Hurwitz then scored on an endaround for his second touchdown of the game, putting PHS up 14-7. However, the Highlanders’ joy was short-lived after the Mustangs answered with a touchdown of their own on the next possession. But on the ensuing kickoff Piedmont relinquishing a crucial fumble to Middletown, giving them great field position. The Mustangs ran the ball through the Highlander defense to score a go-ahead touchdown, 21-14. On the Highlanders’ next possession, Middletown nabbed an interception to take it all the way to the end zone increasing the deficit to 27-14 with two minutes to go. The Highlanders look to bounce back this Friday against Mt. Eden of Hayward. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1-1) hosts Mt. Eden on Friday, September 13 for a 4:00 p.m. game. articles.title: JV Highlanders lose 27-14 to Middletown

He finished with 149 all-purpose yards with seven receptions for 118 yards, to go along with four rushing attempts for 31 yards. Perhaps his marquee play was a huge 34-yard reception when he switched from one side of the field to another for a big gain. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse launches its 2024-25 season with The Prom, performing now through Sunday, October 13. The Prom is a musical telling the story of four Broadway actors and actresses who visit a small town in Indiana to champion a local high school student’s right to bring her girlfriend to the prom. The play, based on a book by Bob Martin, was originally performed on Broadway in 2018 and was later made into a movie featuring Meryl Streep and Nicole Kidman. The Berkeley Playhouse production is co-directed and co-choreographed by Megan McGrath and Christina Lazo, with music directed by Daniel Alley. Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley said she was thrilled to select The Prom as the theater’s celebratory season opener. “This musical is bursting with so much heart and humor, plus it’s full of laughter and fantastic dancing,” said Dooley. “It’s the perfect show to open our new season for its messages of acceptance, joy, friendship and love for all.” “There have been instances over the years across the country of parents pulling their students from high school productions and local theaters canceling their shows due to the material,” said co-director Christina Lazo. “So we have to keep doing shows like this. I can’t wait for audiences to see the sparkle and the beauty of the world within The Prom.” The play features Arri Toshiko Glenn as Emma Nolan, Aleshani Altan as Alyssa Greene, Taylor Bartolucci as Dee Dee Allen, DC Scarpelli as Barry Glickman and Mary Kalita as Angie Dickenson. To purchase to tickets and see showtimes, visit https://tickets. berkeleyplayhouse.org/
articles.title: The Prom at Berkeley Playhouse through Oct. 13

articles.text: The de Young Museum, one of the fine arts museums in San Francisco, is exhibiting impressionist and realist artworks spanning the period of 1848 to 1960 in an exhibition entitled American Beauty now through October 20. American art in the 19th and 20th centuries presents a variety of artistic responses during a complex period in US history. Artwork featured is borrowed from the collection of Bernard and Barbro Osher, which enhances the de Young’s American art collection with several significant firsts. The exhibition includes the first large-scale oil painting by Winslow Homer (The Angler, ca. 1874), the first genre picture by William Merritt Chase (Spanish Bric-à-Brac Shop, 1883), the first major George Bellows landscape (In Virginia, 1908), the first Georgia O’Keeffe images of the Southwest (Front of Ranchos Church, 1930 and The Patio, 1940), as well as 13 artists on display at the museum for the first time. To learn more about the exhibition and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.famsf.org/exhibitions/osher-american-art. The American Beauty exhibition will be on view at the de Young through October.
articles.title: De Young Museum hosts American Beauty exhibition

articles.text: AXIS Dance Company, an acclaimed ensemble of disabled and neurodiverse dancers, will perform Friday-Sunday, October 11-13, at San Francisco’s ODC Theater. A Bay Area-based dance company, Axis was founded in 1987 and has toured over 100 cities in the U.S., the United Kingdom, Europe and the United Arab Emirates. AXIS’s mission is to create world-class productions that challenge perceptions and redefine dance and disability. Next month AXIS will perform new choreography for its home season Ecos, with Berkeley-based contemporary dance company “Post:ballet” serving as special guests. “Ecos brings together extraordinary artists to explore the complexities of our shared human experience,” said AXIS Dance Company’s Artistic Director Nadia Adame. “Each piece in this Home Season reflects a unique perspective, yet together they resonate with a powerful, collective spirit. This season is a heartfelt invitation to connect, reflect, and be moved together.” Tickets for Ecos are available now at www.axisdance.org. AXIS Dance Company artists perform onstage. Photo courtesy of AXIS Dance Company Violinist Shoshana Kay vain. Philosophers such as Maimonades attempted to coalesce human frailties with science. Diogenes, Hippocrates and Rodon were brainstorming one time. Diogenes used his lantern in the search for honesty. Hippocrates sought good health and endeavored to achieve it. Despite the publicity, neither Diogenes nor Hippocrates were successful at the plate. Then Rodon came to the plate and hit it out of the park. In case you haven’t guessed, Rodon is the Greek word for Shoshana.

She graduated from Piedmont High in 2004 and continued her musical education at the Cincinnati Conservatory and then to Indiana University. Professional musical engagements continued both in Indiana and in Miami Beach and then a return once again to Indiana. Along the way Shoshana met Emmet Hanick, a bass player, who became the love of her life. For many of us, music is the center of our lives. It is the center of our universe. And so it is with Shoshana. She returned to Indiana in 2013 and continued her professional violin playing with the Indianapolis Symphony and the Indianapolis Opera in addition to studio work. articles.text: A scene from Pirate Radio On any given Friday or Saturday night in the 1950s and early 1960s, it was not unusual to pull into a drive-in restaurant filled with cars and kids, some leaning against fenders, others deep in conversation, and hear on more than one car radio Wolfman Jack, a rock & roll DJ legend. “Let’s git nakkid” he’d call out as he segued into “It’s All Right (Mama)” by Elvis Presley, one of the first and perhaps greatest rock & roll songs ever. Wolfman Jack with his signature gravelly voice and a diabolical laugh. No one had ever seen him. He was an enigma. Rumor had it that he was on some ship off the coast of Mexico, staying one record spin ahead of the culture cops. Or possibly he was holed up in a beachside, cinderblock shack with a monster antenna, south of Tijuana. And, as it turned out, that’s exactly where the Wolfman was, in Mexico, slammin’ and jammin’ at station XERB-AM, sending out a powerhouse signal to all places north, up the coast of California, even reaching Alaska on a clear night. What was undisputed was that the discs Wolfman played captured the essence of being young during the late 50s and early 60s. Rock & roll was transcendent. It was heart wrenching, spine-tingling, drop to your knees wonderful. And more. There was Big Joe Turner’s Shake, Rattle & Roll and Bill Haley and the Comet’s Rock Around the Clock, all precursors of some of the most vital, Motown inspired music to ever come out of the 50s, soon morphing into the Stones, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, James Brown and the Beach Boys. Rock & roll was the cresting wave, a cultural zeitgeist. It defined a generation. Great Britain, in so many ways, mirrored America, creating its own unique version of rock & roll, led by groups such as The Who, The Kinks, Cream, Pink Floyd and, of course, The Beatles. And for a time, in the 60s, British kids tuned in late at night to a rogue rock & roll station, beamed from a ship somewhere off the coast. And that is the essence of the film, Pirate Radio. An improbable group of disc jockeys who kept rock & roll on the radio 24/7, to the absolute delight of the nation’s listeners and to the consternation of the British government and the BBC, which took great umbrage at the airways being filled with such “rot.” Led by Cultural Minister Alistair Dormandy (Kenneth Brannagh), a concerted effort is set in motion to sink the renegade ship, so to speak, and shut down the illicit music once and for all. Rock & roll, it was decided, posed a threat to homeland security. Meanwhile, on board, the DJs are running a floating animal house, engaging in pranks and fun and music. The housemother, so to speak, is Quentin (Bill Nighy), the captain and titular head of this ragged crew, with The Count (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and Gavin (Rhys Ifans) filling the prime time radio slots. While the story is thin – there is a subplot, a sort of coming-ofage saga about young Carl, the nephew of Quentin – the energy and sheer delight conveyed by the film makes for sweet entertainment and the sound track, meaning the platters spun, is, simply, top drawer. Pirate Radio. Starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, Bill Nighy, Rhys Ifans, Talulah Riley and Tom Sturridge. Directed by Richard Curtis. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Streaming on Fandango/apple tv/prime. The summer of 2024 is behind us. Fall beckons. You can feel the mornings are cooling, edged ever so subtly with winter. So why not find an evening to stream a movie. But not just any movie. Find something wonderfully pulpy, an upscale B-movie where you can blissfully ignore the thin plots. I suggest Angel Has Fallen. It’s just about a perfect B-movie, with minimum exposition. It relies on familiar tropes, lacks nuanced characters, demands you not overthink and asks only that you sit back and enjoy what it does best: entertains If you have already had the pleasure of seeing the previous two Mike Banning Secret Service installments (now called the Angel Trilogy), then you will recognize Gerard Butler with his game face on as Banning, doing what he does best: guarding the American President, who, in this iteration, is Allan Trumball, portrayed by the always exceptional Morgan Freeman. Banning, after years of getting banged up is now stoically suffering from a compressed vertebrae and serious aches and pains plus a growing addiction to painkillers. But no matter, he stands his post. In Angel Has Fallen, a very lethal attempt, using weaponized drones, is made on the President’s life and Banning is once again put through the protect-the-president-at-all-cost Cuisinart. The audience is only told that the reason for the attempt is that President Trumball is way too soft, choosing diplomacy over hard power. As a result there is a group of hawks, one in particular, within the government that take exception to such policies and hire some very nasty off-the-grid mercenaries to take out Trumball, setting in motion sustained mayhem with lots of collateral damage. And as it turns out, Mike, who is the lone Secret Service agent who survives, is thought to have gone rogue. It’s a stretch plotwise, but the audience, from the get-go, knows better. One last thing: Look for the durable and seriously weathered Nick Nolte portraying Banning’s dad, Clay, hiding behind a massive beard, his face possessing more crevices than a topography map. He’s a hermit, living in a shack in the mountains of Virginia, and possesses more unpacked suitcases of issues than a hotel lobby. Nolte chews up every scene, and is definitely enjoying himself. He’s wonderful. Angel Has Fallen. Directed by Ric Roman Waugh. Starring Gerard Butler, Morgan Freeman and Nick Nolte. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ apple tv.
articles.title: Morgan Freeman at his best in Angel Has Fallen

articles.text: Castle in the Sky is a swashbuckling, Indiana Jones steampunk adventure that also manages to weave into its narrative a subtle ecological message. But above all it’s for kids. From the get-go, the story is gripping and in the first opening scenes there’s a kidnapping attempt of a young orphan girl Sheeta (Anna Paquin) by a secret, nefarious agent called Muska (Mark Hamil). She is flown via airship to a military fortress, but on the way the ship is attacked by a cohort of air pirates, all led by captain Dola (Cloris Leachman). The reason for the raid is to steal a precious, mysterious amulet that Sheeta wears around her neck, a gift to her from her grandmother. During the attack, Sheeta falls from the ship and instead of crashing to earth she floats gently down into the arms of a dreamy teenage boy, Pazu (James Van Der Beek). Together they set out on a hold your breath, hide from the pirates adventure, a quest that leads them to a floating mythical, steampunk island called Laputa that hovers just above earth. Its source of power is a crystal, not unlike Sheeta’s amulet. Sheeta and Pazu are scrappy, courageous protagonists who relish getting into and out of sequential jams. The story is fast-paced and while there is gunplay, and the bad guys and designated villains bite the dirt, so to speak, Miyazaki is never relies on graA scene from Studio Ghibli’s Castle in the Sky tuitous, wham-bang, shots-fired action drama. It’s all in service of a let’er rip story. Castle in the Sky is no exception. It’s pure fun fantasy. The artwork is hand-drawn (part of Ghibli’s brand) and astonishingly good (in many ways richer than those works created by CGI) depicting some wonderful chase scenes featuring a train racing across a wobbly trellis, dogfights between massive airplanes and shoot-outs between floating dirigibles and war ships. Meanwhile, as Sheeta and Pazu discover, Laputa is a remarkable medieval place, with crumbling castles, overrun with weeds and vines, marginally maintained by a crew of robots. Underground they discover that the technology that keeps Laputa afloat is not dissimilar from Sheeta’s magical amulet. If you have not introduced your youngsters to the amazing work of Studio Ghibli and the extraordinary art and storytelling of Mayao Miyazaki, Castle in the Sky is a fine beginning. Castle in the Sky. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Animé fantasy from Studio Ghibli. With voices of James Van Der Beek, Anna Paquin, Cloris Leachman, Mark Hamil and Mandy Patinkin. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019, Now streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Big adventure in Castle in the Sky

articles.text: Before discussing the latest entry to the Marvel Comics Universe (MCU), I pause to make full disclosure. When I was a kid my favorite superhero was, indeed, Captain Marvel. As drawn and written in Marvel comics the Captain was a guy. He had the physique of Superman with an orange cape, matching tights with a lightning bolt in the center of his chest. Very cool. He possessed, like Batman and Superman, superhuman abilities. I recall that my mom sewed an orange cape for me with silver piping at the edges. It sat perfectly on my shoulders with some flare. That was, of course, then, and this is definitely now. This new incarnation of Captain Marvel is a woman, equally awesome, sans that signature cape, but decked out to be sure in some pretty nifty tights. Superhero, superheroine, no worries. The MCU is inclusive. No suspension of disbelief necessary. The buzz was that this first film – what will surely be a franchise – would be an origin story. Truth is, I have always favored the origin tales of any superhero. None has done it better than Superman in which Diane Lane and Kevin Costner play Clark’s parents and find the little guy in a capsule in a cornfield. Young Clark Kent, a kid, going to school, pushed around by bullies, and counseled by his folks to keep his powers a secret and exercise restraint. Unfortunately, the origin story for Captain Marvel has to ignore such early grand moments. Carol, the new Capt. Marvel, only acquired her powers much later. So, as she was growing up, played baseball, rode a bike, dealt with taunting boys, all she could call Brie Larsen as Captain Marvel For advance tickets, go to https://bpt.me/6383991 or use this QR code:

Lucky in Love celebrates the centennial anniversary of legendary French composer Gabriel Fauré by highlighting one of his most important song cycles: La Bonne Chanson . Inspired by his passionate love for soprano Emma Bardac and based on the exquisite poetry of Paul Verlaine, Fauré called La Bonne Chanson his “most exuberant writing.” Mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and pianist Jeffrey LaDeur present this work, alongside other beloved scores that explore l’amour!
