The reason for the raid is to steal a precious, mysterious amulet that Sheeta wears around her neck, a gift to her from her grandmother. During the attack, Sheeta falls from the ship and instead of crashing to earth she floats gently down into the arms of a dreamy teenage boy, Pazu (James Van Der Beek). Together they set out on a hold your breath, hide from the pirates adventure, a quest that leads them to a floating mythical, steampunk island called Laputa that hovers just above earth. Its source of power is a crystal, not unlike Sheeta’s amulet. Sheeta and Pazu are scrappy, courageous protagonists who relish getting into and out of sequential jams. The story is fast-paced and while there is gunplay, and the bad guys and designated villains bite the dirt, so to speak, Miyazaki is never relies on graA scene from Studio Ghibli’s Castle in the Sky tuitous, wham-bang, shots-fired action drama. It’s all in service of a let’er rip story. Castle in the Sky is no exception. It’s pure fun fantasy. The artwork is hand-drawn (part of Ghibli’s brand) and astonishingly good (in many ways richer than those works created by CGI) depicting some wonderful chase scenes featuring a train racing across a wobbly trellis, dogfights between massive airplanes and shoot-outs between floating dirigibles and war ships. Meanwhile, as Sheeta and Pazu discover, Laputa is a remarkable medieval place, with crumbling castles, overrun with weeds and vines, marginally maintained by a crew of robots. Underground they discover that the technology that keeps Laputa afloat is not dissimilar from Sheeta’s magical amulet. If you have not introduced your youngsters to the amazing work of Studio Ghibli and the extraordinary art and storytelling of Mayao Miyazaki, Castle in the Sky is a fine beginning. Castle in the Sky. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Animé fantasy from Studio Ghibli. With voices of James Van Der Beek, Anna Paquin, Cloris Leachman, Mark Hamil and Mandy Patinkin. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Lucky in Love celebrates the centennial anniversary of legendary French composer Gabriel Fauré by highlighting one of his most important song cycles: La Bonne Chanson . Inspired by his passionate love for soprano Emma Bardac and based on the exquisite poetry of Paul Verlaine, Fauré called La Bonne Chanson his “most exuberant writing.” Mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and pianist Jeffrey LaDeur present this work, alongside other beloved scores that explore l’amour! articles.text: Ongoing Elena Doronkina New Work Exhibition Returning to PCA for their second exhibition, Russian-born Elena Doronkina and Alexander Zimin have an exhibit that is open through September 22. Elena drew rave reviews in the summer of 2023 with her first exhibition here with still-lifes, figurative works, and landscapes. An award-winning artist and member of American Women Artists, she is also Program Director at the Alamo Danville Artist’s Society and manager at Blackhawk Gallery in Danville. The exhibit will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. The artists will host an opening reception on Saturday, September 7, from 6 to 9 p.m., during which Natalya Biktairova will show her fabric works also. September 14, 4:30 p.m. Boon Hiker Band Concert The Boon Hiker Band – John Bidwell, Clare Broussard, J.T. Devine, Robin Eschner, Natasha Haugnes, Dennis Hysom, Chris Smith, and John Tuttle – bring dynamic vocal harmonies with guitar, bass, keyboard, banjo, accordion, dobro, lap steel, and percussion. The songs lean toward Americana and folk traditions. The five North Bay members enhance the vocal textures and harmonies. Advance tickets for this concert can be found on Brown Paper Tickets at https://bpt.me/6383991. Doors will open at 4 p.m. September 21, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Fall Celebration To celebrate the Fall Equinox, Mexican Independence Day, and to welcome new drummer Albert Brooks, the jazz and pop piano trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. A narrative ties all the tunes into the autumn theme. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a late Saturday afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 p.m. Tickets $25 at https://bpt. me/6214927 or $30 at the door, cash or check ONLY. September 22, 4:00 p.m. Festival Opera Vocal Recital Lucky in Love kicks off a series of three vocal recitals with mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharichn and pianist Jeffrey LaDeur as they perform the music of Gabriel Fauré, focusing on one of his most important song cycles, La Bonne Chanson. The program will include an assortment of music centered on l’amour. Patrons are invited to a wine reception to meet the artists immediately after the performance. articles.text: Weather in the Bay Area may never be better for an outdoor read than in September. Begin your search for your next book, by consulting the Indie Next List’s recommendations for the month. The list of new releases is curated by independent book store owners and staff. This list for September has an extra helping of romance and fantasy titles this month, perfect for whisking the imagination elsewhere. The Indie Next List consists of only the newest releases, with rave reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small bookstore culture. familiar heritage and connects it to the larger social issues of the Métis and other Indigenous peoples. This book is an accomplishment.” —Mara Panich-Crouch, Fact & Fiction Downtown, Missoula, MT The Night Guest Robinette Kowal (Transl.), Tor Nightfire, Horror “Why are we all so tired all the time, even after sleeping for a full night? For one woman, the answer is much darker and tied into family history and the misdiagnosis of doctors. A compelling novella that demands to be read in a single sitting.” —William Carl, An Unlikely Story, Plainville, MA The Examiner Thriller Tell Me Everything House, Fiction “I’ve just spent the last few days observing a grand reunion in this gorgeous book! All my old friends showed up: 90-year-old Olive, Lucy Barton, the Burgess brothers, even Amy and Isabel! Strout probes human nature and the many meanings of love.” —Carol Katsoulis, Anderson’s Bookshops, Naperville, IL Blue Sisters Books, Fiction “I’ve always wanted a sister; this book gifted me four. Four unique characters, each flawed but lovable in their own way, who seem like they would never be able to get along. Pick up this book, then call your therapist. Better yet, your sister.” —Caroline Giblin, Thunder Road Books, Spring Lake, NJ There Are Rivers in the Sky Fiction “Water: the omnipresent witness to the reverberation of the underdog and the valorized, to the drenched disorderedness of security throughout civilization. Elif Shafak tackles the toxicity of human greed, cruelty, and survival through water.” —Kayleen Rohrer, InkLink Books, East Troy, WI Bluff: Poems Poetry “Danez Smith is an artist grappling with the role of art at the end of the world. These poems shine a soft light into the darkest tunnels of our history, into the precise cuts they made into your soul, and leave you with something better than hope.” —Michelle Carroll, Powell’s Books, Portland, OR The Wildes in Five Acts Books, Historical Fiction “Bayard transports us to the British countryside, an Italian villa, the trenches of France, and back to London. Told in the language of the late 19th & early 20th centuries, The Wildes involves the entire Wilde family and the scandalous drama that ensues.” —Mindy Ostrow, The River’s End Bookstore, Oswego, NY The Life Impossible “Matt Haig’s wonderful book about climate change, aging, and recovering from guilt. Widowed Grace is left a house in Spain by a friend she hasn’t heard from in over 30 years. She heads out on an adventure where new friends and life-altering changes await.” —Kathy Clemmons, Sundog Books, Santa Rosa Beach, FL Books, Fiction “A fascinating story of a woman who may have written many of the works attributed to Shakespeare. While this book is fiction, Picoult digs deep into the research that’s been done to present an interesting and intriguing tale of what might have been.” —Camille Kovach, Completely Booked, Murrysville, PA Where the Forest Meets the River Editions, Fiction “In Where the Forest Meets the River, Bowring takes us back to Dalton, Maine, where some of my favorite and not-so-favorite people live. Dalton has its secrets, but Bowring spins a tale full of love, sorrow, and laughter.” —Jayne Rowsam, Mystery to Me, Madison, WI Madwoman and Company, Fiction “This incredible story of domestic violence survivors had me on the edge of my seat. Fans of Godshot will recognize Bieker’s humor and depth. But in Madwoman, there’s growth, not always for the better, of a character trying to forget her dark past.” —Emily Berg, Books & Books, Key West, FL That Librarian: The Fight Against Book Banning in America Publishing, Memoir “Fierceness and bravery should not be a requirement for librarians. In this era of book banning, however, a librarian must be a warrior. Jones is fighting the good fight to give everyone freedom to read and feel safe in a library space.” —Pamela Klinger-Horn, Valley Bookseller, Stillwater, MN “When faced with a new Janice Hallett mystery, there’s nothing to do but dive in and swim for the end. There’s no stopping along the way — you don’t want to get lost in the clues before you’ve figured out the solution. (Ha! Good luck with that.)” —Linda Bond, Auntie’s Bookstore, Spokane, WA William Sons, Horror “Henry, an engineer, has created an AI marvel with William. His wife, who’s been standoffish since her pregnancy, invites some colleagues over for lunch. Suspicious of his wife, he decides to introduce them to William. This dark tale will leave you guessing.” —Jason Kennedy, Boswell Book Company, Milwaukee, WI Becoming Little Shell: A Landless Indian’s Journey Home Editions, Biography “With Becoming Little Shell, Chris La Tray takes a very personal journey of introspection and We’re Alone: Essays Press, Essays “In so few pages, Edwidge Danticat weaves language that situates us in the moment with compassion and clarity. From odes that ache and appreciate the humanity of brilliant authors, to writings about Haiti and storms to come, Danticat threads it all.” —Mari Guzman, Politics and Prose Bookstore, Washington, DC I’ll Have What He’s Having Romance “A substitute teacher turned restaurant owner meets a sommelier in this completely charming ‘friends with benefits…oh, oops, we’re in love’ rom-com! Khorram’s impeccably-titled adult debut will surely be a big hit this fall.” —Kate Storhoff, Bookmarks, Winston-Salem, NC Spirit Crossing Books, Mystery “A work of fiction can hold an abundance of truth. In this story, it’s not until the body of a missing white girl from a prominent family is found that a missing Indigenous woman gets attention from law enforcement. Lives are at stake on the path to the truth.” —Casey Luke, The Book Shoppe, Boone, IA The Instrumentalist Schuster, Historical Fiction “Inspired by a true story, The Instrumentalist immediately pulled me into 18th-century Venice. Anna Maria’s journey to find love, meaning, and purpose in life kept me turning pages. It’s so satisfying watching her learn to use her gift for good.” —Michelle Ratto, A Thousand Stories, Herndon, VA The Story of a Heart: Two Families, One Heart, and a Medical Miracle Biography “An emotionally complex tribute to an unfathomable loss, a profound love, and a choice that offers up a miracle. Dr. Clarke interweaves the emotional story with the medical history that has led up to this lifesaving gift. A stunning, memorable read.” —Maxwell Gregory, Madison Street Books, Chicago, IL Under the Eye of the Big Bird Yoneda (Transl.), Soft Skull, Fiction “What will the world look like when humanity is near its end? In short glimpses, this book gives us insight to small groups of people and how they live and survive in an ever-changing, increasingly dystopian world. This is speculative fiction at its best.” —Miranda Myers, Changing Hands, Tempe, AZ The Book Swap House, Romance “I am a sucker for a well-written and meaty romance and The Book Swap delivers. Erin and James are both imperfect people, but they also both have such a capacity for love and growth. Them falling in love through margin-writing in books is just the cherry on top.” —Amelia Yasuda, Queen Takes Book, Columbia, MD Best Copy Available: A True Crime Memoir of Georgia Press, True Crime “Do not shy away from this memoir. It’s a hard read but it’s so worth it. Nicorvo is masterful in his ability to share the trauma of his childhood. Part memoir, part true crime, completely unforgettable!” —Julie Slavinsky, Warwick’s, La Jolla, CA

articles.text: Jean Anderson McIntyre, 94, the mother of former Piedmont resident Claire Kostic and a longtime Atherton resident, passed away peacefully on August 28, 2024 in Palo Alto, after a short illness. She will be sorely missed. Jean will be remembered for her passion for music and music education. She was an accomplished pianist and loved Debussy, Chopin and Beethoven. She practiced at least one hour every day and filled the house with beautiful music. Jean shared her love of music through teaching piano to many children, including her own. She also loved the opera and symphony and was an active supporter of the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, and San Francisco Ballet. Jean was born on November 20, 1929 to Niles and Olga Anderson in Everett, Washington. At age 12 her family moved to Toronto where Jean graduated from The Bishop-Strachan School. She went on to study music at Vassar College, graduating in 1951 after completing a thesis comparing personality traits to musical tastes. After graduation, Jean landed her first job in Chicago doing research on how music could help with mental illness. In 1953, Jean moved to San Diego, where her parents had retired. There, she met and married Ray Stewart. They moved to the San Francisco peninsula a year later when Ray started his career with Ampex. In 1963, Jean and Ray bought their home in Atherton, where they raised their five children. Jean was very active with her children’s education and served on the PTA of Selby Lane School and Menlo School and was a board member of Castilleja School from 1971–1982 and longtime supporter of her grandchildren’s schools in Piedmont. Jean started a legacy at Camp Four Winds on Orcas Island where all of her children either attended as well as her granddaughters. She also enjoyed gardening and was a gracious hostess to her circle of friends. In 1973, Jean married Dr. Harold Christian Zweng, who passed away in 1977. As a new widow, she became a successful real estate broker in the mid-peninsula. In 1996, she married Henry McIntyre. Throughout their marriage, Jean and Henry enjoyed extensive travel throughout the world. They loved living in their winter home in Indian Wells playing golf, bridge, and tennis and at their El Dorado Country Club, Cypress Point in Pebble Beach, Burlingame Country Club, and Menlo Circus Club. Henry passed away in 2003 and Jean never remarried but had a long-time companionship with Dr. Norman Snyder of Atherton for over ten years until he passed away in 2014. Jean loved card games, especially bridge. For those who did not share her bridge passion, she taught them to play the card game “Onze”. She also loved having her children and grandchildren over for pool gatherings, including salmon barbecues. Jean’s last 10 years included a move to the Vi in Palo Alto. She continued to enjoy traveling on many San Francisco Ballet tours all over the world with her daughter, Claire. Jean Anderson McIntyre passed away on August 28 at the age of 94. She is survived by her five children: Sandra Stewart MacPhail (Jack) of Portland, OR; Claire Stewart Kostic (Mark) of Atherton, Sharon Stewart of Ukiah, Kim Stewart of Los Altos, and David Stewart of Barcelona, Spain. She also is survived by nine grandchildren: Sheldon Stevenson (Suzanne), Jeffrey Stevenson (Erin), Creighton Stevenson, Kirsten Hanafee, Sean Hanafee, Emily Bortz, Eddie Bortz, Camila Stewart, and Giana Stewart, as well as two great-grandchildren, Finn Stevenson and Charles Stevenson. Jean is predeceased by her husband, Henry, and by her sister, Laurel Bates. A private service will be held with family and friends at the Menlo Circus Club in Atherton. In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial donations be made in her name to San Francisco Ballet, San Francisco Opera, and San Francisco Symphony.
articles.title: Jean McIntyre dies at 94

articles.text: Of all the AVAs in the Rhone Valley none is as historic and storied as Hermitage. Legend has it a knight returning home wounded from the Crusades in 1224 was given permission to build a small refuge to recover in on this grand hill in a bend in the Rhone River across from the town of Tain. In 1937 it was established as one of France’s first wine appellations. The vines grow on the southwest side of the steep granite hill facing the afternoon sun and are divided into a number of smaller vineyards. Syrah is the primary red grape and Marsanne and Rousanne are the white grapes. Hermitage reds tend toward being very earthy with aromas of leather, red berries, earth and coffee. They have a high level of tannins and are considered the longest lived within France. The Sorrel family’s roots in Hermitage go back to 1893 when they purchased land on the hill. Today the family’s third generation of winemakers, the three Sorrel brothers, tend the family’s few acres of land producing only a handful of bottles each vintage. Production methods are very traditional, and the wine is aged in four-year-old neutral barrels and limited to fewer than 4,000 bottles each vintage. • 2020 JMB Sorrel Hermitage Le Vignon, $75 A selection of fruit from three separate parcels: “Les Plantiers” sandy and stony, “Les Greffieux” with glacial stones and clay, and “Les Bessards,” south facing granitic soils. It shows lovely aromas of violets, leather, cured meat, blackberries and black olives. Full-bodied with a rich, velvety feel on the finish, it is bursting with life and totally enjoyable now but will age for many decades in the cellar.

articles.text: When drawing up your estate plans, you might find it useful to create a revocable or irrevocable trust, either of which can help your estate avoid probate court and give you significant control over how and when your assets are distributed. But who should oversee your trust? As the person who established the trust — known as the “grantor” or “settlor” — you can also name yourself as trustee. However, this may not be the best move, particularly if the trust is irrevocable. An irrevocable trust protects the assets in the trust from creditors and civil judgments, but if you serve as trustee, this protection will disappear. It might be more advantageous for you to be the trustee of a revocable (living) trust, which can be modified without much trouble and allows you to move assets in and out of the trust and to change trust beneficiaries. You should work with a qualified estate-planning attorney to determine which type of trust, if any, is appropriate for your situation, and to get some guidance on the wisdom of serving as your own trustee. If you decide to choose someone else as trustee, you’ll want to consider the following factors: • Trust In thinking about whom you might want to serve as your trustee, the most important attribute is trust. Do you trust that this individual will always act in your best interest? If so, then they may be a good trustee candidate, but you’ll also need to look at other considerations. • Financial management skills The person you choose to be your trustee doesn’t have to be an accountant or a financial professional — but they should be skilled at managing their own finances. And they should be well-organized and good with details. • Mental and physical fitness Your trustee could serve in that position for many years, so you’ll want to name someone who is in good physical and mental health. Of course, things can change over time, so if you observe that your chosen trustee has begun to suffer physical or mental decline, you may need to name a successor trustee in your trust document. • Conflict of interest You want your trustee to carry out your wishes in a fair manner — so, you should pick someone who doesn’t have a conflict of interest with any of the beneficiaries you’ve named in your trust. Of course, this can be tricky if you want to name a family member as trustee. So, if you do, you’ll need to spell out your wishes clearly — to the trustee and to other family members. Here’s something else to think about: Instead of choosing an individual, you could name a corporate trustee. By doing so, you can receive some key benefits, such as objectivity and potentially avoiding some of the family-related disputes that can arise when an estate is settled. Also, corporate trustees have the expertise and resources to navigate the various tax and inheritance laws affecting living trusts. Whether it’s a trusted individual or a corporate entity, the right trustee can make a big difference in the effectiveness of your living trust — and, by extension, the outcome of your comprehensive estate plans. So, start your search, get the help you need and take the steps necessary to arrive at a choice for trustee that’s right for you and your family. articles.text: Most East Bay wine lovers have probably discovered the North Berkeley Imports wine shop on Shattuck Avenue in Berkeley comfortably located in the “Gourmet Ghetto” neighborhood. The cozy little shop provides a convenient place to shop for mostly French and Italian wines. What many people may not know is that affiliated with the shop is a wine importing company that searches out interesting wines in France and Italy and imports them into the U.S. market. They are also a wholesaler with a national distribution network that provides wine to many of the nation’s best restaurants and wine bars. Founded in 1979, the company was purchased by Billy Weiss in 1999. The importing business has grown, and they now have a portfolio of over 120 producers. One of the nice things about the North Berkeley shop is the staff are extremely well educated about the wines and immensely helpful in helping the shopper select the right wine for the occasion. There are no stupid questions and no wine snobbishness in sight. As readers know, one of my favorite wine regions in the world is the Northern Rhone. The Syrah wines from that area are marvels of complexity and deliciousness. I recently had the opportunity to review some of the wines from that region that are in the North Berkeley Imports portfolio. The following wines are all available. comes, the family stomps the grapes with bare feet in ancient wooden fermentation vats - in other words they give new meaning to the term “old school.” The Delos family, who established the estate in 1933, do this not because it is “romantic” but because they believe it is the most efficient and effective way to make their wine. The winery, located high above the village of Saint-Jean de Muzols, is a throwback to another century. So, it’s not surprising that the wines put forth the taste of Syrah d’antan – flavors pulled from the earth with no makeup or modern frills. Their wines are rustic and real and bursting with character. They make a Saint Joseph Blanc, a Syrah “Gabouillon” a second label wine, a regular Saint Joseph rouge and the flagship wine listed below. The wines all represent amazing value with a big bang for the buck. North Berkeley Imports 1505 Shattuck Ave. Berkeley, CA 1-800-266-6585 www.northberkeleyimports.com • 2022 Domaine de Gouye Saint Joseph Vielles Vignes $40 Made from fruit selected from the oldest Syrah vines, some as old as 100 years. The wine is crushed by foot and aged 16 months in neutral barrels and bottled unfined and unfiltered. The wine boasts licorice, meaty, herb-laced aromas and plenty of succulent blackberry fruit. Full-bodied, rich and velvety with soft tannins, it’s concentrated and long on the finish. Will improve for two decades in the cellar. The winery, located high above the village of Saint-Jean de Muzols, is a throwback to another century. So, it’s not surprising that the wines put forth the taste of Syrah d’antan – flavors pulled from the earth with no makeup or modern frills. Their wines are rustic and real and bursting with character. They make a Saint Joseph Blanc, a Syrah “Gabouillon” a second label wine, a regular Saint Joseph rouge and the flagship wine listed below. Legend has it a knight returning home wounded from the Crusades in 1224 was given permission to build a small refuge to recover in on this grand hill in a bend in the Rhone River across from the town of Tain. In 1937 it was established as one of France’s first wine appellations. The vines grow on the southwest side of the steep granite hill facing the afternoon sun and are divided into a number of smaller vineyards. Syrah is the primary red grape and Marsanne and Rousanne are the white grapes. Hermitage reds tend toward being very earthy with aromas of leather, red berries, earth and coffee. They have a high level of tannins and are considered the longest lived within France. The Sorrel family’s roots in Hermitage go back to 1893 when they purchased land on the hill. Today the family’s third generation of winemakers, the three Sorrel brothers, tend the family’s few acres of land producing only a handful of bottles each vintage. When drawing up your estate plans, you might find it useful to create a revocable or irrevocable trust, either of which can help your estate avoid probate court and give you significant control over how and when your assets are distributed. But who should oversee your trust? As the person who established the trust — known as the “grantor” or “settlor” — you can also name yourself as trustee. However, this may not be the best move, particularly if the trust is irrevocable. An irrevocable trust protects the assets in the trust from creditors and civil judgments, but if you serve as trustee, this protection will disappear. It might be more advantageous for you to be the trustee of a revocable (living) trust, which can be modified without much trouble and allows you to move assets in and out of the trust and to change trust beneficiaries. You should work with a qualified estate-planning attorney to determine which type of trust, if any, is appropriate for your situation, and to get some guidance on the wisdom of serving as your own trustee. If you decide to choose someone else as trustee, you’ll want to consider the following factors: • Trust In thinking about whom you might want to serve as your trustee, the most important attribute is trust. Do you trust that this individual will always act in your best interest? If so, then they may be a good trustee candidate, but you’ll also need to look at other considerations. • Financial management skills The person you choose to be your trustee doesn’t have to be an accountant or a financial professional — but they should be skilled at managing their own finances. And they should be well-organized and good with details. • Mental and physical fitness Your trustee could serve in that position for many years, so you’ll want to name someone who is in good physical and mental health. Of course, things can change over time, so if you observe that your chosen trustee has begun to suffer physical or mental decline, you may need to name a successor trustee in your trust document. • Conflict of interest You want your trustee to carry out your wishes in a fair manner — so, you should pick someone who doesn’t have a conflict of interest with any of the beneficiaries you’ve named in your trust. Of course, this can be tricky if you want to name a family member as trustee. So, if you do, you’ll need to spell out your wishes clearly — to the trustee and to other family members. Here’s something else to think about: Instead of choosing an individual, you could name a corporate trustee. By doing so, you can receive some key benefits, such as objectivity and potentially avoiding some of the family-related disputes that can arise when an estate is settled. Also, corporate trustees have the expertise and resources to navigate the various tax and inheritance laws affecting living trusts. Whether it’s a trusted individual or a corporate entity, the right trustee can make a big difference in the effectiveness of your living trust — and, by extension, the outcome of your comprehensive estate plans. So, start your search, get the help you need and take the steps necessary to arrive at a choice for trustee that’s right for you and your family. articles.text: It was going to be hot last Wednesday, so the Walking on Wednesdays group decided to take a shorter walk through the central part of Piedmont, and walk to the home of Hugh Craig on Craig Avenue and hear the story of Piedmont’s first mayor. He was a central figure in the City of Piedmont’s first years in the aftermath of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake when many people moved to Oakland and Piedmont. Oakland was looking for property taxes to pay for the additional services it needed to provide. It wanted to annex Piedmont, but some Piedmont residents wanted to incorporate it as a separate city. It was a race and those who favored incorporation had to move quickly. They needed a map to file incorporation papers in Sacramento, so they used a map from the Piedmont Sanitary District. This explains why some Piedmont homes are partially in Oakland. On January 7, 1907, Craig and another Piedmonter went to Sacramento to file the incorporation papers with the State. This incorporation had to be approved by the voters, and on January 26, 1907, 79 Piedmont men voted for incorporation and 38 voted against it. It was all men because women didn’t get the right to vote until 1920. On January 31, 1907, the State approved Piedmont’s incorporation. However, immediately there were problems and some Piedmonters wanted to vote again about being a separate city. On September 5, 1907 a vote on disincorporating and becoming part of Oakland was held. Approval required a 2/3 vote. Ninety-two men voted to disincorporate and 62 voted to stay a separate city. The vote to disincorporate failed by only 10 votes. For the Wednesday Walkers, it was a short stroll up Highland and Mountain Avenues to Craig’s house. He was one of the first five Piedmont settlers. He was also a San Francisco insurance man and twice president of the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce. Craig was born in Sydney, Australia in 1841 to Scottish parents. He grew up in New Zealand before moving to Oakland in 1874 to work in San Francisco for the New Zealand Insurance Company. He bought five acres and built a house in 1879 on Vernal (now Highland) Avenue. However, Highland was widened in 1912, so Craig had his home put on log rollers and pulled by horses to its current location at the corner of Craig and Mountain Avenue. Craig is known as the first Mayor of Piedmont, but there were one or two men who held the position before him. Varney Gaskill was elected mayor by the A group of 42 walkers and three K-9 best friends were on hand for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays. Among those participating were Noemi Alvarado, Charlene Louie, Priscilla Wanerus, Lois Price, Chuck Oraftik, Garrett Clifford, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Lorek Haghnazarean, Mark Davis, Robert Lang, Judy Sokoloff, Jim Kellogg, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Jim Kellogg, Lisa Euphrat, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Albert Chen, Sean Brient with K-9 best friend Pip, Melba Yee, Gary Rogers, Jack Fischrup, Sharona Fischrup, Nancy Henn, Denny McGee, Kat Lang, Sherry Jacobs, Karin Fetherston, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Claudine Bach, Martin Levy, Irene Thompson, Alicia Rivera, Dave DeRoche, Greg Slatoff, Mark Frost, Peggy Shultz, Jim Kuo and Dick Carter. Hugh Craig is known as the first Mayor of Piedmont. Piedmont Board of Trustees on February 8, 1907, and Craig was later elected in 1907 and served until 1914. To fund the new city, Craig instituted a new property tax based on the size of the home’s parcel. Prior to incorporation, all residents paid the same, small tax to the County. Newspaper articles provide an understanding of what happened. On January 28, 1914 the Sacramento Star proclaimed, “Single Tax Successful in City of Millionaires – Mayor of Plutocrat Principality Forces Rich Men to Bear Just Share of Taxes - Imagine the storm of protest … when Craig, ‘a nut on the subject of taxation,’ … raised the assessments of the rich men of Piedmont.” Land assessed at $150/acre was raised to $3,000 when its market value was $8,000 to $16,000/acre. Some people were not happy. The Oakland Tribune reported on April 21, 1914, “Hugh E. Craig … was not reelected to the chairmanship of the trustees and quit his place on the board.” Craig died on November 11, 1920 at his home at the age of 79 years. This original Craig house is a beautiful Stick Italianate Victorian and surprisingly large with five bedrooms and four and a half baths in a total of 4,359 square feet. Now, it also has solar panels. On their first walk in 2018, nearly 20 Wednesday walkers posed for a group photo in front of the house and the larger group did it again last Wednesday. With all this history shared, it was time to really walk. The group went up Craig and Oakland and Moraga Avenues. At Estrella Avenue, Jim Kellogg, who led a past walk featuring residential architecture, pointed out some additional homes that he hadn’t been able to get to. They were three, identical cedar shake shingle homes built by a man who bought a larger plot and subdivided it. Further down Estrella were twin California Mission Revival homes built in 1923. It was warming up, so the group went up Ramona and Bonita Avenues for a leisurely walk back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

Wearing the pancake suit feels like quite an honor,” said Gross, who added that the costume can get quite hot. “I may want to get it drycleaned before I put it on next year,” joked Wilhelm while looking in his direction. For the Beach Dads, the pancake breakfast is nothing short of a labor of love. Between renting the grills, coordinating the club’s manpower, early mornings and the extensive preparation in the days leading up to the event, the breakfast requires many volunteers to put on. Many of the dads were at a “batter mixing party” the previous day to prepare food for the event and still showed up to Beach at 6:30 a.m. to set up tables. “For me, it’s about spending time with the other dads and just having a good time,” said Mario Ortiz, a Beach Dad who worked the grill at the breakfast. This was his third year volunteering at the event. “I have two more kids going through the system, so I’ll be here for quite some time,” he said. Although many of the dads enjoyed the opportunity to raise money for Beach, just as many say they came for the camaraderie. “We all share a special bond by making sure that the community is together, having a good time. It’s good to see smiles all around and that people’s bellies are fed. Not all heroes wear capes. Sometimes they wear pancake costumes.” However, this sense of community isn’t just felt by the Dads. Christine Schooley and her family have attended the event for close to 15 years now and plan on continuing, even though they haven’t had a child at Beach in four years. “It’s just great community, great food, and the opportunity to reconnect with old friends,” said Schooley. We had gradual improvement and playoff maturity formed. The program just developed over the years. It was a perfect story with making some mistakes in my first year, learning a lot, managing to stay in the job and make adjustments to develop the program,” he said. “Now we’re one of the most competitive teams in the Foothill and up to D3; it brings a proud moment to take a step back and see where the program is now,” Sullivan said. The changes began to work by 2019 when PHS went 12-2-5 overall and was undefeated with a 9-1-0 record while winning the Shoreline banner. The Highlanders finished second in the Shoreline in 2020 prior to the pandemic with a record of 9-2-9, then returned for the shortened 2021 spring season with a. perfect 10-0-0 record, Sullivan’s team then went 15-2-4 overall and 13-0-3 in league for another Shoreline banner and went on to win the NCS

We prevailed upon the camp to give us a new baton, and I swam the final leg of the race, handed the baton off to Nick and he then ate the baton at the end of the race, capping off our last place finish. All in all, Troop 6 had an eventful summer. Our planned expedition next summer is to the Northern Tier in Canada for a canoeing trip. Hopefully, our canoeing skills are better than our kayaking skills. Nico Salvadei and Benjie Chien complete camp evaluation forms at the end of the week. Campers wait for the boat to take them home. Todd Sullivan Continued from page 12 creating a high-pressing and possessive style. “That first season was a learning curve, I learned a lot in that first season and it set us up for future success. We had gradual improvement and playoff maturity formed. The program just developed over the years. It was a perfect story with making some mistakes in my first year, learning a lot, managing to stay in the job and make adjustments to develop the program,” he said. “Now we’re one of the most competitive teams in the Foothill and up to D3; it brings a proud moment to take a step back and see where the program is now,” Sullivan said. The changes began to work by 2019 when PHS went 12-2-5 overall and was undefeated with a 9-1-0 record while winning the Shoreline banner. The Highlanders finished second in the Shoreline in 2020 prior to the pandemic with a record of 9-2-9, then returned for the shortened 2021 spring season with a. perfect 10-0-0 record, Sullivan’s team then went 15-2-4 overall and 13-0-3 in league for another Shoreline banner and went on to win the NCS title as the tournament’s favorite in 2022. The 2023 team went 13-6-5 and but upset higher ranked teams on the way to the NCS title as the No. 8 seed. They beat No. 1 Cardinal Newman, and No. 5 Healdsburg before taking down University at the Beach Chalet Field in Golden Gate Park. Although 2024 didn’t bring any banners, his team went 12-3-3 in its most recent season and challenged for the Foothill title at 7-3- 2, finishing third. Their 1-nil win over Berkeley marked the first time Sullivan’s team had defeated the Yellowjackets and showed how far Piedmont soccer had come. “Definitely the Berkeley win is up there as a favorite memory. It was massive for the boys and me as well. Another favorite memory was the NCS win at Witter under the lights,” Sullivan said. In addition to Sullivan’s collection of championship banners, he finishes his time at Piedmont with 87 wins and 155 matches as head coach. He closes with a record of 87 wins, 19 ties, and 49 losses. Piedmont High School is in the hunt for its next boys’ soccer coach. The season begins in mid-November. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, September 11, 2024 Captain Marvel Continued from page 19 upon were her powers of tenacity and courage. The movie begins with Carol, aka Ver (Brie Larsen), as a soldier on Kree, about to take part in a mission that sets out to rescue a fellow soldier being held by the Skrulls. One thing leads to another and Ver finds herself spinning toward planet C-53, known to us as earth. She free falls through the roof of a Blockbuster video store, landing among rows of boxed tapes. Apparently this is the 1990s, back when there were Blockbuster stores on lots of corners. Unbeknownst to Ver, a number of Skrulls have followed her to earth and are in the hunt for her. Enter Nick Fury (Samuel L. Jackson) as a S.H.I.E.L.D. cop, called to investigate the store break-in. If Captain Marvel has a weakness, it’s in the writing. It’s all pretty generic. Brie Larsen gives the script her best effort as an empowered woman who discovers that her powers are more than extraordinary. But tangentially, here’s the issue with superheroes in general, and why the origin stories can be so compelling: Captain Marvel, and Superman, et al., have no natural enemies. They’re bullet-proof. Okay, there’s kryptonite. So they are never in mortal danger. Tough to write around that quality. What are the stakes? Sure all powerful is an exciting strength; but it’s also a weakness. And it is what makes this new Captain Marvel film good, but not great. But that’s from an adult point of view. As for kids, girls and boys, tweens and teens, this Captain Marvel will entertain. The new Capt. Marvel even appears in the next MCU installment, Avengers: End Game. Captain Marvel. Directed by Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck. Starring Brie Larsen, Samuel L. articles.text: Applications for full-time position due this Friday, Sept. 6 The City of Piedmont recently posted a job listing for a “Video Communications Specialist / Television Station Manager” on its website and multiple job recruiting sites. This move comes on the heels of new information that the previous KCOM Station Manager, Jesse Rosenberg, left his position with the city in late July. His departure was confirmed by Communication Manager Echa Schneider. “Jesse was a great asset to the city and we will miss him. We’re looking forward to filling the role soon, hopefully with somebody who can continue to push us forward,” said Schneider. Rosenberg was with the station for less than a year, hired in September 2023. However, his departure may not necessarily signal less coverage of city events in the future. The City is now looking for a new station manager to fill the full-time position. “Video is one of our most powerful storytelling tools, and we know more and more this is how our community digests information,” said Schneider.
articles.title: City searches for new KCOM manager

articles.text: Beach School students from Ms. Quintella and Ms. Rinehart’s first grade classes spent Labor Day weekend camping at Mandala Springs, a wellness retreat center near Napa. Over 30 people joined for a weekend of outdoor fun including hiking, swimming, and of course making s’mores. Mandala Springs has a variety of lodging options including houses, cabins, and tents. A few of the families rented the Glenbrook Lodge and used that house as the base camp to cook, eat, and hang out. Both experienced and firsttime campers joined the trip. A small creek ran through the campsite that kids loved exploring. It was a hot weekend but there were plenty of water activities to keep everyone cool. All the kids were amazed by how many stars they were able to see at night, including the excitement of seeing some shooting stars. The families saw all sorts of animals including deer, turkeys, frogs, and lizards. It was a great weekend being with classmates outdoors at the start of the school year. 10.
articles.title: Beach first grade families spend Labor Day weekend camping

articles.text: The 19th Annual Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast will take place this Sunday, September 8, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. As with every year, hundreds of community members will enjoy plates of buttermilk, blueberry, chocolate chip or oatmeal pancakes, plus sausage, bacon, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee. A student jazz band will serenade breakfast-goers as they eat. The cost is $15 for adults and $10 for kids and seniors. Tickets will be sold on-site, and no pre-registration is needed. All proceeds will benefit the Beach Parents Organization (BPO) which provides funding assistance for Beach Elementary School’s educational programs and sponsors after-school enrichment classes. “I want to go all in and help the community as much as I can with this fundraiser,” said Michael Wilhelm, president of the Beach Dads Club, a position known affectionately to the other club members as “Padre Grande.” Wilhelm took over the role from the previous president, Michael Gross, at the Beach Dads’ Welcome Night on August 21. Funds raised will go toward classroom materials, library support, STEM resources, science materials, lunchtime activities, assemblies, speakers, musical instruments, art and library supplies, and teacher and staff appreciation activities. The annual pancake breakfast is a major fundraiser for the school and Wilhelm said he’s never felt out of his depth because of the help he’s received from former presidents. “[One of the previous presidents] has been calling me to make sure that I have all of my T’s crossed and I’s dotted leading Last year’s event drew more than 500 breakfast-goers to Beach. Staff photos

articles.text: On August 28 I got to ring the gong at the Golden Gate Cancer Center signaling the completion of my 28 radiation treatments for prostate cancer. My gong stroke was unremarkable but solid. What is remarkable is the care I received by the team at the center and encouragement I received from family, friends and community. I am a grateful human being. My colleague, Dr. Scott Arnold, the Senior Minister at the First Baptist Church of Los Angeles, is a cancer survivor and the author of Soul Fruit: Bearing Blessings Through Cancer. He writes. “Cancer is a disease, and blessings can be discovered when facing disease, trials, or troubles in life. I am not saying that cancer as a disease is the blessing, what I am saying is that we can experience God’s blessing while dealing with cancer or any other illness.” – Pastor Jim Hopkins I appreciate Scott’s insights and certainly like his title of Soul Fruit. SAMMY RAGONES, 10th grade I’m going to Tahoe to see my grandparents. PETER LEE, 11th grade I’m leaving this weekend to start my junior year of high school at Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire. RELIGION CORNER Ringing the gong By Pastor Jim Hopkins On August 28 I got to ring the gong at the Golden Gate Cancer Center signaling the completion of my 28 radiation treatments for prostate cancer. My gong stroke was unremarkable but solid. What is remarkable is the care I received by the team at the center and encouragement I received from family, friends and community. I am a grateful human being. My colleague, Dr. Scott Arnold, the Senior Minister at the First Baptist Church of Los Angeles, is a cancer survivor and the author of Soul Fruit: Bearing Blessings Through Cancer. He writes. “Cancer is a disease, and blessings can be discovered when facing disease, trials, or troubles in life. I am not saying that cancer as a disease is the blessing, what I am saying is that we can experience God’s blessing while dealing with cancer or any other illness.” “The call of faith is the call to trust.” – Pastor Jim Hopkins I appreciate Scott’s insights and certainly like his title of Soul Fruit. If my cancer has borne any Soul Fruit. that fruit looks like this: 1. It is good just to be among people ­ – the people I ride BART with to SF for my treatments, the people who live along Mission Street where I walk to the cancer center, my fellow patients, the cancer center staff, my congregation, my family. Some are close friends. Some are acquaintances. Most are strangers I will never meet. Yet, we all share this amazing journey called life. It is a gift to be among them. It is good to be among you. 2. After the death of his son in an automobile accident, the great preacher William Sloane Coffin wrote, “God may not protect us in the ways we’d like, but God sustains us in the ways we need. I have been sustained. I have been upheld.” Indeed. It is a gift to be upheld. 3. There is so much I will never understand. The why of bad things, the how of cancer treatment, the steadfast presence of God’s love in all things. Yet, I trust. There is a great difference between trusting and understanding. The call of faith is the call to trust. See Religion Corner on page 31 LUKA PEÑA, Piedmont Post Delivery Kid I’m going to be celebrating my mom’s birthday this weekend. We are going to Claremont to sit by the pool and relax. NICO LIEBSCHER, 12th grade When is Labor Day? Monday? ADAM QUIBELAN, 11th grade I’ll probably be playing tennis either with my dad or friends. articles.text: The parent-run Piedmont School District Wellness Center is hosting a pickleball tournament titled Positively Pickled on Saturday, September 21, with three divisions of play (beginner, intermediate and competitive). Every team is guaranteed one hour of play. All matches will be held at the courts at the middle school. Winners from Saturday’s Intermediate and Advanced hourly round robins will battle it out on Sunday morning in a single elimination tournament with tournament prizes at the end. Beginners will play Saturday only. Coaching will be provided to help with rules, scoring and game play. The first five teams (doubles) to register in the Beginner division will receive a free Selkirk SLK Nexus Paddle from Montclair Sports Tennis & Pickleball. After a five-minute warmup each team will play three matches against similar teams. Team registration is $100. Last school year, the Wellness Center provided over 2,000 therapy sessions to Piedmont students; this fundraising effort helps ensure that Piedmont students continue to receive the mental health support they need. The Wellness Center delivers free counseling and mental health services to Piedmont High School, Middle School, and Millennium High School students. The center helps students manage emotional and social challenges, including stress, depression, grief, relationship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Register at htt ps://pef. schoolauction.net/wow24/register/ticket_sales. Pickleball players Asher Shalev (left) & Henry van den Bos are ready for the tournament. articles.text: The 23rd annual Chalk Art Festival will return to the Beach School playground this Sunday, September 8, between 9 a.m. and Noon. The school’s blacktop will be divided into roughly 100 squares that parents can purchase for their child to draw on with boxes of brightly colored pastel chalk provided by Flax Art & Design. Individual squares are available for $20 each at the time of the event. All proceeds will benefit the Piedmont Arts Fund, a part of the Piedmont Education Foundation that supports art in Piedmont schools. “It’s a great community event,” said Jon Schleuning, who organizes the Chalk Art Festival. “Every year, the blacktop literally transforms into this amazing kaleidoscope explosion of color.” Three artists pay homage to the Pixar film Elemental with chalk art in 2023. Founded in 2002, by Havens school art teachers Raul Jorcino and Karen Stanton, the Chalk Art Festival has become a well-loved tradition among Piedmont families. “People come back year after year for generations. It has A pair of girls work on their chalk square in 2023. become this event where people, parents and their kids habitually come back and do their squares together each year,” said Schleuning. Schleuning added that he believes that the opportunity for kids to express themselves artistically is what keeps people coming back. “You literally start with a blank square and you have permission to do pretty much anything you want,” he explained. Subject matter for artists’ chalk squares in the past has ranged from pancakes and rainbows to spooky graveyards and Halloween costumes. The Chalk Art Festival is held in conjunction with the Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast. Both are hosted at the same time at Beach School. For more information about the Piedmont Arts Fund, visit their website at www.piedmontartsfund.org. A girl focuses on blending colors together with a paintbrush. articles.text: Introducing one-year-old Chihuahua mix Tater Tot. This 13-pound affectionate cutie is available for adoption or foster. Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers say Tater Tot can be a bit shy when meeting new people, but once he knows someone he loves to sit in laps and cuddle. He enjoys playing with other small dogs and would do well in a home with a playful doggie sibling to show him the ropes. Tater Tot has had a chance to go on a couple of outings where he demonstrated good progress in leash walking skills and was not reactive to other dogs, bicycles or people. On a trip to Tilden Park, Tater Tot easily hiked 3+ miles in the company of a volunteer and a 10-year-old child. At an ice cream stop, he sat contentedly on a bench next to the volunteer and accepted pets, patiently waiting and not begging while they ate their snack. He was an ideal al fresco dining companion! Tater Tot, a Chihuahua mix, at Oakland Animal Services. If you would like to foster Tater Tot email dogfostering@ oaklandsanimals.org. If you would like to adopt him, come meet him Thursday from 12 - 7 pm, or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Tater Tot must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. articles.text: The 23rd Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will take place in Piedmont Main Park on Sunday, September 22, featuring musicians performing on a stage near the Piedmont Community Center. The event is free to the public. The first performers will take the stage beginning at 11:00 a.m. This city-sponsored event occurs in conjunction with the annual Piedmont Harvest Festival. “It’s a celebration of the musical talent of Piedmont,” explained the festival’s longtime organizer, Greg Slatoff. The first performance will be Carlos Caminos, a local jazz-flamenco fusion guitarist originally from Venezuela. “He’s going to be opening the show with an acoustic set that should be quiet and even,” said Slatoff. “We don’t want to blast the city awake at 11 o’clock in the morning.” Next, the Piedmont High School Jazz Band under the direction of new PHS Band director Trevor Messeroll. A recent graduate of Berklee College of Music, he took over the role in September 2023 after the departure of long-time PHS band director Andria Mullan. The Puckett Family Project will be the penultimate act of the festival. Originally started in 1998 as a solo project by frontman and Piedmonter Tod Puckett, the band, now with nine members, is known locally for its high-energy brand of Americana rock and funk. The band has shared bills with a wide range of bands including Ricky Skaggs, Tea Leaf Green, Acoustic Junction and The Will Bernard Trio. The band also recently released its fifth album, No Invite, now available on Spotify and Apple Music. Local tango band Molinete, with five musicians, will close out the festival, which should finish around 3:00 p.m. For more information about the Jazz Festival, contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@yahoo.com. 11:00 – 12:00 12:00 – 1:00 1:30 – 2:15 was taken.

articles.text: During the August 28 school board meeting, Teachers Union President Elise Marks used her allotted time to ask district leadership about the absence of gay pride flags flying above Piedmont campuses. Marks’ comments were only the beginning of a board meeting in which community members, teachers and students used public comment in defense of LGBTQ rights. Marks said she understood that a formal board resolution passed years ago, ensured that the flags would be flown in June, during Pride month. “Though many of us had understood, at least informally, that the plan had been to keep the flags flying year round as they have for the past couple of years,” she added. Marks, who effectively advocated for teacher salary raises last year, has taken up the torch of LGBTQ rights to start this school year. The school board room was filled with students and allies raising the question of why the pride flag isn’t on the flag pole at the entry to the campus. “For several years at the start of my career in Piedmont (in 2000), there were no openly LGBTQ students or staff at Piedmont High School. None – not one,” said Marks. Marks told of the first student to openly insinuate his homosexuality in an AP Art class project and the first teacher at PHS to tell her students about her female partner. Marks spoke of the bravery of these two and how far the district has come. Despite Piedmont being in the progressive Bay Area, LGBTQ advocates sensed the need to speak out. They came in droves to supply personal stories and explain what the presence of the flag means. “It is important to recognize, that the pride flags flying for so many years, were not flying as some sort of overly-long Pride month celebration,” said PHS Sophomore Mimi Crawford-Jakubiak. “I know in my heart how much this has hurt my son,” said parent Kim Hunter. “That flag means freedom, free to be exactly who they are, every part of them.” “Taking down the Pride Flag would take back years of action and years of work for these students,” said PHS student Abigail Kauffman. articles.text: Camp Augusta will host its annual Wish, Wonder & Wine fundraiser on Saturday, September 21 from 5:00-7:00 p.m. in the courtyard at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Tickets are $50 and are available at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/wish-wonderand-wine-tickets-945283286757 ?aff=oddtdtcreator. As school begins, keep an eye out for the cornflower blue shirts around town worn by the hundreds of Piedmont children who attended Camp Augusta this summer. They may not know it, but they are continuing a long tradition in the community. You are invited to learn more about this special place that so many children call home each summer. Join us on September 21st for Wish, Wonder & Wine, an adult evening of fun in Piedmont. Enjoy wine, appetizers, and auction prizes while building community in support of Camp Augusta. You’ll hear from staff and campers with exciting updates from this summer, including the hugely popular new ropes challenge course. Camp offers amazing programming and some of the highest trained camp staff in the world to run the program. Help us meet our goal of upgrading our staff housing and to kick off a two-year capital campaign to replace those structures and the Cedar Bath house. Piedmont History Camp Augusta was originally donated to the girls of Piedmont almost 100 years ago. In the early years, the camp’s main use was by the Piedmont Council of Camp Fire. Virtually all the young Piedmont women spent their summers at the camp. After the site was shuttered by the Camp Fire organization, a group of dedicated Piedmonters formed an oversight board and began the long legal battle to win the property back for the children of Piedmont. While the site sat dormant for decades, the facilities fell into disrepair. However, with hard work and the support of the community, the 90 acre facility located in the beautiful forested foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains has received a variety of improvements over the years: the restoration of the original Lodge where campers hang out in aerial silks; a kitchen where our chefs cook delicious organic food that campers get excited about (have you ever tried Australian pizza with bananas on top!?); and this year’s incredible new high ropes challenge course with over 40 elements to ascend. We hope to see you at Wish, Wonder and Wine. Can’t make the event in person? Please consider making a contribution to support our efforts at www.campaugusta.org/gifts. articles.text: The co-ed “Wild Things” adult softball team won the summer league on Thursday, August 15. The team defeated the “Saints & Sinners” team 4-3; and continued a tradition which dates to 1979. The coed softball league competed against four other teams this summer in 7-inning games. Other teams participating included Beach Bums, the Baja Bombers, and Game of Throws. The Wildwood Dads Club team also defeated slow-pitch softball foes from Havens and Beach at the end of the school year. The team added some moms to the diamond and became a summer league team. “The team started because (I think) many of us were super disappointed in our near decade losing streak,” said team manager Alex Shartsis. “We wanted a chance to win a game, so we signed up for the coed league.” Shartsis got the requisite signups and the rest is history. “In the winter of 2022-23,” explained Team Manager Adam Schwarz, “we played lots of ‘Eye of the Tiger,’ and recruited more talented and fun Wildwood parents and friends. We pirated a logo, ordered jerseys, destroyed a set of practice balls, and broke a window in Adam’s back yard.” Members of the WiId Things softball team: Abigail Johnson, Alex Shartsis, Brian Trowbridge, Cecilia Coronado Blake, Dirk Van Den Bos, Greg Wheeler, Jacqueline Perez Kalafate, Jennifer Gregovich, Matthew Deutsch, Megan Walsh, Mike Stearns, Morgan Driskill, Noah Schwartz, Roberto Kalafate, Steve Driskill

pages.text: Wednesday, September 4, 2024 7 Camp Augusta event in Piedmont Sept. 21 Camp Augusta will host its annual Wish, Wonder & Wine fundraiser on Saturday, September 21 from 5:00-7:00 p.m. in the courtyard at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Tickets are $50 and are available at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/wish-wonderand-wine-tickets-945283286757 ?aff=oddtdtcreator. As school begins, keep an eye out for the cornflower blue shirts around town worn by the hundreds of Piedmont children who attended Camp Augusta this summer. They may not know it, but they are continuing a long tradition in the community. You are invited to learn more about this special place that so many children call home each summer. Join us on September 21st for Wish, Wonder & Wine, an adult evening of fun in Piedmont. Enjoy wine, appetizers, and auction prizes while building community in support of Camp Augusta. You’ll hear from staff and campers with exciting updates from this summer, including the hugely popular new ropes challenge course. Camp offers amazing programming and some of the highest trained camp staff in the world to run the program. Help us meet our goal of upgrading our staff housing and to kick off a two-year capital campaign to replace those structures and the Cedar Bath house. Piedmont History Camp Augusta was originally donated to the girls of Piedmont almost 100 years ago. In the early years, the camp’s main use was by the Piedmont Council of Camp Fire. Virtually all the young Piedmont women spent their summers at the camp. After the site was shuttered by the Camp Fire organization, a group of dedicated Piedmonters formed an oversight board and began the long legal battle to win the property back for the children of Piedmont. While the site sat dormant for decades, the facilities fell into disrepair. However, with hard work and the support of the community, the 90 acre facility located in the beautiful forested foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains has received a variety of improvements over the years: the restoration of the original Lodge where campers hang out in aerial silks; a kitchen where our chefs cook delicious organic food that campers get excited about (have you ever tried Australian pizza with bananas on top!?); and this year’s incredible new high ropes challenge course with over 40 elements to ascend. We hope to see you at Wish, Wonder and Wine. Can’t make the event in person? Please consider making a contribution to support our efforts at www.campaugusta.org/gifts. Saturday, September 21st at 5:00 PM Piedmont Community Church Come join us for an adult Tickets $50 evening of fundraising with wine, appetizers, auction prizes, and fun and more while building community support for Camp Augusta. articles.text: Troop 1 inaugurated its first trip of the school year with a tubing trip at Caswell Memorial State Park in the Central Valley. The plan was to float for about a mile down the Stanislaus River, get out at a downstream beach and then walk a half mile back to do it all over again. Upon arrival, the Scouts couldn’t contain their excitement to wade or jump into the water. It was a great time with some Scouts preferring to just relax in their inner tubes and float down the river chatting with friends while others liked to be out and about, playing catch and swimming in the current. The water was crisp and refreshing with an occasional fallen tree or tree branch jutting out ominously from the river bed waiting to pop inner tubes of unsuspecting floaters. After spotting a lone cow by the riverbank, the Scouts stopped at a beach halfway through the trip to splash in the water. While many of the trees in the water posed hazards, one particular clump of trees and branches rose high out of the water, enabling the Scouts (and the scoutmaster) to climb up and jump several feet into the Keira Spina (left). Ben Callaway, Sawyer Heppner, Zeke Stein, Gabi Stein, Dylan Wallway, Theodore Cost, Zack Fisher, Kian Spina, Sammy Donnelly, Jack Chauncey, Finn Holder, Susannah Cantrill and Teo Wickner are excited to start floating. Troop 1 Scouts Samantha Pell, Susannah Cantrill, Moning Wang, Sasha Liu, and Julia Bencher enjoyed floating together. Troop 1 Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill leaps into the river while Susannah Cantrill and Kiera Spina wait to jump in. water – the highlight for many on the trip (see photo). After a second floating trip down the river, the Scouts changed out of their waterlogged clothing and set up their tents. Some Scouts cooked dinner, working to earn a Cooking merit badge, while others enjoyed a game of Three Flags Up with a frisbee. After a hearty dinner, the Scouts created a fire and roasted smores. As the night went on, the Scouts performed skits they had created such as “Crazy Uno.” To finish it off, one Scout relayed a classic Troop 1 story, “The Pink House”, to the new 6th graders participating in their first outing. Early the next morning after taking down camp, most Scouts embarked on a final float down the river while others waited at the downstream beach. The final trip down the river was just as good as the earlier floats, if not better. After reluctantly exiting the water, the Scouts formed a circle to discuss the trip highlights. All in all, it was a great introductory trip for Scouts new to Troop 1 and a fun new experience for the older Scouts. Theodore Cost is an 8th grader and a member of Piedmont Scouts Troop 1. Troop 1 Scouts Ben Callaway (left), Zeke Stein, Finn Holder, Gabi Stein, Theodore Cost, Kian Spina, Ciaran Gallagher, Cade Ogles, Ronan Price, Dylan Wallway, Sammy Donnelly, Teo Wickner, Susannah Cantrill, Moning Wang, Keira Spina, Sasha Liu and Julia Bencher celebrate after finishing their final float.

articles.text: Troop 6 Scouts at Sea Base in the Bahamas: Walid Abdul-Rahim (left), Sammie Do, Devan Salazar, Eva Abdul-Rahim, Alek von Komarniki, Nolan Walsh, Jason Throne, Dr. Sellman, Matthew Goldweber, Emme Throne, Sebastian Guzman, Logan Asport: (back) Jack Throne, JD Sellman, Conner Hulsy, Nate Norvell, Martin Gustavson, Lisa Gros This summer, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 6 traveled to Sea Base in the Bahamas to spend five days on a 60-foot Catamaran. Upon our return and after just a few brief nights in our own beds at home, we then traveled to Camp Oljato in the San Joaquin Valley for another week of adventure. On June 28, 15 members of Troop 6 (11 boys and four girls) and five lucky adult chaperones took a red eye flight to Charlotte, North Carolina, where we then flew to Marsh Harbour to board our catamaran. We dressed in our Class A formal uniforms and, although we looked sharp, the wave of humidity that hit us as we exited the plane made us quickly want to change into our shorts and t-shirts. Every Scout had a job on the catamaran. I was one of three Patrol Leaders who assigned daily tasks, such as cooking and cleaning. We spent our days sailing around the Abaco Islands, snorkeling and exploring shipwrecks. We saw sharks, did some fishing and ate lots of really good food we made on the deck-top grill. Although I loaded the catNate Norvell and JD Sellman enjoy the Bahamian breezes. amaran with fishing rods and am an avid fisherman, the fishing was not great. The boat’s Captain taught me another fishing method called Handlining where you snorkel with a line in your hand. I caught a snapper that way. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys water polo team, the defending North Coast Section champion, got its 2024 campaign underway on Friday and Saturday, August 30-31 at the Labor Day Bash tournament hosted by James Logan HS and Mission College in Fremont. They won two of four games, beating Marin Catholic 15-13 and losing 16-2 to James Logan on Friday, and beating Mission San Jose 12-7 and losing 12-8 to Alameda the following day. 12-7 win vs. Mission San Jose Piedmont got out to a 4-2 lead in the first quarter and went into halftime up 7-2. Both teams added a goal in the third quarter, 9-3, while PHS added three goals and conceded four in the final going. Final stats: Freshman Henry Stein led scoring with three goals, two assists, and a steal. Fellow freshman Rylan Patty had two goals, one assist, and three steals. Charlie Wright had two goals and an assist. Leo Hurwitz had a goal, two assists, and two steals. Elles Krieckhaus scored two goals. Yotam Kariv had one goal. 12-8 loss to Alameda Piedmont’s meeting with Alameda was a rematch of the D2 NCS Championship game, this time going in favor of the Hornets. Alameda led 5-2 by the end of the first quarter and 7-4 by halftime. Piedmont couldn’t cut away at the deficit in the third quarter, trailing 10-7 going into the fourth. PHS could only amass one goal in the final going, allowing two. Final stats: Krieckhaus had three goals, one assist, and one steal. Stein had two goals and an assist. Hurwitz had two goals and a steal. Kariv scored once. Goalie Luke McAuliffe had five goals and a steal. 15-13 victory over Marin Catholic Both teams battled to a 3-3 tie through the first quarter and the match stayed deadlocked 8-8 into halftime. Both teams added Staff photos The boys’ water polo team opened its season at the Labor Day Bash tournament. three goals in the third quarter to continue the barnburner 11-11. Piedmont added four goals in the fourth quarter on its way to a 15-13 victory. In the fourth quarter, Marin Catholic scored to take a 12-11 lead with 4:36 left in the game after back and forth possessions. But the Wildcats committed a foul and ejection with 4:20 on the clock, leading to a goal by Krieckhaus 12 seconds later to tie. After Piedmont forced a quick turnover, Krieckhaus scored again with 3:42 on the clock to give PHS a 13-12 lead. 42 seconds later, Charlie Wright gave Piedmont a 14-12 cushion. Marin Catholic drew one back at 2:28 to make it a one-goal deficit, but #3 put the game away for Piedmont with a final goal with 1:02 left in the game. Final stats: Krieckhaus scored four goals. Wright had two goals. Kariv had two goals, one steal, and two assists. Dupree had a goal and assist. Stein also had two goals and two assists. Hurwitz had two goals and an assist. Patty had two goals and a steal. McAuliffe finished with nine saves. 16-2 loss to James Logan James Logan led 7-1 through the first quarter and 10-1 by halftime. JLHS made it 13-1 in the third quarter and closed with four goals in the fourth. Final stats: Krieckhaus and Kariv had individual goals. McAuliffe recorded nine saves. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team claimed a pair of wins in their first two matches of the season. The squad defeated non-league opponent Las Lomas 8-1 in Walnut Creek on Wednesday, August 28, then showed improvement from last year by beating crosstown rival Head Royce 5-2 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center the following day. “We are off to a great start,” said coach Jim Landes. “Thursday’s match against Head Royce was long with an 8 pm finish, but at least it wasn’t 100 degrees like in Walnut Creek on Wednesday.” The win over Head Royce was closer than the 5-2 score indicates. Of the seven matches, three went to three sets. The clinching match came down to No. 3 singles, where junior Arianna Kortum defeated the Jayhawks’ Darya Mooshed in straight sets, 6-2, 7-6 (8-6). Kortum dominated the first set 6-2, but trailed 6-5 in the second set. After tying the set 6-6, she won the seven-point tiebreaker narrowly 8-6. “It’s definitely good to get the win, but definitely was stressful. Good thing I didn’t know I was the clinching match until now,” Kortum said with a laugh after the match. It was also a strong match for No. 1 singles starter, Carolina Romanczuk, who rallied after losing the first set 7-5 to win 6-4, 6-1 against Head Royce’s Mia Wang. After dropping the first set, Romanczuk settled in with her usual array of powerful forehands and backhands. “I lost the first set 5-7 and it was a really tight match. The second set was close again. I really just stayed focused. Getting the first serve in really helped after struggling in the first set. Once I Staff Photos Arianna Kortum won the clinching fourth match in Piedmont’s 5-2 win over Head Royce. No. 1 singles starter Carolina Romanczuk claimed victories against both Las Lomas and Head Royce. Emma Eisemon sends a forehand against Head Royce. She won her No. 1 doubles match with teammate Samantha Huynh.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team opened its season on Friday, August 30 with a one-sided 46-14 loss to Salesian in its first game at Witter Field since 2022. After scoring the game’s opening score and clinging onto a 14-14 tie in the third quarter, the Highlanders gave up 32 unanswered points in the second half. “It was a tough game. We had ample opportunities to take control but it just didn’t happen. Whether it was a variety of play calling, some miscommunication, or bad snaps, we really shot ourselves in the foot,” said PHS head coach Jordan Seiden. Despite the loss, it was a packed house at Witter and brought together a loud student-cheering section to embrace Piedmont’s renewed football culture. “It would have been nice to be back at home with a W,” Seiden said, “but, it was nice to see the JV team come out and fight. That was really inspirational just to see how far they have come.” Although the Highlanders struck first and held a tie into the third quarter, things fell apart as the size and skill of Salesian began to take its toll. PHS was held to one first down following their tying touchdown in the third quarter. The Highlanders look ahead to another tough test this Friday against Middletown. The Mustangs started their season with a 33-14 win over Piner and finished Piedmont’s Xavier Anderson (13) celebrates after the defense forced a turnover. Photos by Jonathan Comeaux and Ken DeCrosta Sam Shelby (2) scores Piedmont’s opening touchdown. last year with an 8-3 record and advancing to the North Coast Section playoffs. “Middletown will be a tough, physical game,” predicted Seiden. “They are physical up front, they run a lot of Wing T, run it straight down at you, and have a lot of movement. But we have to come out and play football; it’s not about what the other team is doing, it’s what we’re doing. We have to do our job and give ourselves a chance,” Game Recap Piedmont led 7-0 at the end of the first quarter but trailed 14-7 by halftime. PHS tied the game 14-14 early in the third quarter, but Salesian scored five straight touchdowns to put the game away. The Highlanders struck first after recovering an onside kick to open the game. From the 50-yard line, quarterback Markos Lagios threw a touchdown pass to Brandon Dicke wide open on a broken play. After Lagios reeled in a high snap, he rolled to the right toward the line of scrimmage. Salesian’s defensive backfield didn’t account for Dicke, allowing Lagios to toss a ball over the defense to Dicke— who ran about 20 yards after the catch into the end zone. An extra point by Sam Shelby made it 7-0 after just 21 seconds of play. PHS forced a punt on Salesian’s opening possession and drove to the Pride’s 14-yard line following a trick play where Shelby threw a pass as a receiver to Dicke for a big 28-yard gain. However, the drive stopped with a turnover on downs at the 10-yard line. articles.text: Piedmont’s flag football team opened its season on Wednesday, August 28 at Witter Field with a 28-6 loss to Las Lomas. PHS got on the board late in the game, showing improvement after suffering some jitters in the first game of the season. “Our goal of this game was execution. We’ve built an offensive system and have practiced it. We struggled with it last week at our scrimmage, but we were able to execute today. We looked like a football team, looked tough, and are moving in the right direction,” said coach Beth Black. The game included a positive performance by running back Kalyani Spieckerman and receiver/defensive back Dahlia Osman. Spieckerman led the team offensively with several long runs, while Osman had some critical first-downs and led the defense in tackles (flags pulled). “She picked up a lot of yards. She didn’t play at the running back spot much last year and mostly caught short passes. She also stepped into the role with our usual starter, Miya Fujimoto, out,” Black said of Spieckerman. Scoring Piedmont’s touchdown was tall receiver Dorothy Nemeth, reeling in a pass from Edie Elmquist. The Highlanders look ahead to a game at Berean Christian in Walnut Creek on Tuesday, September 10. PHS starts their Western Alameda County Conference league schedule the following week on September 17 when hosting Encinal.
