articles.text: The Piedmont Highlanders JV football team started the 2024 season with a hard fought 14-14 tie against Salesian on Friday, August 30 at Witter Field. This year’s JV team is ripe with young talent, including 19 freshman pumped up to get experience on the gridiron. It was a memorable day for many, joining in on their very first High School football game. Piedmont’s returning sophomores Daniel King, Noah Hussain, Colby Hong, and Diego Hurwitz were named team captains by head coach Pouyan Assadi. PHS won the toss and decided to kick off to open the game. Salesian started on its own 37 yard line and drove all 63 yards for a touchdown in just two plays, including a 58-yard passing touchdown up the sideline. Salesian led 8-0 after a successful two-point conversion. But the Highlanders were ready to return the favor on Salesias when freshman quarterback Jimmy Lagios stepped to the line on their first play from scrimmage. With just enough blocking, Lagios tossed a perfect throw to Hurwitz, taking it 52 yards to the house for a touchdown. Piedmont trailed 8-6 after coming up short on a two-point conversion. The rest of the first quarter remained scoreless with both teams were playing good defense. It wasn’t until late in the second quarter when Salesian marched Photo by JC Curran Returning sophomores Diego Hurwitz (left), Daniel King, Noah Hussian, and Colby Hong were named captains ahead of JV football’s season-opener against Salesian. their way to the four-yard line on a multiple-play drive with broken tackles, punching it into the end zone with a little over three minutes left in the half. The Pride went into halftime holding a 14-6 lead. Salesian’s 14-6 lead remained through the third quarter with back-and-forth possessions and fumbles for both sides. In the fourth quarter, inside freshman linebacker George Saunders recovered his third fumble of the game to put Piedmont in a great position in the Pride’s red zone. Piedmont took advantage, scoring their second touchdown on a pass from Lagios to tight end George Saunders. Now trailing 14-12, PHS was forced to go for a two-point conversion. They went right back to the man, Saunders, converting the two-point conversion and touchdown reception for a rare ‘octopus’. But it wasn’t yet over. In the waning minutes, Piedmont’s defense came through again when recovering another fumble in Salesian’s red zone. Unfortunately, a victory wasn’t in the cards for the Highlanders as time expired before PHS could get across the goal line. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-0-1) hosts Middletown on Friday, September 6 at Witter Field at 4:00 p.m. Colby Hong is a sophomore and a member of the Piedmont JV football team.

articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country team returns this week for the 2024 season with some familiar and new faces. Both the girls’ and boys’ teams had former captains, Xander Schulte-Sasse and Jamie Schwarz graduate, meaning both teams have a new group of leaders. The Highlanders get their season started this Saturday, September 14 at the Ed Sias Invitational at Hidden Valley Park in Martinez. For the girls, coach Steve Zirkelbach has an intriguing cast of young runners. He expects the squad to have a solid group of eight runners: Skylar Best, Leighton Mand, Cora Chan, Gladwin Horsley, Amalia Gray, Caroline Taylor, Cora Brozowski-Schrader, and Nasreen Schulze. “We really only lost one runner in Jamie and we have eight or nine girls who will vie for the top seven spots. In our time trials, they’ve all been very close, so that bodes really well for the season. All seven runners matter on race day, and we have a good group,” Zirkelbach. Taylor and Best were named captains for the girls’ team, Sophomore Sebastien Swain is back after winning the Post’s Freshman of the Year award. Staff Photos Skylar Best, a junior, has been named a captain of the girls’ cross country team. while Oliver and Henry Horsley are captains for the boys. Best, most notably, reached the 2022 CIF State Championship as a freshman and was our Honorable Mention for 2022 Freshman of the Year. She’ll likely lead the girls’ team. “Skylar is a great personality on the team. She brings a lot of positive energy and I’m looking forward to see her use that friendly and positive energy to excite the rest of the team,” Zirkelbach said of Best. Zirkelbach could see Piedmont competing at the NCS Championship meet at Hayward. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, September 4, 2024 JV Highlanders open season with 14-14 tie against Salesian By Colby Hong The Piedmont Highlanders JV football team started the 2024 season with a hard fought 14-14 tie against Salesian on Friday, August 30 at Witter Field. This year’s JV team is ripe with young talent, including 19 freshman pumped up to get experience on the gridiron. It was a memorable day for many, joining in on their very first High School football game. Piedmont’s returning sophomores Daniel King, Noah Hussain, Colby Hong, and Diego Hurwitz were named team captains by head coach Pouyan Assadi. PHS won the toss and decided to kick off to open the game. Salesian started on its own 37 yard line and drove all 63 yards for a touchdown in just two plays, including a 58-yard passing touchdown up the sideline. Salesian led 8-0 after a successful two-point conversion. But the Highlanders were ready to return the favor on Salesias when freshman quarterback Jimmy Lagios stepped to the line on their first play from scrimmage. With just enough blocking, Lagios tossed a perfect throw to Hurwitz, taking it 52 yards to the house for a touchdown. Piedmont trailed 8-6 after coming up short on a two-point conversion. The rest of the first quarter remained scoreless with both teams were playing good defense. It wasn’t until late in the second quarter when Salesian marched Photo by JC Curran Returning sophomores Diego Hurwitz (left), Daniel King, Noah Hussian, and Colby Hong were named captains ahead of JV football’s season-opener against Salesian. their way to the four-yard line on a multiple-play drive with broken tackles, punching it into the end zone with a little over three minutes left in the half. The Pride went into halftime holding a 14-6 lead. Salesian’s 14-6 lead remained through the third quarter with back-and-forth possessions and fumbles for both sides. In the fourth quarter, inside freshman linebacker George Saunders recovered his third fumble of the game to put Piedmont in a great position in the Pride’s red zone. Piedmont took advantage, scoring their second touchdown on a pass from Lagios to tight end George Saunders. Now trailing 14-12, PHS was forced to go for a two-point conversion. They went right back to the man, Saunders, converting the two-point conversion and touchdown reception for a rare ‘octopus’. But it wasn’t yet over. In the waning minutes, Piedmont’s defense came through again when recovering another fumble in Salesian’s red zone. Unfortunately, a victory wasn’t in the cards for the Highlanders as time expired before PHS could get across the goal line. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-0-1) hosts Middletown on Friday, September 6 at Witter Field at 4:00 p.m. Colby Hong is a sophomore and a member of the Piedmont JV football team. There are an estimated 15,000 trees in El Retiro Park in Madrid. (Great Pond). The pond is 280 meters long, 140 meters wide, with restaurants along the edges, bands looking for tips, and boats in the water. Standing tall at the east edge of the Great Pond is the Monumento a Alfonso XII – the largest monument of the park at 30 meters high, 86 meters long, and 58 meters wide. At its center is the cast bronze equestrian statue of King Alfonso XII, who was the King of Spain from 1874-1885. You can find the Paterre Garden on the Western edge of the park. On the opposite side is the Cecilio Rodriguez Garden, where you will see peacocks walking around. On the southern edge is its famous rose garden, La Roseleda. In the center of the park just a short walk from the Great Pond are two museums, the Velasquez Palace, a museum of modern art which is free, and the magnificent Palacio de Cristal. Palacio de Cristal museum was undergoing renovations during our visit, and is one of the most popular sites of the park. This puts an end to our summer series of hiking trails. articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek will host a plein air workshop, where guests are invited to paint on garden grounds under the supervision of a local artist. Nancy Roberts, the Garden’s Artist in Residence this Fall will lead the outdoor workshop. A retired architect, she is a local professional artist, educator, arts community volunteer who exhibits her work in several Bay Area galleries. She organizes “paintouts” for the Contra Costa Plein Air group. Attendees will learn how to capture the shapes, colors and patterns on location with the versatile and expressive medium of acrylic paint. Roberts starts the workshop with a demonstration, then attendees will create their own painting with the instructors’ help and engagement. The workshop will be held on Wednesday, September 18, from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. Students are asked to bring their own portable easels and paint supplies. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ event/workshop-plein-air-in-thegarden/. Artist Nancy Roberts at work outside at Bancroft Gardens ®
articles.title: Bancroft Gardens hosts Plein Air workshop on Sept. 18

articles.text: SF Opera in Golden Gate Park celebrates SF Opera’s 101st season San Francisco Opera’s famous free performance in Golden Gate Park is this Sunday, September 8, featuring stars from the company’s 2024–25 season. “Opera in the Park,” is now in its 48th year and is presented by the opera company and by the San Francisco Chronicle. The free concert celebrates the opening of the San Francisco Opera season, and traditionally draws thousands of attendees annually for a free afternoon of arias, duets and popular songs at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. Featured vocal soloists include sopranos Julie Adams, Aleksandra Kurzak and Olivia Smith; mezzo-sopranos Hyona Kim and Daniela Mack; tenors Roberto Alagna, Arturo Chacón-Cruz and Moisés Salazar; baritone Brian Mulligan; and bass-baritone Jongwon Han. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the performances, with Company General Director Matthew Shilvock serving as emcee. A rendition of the brindisi (drinking song) from Giuseppe Verdi’s La Traviata traditionally ends this time-honored Bay Area tradition. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and their own food and beverages. Food trucks will also be onsite. The event is free and no tickets are required. Visit https://www. sfopera.com/seasons/opera-inthe-park/ to learn more. The event begins at 1:30 p.m.

articles.text: Unique event in Golden Gate Park is Sept. 13-22 San Francisco Botanical Garden will host its annual Flower Piano Lounge music series beginning September 13 in Golden Gate Park. This unique event merges botanical beauty and classical tunes against the backdrop of San Francisco’s most famous park. Flower Piano Lounge transforms San Francisco Botanical Garden into an alfresco concert hall where everyone is invited to play and listen. A dozen pianos will be placed across the 55-acre garden, inviting visitors to explore San Francisco’s collection of diverse plants and foliage while seeking out the hidden instruments’ location. Sunset Piano, which hosts the event in partnership with the Botanical Garden places grand pianos throughout the gardens where musicians can play. The event has enjoyed eight successful years of turnouts. A limited number of chairs, as well as lawn seating, are available. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets or folding chairs. For a full list of programming, visit https://gggp.org/flowerpiano/. Musicians and attendees play grand pianos placed throughout San Francisco Botanical Garden by Sunset Piano.

articles.text: Violist Darcy Rindt will lead Berkeley Symphony musicians in the opening concert of the season in the ongoing Chamber Music Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, September 29, at 4 p.m. Founded in 2012 by former Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel, the chamber music concerts have provided a balance to the symphonic concerts typically held at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley. The ensemble of violinists Emanuela Nikiforova and Sarah Elert, Rindt on viola, cellist Sephanie Wu, and Kymry Esainko on piano will perform a program of music that includes Piano Trio in G minor, Op. 17 by Clara Schumann, Concerto for Piano and Strings by Caroline Shaw, and Joaquin Turina’s Piano Quartet in A minor, Op. 67. Tickets are $128 for the series and $40 per concert. Tickets are available at http://www.berkeleysymphony.org. Darcy Rindt has a wide scope of musical interests and activViolist Darcy Rindt will lead the Berkeley Symphony & Friends chamber concert on September at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. ities, beginning with the usual classical orchestral and chamber music canon. She composed and arranged for her alternative string quartet, Squid Inc., has been a member of the singing/playing group “Real Vocal String Quartet,” performed at the Hollywood Bowl and in New York’s Central Park with Jazz Mafia, and toured the country with the musical, “Hamilton.” She currently serves as Executive Director of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra. articles.text: The wildly popular play Hamilton returns to San Francisco’s Orpheum Theatre this November with performances November 27 through January 5. The acclaimed musical by Lin-Manuel Miranda is based on the 2004 biography Alexander Hamilton by Ron Chernow. The sung-and-rapped musical tells the story of American founding father Alexander Hamilton. Miranda said he was inspired to write the musical through reading Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography about the man. The show draws heavily from pop, soul, hip-hop, and traditional-style show tunes. Hamilton received Tony Awards for Best Musical and Best Original Score, and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. The musical routinely receives positive and rave reviews in publications across the country. A review in The Economist summed up the response to Hamilton as “near-universal critical acclaim.” The musical is produced by Jeffrey Seller, Sander Jacobs, Jill Furman and The Public Theater. Visit www.broadwaysf.com for tickets and showtimes. The original cast of Hamilton on Broadway

articles.text: A tongue twisting dance tune from Brazil. A centuries old Korean folk song. An ode to pigeons from Zimbabwe. These were among the songs performed by World Harmony Chorus (WHC) at its most recent concert in June. All were sung in their original languages, in four-part harmony with no instrumentation sung by an enthusiastic, non-auditioned community chorus, many of whom were singing in a chorus for the first time. In the hands of any lesser director, this combination could be a recipe for disaster. But under Betsy Blakeslee’s masterful direction, a capacity audience at the Piedmont Center for the Arts thrilled to the diverse musical repertoire. The East Bay branch has been fortunate to have Betsy Blakeslee as its director for 16 years. World Harmony Chorus was founded in 1999 by Daniel Steinberg, who wanted to bring music-making into the lives of people who never thought they could sing. Twenty-five years later, WHC has branches in Palo Alto and Santa Cruz, directed by Steinberg, and in Berkeley, directed by Blakeslee. Steinberg arranges nearly all the music himself. Chorus members are sometimes bewildered at the beginning of the semester, but with patient teaching, over 100 amateur singers from around the Bay Area find joy in mastering the material and bringing the music to life. The fall semester starts Tuesday, October 1. The East Bay branch rehearses weekly on Tuesdays from 7:00-9:00 p.m. at the Berkeley Shambhala Meditation Center in in downtown Berkeley at 2288 Fulton Street. Arrive between 6:45-6:55 p.m. No auditions, no experience needed, no sight reading required. Musical adventures await for adults and children eight and above accompanied by a participating adult. For information, see https:// www.instantharmony.com/chorus.html. The fall semester for World Harmony Chorus starts Tuesday, October 1.
articles.title: Openings available in World Harmony Chorus

pages.text: Wednesday, September 4, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet Food for thought By Joseph Gold The inspiration came at the right time. It came in the person of a blonde Viking – perfect of form and personality, and a musical genius as well. This guy was generous, friendly and diplomatic, with perfectly timed humor. There was even a popular song about him - “Oleanna.” There were other popular musical super stars at the time. They played hundreds of concerts every year. Classical music was the thing that everyone wanted. But it was Ole Bull who became the most Americanized and did the most to bolster our national spirit. He gave the people what they wanted musically, and he The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet educated them at the same time. It was brilliant. This genius of the past is often ridiculed by the iconoclasts of today. Fortunately, a friend made an historical discovery which caused me to reevaluate some individuals, and Ole Bull is one of them. A Norwegian virtuoso violinist and composer (1810-1880), Bull did not have a huge repertoire as a violinist. He was happy to play the same pieces over and over again. The public didn’t mind, and they applauded vociferously. The thousands of dollars that he earned were given to charities around the world. What impresses me the most is that Ole Bull was one of the most deeply profound observers in the history of music. He was a violinist Sherlock Holmes. Every violinist would be advised to read his brilliant observations. Sadly, there is no recorded documentation of how he sounded. Generally speaking, artists of the past combined a brilliant technique with poetry to convey their art. Success today relies on speed, superficiality, and ridiculous stage deportment. I try to keep myself up-to-date musically. The pop music of the past was very interesting, and the artists of those days had very thorough musical training. Not so today. A musical example comes to mind. I was in a store the other day and listened to some music. The song was the usual type. As I listened, I noticed that the song had just one chord. It kept repeating over and over again… the same chord. Some people told me they like that song. Genius gives us food for thought. If we continue down the other road, we will have coprophagia. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, September 4, 2024 MOVIES FOR ADULTS By Chris Honoré Ready Player One, directed by Steven Spielberg, begs for exposition. In fact, it’s crammed full of stuff to comment on; the challenge is how to best sort it all out so that the commentary coheres on this one-dimensional page. First, the film is based on the best-selling Ernest Cline novel of the same title. Cline also partnered with Zak Penn to write the screenplay. Adapting Cline’s story for the screen, however, poses a problem because it is really two stories offered as one. Ready Player One (great title) opens with 18-year-old Wade Watts (Tye Sheridan) heading home. The year is 2045, the place is Columbus, Ohio, and Wade’s neighborhood is definitely not Spielberg’s archetypal burb, one with trimmed grass and affluent two-story houses. Housing is called “the stacks,” meaning towers of rusting RVs and mobile homes, placed precariously, one on top of the other. Wade lives in one and his hood looks like an overgrown junkyard, discarded detritus, and a warren of old cars and garbage. His reality is oppressive and seemingly hopeless. He is also without parents and living with a sketchy aunt and her boyfriend du jour. So it is no wonder that every chance Wade, who is part of what is referred to as the “missing milOlivia Cooke, Win Morisaki, Lena Waithe and Philip Zhao in Ready Player One Ready Player One lions,” literally and virtually goes missing into a reality known as the Oasis (Anthropocentric Sensory Immersive Simulation). It’s a virtual world of kaleidoscopic colors, avatars, a small cohort of friends, and a level of intensity that will likely never exist in his real dystopian world. The Oasis knows no limitations other than one’s imagination. It’s spectacular as well as a spectacle. And woven into the Oasis is an announced Easter Egg hunt, defined as three keys hidden by its late creator, James Haliday (Mark Rylance), somewhere in this virtual reality. The person/avatar who finds all three keys will inherit all the rights to the Oasis as well as Haliday’s half trillion-dollar fortune. Also in the hunt is Wade’s nemesis, Nolan Sorrento (Ben Mendelsohn), CEO of Innovative Online Industries, who wants ownership of the Oasis for commercial purposes. Its inherently positive construct is what attracts Wade, whose avatar is Parzival, the mythical seeker of the Holy Grail. So the race for the three keys is on. Most of the story will be spent in the Oasis with Parzival and a girl, Art3mis (Olivia Cooke), known in the real world as Samantha. Their interaction is far more compelling when it is set in the Oasis than those brief breaks back on the mean streets of the stacks. Or those moments spent with Wade in his narrow room when he’s hooked up to his virtual reality gear. Win Morisaki stars in Ready Player One Parzival, as we learn, is far more animated and cool than Wade, as portrayed by a somewhat flat Sheridan. Another example would be Art3mis, with her anomie eyes, lots of attitude, and spiky, multi-colored hair; she’s wonderful to watch and it’s clear why Parzival is attracted to her. Plus she fearlessly rides a very hot, red Shotaro Kaneda motorcycle. Parzival’s ride is a tricked out DeLorean, straight out of Back to the Future, the hit 80s blockbuster. Ready Player One is stuffed full of 80s pop culture artifacts and references. I found the Oasis and its multitude of characters appealing. The only downside was the writing. The plot, both virtual and real, was pretty thin, The narrative is held together by a series of vignettes: battles and races and chases all taking place for the most part in the Oasis. True, act three does take Wade/Parzival and Samantha/ Art3mis back to the real world for the finale (a prolonged chase) as well as the story’s denouement. It’s an uplifting ending; but the question is, will they stay there? Ready Player One. Directed by Steven Spielbrg. Starring Tye Sherman, Olivia Cooke, Ben Mendelsohn. 2 hrs., 20 min. Rated PG-13. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not at her part-time job or going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around that local, junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday!, he says), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is that classic and wondrous reveal (wonder is a thread that stitches this film together). As Charlie is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Pom Poka Pom Poka is a strange, convoluted film, perhaps best suited for older tweens, teens, and adults. And even then its audience may indeed be those who find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that for decades has been the signature of Studio Ghibli from Japan. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poka is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. The weakness of the film resides not with its art but in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine. They are thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog. These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting in which they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals. The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki on the outskirts of Tokyo is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes in 1990 when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the warlike chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous, but often lack focus. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. It’s a spectacle leading to a dour denouement which sums up what proves to be a not-family friendly fable. Pom Poko. Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahata. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. Released in 1994, Now streaming on prime/ MAX/apple tv/Fandango.

In every way, Bumblebee (an origin prequel) is not only redemptive, but resurrects that sweet spot mined by Shia LaBeof as Sam Witwicky, in the first Transformers when he negotiates with his dad for a car, He finds a hard-used, yellow Camaro on a lot and convinces his dad that this rusty ride works for him. And so, his adventure begins. Ditto Charlie Watson (Hailee Steinfeld), who is on the cusp of turning 18 and declares that, like Sam, all she wants is a car. Any car. After a brief lead-in segment where the Autobots/Optimus Prime and the Decepticons/Megatron are locked in a destructive battle on their home planet, Cybertron, the narrative shifts to 1987. The place is the San Francisco Bay Area. Charlie is grieving for her father who died two years before of a heart attack while they were restoring a vintage Corvette that still sits in the garage. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not at her part-time job or going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around that local, junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday!, he says), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is that classic and wondrous reveal (wonder is a thread that stitches this film together). As Charlie is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the See Bumblebee on page 31 Pom Poko – animation from Ghibli for older teens Hailee Steinfeld in Bumblebee A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Pom Poka By Chris Honoré Pom Poka is a strange, convoluted film, perhaps best suited for older tweens, teens, and adults. And even then its audience may indeed be those who find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that for decades has been the signature of Studio Ghibli from Japan. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poka is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. The weakness of the film resides not with its art but in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine. They are thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog. These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting in which they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals. The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki on the outskirts of Tokyo is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes in 1990 when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the warlike chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous, but often lack focus. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. It’s a spectacle leading to a dour denouement which sums up what proves to be a not-family friendly fable. Pom Poko. Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahata. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. Released in 1994, Now streaming on prime/ MAX/apple tv/Fandango. articles.text: A slice of a freshly baked Summer Fruits Cake Photos by Deborah Quok As summer wanes, so do my favorite summer fruit crops of peaches, nectarines and plums. This cake, which is pretty forgiving when it comes to making substitutions, is a brilliant showcase for perfectly ripe stone fruits. I appreciate the versatility of this cake: it can be dressed up for fancy presentation, or served simply to allow the fragrant fruit and tender cake to make a statement on their own. The other bonus for making this now is that many of these fruits are at seasonal low pricing from your local farmers markets. Summer Fruit Cake with Peaches and Nectarines Inspired by Marion Burros’ Original Plum Torte Makes one 9″ round cake INGREDIENTS • 1½ cups all-purpose flour • 1 teaspoon baking powder • ½ teaspoon baking soda • ¼ teaspoon salt • ½ cup granulated sugar • ½ cup unsalted butter, softened to room temperature • 2 eggs, room temperature • ½ cup whole milk yogurt, room temperature (substitute sour cream) • 3 medium peaches or nectarines, or large plums • 1 tablespoon lemon juice, freshly squeezed • 1 teaspoon lemon zest • ½ teaspoon cinnamon or ginger or “Dusk” Local Spicery blend • 1 tablespoon Turbinado sugar, or any coarse grind sugar • Additional butter for the pan remove the pit. Slice into about ⅓″ to ½″ thick wedges. Place in a medium sized bowl; add the lemon juice, lemon zest and spice. Stir gently to evenly coat the fruit. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, using a handheld electric mixer, cream the butter until smooth. Add the sugar and beat on medium until light and fluffy. Add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each. Add the vanilla. Add one-half of the flour mix, blend in slightly; then add one-half of the yogurt. Repeat with the remaining flour mix and yogurt, taking care to just mix thoroughly, but do not over beat the batter. The batter will be thick. Pour the batter into the prepared springform pan, leveling it with a spatula. Arrange the sliced fruit atop, avoiding too many overlapped pieces. It is okay if some batter is uncovered, where it will rise during baking. Bake for about one hour. Test doneness by inserting a toothpick into the center of the cake. If it comes out clean, or with a few dry crumbs clinging to it, the cake is ready. Remove and cool on a wire rack. After 10 minutes, remove the sides of the pan. It may be served slightly warm, or completely cooled. Finish with additional fresh fruit, or a dollop of whipped cream or vanilla ice cream. And if there is any left over – and good luck with that – it makes a delicious breakfast fare. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com Previously printed in the PiedINSTRUCTIONS: mont Post on September 6, 2017. Position an oven rack into the center of the oven, preheat oven to 350°F. Line the bottom of a 9-inch springform pan with parchment. Make sure the pan is securely fastened, then generously butter the sides of the pan. Set aside. Combine the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a small bowl. Set aside. Slice the fruit lengthwise and Summer Fruit Cake with Peaches and Nectarines

articles.text: If you’re an avid gardener, you know that growing your own food is just a gateway to raising egg laying hens. It was about this time last year when I brought home two fluffy little chicks. Now a year later, I have two sweet hens, Clucky and Ginger, who add so much enjoyment to my little backyard farm. Here are a few tips if you’re thinking of raising a flock of your own. First and foremost, keeping chickens is a community affair. While you may like the sound of a hen’s egg call in the morning, your neighbors might not. To keep the peace, propose your new plans to neighboring homes. This way you can ease any concerns before they begin and even persuade them with the promise of sharing your fresh egg bounty. The City of Piedmont currently allows backyard chicken keeping. However, to keep your chicken coop exempt from additional permits, you must keep the coop within your backyard, away from street view. They also require your coop to stay below five feet in height and have a combined footprint of one hundred square feet with any other with a fully protected chicken run made with hardware cloth so no stealthy predators have a chance of breaking in. Whether you bring home little chicks or full grown hens, let the utter enjoyment of chicken keeping begin. Not only are these birds full of personality, they also bring great benefits to your garden. Chickens love to eat many types of garden scraps as a supplement to their feed. Their droppings also make amazing fertilizer when fully composted. Nearly every morning you’ll be greeted with a farm fresh egg full of nutrients. But the best reason to get chickens is the companionship you’ll find in these charming pets. If you’d like to learn more about how we built a chicken coop from scratch and other backyard gardening tips, check out our Youtube channel, Girl And Her Dog Farm. articles.text: Remakes of old movies can be disappointing, but sometimes they’re terrific. Take the great comedy classic, Some Like It Hot, for example, which is a retooling of a 1930s German musical. Another irresistible remake is 1996’s The Birdcage, an American take on the French comedy hit, La Cage au Folles. No one is disappointed by the American version – they’re laughing too hard, and locals will get a chance to laugh, too, when the film is shown at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at the next Flix Fest. Directed by Mike Nichols from a screenplay by Elaine May (remember Nichols and May?), The Birdcage won a Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast. It stars Robin Williams and Nathan Lane as a gay couple whose son arrives at their Miami nightclub with the surprise announcement that he plans to marry soon. The problem is that his fiancee’s parents are an ultraconservative couple, deftly played by Gene Hackman and Diane Wiest. (If you’ve ever wanted to see Gene Hackman in drag, here’s your chance.) The Birdcage was released on March 8, 1996, to positive reviews and significant commercial success. It debuted at the top of the North American box office and stayed there for the following three weeks, grossing $185.3 million on a $31 million budget. It’s seen as groundbreaking, because it was one of few films from a major studio to feature LGBTQ characters at its center. The Birdcage will be screened on Thursday, September 12, at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the Rec. Dept. can be done at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. Piedmont Flix Fest movies are scheduled on the second Thursday of each month and are free. The next movie is the 2003 German comedy, Schultze Gets the Blues, to be shown on October 10.
articles.title: Robin Williams classic comes to Piedmont Sept. 12

articles.text: A new class at Piedmont Adult School, “Building Skills for Successful Family Research,” aims at helping aspiring family historians who want to learn about the lives of their ancestors. The class will focus on teaching foundational skills to identify relevant records and where to find them, documenting sources, and assessing record reliability. The course will consist of six classes plus optional field trips to the Oakland Family Search Library and the California Genealogical Society Library. The class will be taught by Pam Brett, who has been researching her own family history for the last 25 years. She has taught numerous classes for the California Genealogical Society and has traveled extensively to attend genealogical conferences and workshops and to conduct on-site research. “Many people have dabbled in genealogy,” says Brett, “but they often hit a brick wall or lose interest when results are slim. This class goes far beyond what you can accomplish on a genealogy website. Students will learn how to dig deep and uncover the inforInstructor Pam Brett’s ancestors came to America in colonial times and moved often, leading her toward research in 29 states and the District of Columbia. mation that really makes family histories come alive.” Are you interested in researching your family history, but not sure how to get started? Have you tried some genealogy websites, with unsatisfying results? Do you want to get off your computer and into the fascinating world of libraries, courthouses, archives and town halls? To register for this class and others, visit Piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655. Building Skills for Successful Family Research Instructor: Pam Brett 6 Wednesdays, Sept. 25 to Nov. 6 2 field trips - optional $360
articles.title: New Adult School class lets you explore family history

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group tries to get to every safe walking Piedmont street during the year, but they hadn’t been to some of the streets west and north of Dracena Park. This part of Piedmont, like a lot of Piedmont, was developed after the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake through the 1920s. The walkers thought it would be fun to see the streets and consider some of the homes on them. Zillow research of a random set provided when they were built, their sizes, and estimated selling prices. With information shared about the other homes, the walkers could have fun guessing its listing price. However, before the group started walking some background information was shared. In 2020, Piedmont’s population was 11,270 with 3,924 housing units according to Wikipedia. The median price of homes sold in the last 12 months was $2,550,000. The walkers went across Carmel Avenue to Blair and Ricardo Avenues for their first selected house to consider. Architect Jim Kellogg called it a “bungalow beauty,” a 3 bedroom/3 bath built in 1907 with an estimated value of $2.4 million. The next Ricardo house up the street (by coincidence) was Sharona and Jack Fischrup’s original clapboard brick exterior home of 33 years. Then it was over to Arroyo Avenue to York Drive and a 5 bedroom/3 bath house built in 1959 on rightof-way land made available when the Key System trains stopped running. Further up York was a 1922, 5 bedroom/7 bath being completely remodeled. The walkers went down Cambridge Way to Manor Drive for their last home before the actual “for sale” home and their guessing. This last one was built in 1915, has 3 bedrooms and 3.5 baths, and is worth 3 million according to Zillow. Finally they came to the house with a For Sale sign in the front yard. It is a Tudor style house with 2,521 square feet and was built in 1921. All the walkers fell for the flowery language and guessed more than the listing price of $2.295 million. Thankfully, no one had brought a checkbook. It was all in fun, but it was time for the walkers to make their return to the Exedra. They went back via Holly Place, a hidden 272-foot path from York to Ricardo, and then had a delightful walk through Dracena Park to Park Way, Hillside and Magnolia Avenues. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A record 49 walkers and three K-9 best friends showed up for the last Wednesday Walk of the summer on August 28. Among those participating were Sharona and Jack Fischrup, Denny McGee, Karin Fetherston, Charlene Louie, Nancy Henn, Mari Negron with K-9 best friend Dakota, Lisa Euphrat, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Peggy Shultz, Adrienne Hamlin, Martin Levy, Judy Sokoloff, Claudine Bach, Linda Peacock, Elizabeth Richter, Pat Keller, Dottie Hutch, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Nancy Olsen, Lois Price, Meghan Bennett, Larry Olsen, Mark Frost, Rick Eigenbrode, Pat Nicholas, Gloria DaSilva, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Angela Tom, Robert Lang, Gary Rogers, Melba Yee, Kat Lang, Garrett Clifford, Matt Gerhardt, Ken Hubbert, Brenda Ferrero, Chuck Oraftik, Greg Keller, Bill Ahern, Irene Thompson, Lori Rubens, Patsy Forsyth and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Eric Behrens brought his sister, Yvonne Behrens, who was visiting from Virginia.
articles.title: Wed. Walkers head to Ricardo neighborhood

articles.text: Dear Abby: What’s this doggy yap about a Pawsome Day for Dogs at the Giants? I’ve heard that I’ll get a free leash with the Giants logo if my parents take me. Is that fur real? And when is it? –Jennifer and Charlie the Frenchie Dear Jennifer and Charlie: Yes, It’s true. This year the Giants are hosting two Dog Days. The second one is on Saturday, September 28th at 1:05 against the feathery Cardinals. Come early and walk in the pawsome pre-game parade on the field. All furry costumes are welcome and some of the proceeds from your ticket purchase will benefit the SF SPCA. When you’re done barking, take a seat and cheer the Giants onto victory as they take on St. Louis. All dogs are welcome. If you get hungry your mom can always buy you a hot dog and you’ll receive a lovely orange Giants leash to show off to all your canine friends. Learn more at Dog Days at sfgiants.com. It’ll be a doggone good time. Lots of sniffs and howls. Go Giants! –Abby Dear Abby: I’ve seen a lot of mobile groomers in Piedmont. Do you have any opinions? It seems like a nice option for my Ulti-Mutt, but am I barking up the wrong tree? Woof. –Thug the Pug and Dad Dear Thug and Dad: I haven’t used any of the mobile groomers. I’ve seen a Groom Buggy van around town and Tiffany’s Mobile Grooming van too. When I’ve asked owners, they seem to be pleased with the results. We use a groomer near Park Boulevard. It used to be called Poodles ala Pamela and is now Elegant Grooming at 1310 Glenfield Avenue (Oakland 92602, tel. 510-612-5027). We have had excellent results, with fragrant fur as well as a very happy, clean dog. Drive to Park Blvd. and park near Marzano Restaurant. Our experience has always been great, the groomers are kind and it’s reasonably priced. We’ve had good luck, and grooming is good for the soul. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.
articles.title: Let’s talk about groomers, near and far

Students will learn how to dig deep and uncover the inforInstructor Pam Brett’s ancestors came to America in colonial times and moved often, leading her toward research in 29 states and the District of Columbia. mation that really makes family histories come alive.” Are you interested in researching your family history, but not sure how to get started? Have you tried some genealogy websites, with unsatisfying results? Do you want to get off your computer and into the fascinating world of libraries, courthouses, archives and town halls? To register for this class and others, visit Piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655. I’ve heard that I’ll get a free leash with the Giants logo if my parents take me. Is that fur real? And when is it? –Jennifer and Charlie the Frenchie Dear Jennifer and Charlie: Yes, It’s true. This year the Giants are hosting two Dog Days. The second one is on Saturday, September 28th at 1:05 against the feathery Cardinals. Come early and walk in the pawsome pre-game parade on the field. All furry costumes are welcome and some of the proceeds from your ticket purchase will benefit the SF SPCA. When you’re done barking, take a seat and cheer the Giants onto victory as they take on St. Louis. All dogs are welcome. If you get hungry your mom can always buy you a hot dog and you’ll receive a lovely orange Giants leash to show off to all your canine friends. Learn more at Dog Days at sfgiants.com. It’ll be a doggone good time. Lots of sniffs and howls. Go Giants! –Abby Dear Abby: I’ve seen a lot of mobile groomers in Piedmont. Do you have any opinions? It seems like a nice option for my Ulti-Mutt, but am I barking up the wrong tree? Woof. –Thug the Pug and Dad Dear Thug and Dad: I haven’t used any of the mobile groomers. I’ve seen a Groom Buggy van around town and Tiffany’s Mobile Grooming van too. When I’ve asked owners, they seem to be pleased with the results. We use a groomer near Park Boulevard. It used to be called Poodles ala Pamela and is now Elegant Grooming at 1310 Glenfield Avenue (Oakland 92602, tel. 510-612-5027). We have had excellent results, with fragrant fur as well as a very happy, clean dog. Drive to Park Blvd. and park near Marzano Restaurant. Our experience has always been great, the groomers are kind and it’s reasonably priced. We’ve had good luck, and grooming is good for the soul. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: It was an extraordinary day of community connection and celebration as local real estate agent Lisa Chan Carnazzo recently hosted not one but two neighborhood parties to welcome new residents to Piedmont. The festivities were made even sweeter with the addition of a Kona Ice truck, bringing joy and shaved ice to everyone who attended. The first stop of the day was on Fairview Avenue, where Carnazzo welcomed the Bowman family to their new home. The party was made all the more lively by the presence of Denise Fullerton, a former Berkeley High School teacher who now owns and operates the Kona Ice truck. Kona Ice isn’t just about fun. The company has given over $200 million to communities across the country. Fullerton shared, “I knew I wanted to retire but wanted to work in the community and schools, so this was a good way to do that.” The event on Fairview Avenue brought together long-time neighbors, friends of the home’s previous owners, and new faces, all bonding over shared stories Officer Tyler Petit, with Tam Thao Pham and realtor Lisa Chan Carnazzo Rory Tait Pham and Lydia Bowman, a new neighbor on Fairview Avenue and shaved ice. The celebrations continued on Ricardo Avenue, where the Torosean family was warmly welcomed to their new neighborhood. Neighbors shared stories of living there since the 1970s, while others newer to the community met fellow residents for the first time. “I always tell my clients when they move to Piedmont how amazing the Piedmont Police Department is,” said Carnazzo. “They not only respond to every call but always show up to my ‘Welcome to Piedmont parties.’” Officer Tyler Petit expressed his appreciation for the community. “What makes Piedmont so New Ricardo neighbors Noah and Arthur Torosean special is the people who work here. Everyone I work with has a passion to serve the community, and it’s nice to be part of this family. Having a community that backs us and makes this family is what makes it so special,” said Petit.

articles.text: Troop 11 Scouts just backpacked 35 miles through the Grand Canyon of the Tuolumne in Yosemite. On the first day, the backpackers began by descending 3,000 feet down the steep walls of the valley over the course of 12 slightly smoky miles. At the bottom, Scouts were met with their first view of the Tuolumne River and immediately everyone jumped in the water to cool off and to relieve their aching muscles. The next day, the group had a late start at 11 a.m. The Scouts hiked alongside the river where gorgeous pools and beautiful views of cliffs could be seen. After lunch, the crew decided to push on for a 1200-foot climb. It was well worth the effort because there were 40-foot waterfalls from a creek to swim under and incredible views of the canyon at the top. On the way up, Scouts Top row: Elles Kreickhaus (left), George Stein, Henry Stein, Sean McKee, Drew Kobal, Jack Shim, Oliver Amen, Colin Amen, Ted Eisemon, Justin Amen. Bottom row: Julie Stein (left), Rob Amen, Laura Amen, Jason Stein, Eric Eisemon Scouts carry all their gear for 35 miles. Playing in water slides Drew Kobal at LeConte falls spotted their first rattlesnakes of the trip. The hike on Thursday totaled eight miles and 1,500 feet of elevation. At the end of day, everyone was delighted to find a lovely campsite with what one Scout described as “some of the best natural water slides I’ve ever been on.” Slippery granite slabs sloping into a deep pool of water were the perfect combination for epic slides down the rocks. After a dinner of freeze dried food, the Scouts fell asleep under an unparalleled view of the stars and frequent meteors shooting by. Friday also included some epic scenery. Starting out it felt like hiking ln the middle of a desert, but it soon changed into a bug-infested rain forest. The crew escaped by hiking up a completely barren granite rock face, and then climbing under boulders the size of houses. Lunch was the pinnacle of the day. The Scouts found a perfect place to eat after their enormous climb. The spot was a wide section of the river that led into an incredible waterfall that cascaded down the same cliffs the crew had just hiked. But the climb was not over. Another 1000 feet had to be ascended before the group could pitch a campsite. The work did not go unrewarded. Incredible Troop 11 Scouts hike alongside the river. Swimming in a waterfall at a creek

Starting at 4:30 a.m. the next morning, the first hour was spent hiking by flashlight in complete darkness with rain pouring down. As the woods opened up to Tuolumne Meadows, the jagged peaks and magnificent domes of Yosemite could be seen. After a sleepy bus ride back to the start of the trail, the troop gathered at the trailhead where they met a few people about to hike the same route. articles.text: In recent years, KCOM’s coverage has largely been recordings of public meetings. The road to reviving and expanding KCOM has been a long one. In the past, city staff have had to deal with aged equipment which has required extensive maintenance and troubleshooting. This year the City Council has approved a budget that allows for crucial upgrades in equipment, including a new broadcasting system that will allow public meetings to be broadcast in high resolution. Additionally, the City has hired two new broadcast technicians, Richard Daniels and Dreu Towan, to assist with regular broadcasting by the station. Overall, Schneider believes that with the support of the community and City Council aligned, KCOM should have the support it needs to play a more important role in the city. “I’m very grateful for the council’s support for modernizing and upgrading the setup,” said Schneider. “It’s only going to pay dividends,” she stated. Applications are currently open for the new Video Communications Specialist / Television Station Manager role with the City of Piedmont. The position will pay between $98,000 and $117,000 depending on experience. Applications are due by this Friday, September 6. For more information about the position, contact Echa Schneider at eschneider@piedmont. ca.gov or call City Hall at 420- 3040. articles.text: Piedmont Post’s intern reporter and photographer, Sophie Hess, spent the final weeks of her summer vacation in a class taught by New York Times reporters and editors. The newspaper runs a Summer Academy for high school students, with dozens of areas of focus for budding journalists to explore. Along with 20 students from across the world, Hess enrolled in a course called “Writing About Food Culture in N.Y.C.” from July 7-19. Afterwards, back in Piedmont with some final hours left in summer vacation, the PHS senior generously shared her tales of exploration and some of the photos she captured. The course was focused as much about the Big Apple, and dorm life, as the title topic – how to write about food within the scope of culture. Most Summer Academy students bunked up in dorms at Fordham University near Lincoln Center in Manhattan. “I really love New York; It feels like what a city should feel like. It combined all the differPhotos by Sophie Hess Manhattenhenge, witnessed on July 12, when the sunset perfectly matches with a handful of streets in New York. articles.text: On Monday, August 19, City Council voted unanimously to approve a contract for $206,800 to restripe and resurface the Linda Beach pickleball courts despite a pending lawsuit filed by members of the surrounding neighborhood. Although the move has been warmly received by local pickleball players, neighbors involved in the lawsuit are troubled by what they see as a premature move by the City. “It seems unwise, at the very least,” said Richard Drury, an attorney who represents the neighbors. “If we win, the court is likely to rescind the project, and they’ll have to go back to the drawing board, which means they might spend $200,000 for nothing if they either have to stop the project, move it elsewhere or make significant changes.” “It seems like they’re really jumping the gun here,” he added. articles.text: Demolition began at the Shell Station on Monday, August 19, as teams from Shell Recharge moved forward with their plans for an electric vehicle hub on the corner of Grand and Wildwood. The gas pumps that served Piedmont vehicles for over 17 years have been removed, as have the metallic canopies that covered them. Excavators on-site have also begun to remove the asphalt paving to expose the fuel tanks below ground for removal, covering the site in a dusty mixture of concrete and dirt. “We’re going to keep going until it’s just dirt,” said Shane Moore, an operator with Central Valley Demolition, one of several companies scheduled to do work on the property. On September 9, a different company, Wayne Perry Construction, will begin removing the underground fuel storage tanks in a six-week project. Contractors are still waiting for a conditional use permit from Piedmont’s Building Dept. Once approved, it will allow workers to complete the demolition by removing the station building on site. This new demolition is intended to make way for the construction of a new electric vehicle hub from Shell Recharge. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief As the weather turns hotter and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. Even if you took these steps earlier this summer, it’s a good idea to do another round of clearing as fall nears. The East Bay hills have seen significant wildfires throughout September and October multiple times in the last 150 years. Those events and recent wildfires across California have taught us that our communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, an action that helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. You can do your part and increase your own home’s chance of surviving a wildfire by taking a few simple protective measures in your yard every year. Please make time in the next few weeks to prepare your property with the following: Create space between plants and your home Remove branches that hang over your roof or are within 10 feet of your chimney. Prune plants away from buildings. This buffer area will help protect your house and give firefighters an area to work in to defend your home during a fire. Create space between plants Trim trees so the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground or three times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. This helps prevent fire from moving from the ground to the treetops, where it can spread more quickly. Clear debris and flammable materials Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your yard. Clear leaves and pine needles from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove flammable materials, such as paint or propane containers from under decks and away from buildings. Trim plants of any dead or dying material It’s important to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Remove any dead or dying vegetation. If you have eucalyptus trees in your yard, remove any shedding bark or leaves. Download a checklist for preparing your yard at piedmont. ca.gov/YardChecklist. For more information and links to additional resources on preparing your property for fire season, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ vegetation. If you need help identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Fire Department at (510) 420-3030 to request an inspection. PREPARE YOUR YARD FOR FIRE SEASON The best practice in vegetation management is to remove all vegetation within five feet of your home. Even if this is not currently feasible for you, taking protective measures in your yard will increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire and reduce risk to our whole community. Use this checklist to prepare your yard. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! articles.text: The 23rd Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will take place in Piedmont Main Park on Sunday, September 22, with musicians performing on a stage near the Piedmont Community Center. The city-sponsored event will take place in conjunction with the annual Piedmont Harvest Festival. The Jazz Festival will make full use of Piedmont’s wide musical talent. This year’s event will include the first appearance by Piedmont High School Music Director Trevor Meseroll conducting the PHS Jazz Band. The audience will also be treated to the rocking rhythms of the Puckett Family Project, the solo guitar stylings of Carlos Caminos, and the sultry tango of Molinette. This year a watermelon eating contest will be held between sets that should add to the energy of the event. For information contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@yahoo.com. 11:00 – 12:00 12:00 – 1:00 1:00 – 1:30 1:30 – 2:15 2:15 – 3:00 Molinette

Much of the damage, he explained, has been caused by nearby trees whose roots have grown under the court, causing cracks and uneven playing surfaces. Gonzales added that his department “never likes removing trees,” but that in some situations it is unavoidable. The project was awarded to Vintage Contractors Inc. who also did the Corey Reich tennis court surfaces in 2019. Gonzales estimates work will begin in late September. “The agreement allows up to 10 weeks for construction and I believe that finishing the project around Thanksgiving is realistic,” he said. Ongoing Controversy This vote by City Council is the latest in an ongoing controversy between City Hall and the neighbors of the Linda Beach courts. Since 2018 when the Walnut Creek Pickleball Club held a demonstration for the Piedmont Recreation Department, the sport’s popularity has taken off in Piedmont and efforts have been mounting to accommodate the number of new players that the city now has. From February through July 2023, the Piedmont Recreation Commission held a trial of fulltime pickleball play at the Linda Neighbors like Chris Free, who lives near the courts, attended the City Council meeting to voice their opposition to the development of the courts as full-time Pickleball courts. Staff Photos The Linda Beach Courts have sparked controversy once again as the city council approves a $200,000 contract to renovate the courts ahead of a pending lawsuit. Beach tennis courts to gauge if it would be a suitable candidate for pickleball usage. During this time, multiple complaints were registered by members of the surrounding neighborhood about matches taking place outside of scheduled hours. Neighbors sent several letters to City Council and reported several noise complaints to the Piedmont Police Department. In August 2023, the City created a series of “working groups” of neighbors and pickleball players to resolve complaints about unreasonable noise at the courts. The meetings were mediated by City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore and Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. The talks fell apart after two meetings. In October 2023 a group of residents filed a lawsuit against the City claiming that the City unlawfully violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The residents are currently seeking an injunction to stop the development of the courts as full-time pickleball courts. Community reacts In anticipation of the vote, the city council meeting was attended by both supporters and opponents of the Linda Beach pickleball courts who were keen to voice their opinions. “It seems to me that it’s not economically responsible to proceed with spending approximately $200,000 on a court renovation for permanent pickleball when there are outstanding lawsuits present,” said Brian Kotlyar, who lives above the courts on Sunnyside Avenue. “This process has been long and thorough to get to this item before you tonight…The end result is that a previously little-used space is now joyously used by many for the betterment of the entire community,” said Rick Schiller. As a matter of policy, the City of Piedmont does not comment on pending litigation. articles.text: Camp Augusta will host its annual Wish, Wonder & Wine fundraiser on Saturday, September 21 from 5:00-7:00 p.m. in the courtyard at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Tickets are $50 and are available at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/wish-wonderand-wine-tickets-945283286757 ?aff=oddtdtcreator. As school begins, keep an eye out for the cornflower blue shirts around town worn by the hundreds of Piedmont children who attended Camp Augusta this summer. They may not know it, but they are continuing a long tradition in the community. You are invited to learn more about this special place that so many children call home each summer. Join us on September 21st for Wish, Wonder & Wine, an adult evening of fun in Piedmont. Enjoy wine, appetizers, and auction prizes while building community in support of Camp Augusta. You’ll hear from staff and campers with exciting updates from this summer, including the hugely popular new ropes challenge course. Camp offers amazing programming and some of the highest trained camp staff in the world to run the program. Help us meet our goal of upgrading our staff housing and to kick off a two-year capital campaign to replace those structures and the Cedar Bath house. Piedmont History Camp Augusta was originally donated to the girls of Piedmont almost 100 years ago. In the early years, the camp’s main use was by the Piedmont Council of Camp Fire. Virtually all the young Piedmont women spent their summers at the camp. After the site was shuttered by the Camp Fire organization, a group of dedicated Piedmonters formed an oversight board and began the long legal battle to win the property back for the children of Piedmont. While the site sat dormant for decades, the facilities fell into disrepair. However, with hard work and the support of the community, the 90 acre facility located in the beautiful forested foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains has received a variety of improvements over the years: the restoration of the original Lodge where campers hang out in aerial silks; a kitchen where our chefs cook delicious organic food that campers get excited about (have you ever tried Australian pizza with bananas on top!?); and this year’s incredible new high ropes challenge course with over 40 elements to ascend. We hope to see you at Wish, Wonder and Wine. Can’t make the event in person? Please consider making a contribution to support our efforts at www.campaugusta.org/gifts. articles.text: With another three days left in the month of August, Piedmont High School is halfway through its third week of class. The 2024-25 instructional year comes to life as teachers, administrators and students continue to start the new year. articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team is back for the second year and first time with Witter Field as its home field. Their 15-game regular season schedule gets starts tonight, August 28, hosting Las Lomas under the lights at 7:30 p.m. Piedmont played Foothill of Pleasanton last Friday, August 23 in a preseason scrimmage. Final results of scrimmages cannot be reported, but Piedmont had its bright moments after a slow start. With only a couple of weeks of practice, head coach Beth Black knew it would take a little to get rolling. “We’re back at it. That was our first Friday Night Lights on Witter Field – that’s something to be proud of. We are two weeks in and knew it was going to be a learning experience. We threw an interception, and thought will their confidence break? It didn’t. and they knew it was working,” Black said. Returning players include a group of playmakers led by receivers Miya Fujimoto and Dorothy Nemeth, both of whom earned second-team honors last season. Mary Schickedanz recorded an interception in the scrimmage and Ella Yasar is another defensive returner. “Mary Schickedanz is bringStaff Photos Piedmont High’s flag football team embarks on its second season. They will play a schedule of 15 games, starting tonight against Las Lomas at Witter Field. ing a lot of positivity and helping out on defense. She’s strengthened by Ella as well. On offense, we have Dorothy Nemeth and Miya. She’s really sharp and a playmaker with the ball” Black said. Playing on offense and defense will be junior Dahlia Osman, who we named as one of last year’s breakout stars after emerging as a key cornerback in defense. Osman made a long touchdown reception in Friday’s scrimmage against Foothill. She grabbed a pass in traffic, catching the ball at its high-point despite being one of the shorter players on the team. It was a moment similar to a few of Photo by Sophie Hess Dahlia Osman takes off on a touchdown reception in Piedmont’s recent scrimmage with Foothill. Staff Photos Miya Fujimoto earned All-League honors last season as a receiver. her interceptions in 2023. “It’s nice to see Dahlia get time on both sides of the ball this year. We kept her on defense last year and had her involved on a few plays on offense. This year, we told her she’s playing both sides. She has the energy, the grit, can catch, and its beautiful to watch,” Black said. This year marks the first time the North Coast Section offers a postseason for the sport. There are currently no divisions set for all 54 schools competing in NCS, and 16 schools are eligible to qualify for a playoff tournament. Piedmont’s league, the Western Alameda County Conference, goes into 2024 with some alterations. They’ve split the 10 teams into two divisions. PHS will compete in the North Division with Alameda, Berkeley, Encinal, and San Leandro. Instead of a season-end jamboree, the WACC Tournament will follow a more traditional format with brackets. The first round of WACC playoffs start on October 28, with finals scheduled for Saturday, November 2 at Burrell Field in San Leandro. Without former athletic director and offensive coordinator Bradley Smet helping coach the flag football team this year, Black has brought on two new assistants Reggie Smith and Lauren Dutton. Last year’s assistant, Hayley Adams, is also back in the fold. “Lauren Dutton is a Piedmont resident and believes in women’s sports. Both of her boys graduates from Piedmont, she’s a great force for the girls. Reggie comes in with flag football experience, having worked with East Bay Flag Football. He brings great knowledge,” Black said. PHS finished 4-6 overall last year and fourth-place in the WACC. They fought down to the end, entering the league tournament as the fourth seeded school. They opened with a nail-biting one-point 13-12 loss to top-seed Berkeley, while they fell 22-6 to third- seed San Leandro in the battle for third place. In the previous round against Berkeley, the Highlanders rallied from a 13-0 deficit to make it 13-12 with 36 seconds left in the game, but fell short on its 1-point conversion. “This year it’s not that the newness has worn off. They are athletes who are going to come out and represent their school. You can see the difference in that already,” Black said.
articles.title: Flag Football back for its second season

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team returns for its 2024 season fresh off winning last year’s Division 2 North Coast Section title. – even without a pool in town. With a senior-heavy roster in 2023 comes change, meaning PHS will have a new cast of starters for the upcoming season. “It’s a new team and new challenges. It’s a new team, but the guys who are filling in have been with the program for years. We have some seniors and juniors who were key elements in the last few years. They know exactly what we do; the quality of polo I’m seeing in practice is still very high,” said coach Rik Krumins. Last year, Piedmont reached the North Coast Section finals for the first time in school history after making back-to-back semifinals appearances. They upset No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals, marking their first win over the Wildcats. In the Finals on November 11, PHS defeated league rival No. 3 Alameda 10-8 on their way to the title. Declan Linnane and Peter Krumins graduated and ere named by the Post as honorable mention for 2024 Athlete of the Year. Piedmont will need to replace them and classmates George Stein, Finn Burke, Quincy Scherman, Burke, Daniel Banin, Spencer Barlow, and Evan Dickason. But returning to the fold is goalie Luke McAuliffe, who we named as Sophomore of the Year after emerging as a starter. He provides defensive stability and insurance. “Luke is a huge player for us; he came into that starting role by the end of last season and that’s continuing this year. Goalies are so important in every sport, but especially water polo. We’re looking at him as a captain this year, we’re hoping he can lead and command that defensive role. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, August 28, 2024 Sports Flag Football back for its second season By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s flag football team is back for the second year and first time with Witter Field as its home field. That was our first Friday Night Lights on Witter Field – that’s something to be proud of. We are two weeks in and knew it was going to be a learning experience. Returning players include a group of playmakers led by receivers Miya Fujimoto and Dorothy Nemeth, both of whom earned second-team honors last season.
