articles.text: The newly launched non-profit group, the Piedmont Gridiron Club, looks to foster the growth of Piedmont High School football. Two years ago there was real concern about the future of football at Piedmont High School. Covid had scared of many families, and signups for the sports were at an all-time low. But now in 2024, there’s a different energy in the program as they return to a full-time program intent on winning championships. The newly created non-profit Piedmont Gridiron Club aims to sustain the return to glory of Piedmont football. “We’re hoping this gives our players the support they need,” said Greg Dietrick, the Gridiron Club co-founder and president, “The last few years have been really challenging. For a while, it felt like the community just wasn’t with us and there were constant challenges. “Now, it feels like the community is behind us. This is about building the culture, keeping the Piedmont community interested in football, and we feel it’s going to snowball. We had a lot of success last year, we’re winning. Having the PGC will give that little extra something to the kids,” he added. “We had a really good season last year,” said co-founder Roderick Alemania, “We were asking ourselves how we can avoid being a one-trick pony and how we could emulate nearby programs. Our mission is to grow and foster both football and girls’ flag football. It’s not just about the boys; several parents have kids on both teams. When you look at where football and flag football is going, there are real college opportunities.” A common thread among successful football schools like Acalanes, Campolindo, and Miramonte is that each of them have groups dedicated to funding its football programs. As an assistant coach for Piedmont’s Junior Varsity team and got a first-hand look at operations. “Throughout all of last year, I was doing research on other schools. I looked at schools primarily across the tunnel like Acalanes, Campo and Miramonte because they were similar communities, albeit bigger schools than us. I found what they all had in common was a football-only boosters club. After a year with the program, I had a good sense of what the program needed from a resources perspective,” Dietrick described. Coming out of the pandemic, PHS finished 2021 at 2-7 with a roster that fluctuated between 15-19 available players. The following season in 2022, depleted roster issues continued, leading to the varsity program shuttering for the first time in the school’s 100-plus year history. But since then, Piedmont won the 2023 WACC Shoreline title, earning a promotion to the WACC Mission division for the upcoming 2024 season. Dietrick has kids at Piedmont Middle School. He remembers visiting a Piedmont High football game around 12 years ago. “We were living in San Francisco and we were picking towns where we wanted to live. My wife wanted to move to Piedmont and the first thing I did was go to a Friday Night Lights game, it was awesome. I found there’s a nice community that supports its football program, which is something I never had growing up until I got to college. When the football program started dying, I thought, ‘Oh no.’ This was one of the reasons I moved here. Fast forward years later, both of my sons are very interested in football, and I started getting worried about whether we would have a team. It started the discussion on how we were going to get football back to its stronger days,” Dietrick said. His visit clearly left a lasting impression. In fact, 12 years ago was around the start of Piedmont football’s heyday following the close of Kurt Bryan’s A-11 offense from 2006-2010. From 2013-2017, Piedmont never finished with a losing record. In 2014 under Scott Coats, PHS went 12-1 overall, reached the Division 4 NCS Semifinals, and won the Shoreline’s championship. 2014 has remained the Highlanders’ peak over the last decade. James Holan took the reins from 2015-2017 after serving as Coats’ offensive coordinator. In 2015, Piedmont went 9-3, reached the quarterfinals of the D4 NCS playoffs and won its second-consecutive Shoreline title, which earned them a promotion to the Foothill Division, where they resided until 2021. In 2016, Piedmont went 8-5 and made the semifinals of the D4 playoffs, falling to No. 1 seed Cardinal Newman. In Holan’s final year in 2017, PHS went 7-5 and reached the quarterfinals of the D4 playoffs before losing to No. 3 Harker in San Jose. PHS promoted former offenStaff Photos sive coordinator John Trotman to head coach in 2018, finishing 5-6. They went 3-7 the following season under Jerome Johnson with a cast of players called up from JV, Ut was the start of a decreasing interest in football. Johnson’s team returned from the pandemic in the spring of 2021 and went perfect, 5-0, in its shortened season. However, the team suffered from low roster turnout, which led canceling JV. The following fall season, the downfall of football began until winning the Shoreline title under Jordan Seiden in his second year at the school. Now, there is a renewed spark of interest in the longest running sport at the school with extra support from the coaches. Offensive and defensive line coaches, Po and Oski Fotu-Tauaho, spend the entire offseason hosting weekly lifting sessions and building a new football culture. The Gridiron Club helps compensate coaches for the extra time and effort they’ve given to PHS student-athletes. “Our two line coaches are showing up at 6am four days a week out of the kindness of their hearts. We ultimately want to pay all our coaches for the work they do over the offseason when there is no stipend,” Dietrick explained. Dietrick and Alemania hope the Piedmont Gridiron Club will continue promoting and building the sport because in high school sports, there is nothing quite like Friday Night Lights. “We decided the values should be focused around youth development; not just high school youth, but grade school and middle school. Friday Night Lights is such an amazing community experience, not just for the football. It’s an opportunity to get the community together and to build pride in Piedmont and playing for your school,” Alemania said. Dietrick will remain a part of the Piedmont Gridiron Club with his kids reaching PHS in the near future. Like many parents, Alemania will watch his son, Jordan, graduate with the Class of 2025. With the Gridiron Club entering its early days, the two are working to bring more parents into the fold to ensure PHS football continues to shine as bright in the future as it does going into the 2024 season. For more information on the Piedmont Gridiron Club, reach out to Greg at Dietrick@gmail. com and Roderick at Ralemania@gmail.com.

articles.text: For the second consecutive Piedmont High School is searching for a head coach for its highly successful boys’ lacrosse team. Last year’s coach, Jeff Lamb, had to leave after moving to the East Coast. The school is looking for a tested coach who can capture the team’ glory years as a powerhouse in the Western Alameda County Conference, Lamb took over in difficult circumstances for PHS last spring after former head coach Al Yu left the job following the 2023 D2 NCS Finals and six straight WACC titles. An online records search shows that the school never prepared for Yu’s departure, and didn’t post the job on Edjoin.com until November. With a lack of available lacrosse coaches in the area, Piedmont parents scrambled to find Lamb just weeks before the season started. Lamb came to PHS as a firsttime head coach of a varsity program. His only coaching experience was in 2011-2012 as an assistant high school coach after he graduated from Georgetown University. After the job was posted in November, Lamb was officially hired in late-January. Piedmont’s season started just weeks later in February. It was an abrupt and accelerated timeline that left the 2024 team going into its season in a precarious position. PHS still had early success with a six-game winning streak as a new Div. 1 team, but their record dropped to 8-6 by season’s end. It marked the conclusion of an illustrious sixyear run as the WACC’s best team. They finished third in the league for the first time ever, including the school’s first-ever loss to Berkeley, and were beaten by arch rival Bishop O’Dowd in the regular season and first round of the league tournament. Berkeley won it’s first-ever league title; the noise from the Yellowjackets and Dragons’ sidelines was deafening, knowing they have finally turned the tide against the mighty Highlanders’ lacrosse team. Prior to the spring of 2024, the team carried the torch as the school’s most successful program in the WACC. The end of the 2023 marked an official close to the coaching tree that spawned six league titles, the 2019 D2 NCS title, and another NCS finals appearance. Following the 2023 NCS Finals, Yu and assistant coaches David Hafner and Matt Palasek all announced they were departing the school. Yu took a job as a commercial airlines pilot, Hafner moved out of the area, and Palasek accepted a coaching job at Casa Grande closer to his home in Petaluma. Yu was notably brought into Piedmont by former head coach Ryan Price, who the Highlanders hired away from Bishop O’Dowd in 2018. Price notably led PHS to the D2 NCS title in 2019, where the Highlanders defeated Novato 11-6. Price later lured Yu away from O’Dowd in 2021 as an assistant before Yu took over in 2022. Piedmont’s success at the top of WACC began in 2017 under Tim Booth. Price helped win league titles in 2018 and 2019 prior to the pandemic and then won the shortened 2021 post-pandemic season with a 9-8 overtime title win over the Dragons. Yu led PHS to the 2022 WACC title as the underdog, beating O’Dowd 10-9 as the second-seed after losing to BOD in the regular season. Then in 2023, PHS dominated Bishop O’Dowd 14-6 for another WACC title, including an 18-1 regular season win over the Oakland school for the most onesided win in the rivalry’s history. This year, Piedmont posted the job in June, giving ample time for the school to find a qualified candidate. Former coach Jeff Lamb departs from the school after a tumultuous 2024 season. Staff Photos PHS won a pair of WACC titles and made an NCS Finals appearance under coach Al Yu during his stint as head coach in 2022-2023.
articles.title: Can PHS capture its past glory as successful team?

DARCY MCKEE Soccer, Track & Field Photo by Scott Stratman Piedmont High Class of 2026 Darcy McKee is a junior and a two-sport athlete. She competes on soccer in the winter season and also plays on a club team. In the spring, McKee competes on PHS’ track and field team as a sprinter and jumper. McKee earned a role on the PHS soccer team last winter as a sophomore and first-year varsity athlete. As a center back, McKee helped Piedmont go 12-4-2 (W-TL) and reach the second round of the D3 North Coast Section playoffs. As the No. 7 seed, PHS defeated No. 10 College Prep 6-0 in the opening round, but lost to No. 2 Cardinal Newman 2-0 in Santa Rosa. In track, McKee qualified for the NCS Bayshore meet in the 100 meters and high jump. She clocked a 13.26 in the 100 and placed 12th of 20 in the high jump. She was 10th of 46 in the 100 at the WACC Championship in 13.57, and was sixth of 13 in the high jump. What is your workout program this summer? During the summer, I jogged or sprinted on a daily basis. I also did some biking and injury prevention exercises. What are your fitness goals for the summer? articles.text: Piedmont Council’s four Cub Scout Packs are welcoming new youth to join this fall. Cub Scouts is Scouting America’s program for youth in Kindergarten through 5th Grade. Parents and youth are invited to visit the Packs at their first meeting of the year. These meetings are an opportunity to see what a typical meeting is like, learn about the Pack, their regular activities, and meet the Pack members and leadership. Campers at Cub Scout Day Camp enjoy a water balloon buddy toss. Scouts assist in Piedmont’s annual 4th of July parade as flagbearers. Piedmont Scouting delivers a unique program that encourages youth expression, promotes character building, and gets youth to share experiences outdoors. “I love that Cub Scouts is open to any child from anywhere and of any ability,” said Pack 4 Cubmaster Brad Cardon. “All that is required is an open mind, a sense of adventure, and to embrace the Cub Scout Motto: ‘Do Your Best.’” The beginning of the school year is also a great time to start with a Scout Troop, the Piedmont Community Service Crew, or the Piedmont Service Club for middle school students. “Scouting programs offer the chance to build social connections for both youth and their parents,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “As youth get older, they have opportunities for leadership and character development that can give them an edge as they prepare to launch into adulthood.” Families interested in joining Scouting programs are encouraged to contact Piedmont’s District Executive Eris Turner for more information at eturner@ piedmontbsa.org or 510-844- 4752. Additionally, you can visit the webpage at www.piedmontbsa.org, or visit the Piedmont Scout Office at 10 Highland Way in Piedmont. articles.text: Jaz Kalman The beginning of the school year has arrived! At Mountain Music, a Piedmont family-owned business, our mission is to make music and its benefits accessible to our community. Benefits of music have been well researched and include better communication skills, outlet for emotional release, decreased anxiety, improved cognitive function and mental health, and connections to others. Music is a great creative outlet as students navigate academic and social challenges. Listening to and playing music provides an opportunity for self-expression. Playing a musical instrument has been shown to lower cortisol levels and decrease anxiety levels. Creating music involves a sense of camaraderie, as music is a collaborative endeavor. Teacher-student interactions and learning a piece with peers teaches how to work together towards a common goal, gaining skills to connect with those around us. Collaboration is a significant life skill needed as our students move through college, the workplace, and personal relationships. A local hub for learning music provides an opportunity to be a part of their community, introducing them to other students who share the same passions. Studies have linked early participation in music and increased grades in high school exam scores in English, mathematics and science, including exhibiting higher executive function supporting increased academic achievement. Learning music and theory supports skill sets such as memorization, interpretation and improvisation, building blocks of higher learning. We find the benefits of music to be crucial in students’ lives, and strive to meet the needs of our community. With one child through Piedmont schools and one in high school, we see the benefits of art, music, theater and creative outlets in tandem with STEM, an opportunity for our children to experience and discover their strengths. Among our many services, we offer individual and group music lessons for a wide variety of instruments, both in-person and online, and have a stage for practice or performance. We rent instruments to individuMusic is a great creative outlet as students navigate academic and social challenges. als and those in band along with our sister-store: Rockin’ Robbie’s. It is our mission to make the benefits of music accessible for our local students, all family members and our community at large! Mountain Music can help your child with music lessons. They are located at 4444 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland, and can be reached at (510) 655-2263 and online at mountainmusicstore.com. Register for our 2024-25 season today! articles.text: Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year, we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 – Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble, but setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel? Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: – “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” – “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 – Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: – “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” – “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 – Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes - congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s ok. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. This process of checking in with yourself is especially helpful during times of transition and can help you feel empowered to grow not only as a student but as a person! pages.text: 18 Wednesday, August 28, 2024 Back to School in Piedmont By Emily Thompson and Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year, we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 – Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble, but setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel? Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: Feeling empowered in new school year – “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” – “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 – Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: – “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” – “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 – Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes - congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s ok. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. This process of checking in with yourself is especially helpful during times of transition and can help you feel empowered to grow not only as a student but as a person! Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of College Counseling and Emily Thompson is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel has worked in undergraduate admissions at both public and private universities. For more information, please visit www.studysmarter.com, email info@studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Where Challenge Meets Balance Bentley School is an intellectually curious and inclusive K–12 community where teachers embrace the strengths of every student, helping them rise to their full potential by cultivating their unique talents and perspectives. Our students are prepared for success throughout their lives over the course of an enriching educational journey that balances the importance of academic achievement, personal growth, and self-advocacy. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s exhibition !!!!! ends this Sunday, September 1. The exhibition features artwork by British visual artist and painter Rachel Jones, who is known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. Jones graduated in 2013 from the Glasgow School of Art and earned a Masters in Fine Art degree at the Royal Academy in London in 2019. Recent solo exhibitions include the Long Museum, Shanghai, China (2023) and the Chisenhale Gallery, London (2022). This is the first solo museum exhibition for Jones in the United States. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. The artist said she is “using motifs and color as a way to communicate ideas about the interiority of Black bodies and their lived experience.” For more information, and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/rachel-jones. articles.text: Sophia Alawi is cast as the titular character in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Evita. The Tony-award winning musical Evita is being performed on the San Francisco Playhouse stage now through Saturday, September 7. Originally directed by Harold Prince with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, the award-winning show chronicles young and ambitious Eva Perón’s rise from poor illegitimate child to the most powerful woman in Latin America. The play is narrated through the lens of Marxist revolutionary Che Guevara and recounts the story of Argentina’s matriarch Evita as she rallies the heart of a nation to bring about a new era in Argentine history. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English said he selected Evita for the 2023-24 season because “I knew it was going to be an election year in the U.S. and [that] democracy was certain to be on the line.” “I thought, wouldn’t it be interesting to look at another time and place where a very charismatic populist leader rose up with his incredibly charismatic, popular wife to be elected to office and then, at least as the musical and some historical narratives say, began to dismantle essential elements of democracy,” English said. Sophia Alawi is cast as Eva Peron with supporting roles by Jurä Davis, Peter Gregus, Alex Rodriguez, Albert Hodge and Chanel Tilghman. Evita is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through September 7. The venue is located at 450 Post Street, in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. The show is on stage six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2023- 2024-season/evita/ or call the box office at (415) 677-9596.

The San Francisco Symphony opening gala is Wednesday, September 25 and features pianist Lang Lang and Gina Alice performing with the symphony. The internationally-renowned pianist couple take the stage with conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen and the San Francisco Symphony in a celebratory program that includes Saint-Saëns’s Piano Concerto No. 2 and Carnival of the Animals. Born in Liaoning, China in 1982, Lang Lang gained international fame as a pianist through the 1990s. He has performed with major orchestras around the world and was the first Chinese pianist to be engaged with the Berlin Philharmonic, the Vienna Philharmonic and many top American orchestras. Pianist Lang Lang will perform with the San Francisco Symphony on September 25.

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is bringing the museum into your home with weekly, docent-led conversations about exhibitions and permanent collections. The weekly online offering, entitled “Takeout Tuesdays,” connects museum staff with fellow art lovers for interactive lunchtime encounters. Attendees gather on Zoom to observe compelling works using high-resolution images and learn more about artwork from experts at the museum. Guests are encouraged to “unmute” and join the conversation. Each weekly session explores a different topic. The next online session will be held from 12 p.m. to 1 p.m., and will be led by museum docent Etsuko Kobata, who will explore “The Tale of Genji.” Tickets are free. Visit https:// calendar.asianart.org/event/takeout-tuesday-whose-story-thetale-of-genji-sep-10/?_ ga=2. 92149471.457280938.1724524478- 1241342650.1724344952 to reserve your spot.

articles.text: Mads Mikkelsen in Arctic Arctic is a quietly intense yet deliberately measured story of survival and self-reliance. It is set against an unforgiving environment – an enveloping arctic landscape, a stretching snowy white that surrounds a downed single-engine plane that has crashed, intact, its nose scorched, the prop bent. In the opening scene, a man emerges from the fuselage and walks across a flat field of ice and snow to check several fishing lines dropped into ice holes. There is not a hint of backstory regarding who he is or what happened to the plane. He does wear a heavy red parka with the name Overgard on the front, but that could be the name of a company. Clearly, he survived uninjured. Who else was on board, if anyone, is unknown. What is evident is he is alone, surrounded by a penetrating silence that is complete, except for the crunch of snow when he walks from the plane, or the howl of the wind as a storm sweeps through. It appears as if Overgard has been there for some time. Perhaps several months. His face is wind burned and hidden behind a heavy beard. The interior of the plane – it’s a long, rectangular cabin – has been well organized. He has a jury-rigged bed, a down sleeping bag, his parka is weathered and soiled. He also has a few utensils, a knife to filet the fish that he catches and eats raw, and endless amount of melted snow. He’s also dug a massive SOS in the snow near the plane. Part of his daily ritual is to hike to the crest of a nearby hill bringing with him a hand-cranked box that sends out a GPS signal to anyone searching. And then abruptly everything changes. As Overgard is preparing to clean one of his fish, gusts of wind blowing around him, he hears and then sees a helicopter coming over a ridge. Reaching into his parka he takes out a flare and begins waving it frantically. And then, unexpectedly, the erratic wind pushes the approaching helicopter back and then around, as if in the grip of a downdraft. articles.text: When the first of a series of road trip movies appeared in 2010, and Steve Coogan and Bob Brydon took a culinary tour of England, I missed it. That film was followed in 2014 by visits to similar Michelin restaurants and five-star hotels as they wandered through Italy. That led to The Trip to Spain, their third excursion through the rolling, bucolic hills of Spain, once again taking a week to stop at historic stone hotels, each at least several hundred years old, as well as renowned restaurants that serve cuisine on white oval plates that prove to be works of art. But the essence of these trips – adapted from a BBC series – is the conversation that Coogan and Brydon engage in as they sit across from one another, their elbows leaning on white tablecloths while sipping robust local wines. Therein is the full reveal. There is no plot per se. Nada. Okay, there is a fragile, oblique theme in The Trip to Spain, one hidden in all their smart banter and endless impressions of the likes of Michael Caine or Sean Connery, enhanced with spot on Mick Jagger mimicry. That theme? It’s about confronting the reality that they have arrived at that point in life just beyond middle age. pages.text: Wednesday, August 28, 2024 21 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Arctic a gripping tale of survival The Trip to Spain a travelogue with wine, food By Chris Honoré When the first of a series of road trip movies appeared in 2010, and Steve Coogan and Bob Brydon took a culinary tour of England, I missed it. That film was followed in 2014 by visits to similar Michelin restaurants and five-star hotels as they wandered through Italy. That led to The Trip to Spain, their third excursion through the rolling, bucolic hills of Spain, once again taking a week to stop at historic stone hotels, each at least several hundred years old, as well as renowned restaurants that serve cuisine on white oval plates that prove to be works of art. But the essence of these trips – adapted from a BBC series – is the conversation that Coogan and Brydon engage in as they sit across from one another, their elbows leaning on white tablecloths while sipping robust local wines. Therein is the full reveal. There is no plot per se. Nada. Okay, there is a fragile, oblique theme in The Trip to Spain, one hidden in all their smart banter and endless impressions of the likes of Michael Caine or Sean Connery, enhanced with spot on Mick Jagger mimicry. That theme? It’s about confronting the reality that they have arrived at that point in life just beyond middle age. And as much as that seems to matter to them, the improvisational dialogue never takes a deep dive into this existential question, one that is instead studiously ignored in favor of verbal play and clever ripostes. There are private moments when the two pause and make contact with family back home See The Trip to Spain on page 29 Mads Mikkelsen in Arctic By Chris Honoré Arctic is a quietly intense yet deliberately measured story of survival and self-reliance. It is set against an unforgiving environment – an enveloping arctic landscape, a stretching snowy white that surrounds a downed single-engine plane that has crashed, intact, its nose scorched, the prop bent. In the opening scene, a man emerges from the fuselage and walks across a flat field of ice and snow to check several fishing lines dropped into ice holes. There is not a hint of backstory regarding who he is or what happened to the plane. He does wear a heavy red parka with the name Overgard on the front, but that could be the name of a company. Clearly, he survived uninjured. Who else was on board, if anyone, is unknown. What is evident is he is alone, surrounded by a penetrating silence that is complete, except for the crunch of snow when he walks from the plane, or the howl of the wind as a storm sweeps through. It appears as if Overgard has been there for some time. Perhaps several months. His face is wind burned and hidden behind a heavy beard. The interior of the plane – it’s a long, rectangular cabin – has been well organized. He has a jury-rigged bed, a down sleeping bag, his parka is weathered and soiled. He also has a few utensils, a knife to filet the fish that he catches and eats raw, and endless amount of melted snow. He’s also dug a massive SOS in the snow near the plane. Part of his daily ritual is to hike to the crest of a nearby hill bringing with him a hand-cranked box that sends out a GPS signal to anyone searching. And then abruptly everything changes. As Overgard is preparing to clean one of his fish, gusts of wind blowing around him, he hears and then sees a helicopter coming over a ridge. Reaching into his parka he takes out a flare and begins waving it frantically. And then, unexpectedly, the erratic wind pushes the approaching helicopter back and then around, as if in the grip of a downdraft. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 4 It has always been fundamental to childhood entertainment to anthropomorphize animals, whether a Disney nature documentary or an animated feature such as the Lion King. Even Cinderella is helped by intelligent birds and mice. What is extraordinary about the Toy Story feature films, which began in 1995, is that Pixar made familiar toys – Sheriff Woody, Buzz Lightyear, Bo Peep, etc. – all three dimensional characters with emotive personalities, only made manifest when no humans are present. In Toy Story 4, there is actually an ongoing discussion between Woody and Buzz regarding listening to your inner voice for guidance. They live by a code: hope to picked by a child, be loyal and find meaning and purpose in that connection. Stalking Woody and crew, however, is the ubiquitous fear of impending obsolescence, perhaps left in a closet, or sitting on a shelf where dust gathers. Death, so to speak, is just a cardboard box away. Toy Story 4 is simply wonderful, as were its three precursors. Imagine creating four animated features that are stand alone, extraordinary in narrative and animation. Each is an engaging, witty story, heartfelt and in all respects, as best exemplified by Woody (Tom Hanks), posses an abiding sense of compassion, empathy and decency. In writing fiction, be it screenplays or novels, there is a distinct difference between telling and showing. Toy Story 4 “shows” its audience, from youngsters to adults, from the first frame to the last, that caring about your friends before yourself is to be valued. And as Woody points out at a critical moment in 4, “No one gets left behind.” So as the story unfolds, Woody and crew are now part of a new world, their new child, so to speak, is Bonnie. Unlike Andy, now gone off to college, she leaves many of them in her closet collecting dust balls. Of course, kids are fickle (and they grow up); however for Woody, this truth provokes familiar anxieties. His purpose, the meaning of his life, is to be in the room with Bonnie and not in the closet, peering between the slats. He yearns to be held and played with, talked to, taken here and there. When he hears that Bonnie is about to spend one day, reluctantly, being introduced to kindergarten, a week before real school starts, well, Woody hides in her backpack so he can spend the morning keeping an eye on her. And it’s there, sneaking back and forth with discarded stuff found in a trash can, that he helps Bonnie construct what turns out to be her new best toy, Forky (Tony Hale), made out of a plastic fork, red pipe cleaners for arms and wooden sticks for feet. Bonnie is immediately besotted with her new BFF, Forky. As for Woody, helping his child represents mission accomplished and proof that he’s still needed. Of course, that analysis may only present itself in the dimmest way to the little guys in the audience. What they will enjoy is a Winnebago road trip with Bonnie, her parents, which includes Woody, Buzz Lightyear, Forky and the gang. Again, if they’re all to have a life, it must be with Bonnie so where she goes they go. The trip, of course, presents a series of speed bumps and mini-crises: Forky gets lost, Bonnie has a kid meltdown GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2024 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2024 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2024 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2024

articles.text: Kiki’s Delivery Service, adapted by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, is based on a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s animé and prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, must leave home as tradition dictates to complete her magic training in another town. She takes her talking cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, Kiki’s Delivery Service is a wonderful adventure but is also a personal crossroads for Kiki, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. The tale is consistently funny, optimistic and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Voiced by Kirsten Dunst, Debbie Reynolds and Matthew Lawrence. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated G. Released in 2019. Streaming on Fandango/apple tv/ MAX/YouTube. A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Kiki’s Delivery Service

It might therefore be helpful to summarize the work of the various design professions that shape our surroundings to better understand how things fit together and function. Basically, there are six main interrelated design disciplines involved. This work is done by hired professionals on projects like large new homes or the new Piedmont high school buildings, or in the case of small remodel jobs, by contractors or homeowners themselves many times, following the standardized building code requirements, as well as city regulations. All development starts with the field of Planning, which involves design and regulatory requirements at the broadest scale. This work ends up in documents like general plans, zoning documents or design guidelines and forms the basis of the design process for all participating professions. When we submit for building permits, applications are first reviewed by the planning department for compliance and then passed on to the building department for more detailed engineering and code checking. Next is Urban Design, which we have addressed in previous columns. It is a narrower scale consideration, somewhere between Planning and Architecture. Difficult to codify, design guidelines come closest to setting the requirements for this invaluable work. There are urban design specialists but architects and landscape architects also support and contribute to this field. Architecture, of course, is the work of buildings themselves – the scale and discipline with which most people are familiar. Architects, usually known for the design of buildings, have traditionally also led, managed and coordinated the team of professionals from these disciplines whose expertise is needed to deal with all the different specialty issues involved. Landscape Architecture is a discipline whose scope of work is essential and connected to everything, from huge master plans through Urban Design down to individual small homes. Like Urban Design, good Landscape Architecture is critical to the success of any project. but unfortunately is not always given the importance required. Interior Design is the discipline most personal to all of us because we see this work up close. Every day we reach out and touch and use the furniture, fixtures, equipment – everything on the inside of the building – that interior designers specify and design. Engineering is a separate layer coordinated with everything that architects, landscape architects and planners design. Each franchise is independently owned and operated. Design disciplines that shape the built environment interrelated and maybe at times somewhat confusing. It might therefore be helpful to summarize the work of the various design professions that shape our surroundings to better understand how things fit together and function. Basically, there are six main interrelated design disciplines involved. This work is done by hired professionals on projects like large new homes or the new Piedmont high school buildings, or in the case of small remodel jobs, by contractors or homeowners themselves many times, following the standardized building code requirements, as well as city regulations. All development starts with the field of Planning, which involves design and regulatory requirements at the broadest scale. This work ends up in documents like general plans, zoning documents or design guidelines and forms the basis of the design process for all participating professions. When we submit for building permits, applications are first reviewed by the planning department for compliance and then passed on to the building department for more detailed engineering and code checking. Next is Urban Design, which we have addressed in previous columns. It is a narrower scale consideration, somewhere between Planning and Architecture. Difficult to codify, design guidelines come closest to setting the requirements for this invaluable work. There are urban design specialists but architects and landscape architects also support and contribute to this field. Architecture, of course, is the work of buildings themselves – the scale and discipline with which most people are familiar. Architects, usually known for the design of buildings, have traditionally also led, managed and coordinated the team of professionals from these disciplines whose expertise is needed to deal with all the different specialty issues involved. Landscape Architecture is a discipline whose scope of work is essential and connected to everything, from huge master plans through Urban Design down to individual small homes. Like Urban Design, good Landscape Architecture is critical to the success of any project. but unfortunately is not always given the importance required. Interior Design is the discipline most personal to all of us because we see this work up close. Every day we reach out and touch and use the furniture, fixtures, equipment – everything on the inside of the building – that interior designers specify and design. Engineering is a separate layer coordinated with everything that architects, landscape architects and planners design. For retaining walls to not tip over or sewage systems to have the required capacity, they must be ARCHITECTURE: The work of architects shows up on plans and submissions as an isolated building. But good architecture will have incorporated urban design considerations as well as extensive landscape architecture and interior design coordination. LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE: In addition to planting, landscape architects’ work includes hardscape (paving) irrigation, monuments, plazas, fountains, fences, trellises – in short, everything outside the building. INTERIOR DESIGN: Besides furniture selection or design, artwork, and surface coverings, interior designers work closely with architects to design and/or specify the materials, textures, colors and finishes of everything from light fixtures to building hardware. ENGINEERING: Engineers’ drawings are the most detailed and specific since they are responsible for the “nuts and bolts” of construction. They form a coordinated part of virtually all project documentation, alongside the work of all the other professions. engineered. Unlike small residential projects, the list of engineers involved on larger projects can be long and comprehensive, including those in less known fields like life safety, telecommunications and energy systems. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Previously printined in the Piedmont Post on June 2, 2021.

A beautifully rich wine that has an inky purple color, a sweet kiss of crème de cassis, incense, a touch of oak and forest floor. Its gorgeous fruit, medium bodied opulence, impressive purity, expansive texture and broad, savory finish make this a terrific wine to drink over the next ten years. This is the first time in my 23 years of writing this column that I have had the opportunity to review and write about wines from Lebanon. In fact, the only Lebanese wine I have ever tasted is the iconic Chateau Musar, the only internationally famous wine from the country. Historically speaking wine is not a new phenomenon in Lebanon. Lebanon is among the oldest sites of wine production in the world. In the Old Testament book of Hosea the prophet urged his followers to return to God so that “they will blossom as the vine and be like the wine of Lebanon, and their fragrance will be like that of Lebanon.” The Phoenicians who lived in the area were instrumental in spreading wine and viticulture through the Mediterranean in ancient times. During the Ottoman period, wine production in Lebanon was restricted for 400 years. Only after Christians living in Lebanon pursued winemaking as a ceremonial practice did wine consumption and production return in 1857 when a small winery in the Bekka valley was founded by Jesuit priests. During the period of French influence (1920-1946) wine production expanded and French soldiers and diplomats creat4d a significant local market and introduced new grape varieties. The industry faced tremendous challenges due to the Lebanese Civil War, but a few wineries survived and recently many new wineries have opened. There are now over 40 wineries in Lebanon and despite the many conflicts in the region, the country has an annual production of 12 million bottles. I recently received samples from a winery called IXSIR whose vineyards are planted on mountaintops with clay and limestone soil. These distinctive terroirs have provided IXSIR the opportunity to expand beyond the Bekka Valley. The winery blends grapes from a variety of wine regions and all their wines are also a blend of different grape varietals. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of 36 walkers and two K-9 best friends last week. The Shell station on Grand and Wildwood Avenues was being demolished and the conversion to an electric vehicle recharging station had started. History from Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi about this part of Piedmont was shared. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance allowing businesses from the city line just beyond Wildwood Avenue to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand Avenue, and to Fairview Avenue on the east side. Seven months later voters rejected another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the Grand Avenue business district remains the same as it was in 1929. The walkers went down Magnolia to the little visited MacKinnon Place cul de sac. They found a hidden, 110-foot path down to Arbor Drive and continued to Oakland Avenue and Grand. They saw the former site of a beer garden. In 1892 Axel Gruggel built a restaurant on this corner that he called A Mon Chateau (My Castle), and a beer garden in the back on Linda. Over the years, the establishment had different owners, including three bachelors in 1907 who were denied a liquor license when they became available because neighbors didn’t like the restaurant’s noise. However, the bachelors continued to sell liquor. In 1908 they were arrested, and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino,” where poker was played. But gambling was illegal, and the casino was raided in 1912. Nine card players were arrested, and each was fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company and in 1922 the Del Monte Market. The store did well until a Piggly Wiggly supermarket opened down the street at Sunnyside. The competition was too much. The Del Monte Market closed in 1935, and the building was torn down in 1936. A succession of gas stations occupied the space until 1987 when Chevron sold the property, and the current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built on the site. There was also a popular, locally owned Foudy’s Fine Food on the block from 1950 to 1967. The website www.historyofpiedmont.com/grocery provids more history. There were homes where the current Ace Hardware is, but between 1961 and 1963 they were torn down, and in 1963 the 40th store of a local Louis market chain was built on the site. The store was also remembered by walkers being a Big T store, but that store was unsuccessful and closed. In 1985 Ace Hardware move up Grand from where Walden Books is now. The walkers continued down Grand to its corner with Wildwood Avenue. The Shell station had been partially demolished, and workers were doing some clean up. Among those participating in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays were Avelina Buijs, Denny McGee, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Nancy Henn, Mark Davis, Jack Fischrup, Martin Levy, Judy Sokoloff, Yoland Jenkins, Sharona Fischrup, Noemi Alvarado, Judy Live, Nancy Olsen, Charlene Louie, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Lisa Euphrat, Peggy Shultz, Kat Lang, Claudine Bach, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lorek Haghnazarean, Jim Kuo, Adrienne Hamlin, Edith Lee, Margaret Lennig, Shiela Lennig, Elizabeth Richter, Priscilla Wanerus, Dave DeRoche, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Mark Frost, George Epstein, and Donni Rodman who were walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: and in a way those conversations are more engaging than the riffs that take place over dinner. I know that sounds heretical, for it is these back and forth musings and comedic retorts that take stage center and engage what I can only assume is an acquired taste. I do acknowledge that British humor can be dry as day-old toast. Actually, I enjoy most British films and they often do courageous comedy with off-center, character-driven stories that are both brilliant and subtle. But I confess that hanging out with these two Brits for almost two hours, interspersed with a travelogue of Spain, can be tedious and at times seem a bit self-indulgent. One other observation: though the food served looks tasty and so nicely presented, and Brydon is ostensibly going to write restaurant reviews (Coogan is writing a memoir), little is ever said about the food itself. They taste it, nod appreciatively, but are too busy relishing their conversations to comment on what’s before them. My last observation: there were times when I felt that the insipid/clever/smart discussions were a way of avoiding what was really on their minds: old age, meaning mortality. articles.text: The troop of 16+ girls combined two troops of Brownies from Beach, Havens and Wildwood Elementary schools when they were promoted to Piedmont Middle School. Over the past years, Girls Scouts in Troop 33521 volunteered for work at Lake Merritt and beach clean ups, went camping and hiking, learned first aid, made food from their family heritage and worked on many creative projects together. They competed in a regional Girl Scout Camporee and placed in the top 10 for skill, including orienteering, tent building and fire safety. The Girl Scouts celebrated the week before starting high school by sailing to Catalina Island and Ensenada on a cruise August 4-8. Interested in finding out more about Girl Scouts? articles.text: • Monarch, the famed “last grizzly bear” of California, returns to public view for the first time since 2012 and marks the 100- year anniversary of the species’ extinction in California. • Two augmented reality experiences bring the iconic California species condors and bobcats to life inside the museum. • Interactive puzzles and a mock wildlife crossing tunnel (that you and your kids can crawl through!) give visitors a firsthand look at urban ecology. • The Shake House, a fan-favorite earthquake simulator, returns with a new focus on resilient structures in nature. The exhibition also spotlights the Academy’s Thriving California initiative, which aims to regenerate biodiversity, build resilience to climate change, and advance equitable access to nature across the state. Thriving California includes path-breaking work by aquarium biologists raising thousands of sunflower sea stars to improve the health of kelp forests and research by Academy scientists who found biodiversity bounces back more quickly in a wildfire area that was previously treated by a prescribed burn. Learn more about the new exhibit at www.calacademy.org. Ronna Kelly is a Piedmont resident and director of communications at the California Academy of Sciences. articles.text: Piedmont Shell had been in Piedmont for 95 years, but it was announced in November 2023 that it would close that month. The property was sold to Shell Recharge, a division of Shell Oil. The station had three 10,000-gallon gas tanks under the pumps that needed to be replaced by 2025. New tanks would have enabled the station to continue to sell gas for decades, but the increased popularity of electric vehicles made the owner feel uncomfortable with the future of gasoline stations and the investment. Influencing this was California’s plans to achieve 100% new zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035 and have a 25% reduction in smog causing pollution by 2037. Shell is replacing the station with a 14-bay electric vehicle charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. Fast charging will be provided with power up to 360kW. No employees will be regularly on the site. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Wednesday Walkers Continued from page 28 Piedmont Shell had been in Piedmont for 95 years, but it was announced in November 2023 that it would close that month. The property was sold to Shell Recharge, a division of Shell Oil. The station had three 10,000-gallon gas tanks under the pumps that needed to be replaced by 2025. New tanks would have enabled the station to continue to sell gas for decades, but the increased popularity of electric vehicles made the owner feel uncomfortable with the future of gasoline stations and the investment. Influencing this was California’s plans to achieve 100% new zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035 and have a 25% reduction in smog causing pollution by 2037. Shell is replacing the station with a 14-bay electric vehicle charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. Fast charging will be provided with power up to 360kW. Piedmont Real Estate Update August 2024 Interest Rate Update and More As realtors, one of the questions we hear frequently is, “What’s happening with interest rates?” Well, we went right to the source and spoke with local mortgage broker Brady Thomas of LaSalle Mortgage, who explained the current environment of inflation, rates, and the job market. “With inflation falling from 9% to 3% over the past year, the Fed is nearing a point where they’ll feel comfortable reducing rates,” says Thomas. “The key hurdle has been the job market, which the Fed wanted to cool before making cuts. In the last two months, hiring has slowed significantly, and unemployment is up.” Brady continued to explain that the Fed feared cutting rates too soon would reignite inflation. But with unemployment rising, they now believe we’re moving past the inflationary pressure and are shifting their focus to avoiding a potential recession. This brings us to the expectation that rate cuts are imminent. We could see the first cut as early as September, with more likely this year and into early next year. Additionally, the expectation is that the ‘spreads’ charged by banks on mortgage loans will shrink. This reduction in spreads will lead to even lower rates (beyond just the bond market improving). 10-Year Treasury Bond Rate Yield Chart Selling a House with Solar Panels With the knowledge that interest rates might be lowering soon, some readers could be considering a home sale. Lower rates spur action from buyers and help sellers feel more comfortable with their next purchase, whether downsizing, upsizing, or relocating. One feature of the home you may not think too much about is your solar power system. Keeping as much information as possible in your files is essential whether you own or lease solar panels. When properties change hands, the title company will want to see a purchase contract or lease agreement with the solar company, and you’ll need information about monthly payments, payoffs, number of panels, warranties, and more. It’s never too soon to ensure you’ve got the solar-related information you’ll need if you plan to sell at some point. Please contact us if you’d like to learn more about how to be prepared. Calia Homes BBQ Rub Recipe Last month, we had the pleasure of hand-delivering a curated BBQ kit to our clients, which included our own East Bay Rub, a custom blend of spices. Our clients have raved about putting it on everything from beef and salmon to tofu! What makes this an “East Bay” blend? The salt in the recipe mixes sea salt, smoked salt, and a hefty share of Oakland Spice Shop’s “Umami Salt,” which has black garlic and shiitake mushrooms. This rub is quite versatile, working best with beef, pork, and turkey. For those, we recommend a very heavy rub. It still works well for the more delicate fish, just with a lighter touch. Yields about 2.25 cups. Enjoy! articles.text: After many weeks of digging and preparation, construction crews at the site of the future community pool began pouring the concrete floor of its competition pool on Monday, August 15. Besides moving forward with Piedmont’s most high-profile public project, the work results in a visual change in the construction site. The operation went “smoothly, with no issues” said Echa Schneider, the city Communications Manager. “This is a huge milestone and an exciting time to be watching the [online] construction camera as you can really see the site taking shape.” She added that the new facility will have “double the water area” of the old pool. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the concrete floor should be completed by Friday, August 23. Most of them knew that ordinary meant regular, expected and unsurprising. They also knew that sometimes people think of ordinary as boring and unimportant. I asked them to help me name some ordinary things. They came up with breakfast, school, orbits around the sun, bedtime prayers, breathing, going to church and growing. RELIGION CORNER Ordinary Time By Pastor Jim Hopkins This past Sunday, during the Children’s Time portion of worship at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, I talked with the kids about the word ordinary. Most of them knew that ordinary meant regular, expected and unsurprising. They also knew that sometimes people think of ordinary as boring and unimportant. I asked them to help me name some ordinary things. They came up with breakfast, school, orbits around the sun, bedtime prayers, breathing, going to church and growing. They agreed that just because these are ordinary things, it does not mean they are unimportant. I told them that in the Christian liturgical calendar, the calendar that begins with Advent and continues through Christmas, Lent, Easter and Pentecost, we are now in what is called Ordinary time and that the color for the season, as represented by the stole I was wearing, is green. I said green is the color for the season because green is the color of growing. We agreed that ordinary things can sometimes seem a little boring but even then, there are worse things than boring. When it came time for the sermon, I read from Ephesians 5:15-20 in which the writer urges the followers of Jesus in Ephesus to make the most of every opportunity, even in the midst of challenging times. I noted that the writer connected making the most of every opportunity with some really ordinary things like gathering for worship, singing, being part of a faith community and practicing gratitude. I quoted Baptist peacemaker Ken Sehested: “To be sure, dragons need to be slain. Much more often, though gardens need to be groomed, young ones tutored and old ones cherished, watersheds protected, hobbled ones freed and civility practiced. Mostly, it’s these thousand million little things, the minute particulars that, strand by strand, are needed to reweave life’s torn and tattered fabric.” I noted that in our lives one of the most ordinary things is occasional conflict with those we love. I urged us to consider the counsel of Lambers Fisher in the face of this conflict to not go on the attack, get stuck in self-defense or simply give but instead to: 1. articles.text: On July 1 the Presidency of Piedmont Beautification Foundation passed from Karen Sullivan to Patty Dunlap. Sullivan completed a highly successful two years as President of the organization. Under her leadership the importance of PBF to the City of Piedmont increased significantly. Sullivan pushed the organization to increase its role from the more traditional focus on parks. Perhaps the most important undertaking was to support the construction of a new swimming pool. PBF was an early donor to the campaign to cover the shortfall in funding for this vital project. PBF followed by making the pool the focus of its efforts for 2022. It undertook a matching fund drive to raise money for the pool’s landscaping and green infrastructure. Ultimately PBF raised almost $250,000 for the pool, making it the second largest donating organization after Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization (PRFO). Other projects completed under Sullivan’s leadership included completion of beautiful new steps at the Highland/ Guildford entrance to Piedmont Park; safety bulb out landscaping; installation of water bottle filling stations; the planting of an Island Oak at the Mountain/Bellevue intersection; and the installation of a flagpole to honor the late Justice Carl Anderson. Several other projects are pending, including support for the soon to come Dearing Family Memorial and a significant upgrade of the Linda Beach Tot Lot. Throughout Sullivan’s term in office PBF’s long standing memorial bench and tree programs continued. Five memorial benches were installed, and 12 new trees were planted. PBF’s newest project is among the most exciting in recent years – the reforestation of Piedmont. Working in conjunction with Nancy Kent, the City’s Parks and Special Projects Manager (who oversaw the recently completed inventory of trees throughout the city) and incoming PBF President Patty Dunlap, a campaign to reforest the City’s trees has commenced. The initial focus is on Dracena Park, where a loss of many trees has created a huge need for replanting. The plan permits donors to direct their contributions to their own neighborhoods that need new trees. PBF involves many organizations and residents of Piedmont, all contributing to the betterment of the City. The Piedmont Garden Club was the founder of PBF and continues to pull the laboring oar. There are eight Trustees, including three appointed by the City Council (typically two Council members and the Chair of the Park Commission). The Piedmont Garden Club provides the other five Trustees, who also serve as officers. Other garden clubs represented are East Bay Garden Club, Highlanders Garden Club, and Hoe and Hope. Patty Dunlap, PBF’s newest President, will oversee the organization and its ambitious new campaign of reforestation. She is a former member of the Park Commission and served admirably as its Chair. PBF is looking forward to having her pick up the torch. Piedmont Beautification Foundation President Karen Sullivan with incoming president Patty Dunlap
articles.title: Patty Dunlap takes over as President of PBF

articles.text: A rendering of the two main units to be built on the lot, designated as 67 Wistaria Way (left) and 77 Wistaria Way. An ADU will also be built on the property. The design was approved by the Planning Department on December 27, 2023. Neighbors of the controversial housing project at 77 Wistaria Way have recently voiced their distrust of the project’s owner-developers Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead over what they believe is an aggressive attempt to build and quickly resell a large property in the neighborhood. The story of 77 Wistaria Way begins with its original owners, Harold and Genevieve Power. Harold passed away in 1994 and Genevieve in 2020. With no children, the land was given to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Oakland to support Corpus Christi Church. Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead bought the property from the Roman Catholic Diocese on January 4, 2022. The couple, married for 10 years have lived in the Bay Area for 25 and 15 years respectively. On May 2, 2022 Geoff Gibson, Kira Mead and their daughter Mabel introduced themselves to the area by going door to door with gifts of wine and chocolates for their future neighbors. Erin Ashton, who lives nearby, recalled the event. “They were carrying a binder with information about the property next door. They showed me a rendering of their first house design, and they gave us a bottle of wine and chocolates while our daughter played with their child.” When Ashton asked if she could have a copy of the rendering to 2024 September 21, 2024 9 AM - 12 PM 800 MAGNOLIA AVE. PIEDMONT, CA RSVP: coffeecarscops@piedmont.ca.gov show her husband, they refused. “Usually when a neighbor comes to visit regarding a new project, it’s to alleviate any potential impact rather than having everything already designed,” said her husband, David Ashton. On July 11, 2022, Mead and Gibson met with the Planning Commission at its regularly scheduled public meeting for a design review. The couple requested to construct a new four-level, 4,992-square-foot single-family residence with four bedrooms, four and a half bathrooms, two offices, a recreation room, a covered entry porch, and a two-car garage. Many neighbors from surrounding properties appeared to voice their concerns about the size of the house, potential loss of scenic views and sunlight impacts on neighboring properties among others. According to the meeting minutes, their plan was rejected because “the design as submitted is too much of a high impact on the neighbors [...] The applicant should spend more time collaborating with the neighbors to get a more achievable design.” On November 14, 2022, Mead and Gibson met once again with the Planning Commission for another design review. This time, the couple requested to build a three-level, 3,699-square-foot residence with four bedrooms, four-and-a-half bathrooms, an office, and a two-car garage. Once again, many neighbors from surrounding properties appeared to voice their concerns. Gibson said that there had been multiple attempts to meet and talk with people who disapproved of the project, but that not many have come forward to further discuss issues and solutions. Commission Chair Rani Batra said that she appreciated that the couple had made changes, but that the design was still too large. Commissioner Justin Zucker was supportive of the project and voiced his concerns that a subsequent project would come back under the Housing Accountability Act. Ultimately, Gibson and Mead’s design was rejected again for many of the same reasons as in their previous design review. On April 20, 2023, Gibson and Mead submitted their application form and SB9 eligibility package to the City of Piedmont’s Planning Department. The proposed plan split the lot into two properties: one at 67 Wistaria Way, which will be 2,590 square feet, and another at 77 Wistaria Way, which would be 3,418 square feet. On August 23, 2023, lawyer Kurt Peterson sent a letter to the Planning Department on behalf of the neighbors around Wistaria Way urging the City to reject the application. The application was approved on December 27, 2023.

articles.text: Piedmont’s school board met for their first meeting of the new school year on Wednesday, August 14. Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen led the meeting which celebrated the return to school in Piedmont. During the meeting, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn said while touring each of the five campuses on her first day of school frenzy she saw “joyful students returning.” “It really was such a pleasure. Our staff looked joyful, our students and families looked great,” Hawn said. articles.text: Camp Augusta will host its annual Wish, Wonder & Wine fundraiser at Piedmont Community Church on Saturday, September 21, from 5:00-7:00 p.m. Tickets are $50. As school begins, keep an eye out for the cornflower blue shirts around town worn by the hundreds of Piedmont children who attended Camp Augusta this summer. They may not know it, but they are continuing a long tradition in the community. You are invited to learn more about this special place that so many children call home each summer. Join us on September 21st for Wish, Wonder & Wine, an adult evening of fun in Piedmont. Enjoy wine, appetizers, and auction prizes while building community in support of Camp Augusta. You’ll hear from staff and campers with exciting updates from this summer, including the hugely popular new ropes challenge course. Camp offers amazing programming and some of the highest trained camp staff in the world to run the program. Help us meet our goal of upgrading our staff housing and to kick off a two-year capital campaign to replace those structures and the Cedar Bath house. Piedmont History Camp Augusta was originally donated to the girls of Piedmont almost 100 years ago. In the early years, the camp’s main use was by the Piedmont Council of Camp Fire. Virtually all the young Piedmont women spent their summers at the camp. After the site was shuttered by the Camp Fire organization, a group of dedicated Piedmonters formed an oversight board and began the long legal battle to win the property back for the children of Piedmont. While the site sat dormant for decades, the facilities fell into disrepair. However, with hard work and the support of the community, the 90 acre facility located in the beautiful forested foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains has received a variety of improvements over the years: the restoration of the original Lodge where campers hang out in aerial silks; a kitchen where our chefs cook delicious organic food that campers get excited about (have you ever tried Australian pizza with bananas on top!?); and this year’s incredible new high ropes challenge course with over 40 elements to ascend. We hope we see you at Wish, Wonder and Wine. Tickets are available online at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/wish-wonderand-wine-tickets-945283286757? aff=oddtdtcreator Can’t make the event in person? Please consider making a contribution to support our efforts at www.campaugusta.org/gifts. articles.text: Come to the Piedmont Community Service Crew fall kickoff this Saturday, August 24, from 4 to 6 p.m. when youth leaders will describe what the crew does. We’ll offer opportunities for non-members to sign up to try an event as a guest before formally registering. We welcome youth from 6th grade through 12th grade. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is for local high school students and has been serving our community for 20 years, boasting 150 members. Our goal is to provide quality work for people who need it most, while simultaneously taking on full responsibility and funding in our crew. Our events are fun, social, and rewarding, recognizing the diverse interests of our members. Our members gain life skills such as cooking, construction & home Planning and cooking lunch for low income seniors at St Mary’s Center Building planter boxes for Altenheim Senior Community repair, teaching others, event planning, and environmental science. PCSC provides a nurturing learning environment for members who choose to take on leadership opportunities. They are mentored to learn how to delegate, become organized, and work with others. Parents should come to learn about how PCSC will help their kids get a head start on success in life. PCSC not only allows students to give back to their community and connect with their peers, it also gives them opportunities to gain experience in leadership positions. If you are interested in attending, complete this event registration form (https://forms.gle/ dFBMmtQQEgmtBhA98); we’ll respond with the location. If you have any questions, please email us for more details: • Ken Li, PCSC advisor and founder (ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net) • Elena O’Connell, co-President (elenafoc26@gmail.com) • Stephanie Lee, co-President (stephanieww08@gmail.com)

articles.text: On July 11, Scouts and three adults from Troop 15 backpacked a portion of the John Muir Trail in the Sierra Nevada mountains. Each day the group experienced endless views from atop mountains, pleasant weather, and a few encounters with wildlife such as marmots and deer. With over 11,000 feet of elevation gain, the group followed the trail ranging between 9,000 to 12,000 feet. “There were some of the best sunsets I’ve ever seen,” said Scout Davey Ackerman. Each morning Scouts got out of their tents as early as 5:45 a.m. and began packing their gear and having breakfast. Most mornings started with many miles of trekking, up and down the mountains. After the first section, the group stopped for lunch for meals such as pita bread and peanut butter, or the favorite, Ritz, Baby Bell, and salami sandwiches. After lunch, the hiking continued, occasionally stopping for water or a snack. Finally, after hiking up steep ascents and countless switchbacks, they reached their destination for the night and began setThe sunset above Dusy Basin Troop 15 begins the descent into Dusy Basin. pages.text: Wednesday, August 21, 2024 9 Troop 15 Continued from page 8 ting camp. After putting up their tents and filtering water, Scouts went off to have some fun. Many spent the afternoon fishing in a river at the Dusy Basin campsite. “There were many small and hungry Golden Trout in some of the most clear and beautiful streams I’ve ever seen,” said Thomas Moison. Others went swimming in various lakes which were surrounded by towering mountains, casting their reflections in the clear water. In the evenings, Scouts cooked their meals in pots on small camp stoves. Most meals only required boiling water and mixing ingredients. Many Scouts enjoyed the beef stew as well as the longstanding favorite, chili-mac. One of the hardest days was when they climbed up to Bishop Pass, consisting of steep and Assistant Scoutmaster Dave Ragones and Sammy Ragones at the top of Bishop’s Pass Scout Thomas Moision shows off his catch from Dusy Branch. Scout Davey Ackerman and Assistant Scoutmaster Fred Ackerman celebrate their successful climb. Scouts Alex Chin, Thomas Ero, Davey Ackerman, and Sammy Ragones enter the John Muir Wildnerness. rocky inclines, summiting at 11,972 feet. From the pass, Scouts looked out to the beautiful Dusy Basin, scattered with glassy lakes, by far the most memorable view of the trip. One nice surprise was that “the mosquitoes weren’t nearly as bad as last year,” said returning Scout Gianluca Richmond. But it wasn’t all smooth sailing on the trail. Already adjusting to the high elevation, a few Scouts struggled with sunburns, hot spots and blisters. Carrying 50-pound packs took its toll. One pack was broken for part of the trip, and one Scout had boots on the brink of falling apart. Despite the small roadblocks, it was an amazing week of backpacking experience, beautiful views, and loads of fun. The beautiful High Sierra glow as the sun sets above camp Scouts descend down to the Chocolate Lakes.

articles.text: Troop 1 Piedmont Scouts recently embarked on an adventurous Class A High Sierra expedition east of Bishop, California, completing a remarkable journey along the iconic Pacific Crest Trail. An epic journey Five Scouts and three adults covered over 70 miles in seven days, with elevations ranging from 7,626 feet to a breathtaking 14,064 feet. The group enjoyed mild temperatures and clear, smoke-free skies, and totaled 15,712 feet of climbing, surpassing the equivalent climb from Mt. Everest base camp to its summit. First-night adventures Starting from South Lake outside Bishop, each Scout carried Mateo Long shows off one of the dozens of Brook trout landed by the Scouts, with distinctive 11,673- foot Fin Dome stands watch over Arrowhead Lake. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 cross 12,129ft Pinchot Pass: Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill (left), Ayaan Jajodia, Alexander Cantrill, Senior Patrol Leader Miguel Long, Mateo Long, Luke Ironside, Chad Ironside, and Steve Long. approximately 40 lbs. of food and gear. They crossed the 11,960- foot Bishop Pass and made their first camp in Dusy Basin. Ayaan Jajodia earned the title of heaviest pack at 43 lbs. The Scouts were rewarded with stunning views and a crystal-clear lake teeming with elusive Golden Trout. Troop 1 fishing specialist Miguel Long demonstrated his skill catching nearly two dozen Goldens the first evening. Conquering Split Mountain The journey included crossing five major passes. After a challenging 14-mile day, the Scouts were well-positioned to tackle Split Mountain, the eighth highest peak in California at 14,064 feet. With guidance from Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill and adult leader Chad Ironside, the Scouts Troop 1 Scouts prepare to cross the bouncy, 130-foot-long Woods Creek suspension bridge. It spans a stream deep in the mountains between Black Mountain and Mount Pinchot and is a key crossing on the 2,650 mile Pacific Crest Trail. Ayaan Jajodia, Luke Ironside, Mateo Long, Alexander Cantrill, Miguel Long and Chad Ironside wait their turn to cross. Luke Ironside looks on as Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill teaches Scouts a new card game, All Fours, on the shore of Kearsarge Lake.
