articles.text: Piedmont recently experienced a string of burglaries mostly targeted at residents who were on vacation for extended periods of time. On Monday, August 5, around 5:00 p.m., a residential burglary on Requa Road was reported to the police. When the residents returned home they found several items missing. An unknown suspect or suspects entered the home and stole several jewelry items including a Tiffany silver bracelet, a Tiffany silver chain bracelet and a Mikimoto bracelet. The total reported loss was $6,700. On Monday, August 5, at 11:15 p.m., a resident on Grand Avenue returned home from vacation to find his residence ransacked. The victim stated several music instruments, recording equipment and other expensive items were missing. The total value of the loss is unknown. On Thursday, August 8, a resident reported that their house on King Avenue had been burglarized the previous night. The suspect entered the home through a side window and ransacked the office and upstairs master bedroom. The total reported loss is in excess of $5,000 worth of jewelry and purses. The Piedmont Police Department encourages residents who are heading out of town to sign up for their Vacation Home Check program. Vacation Home Check is a service offered to residents who are away from their homes for a period of 4 to 30 days. If requested, members of the police department may periodically check the security of your house. If a problem is discovered, a police officer will respond and handle the situation. Residents may request this service by downloading the Vacation Home Check & Vacant Home Notification Form from the PPD’s website. The completed form may be mailed or dropped off at the Police Department at 403 Highland Avenue or emailed to vacationchecks@piedmont.ca.gov. On the form, please include important information such as who is allowed on the property while you are away, a list of pets left on the property, and the name of any caretaker(s). For more information on the Vacation Home Check program, call the police department’s non-emergency line at 420-3000.

On Monday, August 5, around 5:00 p.m., a residential burglary on Requa Road was reported to the police. When the residents returned home they found several items missing. An unknown suspect or suspects entered the home and stole several jewelry items including a Tiffany silver bracelet, a Tiffany silver chain bracelet and a Mikimoto bracelet. The total reported loss was $6,700. On Monday, August 5, at 11:15 p.m., a resident on Grand Avenue returned home from vacation to find his residence ransacked. The victim stated several music instruments, recording equipment and other expensive items were missing. The total value of the loss is unknown. On Thursday, August 8, a resident reported that their house on King Avenue had been burglarized the previous night. The suspect entered the home through a side window and ransacked the office and upstairs master bedroom. The total reported loss is in excess of $5,000 worth of jewelry and purses. The Piedmont Police Department encourages residents who are heading out of town to sign up for their Vacation Home Check program. Vacation Home Check is a service offered to residents who are away from their homes for a period of 4 to 30 days. If requested, members of the police department may periodically check the security of your house. If a problem is discovered, a police officer will respond and handle the situation. Residents may request this service by downloading the Vacation Home Check & Vacant Home Notification Form from the PPD’s website. The completed form may be mailed or dropped off at the Police Department at 403 Highland Avenue or emailed to vacationchecks@piedmont.ca.gov. On the form, please include important information such as who is allowed on the property while you are away, a list of pets left on the property, and the name of any caretaker(s). articles.text: It’s been a busy offseason for the Piedmont High football team; spending time in the weight room and an excursion to Lake Tahoe for a football camp. It’s all in preparation for the upcoming season as PHS looks for its second straight western Alameda County Conference title, this time in the Mission Division after claiming the 2023 Shoreline crown. “People are watching now, we’re not sneaking up on anybody anymore. People want to see if it was a fluke, and at the end of the day, it’s hard work that gets us here. It’s like that saying, ‘Heavy is the head that bears the crown.’ We don’t have a crown yet, but we changed the expectations,” coach Jordan Seiden said following the close of Piedmont’s first week of practice with pads. When Seiden took over as head coach in April 2022, his Quarterback Markos Lagios takes a snap in practice. Defensive lineman Jordan Alemania was named to the All-Bay Area New Group preseason team. Staff Photos Coach Jordan Seiden (right) talks things over with the team following a recent practice. Piedmont’s football team is eager for more success after winning last year’s WACC Shoreline title. first offseason training camp resembled nothing of his current team. In 2022 they couldn’t running full 11-on-11 drills due to a small roster, which led to the varsity program being terminated that year. This time around, there is visibly a much higher standard for the 2024 Highlanders and a championship mindset from the get-go. “You can’t replace hard work. We say it a million times at practice, hard work begets talent every single time. If you have talent, but they don’t work hard, we’ll look back on this season with a lot of ‘Woulda, Coulda, Shouldas’, and we don’t want that… Our coaching staff laughs about it, but even last year around this time, we’d be in the weight room with just 12 kids. I don’t think we were ever around 25-28 kids throughout the summer,” Seiden said. The Highlanders finished last season with a 7-4 record and as winners of the WACC Shoreline Division after beating Newark Memorial 29-26. They received a lot of headlines with Sam Shelby being named the SF Chronicle’s Player of the Year for the East Bay region and to their All-Metro first-team, while Markos Lagios was a second-team All-Metro selections. This preseason, a pair of Piedmont defenders has already earned honors. Llinebacker Cash Elmquist and defensive lineman Jordan Alemania were named to the Bay Area News Group preseason team. Lagios and Shelby will also likely be named to the offensive group. It’s all built toward the increased expectations surrounding Piedmont in 2024. Seiden is hopeful that the preseason hype doesn’t change the players’ mentality, but to embrace the mindset that gained the notoriety. “Hopefully it’s not changing the mentality. We want them to embrace it and avoid feeling complacent. But that’s not the case with these boys, they understand how to work hard. We could have as many as five players named to the All-Bay Area teams; for a program that was on its death bed a few years ago, that says a lot about our talent,” Seiden said. Piedmont opens its 2024 campaign with a scrimmage at Moreau in Hayward this Saturday, August 24 before starting its full 10-game regular season schedule when it hosts Salesian on August 30. It marks the Highlanders’ return to Witter Field after playing their entire 2023 season on the road due to the ongoing delay of work on Witter Field being completed.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team is back on the courts with eyes on the prize – looking to win the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division title after missing out last year. The squad opened its 2024 campaign with a scrimmage against North Coast Section foe and neighboring school College Prep on August 19. PHS went 13-8 last season and was second in the WACC to Bishop O’Dowd. They reached the D2 NCS Team Championship semifinals, falling 5-2 to eventual champions University. To reach the semis, Piedmont shutout Marin Catholic 7-0 in the first round and beat College Prep 6-1 in the quarterfinals. This year, O’Dowd still shapes up as Piedmont’s main competition for the Foothill Division title, along with Berkeley and Alameda. O’Dowd won in 2021, Piedmont claiming the crown in 2022, and O’Dowd won again last year. “O’Dowd lost their top singles starter and a couple of other girls, so it’ll still be close competition with them. Berkeley has some returners and will be a difficult team and I believe Alameda did too. But we have a good team and look even stronger in doubles,” coach Jim Landes said. Landes has his team captains for this year. Emma Eisemon is a four-year starter and a key doubles player, while Carolina Romanczuk is a three-year singles starter. “Four years down, it’s so crazy and a surreal moment. I’ve played the last three season with my partner Ceci, it’s a bit switched up this year and I’m keeping an open mind to playing doubles and even singles. I’m super excited,” Eisemon said. “Being a captain brings us a lot of responsibility. We have to be role models to the younger girls on the team and that makes me happy to try to become that role model for these girls,” Romanczuk added. Eisemon has played most of her Piedmont career with doubles partner Ceclia DeFazio, who graduated last year. Landes is taking a look at pairing her with Samantha Huynh. “This season, I don’t have any expectations and I’m playing for fun. I’m excited to see how it Staff Photos Senior Emma Eisemon was named a team captain for the upcoming season. Junior Kate Jumper is a three-year starter and a key singles player. looks, we’re moving around the lineup a lot,” Eisemon said. Romanczuk us hoping to be the team’s No. 1 singles starter, and will challenge for the position with junior Kate Jumper. Romanczuk spent time over the summer training and showing some increased power on her forehand. “At the end of last season, I sprained my ankle twice. I’ve been working hard this summer and went to a tennis academy. I’ve been working a lot and practicing,” Romanczuk said. New to the varsity roster are sophomores Emma Chan and Faith Chin, who may round out Piedmont’s doubles lineup. Piedmont gets its season started with two matches next week, at Las Lomas in Walnut Creek on Wednesday, August 28, and home on August 29 with neighbor Head Royce. Senior Carolina Romanczuk is another team captain. She’s a three-year singles starter.
articles.title: Girls’ tennis team returns with eyes on WACC title

Staff Photos compared to my lower body. My workout routine is usually with my football team outside of a few lifts while I was traveling. The football team worked out four days a week, including an hour of lifting and an hour of conditioning. I also attended the Nike Track and Field Camp at Stanford University where I met college and peer athletes and got training tips from some of the top college coaches in the world. I ended the summer with a 70 mile backpacking trip with Piedmont Troop 1 Scouts, carrying a pack of over 40 pounds at altitudes up to 14,056 feet. It was definitely recreational, but hiking at that altitude was great training. What are your fitness goals for the summer? The main goal was to get healthy after the quad injury so it didn’t impact my senior football season. So, I focused on following the routine from my physical therapist of stretching and light lower body resistance training. I was able to focus on upper body work with a goal of increasing my strength and weight for football. I was able to add 10 pounds of muscle over the summer with the weight program and eating healthy. How are you measuring your development? I’m measured my development by seeing how many reps of 135 pounds I can accomplish. Over weeks, that number kept growing. Also, watching the weight scale and paying particular attention to how my quad and body felt to make sure I wasn’t overworking myself. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Our football coaches, Bo and Oski, help guide players in the weight room as the strength coaches, they are incredible. Coach P (Pouyan Assadi) and the Nike track camp coaches provided good track and field specific exercises that I do on my own each week. Additionally, I followed my physical therapy regimen to rehabilitate my quad muscle. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone was overcoming my quad strain, which had been affecting my work output for the last couple of months during the track season, and it was really hard to work through. I’m glad I am back to being healthy again. Also, adding a healthy 10 pounds for football was another accomplishment. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Always have faith in yourself and never give up. Be the first to practice and the last to leave. Get ahead and stay ahead. Trust your coaches and trainers; seek out and follow their advice. We’re very lucky in Piedmont to have amazing facilities, coaches, and our trainer, Bruce. Take full advantage of their experience. SKYLAR BEST Cross Country, Track & Field What are your fitness goals? My fitness goals for the summer were to set a good base for the cross country season ahead. It’s difficult to make the most out of in-season workouts if you’re not in shape because you spend some of that time getting into shape, which sets you back. So, all-in-all, the main goal over the summer was to get as prepared as possible for the upcoming cross country season. How are you measuring your development? Although fitness is hard to measure, I tracked my development throughout the summer by how well I maintained my fitness. Not suffering through running camp workouts and making the most out of preseason training by being prepared for these experiences is one way that I know I am ready for the cross country season. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? When away on vacation, I ran alone or with my dad, who is also a runner. Additionally, my coach is really good about sending workout plans, particularly to those of us who are away and can’t attend summer practice. I also train with my team. Some of my teammates and I went up to Northern California with our coach to attend a running camp where we all trained with other teams in the area. When I’m back in Piedmont, I attend summer practice where we go on runs and complete workouts together as a team. There is always a coach there to help lead and guide us. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I didn’t participate in any races over the summer and only Staff Photo Piedmont High Class of 2026 Skylar Best is a junior and among the top distance runners on the cross country and track teams. Last school year, she earned second-team All-League honors in track and second-team honors in cross country. On the track team, Best qualified for the prestigious North Coast Section Meet of Champions in the 1600 meters and the 4x400 relay team. In the 1600, Best clocked a 5:43.32 to finish 27th while she qualified for the Meet of Champions by finishing eighth of 22 at the NCS Bayshore in 5:26.81. The 4x400 relay team reached the Meet of Champions by placing fourth of 13 at the Bayshore with a time of 4:15.44. At the MoC, the 4x400 team placed 22nd in 4:18.87. Best placed 25th of 120 runners in the NCS Cross-Country Championships, clocking a time of 20:52.9. She helped Piedmont placed second in the Western Alameda County Conference championship by placing eighth of 42 in 19:54.96. What is your workout program this summer? Since I was traveling for the majority of summer, the main goal was to just maintain fitness. I did this by going on a lot of runs between 4-6 miles. In addition, I attended two different running camps where we did a lot of workouts, such as hill repeats, tempos, long runs. My coach also hosts summer practice in town which I attend when I returned from travels.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 21, 2024 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 17th year. High school athletes as well as current and former colSUMMER WORKOUT SUMMER WORKOUT lege athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. MIGUEL LONG Football, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2025 Miguel Long is a two-sport athlete on the football and track teams. On the gridiron, Long is a defensive back and receiver. He is primarily a long jumper and triple jumper on the track team. In football he is set to be a three-year starter and earned second-team All-League honors as a defensive back last season. The Highlanders went 7-4 after receiving the No. 5 seed in the Division 5 NCS postseason, losing 49-14 to No. 4 Alhambra in Martinez. Piedmont won the WACC Shoreline Division title by defeating Newark Memorial in a heated 29-26 battle. Long was a key player in Piedmont’s win over the Cougars to win the Shoreline Division title, He had two interceptions in Newark’s final two offensive drives. In track Long reached the NCS Meet of Champions in the triple jump, finishing 13th of 23 with a distance of 42 feet, 1 inch. In the NCS Bayshore, Long was fourth of 21, logging 43 feet, 1 inch. What is your workout program this summer? My summer workout program consisted of a lot of different exercises, some of which were prescribed to me by my physical therapist which I’ve been attending ever since tearing my quad in April. I put a lot of emphasis on lifting this summer. I tried to work on my upper body because I felt it was a weaker point on my body Staff Photos Miguel Long is a two-sport athlete in football and track. compared to my lower body. My workout routine is usually with my football team outside of a few lifts while I was traveling. The football team worked out four days a week, including an hour of lifting and an hour of conditioning. I also attended the Nike Track and Field Camp at Stanford University where I met college and peer athletes and got training tips from some of the top college coaches in the world. I ended the summer with a 70 mile backpacking trip with Piedmont Troop 1 Scouts, carrying a pack of over 40 pounds at altitudes up to 14,056 feet. It was definitely recreational, but hiking at that altitude was great training. What are your fitness goals for the summer? The main goal was to get healthy after the quad injury so it didn’t impact my senior football season. So, I focused on following the routine from my physical therapist of stretching and light lower body resistance training. I was able to focus on upper body work with a goal of increasing my strength and weight for football. I was able to add 10 pounds of muscle over the summer with the weight program and eating healthy. How are you measuring your development? I’m measured my development by seeing how many reps of 135 pounds I can accomplish. Over weeks, that number kept growing. Also, watching the weight scale and paying particular attention to how my quad and body felt to make sure I wasn’t overworking myself. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Our football coaches, Bo and Oski, help guide players in the weight room as the strength coaches, they are incredible. Coach P (Pouyan Assadi) and the Nike track camp coaches provided good track and field specific exercises that I do on my own each week. Additionally, I followed my physical therapy regimen to rehabilitate my quad muscle. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone was overcoming my quad strain, which had been affecting my work output for the last couple of months during the track season, and it was really hard to work through. I’m glad I am back to being healthy again. Also, adding a healthy 10 pounds for football was another accomplishment. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Always have faith in yourself and never give up. Be the first to practice and the last to leave. Get ahead and stay ahead. Trust your coaches and trainers; seek out and follow their advice. We’re very lucky in Piedmont to have amazing facilities, coaches, and our trainer, Bruce. Take full advantage of their experience. SKYLAR BEST Cross Country, Track & Field What are your fitness goals? My fitness goals for the summer were to set a good base for the cross country season ahead. It’s difficult to make the most out of in-season workouts if you’re not in shape because you spend some of that time getting into shape, which sets you back. So, all-in-all, the main goal over the summer was to get as prepared as possible for the upcoming cross country season. How are you measuring your development? Although fitness is hard to measure, I tracked my development throughout the summer by how well I maintained my fitness. Not suffering through running camp workouts and making the most out of preseason training by being prepared for these experiences is one way that I know I am ready for the cross country season. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? When away on vacation, I ran alone or with my dad, who is also a runner. Additionally, my coach is really good about sending workout plans, particularly to those of us who are away and can’t attend summer practice. I also train with my team. Some of my teammates and I went up to Northern California with our coach to attend a running camp where we all trained with other teams in the area. When I’m back in Piedmont, I attend summer practice where we go on runs and complete workouts together as a team. There is always a coach there to help lead and guide us. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I didn’t participate in any races over the summer and only focused on my base training, so I’m happy with the progress I made these months. I’m excited for what’s to come! What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Not every workout or race is going to feel good, so it’s important that you learn from those times. RAVI SILVERBERG Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2025 Ravi Silverberg is a two-year starter under coach Ben Spencer and made an impact as a shooting guard last season. He can knock down 3-pointer and drive the lane for layups. The Highlanders went 20-11 and made it to the Division 3 NCS Finals as the No. 3 seed before losing No. 1 University, 65-55 on February 23 at University of San Francisco’s War Memorial Stadium. To get there, PHS beat No. 2 Archie Williams 64-61 in the semifinals on February 20, No. 6 Alhambra 67-43 in the quarterfinals on February 16 and No. 14 Sonoma Valley 40-34 in the opening round on February 13. He led scoring in Piedmont’s NCS Finals loss to University with 23 points. Silverberg earned honorable mention All-League honors as a junior and enters a critical senior year as a leader. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program included lifting weights, playing basketball, and conditioning to stay in shape. Piedmont High Class of 2026 Skylar Best is a junior and among the top distance runners on the cross country and track teams. Last school year, she earned second-team All-League honors in track and second-team honors in cross country. On the track team, Best qualified for the prestigious North Coast Section Meet of Champions in the 1600 meters and the 4x400 relay team. In the 1600, Best clocked a 5:43.32 to finish 27th while she qualified for the Meet of Champions by finishing eighth of 22 at the NCS Bayshore in 5:26.81. The 4x400 relay team reached the Meet of Champions by placing fourth of 13 at the Bayshore with a time of 4:15.44. At the MoC, the 4x400 team placed 22nd in 4:18.87. Best placed 25th of 120 runners in the NCS Cross-Country Championships, clocking a time of 20:52.9. She helped Piedmont placed second in the Western Alameda County Conference championship by placing eighth of 42 in 19:54.96. What is your workout program this summer? articles.text: Witter Field off icially re-opened on August 14, 2024, one year after expected. A ribbon-cutting ceremony marked the apparent completion on a new track, new field drainage, and a new playing surface for football, soccer, lacrosse and track. After delays stretched renovations for over a year from June 2023, Witter construction finally reached its conclusion on Friday, August 9. Piedmont’s new principal David Yoshihara opened the ceremony by offering thanks, and then handing the microphone to Piedmont School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, board president Veronica Thigpen, Board of Education member Cory Smegal, and Piedmont Boosters representative Keri Elmquist. Piedmont Director of Facilities Pete Palmer received stark criticism for the delays of Witter Field. Keri Elmquist (left), Pete Palmer, and school board president Veronica Thigpen. “As you can imagine, this project has been in the works for a long time. For those who have lived in Piedmont a while, you’ve known that we suffered through seasons where sporting events had to be canceled, or things had to be delayed and there were a lot of problems with the field,” Smegal said during the ceremony. Renovations began on June 6 of last year and were originally forecasted to reach its completion in December 2023, which would’ve allowed both soccer teams to play its seasons at home and permitted the track team to train at Witter. But, without fail, delays emerged continuously. EBMUD had to install an aqueduct under the field, while 60,000 square feet of substandard asphalt base needed to be replaced before the track could be paved. Paving under the track surface could start in February 2024 and the resurfacing of the track itself was pushed back to June. The subsurface was prepared and ready for paving on June 17, but the field and track were not official open until Friday, August 9 this year, just three days before the start of another school year. An estimated 359 student-athletes were displaced from Piedmont High sports in last year, 2023-24, including the football, cross country, boys and girls’ soccer, and the track program. Girls’ soccer was the first team to play a game at Witter on February 6 – their last scheduled date of the season. Track coach Pouyan Assadi and cross country coach Steve Zirkelbach expressed frustration over the matter. “There seems to be something unpredictable every four weeks. My intention is to be here 20+ years. The willingness to be open and collaborative is critical… We get the disappointing news along with the rest of the public. I’m a coach, I’m also a dad, and I pay property tax. Not just in property tax, but the extra money I spent to have a house here, is because of the great public schools which presumably has excellent decision makers,” Assadi said. “Not having the track’s softer running surface significantly increases risk of injury. I believe some of the injuries we sustained last fall may have been avoided if we trained on a more forgiving surface. It’s a bummer that hundreds of Piedmont kids have been displaced,” Zirkelbach said.

articles.text: Piedmont Council’s four Cub Scout Packs are welcoming new youth to join this fall. Cub Scouts is Scouting America’s program for youth in Kindergarten through 5th Grade. Parents and youth are invited to visit the Packs at their first meeting of the year. These meetings are an opportunity to see what a typical meeting is like, learn about the Pack, their regular activities, and meet the Pack members and leadership. Campers at Cub Scout Day Camp enjoy a water balloon buddy toss. Scouts assist in Piedmont’s annual 4th of July parade as flagbearers. Piedmont Scouting delivers a unique program that encourages youth expression, promotes character building, and gets youth to share experiences outdoors. “I love that Cub Scouts is open to any child from anywhere and of any ability,” said Pack 4 Cubmaster Brad Cardon. “All that is required is an open mind, a sense of adventure, and to embrace the Cub Scout Motto: ‘Do Your Best.’” The beginning of the school year is also a great time to start with a Scout Troop, the Piedmont Community Service Crew, or the Piedmont Service Club for middle school students. “Scouting programs offer the chance to build social connections for both youth and their parents,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “As youth get older, they have opportunities for leadership and character development that can give them an edge as they prepare to launch into adulthood.” Families interested in joining Scouting programs are encouraged to contact Piedmont’s District Executive Eris Turner for more information at eturner@ piedmontbsa.org or 510-844- 4752. Additionally, you can visit the webpage at www.piedmontbsa.org, or visit the Piedmont Scout Office at 10 Highland Way in Piedmont. articles.text: A total of 110 singers from age 7-16 shared music, hikes, arts and crafts at Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s summer camp this year. They challenged themselves to connect, learn and grow for two weeks this past month at Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s annual summer choir camps at Walker Creek Ranch near Petaluma. “Walker Creek is the place everyone learns to connect with choir. “Everyone has about the same memories, with different perspectives,” said 2024 camper Ember. With a daily schedule that wove music throughout, balancing rehearsals and learning with outdoor activities and goofy camp fun, singers and staff bonded and prepared for the coming season. Rafa reflected on his final year as a PEBCC camper: “I have a lot of great memories from camp. Even if you’ve been here a million times, there’s always new places to explore, new things to do with your friends. Musically, the best part is learning all the songs. We’re going to Estonia this year and singing in a big festival there. I already have a billion favorite songs in Estonian.” “I like how funny Mr. Brown is during rehearsals – he makes rehearsals really fun for us. I get to grow in theory, music and singing. I liked getting my mentor- it was making a new friend,” added Zoe. Theory and musicianship classes were a fun challenge for the campers. Campers were so excited to learn about equal temperament and justified tuning. Many of them said it was a highlight from their whole time at camp, even though they described it as “having their brains broken.” “ I like theory and all of the music we’re doing,” shared Laurna. “I’m looking forward to Eric’s new pieces – the parts we’ve done of one of them are really pretty.” At free time, campers enjoyed Turtle Pond adventures, having a blast with swimming and boating. The kayaks were a hit - first time kayaker Emma exclaimed “I love this!!”, and Anar proclaimed “Kayaking is so much fun!” Camp Joyful Voices, PEBCC’s youngest campers, had an afternoon excursion to beautiful Walker Creek (the creek itself), and decided it was so wonderful and pretty that they want to make it a tradition and return to the same place annually. articles.text: McKeegan Autumn is a great time in the East Bay for professional and amateur astronomers, and there’s one place both come together regularly to look up – Chabot Space & Science Center. At 1500 feet in elevation and straddling the border of Alameda and Contra Costa counties, Chabot is the best place possible for an observatory. Since 1883, Chabot has been the Bay Area’s go-to place to learn about and use telescopes. The public has access to three telescopes at Chabot: Leah, an eight-inch refractor telescope, Rachel, a 20-inch refractor telescope (the largest refractor in the Western US regularly open to the public!), and Nellie, a 36-inch reflector telescope. Leah, Rachel, and Nellie welcome the public every Friday and Saturday nights from 7:30 to 10:30 clear weather permitting. Professional and volunteer astronomers and Chabot staff are always on hand to enhance the experience and explain what’s up above. articles.text: It’s back to school time. A time when parents are taking a deep breath. While summer can be super fun, it can also be exhausting because there is so much less structure to the schedule. So, back to the day to day it is for kids and their anxious parents. Get up, get ready, shoes on, out the door and into the classroom on time and ready to learn, As school begins, it can become easy to think that the year needs to follow a specific path and have one set outcome for kids. Of course, we all want our kids to do well in school. But, the definition of “do well in school” can be looked at from different perspectives. It could be a prescribed concept that means one specific path, or it could be a developing idea that shifts and changes daily. School is all about learning. And, as a parent, we can get stuck in believing that the learning journey has a set outcome goal– get good grades, do the right activities, and eventually, get into the right college. This is typically how we all think about school. Every day is one more step towards a set outcome. Therefore, if on any given day your child is struggling with an element of the school process, that becomes a problem. The steps are predetermined, so the path is already made and the child must follow that path. Or, we can see the day to day of growing up and developing, and therefore school, as a creative process. The creative path doesn’t know its end point. It’s the process itself that creates and reveals the end point. If there is no already-predetermined outcome goal, the child is creating the path every day. All of a sudden, a struggle is not a moment where we are fearful of a bad grade, but instead becomes a gift because an opportunity for learning has presented itself. A child’s passions can lead the way, and if those passions change, that’s ok too because the passions are also determining the path. as a creative process, it allows the child’s experience to formulate the path one day at a time and it releases the parent from stressing about every setback. It’s the process of attending school that creates the endpoint. As a result, each step the child takes, even if it is a tiny step or a sideways step or, even a step backwards, is creating the path and the outcome. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Speaker, Consultant and Coach. https:// gocreate.zone. articles.text: On Friday, July 19, a group of the Piedmont Seniors went to visit the Rosie the Riveter Museum, which is part of the World War II National Historic Park, located in Richmond. The Seniors were fortunate enough to meet and have a discussion with 98-year-old “Rosie Jeanne” Gibson, one of two remaining “Rosies” who still volunteer at the Museum. “Rosie Jeanne”, who worked during World War II in Seattle, explained about the dire shortage of housing, thus forcing the Rosies to work in shifts around the clock to share the few available beds. During the visit to the museum, a few of the Piedmont Seniors were shown how to make a rivet and gave it a try. The museum has expanded over the years and now includes a third floor devoted to memorabilia and mannequins of workers in the shipyards. World War II when there was a shortage of workers, young women were recruited as riveters and welders. Sometimes it was difficult for the men working in the industry to accept women as equals and there was a reluctance to overcome Depression-era attitudes about women taking jobs away from men. At that time, men often disapproved of married women working at all. The women were critical workers in the war effort, and Richmond became a vital part of the war effort as ships were being made in large numbers at Richmond’s Kaiser yards. After the war, the women were expected to give up their jobs as men returned home from the war. After the visit to the museum, the Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a relaxing lunch at a nearby bistro before heading to the Red Oak Victory Ship built in Richmond in 1944. This ship carried supplies and troops to the Pacific theater of war. For more information see www.ssredoakvictory.com for hours, fees and directions. The Seniors also visited the Rosie the Riveter Memorial, which included the Keel Walk to the water’s edge, including images and memories of the women who worked there. To find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. Piedmont Seniors at the entrance of the Rosie the Riveter Museum, a National Historic Park in Richmond. Piedmont Seniors try their hands at making a rivet under the instruction of Rosie the Riveter docent Marie Davies. Pictured are Greg Jurin, Sue Getreuer, Carole Jones, Mona Jamieson and Janet Epstein. Janet Epstein and Mona Jamieson with 98-year-old “Rosie Jeanne” Gibson, a volunteer speaker at the Rosie the Riveter Museum.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s free performance in Golden Gate Park is Sunday, September 8, featuring stars from the company’s 2024– 25 season. Opera in the Park, presented in partnership with the San Francisco Chronicle, is now in its 48th year. The free concert celebrates the opening of the San Francisco Opera season, and traditionally draws thousands of attendees for the free afternoon of arias, duets and popular songs at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. Vocal soloists this year will include sopranos Julie Adams, Aleksandra Kurzak and Olivia Smith; mezzo-sopranos Hyona Kim and Daniela Mack; tenors Roberto Alagna, Arturo Chacón-Cruz and Moisés Salazar; baritone Brian Mulligan; and bass-baritone Jongwon Han. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the performances with Company General Director Matthew Shilvock serving as emcee. A rendition of the brindisi (drinking song) from Giuseppe Verdi’s La Traviata traditionally ends this time-honored Bay Area tradition. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and their own food and beverages. Food trucks will also be onsite. The free event begins at 1:30 p.m. and no tickets are required. articles.text: Names like Gianinni, Ratto, Malatesta and Brignole are prominently displayed everywhere, especially on the important buildings. Levaggi built the first opera house. Soon after this, another opera house was built. Wine vineyards and wine production was everywhere. So were olives and olive oil. The small town was famous for its music festivals and people flocked to all the concerts… enthusiastically of course. Musical entertainment was (and is) popular. The restaurants offered excellent pizza and other Italian specialties. Are we in Italy? No. We are in Sutter Creek, California. Even though the town was founded by a Swiss-German named Sutter, the Italian influence remains strong. The restaurant in Hotel Sutter has a mixed reputation. Everything was superb for dinner on Saturday evening. The prime rib was really prime beef. When we asked our waiter to divide the dinner, he gave us a large portion of prime rib. Each of us got a gigantic “loaded baked potato“ and one of the best salads that I have ever had. The “harvest salad” was beautiful to look at and is easy to make. First, you’ll need to roast some peaches. Mix them with lettuce and some dried fruit and use a raspberry vinaigrette dressing. The price was $20 and was a real value. Our waiter, Aaron, was very attentive and even included a complementary apple crisp for our dessert. When I was beginning my musical career, my teachers always spoke of the great musicians of the past. Friends of mine knew the great composer Puccini and they talked about famous violinists such as Joachim and Sarasate, and many other important Dinner in Sutter Creek personages. In those days, everything was done to let the music speak for itself. Performers on stage were reserved. Buffoonery was for the circus. Sadly, things have changed. In today’s classical world, musicians compete with each other to match the buffoonery of the pop culture. It is important to choose which path you want to go. Last Tuesday I went to one of the noontime concerts at Old St. Mary’s at the vortex of the Financial District and Chinatown. The featured performers were cellist Evan Kahn and pianist Amy Zanrosso. Musically, the concert was a complete delight. As they played, a seamless kaleidoscope of emotions became apparent. The program itself was completely balanced, going from Beethoven to Glazunov and concluding with Benjamin Britten. The musical duo did everything that was necessary. They didn’t need amplification. Evan Khan is the new first cellist of the San Francisco Opera. He is first and foremost an elegant performer. Among his assets are a suave and elegant tone. All of these things were increased because of the immense sensitivity of the pianist, Amy Zanrosso. I don’t think it was possible for the ensemble to be better. Pianist Amy Zanrosso and cellist Evan Kahn presented a memorable concert for San Francisco’s noontime concerts.

Admission to OMCA’s Galleries of California Art, History, and Natural Sciences is free on Sunday, September 1, and tickets to special exhibitions in the museum’s Great Hall are offered at a discounted price of $6. articles.text: The de Young Museum, one of the two fine arts museums in San Francisco, is exhibiting impressionist and realist artworks spanning 1848 to 1960 in an exhibition entitled “American Beauty” now through October 20. American art in the 19th and 20th centuries presents a variety of artistic responses during a complex period in US history. Artwork featured is borrowed from Bernard and Barbro Osher, which enhances the de Young’s American art collection with several significant firsts. The exhibition includes the first large-scale oil painting by Winslow Homer (The Angler, ca. 1874), the first genre picture by William Merritt Chase (Spanish Bric-à-Brac Shop, 1883), the first major George Bellows landscape (In Virginia, 1908), the first Georgia O’Keeffe images of the Southwest (Front of Ranchos Church, 1930 and The Patio, 1940), as well as thirteen artists entering the museum’s collection for the first time. To learn more about the exhibition, visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/osher-american-art.
articles.title: American Beauty exhibition on view at deYoung Museum through October

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s new commissioned piece by Stockon-born artist Kara Walker, entitled Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine), is on view through May 2026. Walker is a contemporary painter, silhouettist, printmaker, installation artist, filmmaker, and professor who explores race, gender, sexuality, violence, and identity in her work. She is best known for her room-size tableaux of black cut-paper silhouettes. Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) is a colossal version of her trademark artworks, and marks Walker’s most ambitious large-scale public project to date, as well as the first time the museum commissioned an artist to create a site-specific installation for the Roberts Family Gallery. Walker’s new artwork follows other major exhibitions in the space including Diego Rivera’s Pan American Unity. The commission was organized by Eungie Joo, SFMOMA’s curator and head of contemporary art, who worked with the artists many times over the last 27 years. “Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) emerges out of the abject loneliness of the COVID-19 pandemic and the ominous depopulation of our once thriving downtown San Francisco,” Joo said. Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA’s Helen and Charles Schwab Director, said Walker’s “profound installation grapples with critical subjects relating to our shared humanity, the rapidly expanding role of technology and our aspirations and fears for the future.” “These topics find fresh life and meaning through the distinct lens of her practice, which has for decades confronted challenging histories and realities through formal experimentation and innovation,” he said. The commission is part of the museum’s vision and mission to present work that has strong resonance for Bay Area communities. “With her towering composition of Black automatons enacting ritual and witness amidst a sea of gleaming obsidian, Walker has created a fantastical space of reflection, memorialization and possibility,” Joo said. “I look forward to spending many hours with the work thinking about our shared future.” To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/fortuna-and-the-immortality-garden-machine/. Photo by Ari Macropoulos Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) by Kara Walker
articles.title: Kara Walker artwork on view at SF MoMA

articles.text: Three artists have combined their talents to present a unique art exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening September 7. Elena Doronkina is an award-winning artist and an American Women Artists associate member. For the last five years, she has been a Program Director at the Alamo Danville Artist’s Society (ADAS) and a manager at Blackhawk Gallery in Danville, CA. Elena’s artistic vision: Fine art, in my opinion, is a vehicle for emotional expression, and I strive to elicit the same feelings in the viewer that I encounter during the artistic process. When the viewer experiences a profound emotional connection, I consider my artwork finalized. Alexander Zimin is an Internationally known Artist from Russia. His first significant exhibition was held in Finland in 1994 (Koscengalleria, Imatra). Since then, he has taken part in more than 60 exhibitions in Russia, the USA, China, Finland, Greece, Estonia, Italy. Prizewinner of the landscape art festival (Carmel, CA) in 2001 and 2002. Teaching: since 2008, Zimin has participated in the international educational project “Repin Institute in Kotka” (Finland), and repeatedly held master classes in painting in California. Natalya Biktairova is a unique modern graphic artist and fashion designer. Natalya has a great sense of color and is a virtuoso in drawing. Art is her passion – her air – and she can’t imagine her life without it. Natalya engages in an interactive process with her clients to select the item that will become the ‘canvas’ for the work and understand the concept that the client imagines.

articles.text: Rose Byrne, Ethan Hawke and Azhy Robertson in Juliet, Naked Juliet, Naked is a film that finds its sweet spot early and remains there. It’s subtly comedic (never overtly or obvious) and is in the main all about conversation, even via email. The characters talk, and argue in a kind of discontented, inquisitive manner with an overlay of kindness. The title of the film does not offer any scene where the human anatomy is revealed. Actually, Juliet’s nakedness refers to a song written by a long-ago rocker Tucker Crowe (Ethan Hawke) who was about to make a splash in the world of clubs and concerts. Instead, he walks out of a late night gig and vanishes into the ether of marginally famous Since then, two decades ago, he has been resurrected by a small but obsessed fan base, its leader, Duncan (Chris O’Dowd), a college professor, brags that he is schooled in all facts and rumors having to do with Tucker’s catalog and personal life. For the last 15 years, Duncan has lived in a picturesque, oceanside village with Annie (Rose Byrne), a museum curator, who is finally realizing that her beau is far more enamored of Crowe minutiae than he is of her. And so, over a restaurant dinner, Duncan reveals that he has had an affair with one of his auditing college students and explains to Annie how much better he feels getting the truth out on the white cloth-covered table. Annie leaves understanding that this period of her life is over. Meanwhile, A n nie has received an email from none other than Tucker Crowe – The Tucker Crowe. A fact that she has kept from Duncan. The two begin to share emails and disclose long tamped down emotions, all while discovering that they feel a mutual attraction. They also reveal that they each carry a sense of deep regret – he for the wreckage he’s left behind in his wake – five children and four wives; she for wasting 15 years staying safely with Duncan and fearing living a bit dangerously as well as wishing she had children. Annie and Tucker meet when Tucker comes to London to be with one of his children who is with child. It’s then that the movie earnestly begins and the chemistry foreshadowed through texting and emails is fully revealed. This is a movie with a wonderfully light touch and which relies on the performances of Hawke, Byrnes and O’Dowd. It is charming all the way to its final moments and its very un-Hollywood, un-romcom ending. Juliet, Naked. Starring Rose Byrne, Ethan Hawke and Chris O’Dowd. Directed by J.esse Peretz. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated R. Released in 2018. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/MAX/ apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Juliet, Naked a sweet story of mid-life romance

articles.text: August 24-25, 11:00 a.m. – 2 p.m. Xtra-Dimensions Art Exhibit A local artist and emeritus professor of chemistry at Cal, now living in Montclair, Paul Bartlett has tried for years to find ways to think in three dimensions and has now developed techniques of layering images in ways that show the three-dimensional reality rather than just implying it in only two dimensions. His approach is effective for many types of images: forest scenes with overlapping foliage or trees, cityscapes or abstract images with underlying geometric patterns – in short, any image where additional dimensions stimulate closer inspection and the discovery of something that would be missed in a two-dimensional print. This special exhibition will be open to the public, free, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays through August 25, 2024. Your world has more than two dimensions – so should your pictures. Aug. 31 – Sept. 22 Elena Doronkina New Work Exhibition Returning to PCA for her second exhibition of new works, Russian-born Elena Doronkina brings back a friend and compatriot, Alexander Zimin, to share another PCA experience! Elena drew rave reviews in the summer of 2023 with her first exhibition here, and again will have still lifes, figurative works, and landscapes, all beautifully painted by this true professional. An award-winning artist, an American Women Artists member, a Program Director at the Alamo Danville Artist’s Society (ADAS) for the last five years and a manager at Blackhawk Gallery in Danville, she says, “Fine art, in my opinion, is a vehicle for emotional expression, and I strive to elicit the same feelings in the viewer that I encounter during the artistic process.” The Gallery will be open for viewing every Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on the above dates, and the artists will host an opening reception on Saturday, September 7, from 6 to 9 p.m., during which Natalya Biktairova will show her fabric works also. September 14, 4:30 p.m. Boon Hiker Band Concert The Boon Hiker Band includes John Bidwell, Clare Broussard, J.T. Devine, Robin Eschner, Natasha Haugnes, Dennis Hysom, Chris Smith, and John Tuttle. The eight members of the group bring dynamic vocal harmonies to the heart of the original compositions and the arrangements of covers – all supported by various combinations of guitar, bass, keyboard, banjo, accordion, dobro, lap steel and percussion. The songs lean toward Americana/Folk/Indie traditions, with energetic and vibrant musicianship provided by the three East Bay members - Natasha Haugnes, John Tuttle and John Bidwell (Quake City Jug Band, The Lonestar Retrobates, and Walavista Ave. neighborhood sidewalk jams). The five North Bay members enhance the vocal textures and harmonies with their choral backgrounds (Acorn MusEcology Project, Chimney Full of Birds, Cantiamo). Fans of the Boon Hiker Band recently arrived in fine feather to fill The Abbey at the HopMonk Tavern in Sebastopol for an evening of lively, beautifully performed, inspiring music that brought smiles to the crowd. Several fans even maneuvered to the front for some unanticipated dancing! Advance tickets for this concert can be found on Brown Paper Tickets at https://bpt.me/6383991. Doors will open at 4 p.m. Coming up... September 21… In the Tradition jazz & pop piano trio celebrating Autumn in the Jazz Club September 22… 1st of three Festival Opera vocal recitals with piano September 28 — October 6 (weekends)… Michelle Tholen art exhibition September 28… Jay Krohnengold & Amy Dondy vocal/ piano recital September 29… 1st of four Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concerts October 18… 12th Annual Artisanal Brewing Competition October 19 — November 3 (weekends)… Bill Prochnow Art Exhibition …. And many others beyond, including Big Harp George, Duo Sabu, Michael Stehr’s art, SF Mandolin Orchestra, and Piedmont Chamber Orchestra’s Fall Concert!

articles.text: To watch the work of animator and writer Hayao Miyazaki is to be in the presence of creative genius, a master storyteller who invariably finds that engaging sweet spot: always surprising, perhaps a little scary, and consistently filled with mesmerizing wonder. Made in 1988, My Neighbor Totoro is at the top of the list. If you have yet to sample one of his films Totoro is a solid beginning. The story is absent rough edged villains. There is no conflict, and it is told from the point of view of two young sisters, Mei and Satsuki (Dakota Fanning and Elle Fanning). It is, as well, an extraordinary co-mingling of fantasy and reality, which defines the essence of childhood. Nothing about Totoro is intended to be even remotely spooky. Perhaps touched lightly by sadness, the spare story fits nicely under an umbrella of joy, imagination, and hand-drawn visuals that possess a palate of rich colors and an unfailingly detailed background. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1958. Professor Kusakabe (Tim Daly), a loving father, with his daughters move into an old, creaky house that is filled with enchantment and magic. It sits on the outskirts of a sweeping forest, never forbidding or menacing. The girls immediately take notice of a massive camphor tree that seems to stretch in all directions. The tree, they discover, is the home to a giant, benign creature called a totoro, which can only be described as an amalgam of a penguin, rabbit and owl. The narrative unfolds slowly. We learn that the reason that their father has chosen this particular place to live is that it is close to his wife (Lea Salonga) and the girls’ mother who is in the hospital. At the same time, with the nudging worry about their mother’s illness ever present, the sisters find pure pleasure and excitement in simply hanging out with A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s My Neighbor Totoro For advance tickets, go to https://bpt.me/6383991 or use this QR code:

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty From the world renowned Japanese Studio Ghibli, The Secret World of Arrietty was co-written by two of its principal storytellers, Hiromasa Yonebayashi and Hayao Miyazaki. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, the Borrowers are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure she finds fascinating by the sheer size of the bean world. She is also drawn into Shawn’s personal world and is soon discovered by the bean boy. Surprisingly these two most disparate characters fashion a friendship and a bond of trust. The tree, they discover, is the home to a giant, benign creature called a totoro, which can only be described as an amalgam of a penguin, rabbit and owl. The narrative unfolds slowly. We learn that the reason that their father has chosen this particular place to live is that it is close to his wife (Lea Salonga) and the girls’ mother who is in the hospital. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, the Borrowers are put in real danger and must find a new residence. articles.text: As part of its 20th-anniversary celebration, George Mark Children’s House had its first-ever Hummingbird Awards ceremony to honor individuals who have significantly advanced its mission of caring for seriously ill children and their families. “The Hummingbird Awards were established to recognize and express our deep gratitude to individuals and organizations that have played an outstanding role in furthering the mission of George Mark Children’s House,” read a press release from the event. “Hummingbirds hold a special place in the hearts of our community. They are symbols of healing, comfort and hope, especially when patients, families, and staff need the support most.” The George Mark Children’s House is a nonprofit pediatric hospice in San Leandro that offers comprehensive pediatric medical care to children with serious medical conditions. When it opened in 2004, the house was A row of Hummingbird Awards, cast by local metalworkers at ArtWorks Foundry in Berkeley. the only independent site in the country to provide both medical child care and end-of-life management for children, according to the New York Times. Since then, GMCH has inspired others to follow this type of model in palliative healthcare models across the United States. The Hummingbird Awards were presented by George Mark founder Kathy Hull and George Mark CEO Shekinah Eliassen during a rededication ceremony on Hummingbird Hill, the tranquil and welcoming gardens at George Mark Children’s House named for the presence of hummingbirds on the grounds. This serene setting provided an apt backdrop for honoring the individuals and organizations who have made an impact on GMCH’s mission. Alameda County District 3 Supervisor Lena Tam presented a proclamation honoring George Mark for its 20 years of dedicated service to children and their families and saluted the 2024 recipients of the Hummingbird Award. A framed commendation was presented to George Mark Children’s House by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors in recognition of its two decades of service to patients and their families. George Mark House founder Kathy Hull (left), Alameda County Supervisor Lena Tam and George Mark House CEO Shekinah Eliassen meaningful difference in the lives of George Mark patients and their families. Alyssa Wallace, Manager of Corporate Social Responsibility at Pixar Animation Studios, accepted the award on the studio’s behalf. Wilma Chan, Alameda County Board of Supervisors The late Supervisor Wilma Chan, Alameda County Board of Supervisors, a distinguished advocate and early champion of George Mark Children’s House, played a pivotal role in the organization’s foundational years. Chan’s former Chief of Staff Rachel Richman accepted the award on her behalf. Wilma Chan passed away on November 3, 2021, after she was struck by a vehicle while walking her dog near the intersection of Shore Line Drive and Grand Street in Alameda. Bob Pauley & Jerome Ranft, Pixar Animation Studios Artists These distinguished artists (Toy Story, Finding Nemo, Cars) have contributed their time, sketches, illustrations and maquettes of hummingbirds to George Mark Children’s House pro bono. Cody Lyon, Pixar Animation Studio Artist Known for his work on films like Elemental and Coco, Lyon is a familiar presence at George Mark events where he creates animated versions of families as part of memory-building activities. He has also designed and created a stunning mural in the GMCH Art Room as a poignant tribute to a bereaved family. Kambiz Mehrafshani, Artworks Foundry Mehrafshani has been instrumental in producing the exquisite Pixar-designed bronze statues presented as awards for the Hummingbird Awards, further enhancing the legacy of compassion and artistry at GMCH. Serpico Landscaping For over 15 years, Serpico Landscaping has generously provided pro bono landscaping services, ensuring the gardens and Hummingbird Hill are meticulously maintained. George Mark Children’s House is located at 2121 George Mark Ln in San Leandro. To donate, volunteer or refer a family for care, please visit their website at www. georgemark.org.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Sharon family members Percy Gray painted this watercolor of Casa Montana, the Sharon estate on Mountain Avenue, in the 1920s. The walkers have talked about Frank C. Havens and other early Piedmont real estate developers, but a developer they hadn’t discussed and a street they hadn’t walked this year were William Sharon and Sharon Avenue. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi once devoted an issue of the society’s Piedmont’s History publication to Sharon, his family, and estate. The group decided to walk to Sharon Avenue and discuss its history. The walkers continued to 37 Sharon Avenue where William Sharon’s stories were told. Sharon was born in 1852 and grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he went to San Francisco and then Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, who was a successful banker and silver mine owner. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt in 1876 and they raised a family of 10 children. He became successful in finance and mining and was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. The Sharons initially lived in Virginia City but moved to Oakland in 1890 for better schools. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. In 1897 they hired Frederic D, Voorhess to design their Piedmont home, a magnificent three-story house built in the middle of their property, which they named Casa Montana. In 1914, Piedmont –now an incorporated city – imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property. The Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically, and in 1915 they subdivided their land into a development they called Sharon Terrace. It had 20 lots with frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues, and some family members built homes on them. The driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue, and the address for Casa Montana was changed from 263 Mountain to 37 Sharon Avenue. Sharon died in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home with seven family members and two servants living there. Lillian lived in it until 1934 when she moved to Oakland. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later also built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon, but in 1936 he demolished Casa Montana. The mansion was replaced by three homes at 27, 33, and 37 Sharon. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses remain on the former Casa Montana property, 235 Mountain built in 1908, 56 Sharon built in 1921, and 52 Sharon built in 1922. The walkers took a side trip on Sharon Court. They noted that the exterior 235 Mountain has been updated, and two beautiful red gum eucalyptus trees are in bloom in the front yard. The walkers went up to Pacific, Scenic, and Alta Avenues, with opportunities to enjoy clear views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco. A steep 210-foot set of stairs at 630 Blair got the group back to Pacific, Mountain, Highland, and the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: A few months back I wrote about my recent trip to Burgundy. It is an absolutely beautiful wine region and the wines we tasted there were extraordinary. The Pinot Noir and Chardonnay based wines were complex and interesting and I truly enjoyed the trip. Unlike California, French wineries do not charge for tasting – you also do not just drop in you really need to have a reservation. Being a wine writer, I was treated even better than the average visitor and was always shown great hospitality. The problem was when I got home I was struck with the reality that I could not afford to buy the wonderful wines I had been drinking. The cheapest wines I was served start at around 50 bucks and quickly ascend to the hundreds. They were out of my range as they are for most people. The solution to my problem came when I turned my sights a few miles south of Burgundy and began to focus on the region of Beaujolais. The hilly Beaujolais vineyards stretch out from north to south over 55 kilometers, bordered to the west by the foothills of the Massif Central, and to the easy by the Saone River plain. Located just outside Lyon, the Beaujolais region is less than a 30-minute drive away. Unlike Burgundy, however, the red wines of Beaujolais are based on the Gamay grape variety, which reaches its peak here (even though it’s grown around the world). Most Beaujolais wine is red, but white wines produced from Chardonnay and rosés produced from Gamay grapes are also important parts of the region. Still, it’s the red wines crafted from Gamay that are the calling cards of Beaujolais. There are four key red wine categories from Beaujolais: Beaujolais Nouveau, Beaujolais, Beaujolais-Villages, and Beaujolais Cru. They are all from the Beaujolais wine region, but their origins and styles are notably different. Beaujolais Nouveau is a fresh, fruit-forward wine with light (and often barely perceptible) tannins and a more or less straightforward style. The winemaking technique of carbonic maceration, which is most familiarly used for Beaujolais Nouveau, results in the grapes fermenting within their skins, allowing the winemaker to produce a red wine of freshness and vibrancy. Wines labeled Beaujolais are made from grapes grown throughout the Beaujolais region, especially in the south. These also tend to be quite fruit-forward and are meant to be enjoyed early on. Beaujolais-Villages wines are based on Gamay grapes that were grown in the northern part of the Beaujolais region, specifically 38 permitted villages. And Beaujolais Cru — also called Cru Beaujolais — are grown in any of ten specific locales whose typically granitic soils (though they are far from uniform in composition and character) can produce the most age-worthy and complex of all red wines from Beaujolais. The ten villages, going from north to south, are: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Côte de Brouilly, and Brouilly. Beaujolais also offers a wide range of food-pairing options. Because of the lack of aggressive tannins in Gamay, and the overall character of the red wines of Beaujolais, they tend to work well alongside everything from lighter meats to even fish. Beaujolais Cru, on the other hand, works well with slightly richer foods. The following Beaujolais wines are imported by North Berkeley Imports one of the country’s most reliable provider of French wines. They are available online or at the North Berkeley shop at 1505 Shattuck Ave. in Berkeley. • 2022 Beaujolais Les Grand Coasses. $17 (Great Value) This wine is made by Earl Paul Durdilly et Fils and fills the glass with sumptuous notes of cherries, currants, fig and violets. The medium-bodied palate rolls along the tongue with finesse and impressive concentration that contrasts harmoniously with the delicate tannins and piquant
articles.title: Beaujolais – France’s best bargain

articles.text: Photos by Oakland Zoo August 13 Update: He’s been gaining weight steadily, is now six pounds, sleeps well, and is slowly transitioning from kitten milk replacer to solid food. On the morning of Monday, August 5, Oakland Zoo assisted in rescuing a male mountain lion cub from El Dorado County. This is the 27th mountain lion rescue through the Zoo’s Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT) alliance. The cub, which the Zoo has named Briar, was found by residents on a road in El Dorado County. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) conducted ground and wildlife camera surveillance where the kitten was found, hoping to find a mother or siblings to reunite them. However, no other mountain lions were detected on the cameras. After several days the cub was rescued and brought to Oakland Zoo. The Zoo conducted a full examination and determined that he was 4-5 weeks old, making him one of the Zoo’s youngest mountain lion rescues. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital will continue to care for him and monitor him closely as he adapts to human care. Briar will remain at the Zoo until CDFW identifies a permanent home for the cub. Mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother in the wild to learn survival skills. Because Briar is so young, he lacks those skills and cannot return to the wild. The population of mountain lions faces various conservation challenges in the wild, such as habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict, and climate change. Without information about the cub’s mother, CDFW and the Zoo cannot determine how these factors and many other conservation challenges may have contributed to Briar being orphaned. Photos by Oakland Zoo Briar’s name is inspired by the spots on his fur resembling a blackberry bush.

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, August 21, 2024 The Wine Corner By Pierre DuMont A few months back I wrote about my recent trip to Burgundy. It is an absolutely beautiful wine region and the wines we tasted there were extraordinary. The Pinot Noir and Chardonnay based wines were complex and interesting and I truly enjoyed the trip. Unlike California, French wineries do not charge for tasting – you also do not just drop in you really need to have a reservation. Being a wine writer, I was treated even better than the average visitor and was always shown great hospitality. The problem was when I got home I was struck with the reality that I could not afford to buy the wonderful wines I had been drinking. The cheapest wines I was served start at around 50 bucks and quickly ascend to the hundreds. They were out of my range as they are for most people. The solution to my problem came when I turned my sights a few miles south of Burgundy and began to focus on the region of Beaujolais. The hilly Beaujolais vineyards stretch out from north to south over 55 kilometers, bordered to the west by the foothills of the Massif Central, and to the easy by the Saone River plain. Located just outside Lyon, the Beaujolais region is less than a 30-minute drive away. Unlike Burgundy, however, the red wines of Beaujolais are based on the Gamay grape variety, which reaches its peak here (even though it’s grown around the world). Most Beaujolais wine is red, but white wines produced from Chardonnay and rosés produced from Gamay grapes are also important parts of the region. Still, it’s the red wines crafted from Gamay that are the calling cards of Beaujolais. There are four key red wine categories from Beaujolais: Beaujolais Nouveau, Beaujolais, Beaujolais-Villages, and Beaujolais Cru. They are all from the Beaujolais wine region, but their origins and styles are notably different. Beaujolais Nouveau is a fresh, fruit-forward wine with light (and often barely perceptible) tannins and a more or less straightforward style. The winemaking technique of carbonic maceration, which is most familiarly used for Beaujolais Nouveau, results in the grapes fermenting within their skins, allowing the winemaker to produce a red wine of freshness and vibrancy. Wines labeled Beaujolais are made from grapes grown Beaujolais – France’s best bargain throughout the Beaujolais region, especially in the south. These also tend to be quite fruit-forward and are meant to be enjoyed early on. Beaujolais-Villages wines are based on Gamay grapes that were grown in the northern part of the Beaujolais region, specifically 38 permitted villages. And Beaujolais Cru — also called Cru Beaujolais — are grown in any of ten specific locales whose typically granitic soils (though they are far from uniform in composition and character) can produce the most age-worthy and complex of all red wines from Beaujolais. The ten villages, going from north to south, are: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Côte de Brouilly, and Brouilly. Beaujolais also offers a wide range of food-pairing options. Because of the lack of aggressive tannins in Gamay, and the overall character of the red wines of Beaujolais, they tend to work well alongside everything from lighter meats to even fish. Beaujolais Cru, on the other hand, works well with slightly richer foods. The following Beaujolais wines are imported by North Berkeley Imports one of the country’s most reliable provider of French wines. Dense with flavor and energy throughout the finish, the wine is pleasant in its youth but has more than enough structure to withstand further aging. your Oakland Zoo rescues another mountain lion Photos by Oakland Zoo August 13 Update: He’s been gaining weight steadily, is now six pounds, sleeps well, and is slowly transitioning from kitten milk replacer to solid food. On the morning of Monday, August 5, Oakland Zoo assisted in rescuing a male mountain lion cub from El Dorado County. This is the 27th mountain lion rescue through the Zoo’s Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT) alliance. The cub, which the Zoo has named Briar, was found by residents on a road in El Dorado County. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) conducted ground and wildlife camera surveillance where the kitten was found, hoping to find a mother or siblings to reunite them. However, no other mountain lions were detected on the cameras. After several days the cub was rescued and brought to Oakland Zoo. The Zoo conducted a full examination and determined that he was 4-5 weeks old, making him one of the Zoo’s youngest mountain lion rescues. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital will continue to care for him and monitor him closely as he adapts to human care. Briar will remain at the Zoo until CDFW identifies a permanent home for the cub. Mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother in the wild to learn survival skills. Because Briar is so young, he lacks those skills and cannot return to the wild. The population of mountain lions faces various conservation challenges in the wild, such as habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict, and climate change. Without information about the cub’s mother, CDFW and the Zoo cannot determine how these factors and many other conservation challenges may have contributed to Briar being orphaned. Photos by Oakland Zoo Briar’s name is inspired by the spots on his fur resembling a blackberry bush. Time for R and R After two strenuous days, the Scouts enjoyed three “easy” 10-mile days ahead. They crossed 12,100 foot Pinchot Pass Miguel Long captures a photograph of a spectacular sunset over Arrowhead Lake. (named after the first head of the U.S. Forest Service) and camped at Twin Lakes. An early arrival allowed for swimming, laundry, and fishing. Twin Lakes was filled with aggressively biting Brook Trout, providing plenty of excitement. Spectacular sunsets Day five brought clouds and a spectacular sunset over Arrowhead Lake. Adult leader Steve Long had an epic fishing session, catching 40 trout in just over an hour. The Scouts enjoyed playing their favorite card game, “Deuces,” on a granite rock overlooking the lake and Fin Dome. Final campsite and wildlife encounter After clearing Glen Pass, the group found the perfect final campsite at Kearsarge Lakes, surrounded by water on three sides. A young black bear sighting added to the excitement, reminding the Scouts of the importance of proper food storage. Starry Nights and New Games The Scouts learned a new card game from the Cantrills and played late into the night atop a low granite slab at the edge of the lake. Like other nights, they watched shooting stars, the Milky Way and satellites cross the sky before turning in for a wellearned night’s rest. The expedition was a memorable adventure, filled with challenges, achievements and the beauty of the High Sierra. Scouts Luke Ironside, Migeul Long, Alexander Cantrill, Mateo Long, Ayaan Jajodia are pictured crossing 11,760 ft. Kearsarge Pass. My fitness goals were to increase my vertical, improve my agility and athleticism ,and build more strength. I wanted to be consistent in my training and be as disciplined as possible. How are you measuring your development? I measure my own development by looking back on the previous week to examine where I could improve. An example would be lifting heavier weights and increasing my numbers. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I would occasionally workout with coaches and trainers from basketball, but most of the time I would be on my own. I go to the YMCA to lift and play basketball, but I also frequently workout in a small home gym in our garage. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? In lifting, a recent goal was benching over 200 pounds. In basketball, I would shoot 100 threes from the top of the key, wanting to get 80/100, which I did three times by the end of the summer. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Stay disciplined. You won’t be motivated every day, so maintain a strong work ethic.
