articles.text: Piedmont School Superintendent Dear PUSD Families & Staff: We are back! I am excited to get started and look forward to seeing students and families on the first day of school, August 12, 2024. I confess, I have missed seeing students on campus, and I look forward to a great school year ahead. I would like to welcome new members of our administrative team who’ve hit the ground running and are off to a great start. New Administrators Dr. David Yoshihara – Principal of Piedmont High School. Jamie Van Kleeck – Piedmont Middle School Assistant Principal Tyler Small – PHS Athletic Director Jean Fagin – Director of Special Education We have an outstanding administrative team, and I cannot wait to see what these wonderful educators will accomplish for our students, staff, and community. Our staff and Board have been working hard this summer, including work on our facilities and approval of a parcel tax resolution. The Witter Field renovation project will be completed on August 12th, and I cannot wait to attend our first home football game, August 30th, back on Witter. We also completed roofing projects on the middle school buildings, the Binks Rawlings Gym, and the MHS/District Office building, along with interior upgrades to Millennium HS, a new play structure at Beach, and HVAC on select campuses. Thanks to Pete Palmer, along with our maintenance and custodial staff for their great work. A closer look at the many facilities projects completed can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/ folders/1kxIwMy1OeXYXoGKdZe7YcKuOqFiLnks8 Regarding the parcel tax resolution, our Board has approved replacing Measure H with a new parcel tax that will improve our ability to attract and retain high quality educators along with continued funding for advanced academic programs. In the coming weeks, you will receive more information about this measure, which will provide critical funding for our schools. Part of my summer was spent reading about emerging important topics in education, including Sal Khan’s new book on AI and education and Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation, which offers a deep dive into the effects of technology, including social media and cell phones, on the mental health of our students. We will explore these topics further in community meetings for parents, students, and staff throughout the school year. Speaking of community meetings, I want to update you on our work to create additional opportunities for families to engage and collaborate on programs and key issues throughout this year. articles.text: Piedmont students started the school year on a Monday this year, August 12, after years of confusing mid-week starting days. At Beach, Wildwood and Havens elementary schools a healthy percentage of parents walked their young scholars to campus on Day 1 of the new school year to take dozens of photos of new outfits, haircuts and backpacks. For kids starting school for the very first time, entering Transitional Kindergarten or Kindergarten at 8:30 a.m., parents put aside many common thoughts of work, dinner, bills and everything else to focus on their kids’ first day of school. In such a kidsfirst community, the beginning of the school year brings forth a substantial synchronicity. Students entering Beach School on Lake Avenue walked through a balloon arch of purple and white to see their school’s new playground. At Wildwood, a ceremonial flag- raising ceremony on campus captivated the crowd of parents and students alike. At Havens, kids posed with friends reunited and lined up in single file order for the first time since May. At Havens the steady hand of Principal Anne Dolid led a smooth opening day of the school year. At Beach School, Anne Valva looks more and more at home in the principal’s office in her third year. Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond enters her second year eager to continue the work she began one year ago. The first day of school always brings the possibility of tears from any of Piedmont’s students, parents and siblings at the big change on hand. Nearly all welcomed the new beginning however and the school year in Piedmont has officially begun. For the duration of August, all elementary kids in grades 1-3 will be released from school at 2:00 p.m. This time allows time for teacher assessments. Teachers will be in touch with families to schedule appointments after 2:00 p.m. In September a regular schedule resumes with 3:00 p.m. release times (except Wednesdays) for kids in grades 1-5. (See additional photos in the School Section.)

pages.text: Volume 26, No. 42 Piedmont, California August 14, 2024 91¢ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont Staff photo PHS Assistant Principal Joseph Marik (left), PHS Principal David Yoshihara, PHS Campus Supervisor Michael Bell and Piedmont School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn Supt. Hawn sums up summer, welcomes new year By Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Piedmont School Superintendent Dear PUSD Families & Staff: We are back! I am excited to get started and look forward to seeing students and families on the first day of school, August 12, 2024. I confess, I have missed seeing students on campus, and I look forward to a great school year ahead. I would like to welcome new members of our administrative team who’ve hit the ground running and are off to a great start. New Administrators Dr. David Yoshihara – Principal of Piedmont High School. Jamie Van Kleeck – Piedmont Middle School Assistant Principal Tyler Small – PHS Athletic Director Jean Fagin – Director of Special Education We have an outstanding administrative team, and I cannot wait to see what these wonderful educators will accomplish for our students, staff, and community. Our staff and Board have been working hard this summer, including work on our facilities and approval of a parcel tax resolution. The Witter Field renovation project will be completed on August 12th, and I cannot wait to attend our first home football game, August 30th, back on Witter. We also completed roofing projects on the middle school buildings, the Binks Rawlings Gym, and the MHS/District Office building, along with interior upgrades to Millennium HS, a new play structure at Beach, and HVAC on select campuses. Thanks to Pete Palmer, along with our maintenance and custodial staff for their great work. A closer look at the many facilities projects completed can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/ folders/1kxIwMy1OeXYXoGKdZe7YcKuOqFiLnks8 Regarding the parcel tax resolution, our Board has approved replacing Measure H with a new parcel tax that will improve our ability to attract and retain high quality educators along with continued funding for advanced academic programs. In the coming weeks, you will receive more information about this measure, which will provide critical funding for our schools. Part of my summer was spent reading about emerging important topics in education, including Sal Khan’s new book on AI and education and Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation, which offers a deep dive into the effects of technology, including social media and cell phones, on the mental health of our students. We will explore these topics further in community meetings for parents, students, and staff throughout the school year. Speaking of community meetings, I want to update you on our work to create additional opportunities for families to engage and collaborate on programs and key issues throughout this year. Starting in September, our departments will host open meetSee Supt. Hawn on page 6 Ben Spencer and his 4th grade class for the 2024-25 school year Photo by Tam Bui Students welcome first day of school at Beach, Havens, Wildwood By Jay Russell Piedmont students started the school year on a Monday this year, August 12, after years of confusing mid-week starting days. At Beach, Wildwood and Havens elementary schools a healthy percentage of parents walked their young scholars to campus on Day 1 of the new school year to take dozens of photos of new outfits, haircuts and backpacks. For kids starting school for the very first time, entering Transitional Kindergarten or Kindergarten at 8:30 a.m., parents put aside many common thoughts of work, dinner, bills and everything else to focus on their kids’ first day of school. In such a kidsfirst community, the beginning of the school year brings forth a substantial synchronicity. Students entering Beach School on Lake Avenue walked through a balloon arch of purple and white to see their school’s new playground. At Wildwood, a ceremonial flag- raising ceremony on campus captivated the crowd of parents and students alike. At Havens, kids posed with friends reunited and lined up in single file order for the first time since May. At Havens the steady hand of Principal Anne Dolid led a smooth opening day of the school year. At Beach School, Anne Valva looks more and more at home in the principal’s office in her third year. Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond enters her second year eager to continue the work she began one year ago. The first day of school always brings the possibility of tears from any of Piedmont’s students, parents and siblings at the big change on hand. Nearly all welcomed the new beginning however and the school year in Piedmont has officially begun. For the duration of August, all elementary kids in grades 1-3 will be released from school at 2:00 p.m. This time allows time for teacher assessments. Teachers will be in touch with families to schedule appointments after 2:00 p.m. In September a regular schedule resumes with 3:00 p.m. release times (except Wednesdays) for kids in grades 1-5. (See additional photos in the School Section.) Walkthrough registration prepared these students for a successful first day of school on Friday, August 9. Walk-through registration allowed students in advance to know where to go and what to do on the big first day of class. For the 6th graders, the change was palpable, new classmates, new teachers on a new campus. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has partnered with Ava Community Energy (formerly East Bay Community Energy) to offer an induction burner borrowing program for residents at no cost to the public. Those interested in the Cooktop Lending Program may inquire at the planning and building department front counter at City Hall, Monday-Thursday from 8:30 a.m. - 12 p.m. and 1 p.m. - 5 p.m. to sign up. “The Induction Cooktop Lending Program is a way for East Bay residents to borrow and ‘test drive’ induction cooking in their home for free,” according to the company’s website. “This program is available to all East Bay residents—Ava customers as well as non-Ava customers who receive electric service from PG&E.” Induction burners have been receiving increased attention from home cooks in recent years. Induction appliances are up to three times more efficient than gas stoves, and up to 10% more efficient than conventional smooth top electric ranges according to the Department of Energy. However, many consumers have been slow to embrace them because of the high start-up costs related to converting from gas or electric ranges. The Induction Lending Kit includes a portable induction cooktop, a compatible pan, cooktop operating instructions, recipes and a carrying bag. Residents may also choose between a classic sauté pan and a wok at the time of loan. Induction Lending Kits may be reserved for free at www.tinyurl. com/ava-induction. Burners and cookware may be borrowed for up to two weeks at a time. Wait times to receive burners and cookware may be up to one week. For more information, contact the City of Piedmont Planning and Building Department at 420-3050. articles.text: Pixar studio and artists, former Alameda County Board of Supervisors Member Wilma Chan among those to be honored George Mark Children’s House (GMCH), as part of its 20th-anniversary celebration, will present its first-ever Hummingbird Awards in a ceremony today, August 14, to pay tribute to several individuals and organizations that have played a pivotal role in helping the pediatric hospice provide exceptional care to seriously ill children and support for their families. The ceremony will be held at 11 a.m. at George Mark Children’s House, 2121 George Mark Lane, in San Leandro. The Hummingbird Awards will be part of a re-dedication ceremony for George Mark’s restorative garden, Hummingbird Hill. Hummingbirds hold a special place in the hearts of the community at George Mark Children’s House, symbolizing healing, comfort, and hope. Kathy Hull, founder of George Mark Children’s House, will present the awards with CEO Shekinah Eliassen. Pixar Animation Studios will receive an award for its ongoing commitment and robust volunteer engagement with the organization over the years. “Pixar Animation Studios exemplifies corporate citizenship at its finest, making a meaningful difference in the lives of George Mark patients and their families,” reads a press release from the George Mark Children’s House. The Honorable Wilma Chan, former Alameda County Supervisor, will be honored posthumously at the ceremony. Chan, a distinguished advocate and early champion of George Mark Children’s House, played a pivotal role in the organization’s foundational years. Chan’s former Chief of Staff Rachel Richman will accept the award on her behalf. Alameda County District 3 Supervisor Lena Tam and District 3 Director Silin Huang will also be in attendance. Wilma Chan passed away on November 3, 2021, after she was struck by a vehicle while walking her dog near the intersection of Shoreline Drive and Grand Street in Alameda. Shekinah Eliassen, CEO of George Mark Children’s House, holds a Hummingbird Award. Hummingbird Hill, George Mark Children’s House’s restorative garden, is due for a re-dedication at the awards ceremony. Photos by George Mark Children’s House The first-ever Hummingbird Awards were designed by Pixar artists and cast from bronze by local metalworkers at ArtWorks Foundry. Bob Pauley and Jerome Ranft of Pixar Animation Studios will also receive awards. These distinguished artists – whose work is featured in films Toy Story, Finding Nemo, and Cars – have generously contributed their time, sketches, illustrations and maquettes of hummingbirds to George Mark Children’s House pro bono over the years. Cody Lyon of Pixar Animation Studios (Elemental, Coco) will also be awarded. Lyon is a familiar presence at George Mark events, where he creates animated versions of families as part of memory-building activities. He also designed and created a stunning mural in the GMCH Art Room as a poignant tribute to a bereaved family. Serpico Landscaping will receive an award for generously providing pro bono landscaping services to the GMCH for over 15 years, ensuring the gardens and Hummingbird Hill are meticulously maintained. Kambiz Mehrafshani of ArtWorks Foundry, one of the nation’s leading foundries for the production and restoration of bronze sculptures, reliefs and monuments, will also receive an award. Kambiz has been instrumental in producing the exquisite Pixar-designed bronze statues that will be presented as awards for the Hummingbird Awards, further enhancing the legacy of compassion and artistry at GMCH. Today’s event is closed to the public but open to members of the press. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver You may now subscribe online at:

articles.text: Wistaria Way project specifically does not qualify for SB 9 Mayor Jen Cavanagh has long been a vocal advocate for the environment, consistently highlighting the importance of protecting Piedmont’s natural assets. However, her environmental commitment faces a significant test with a looming decision: Will the city council endorse a developer’s proposal for construction on 77 Wistaria Way, or will it require City staff to comply with Piedmont law and enforce the state and city regulations under SB 9 written to protect the environment? Unless the city council steps in and requires city staff to process the project in compliance with local environmental law, Piedmont will find out by July 16 when construction is set to begin at 77 Wistaria Way. Piedmont’s City staff chose to bypass the Planning Commission’s review of the 77 Wistaria Way project and process it under the State’s SB 9 regulation, which allowed the project to be processed ministerially – by the staff behind closed doors with neither Planning Commission nor public visibility or input. However, per California state law and local Piedmont Code, due to the environmental characteristics of the 77 Wistaria Way property, the project specifically does not qualify for SB 9. According to California state law and local Piedmont law, lots which contain streams, wetland soil or wetland vegetation as defined in Piedmont City Code (Sec. 17.54.050.B 1) and California State Law (SB9) are ineligible for SB9 development. Wildwood Creek and its headwaters traverse this property, a fact well-known to the local community. Many neighbors have actively raised their concerns regarding the staff’s noncompliant decision to process the developer’s application under the expedited and not transparent SB 9 process. Planning staff and City Council received formal notice of the staff’s non-compliance with SB 9 as early as August 23, 2023 – four months prior to the City’s decision to approve the developer’s land-use permit on December 27, 2024. Following the approval of the land use permit, Piedmont residents wrote multiple additional related letters to the city; however, City staff have largely dismissed residents’ concerns, maintaining the site qualifies for processing under SB 9. On June 17 neighbors spoke during the public forum of the city council meeting; the following week they presented a petition to the City, with notice to the developer, requesting to be on the City Council agenda; and again raised their concerns in the July 1 city council meeting. However, the residents’ significant and repeated efforts to urge city council to require City staff to comply with state and local law fell on deaf ears. Piedmont city staff quietly approved building permits for the project last week on July 2. The first offer from the city to engage with residents on the topic came one day later on July 3. It was the day of the Piedmont Post’s first article on this issue, and one day after the City had approved building permits. A meeting between staff and concerned neighbors took place on July 5th. During this meeting, staff asserted confidence in their understanding of the land’s environmental aspects, citing a report from a “licensed biologist” – paid for by the developer – who gave reasons outside the scope of relevant state and local law for why he felt the project should not be disqualified from SB 9 consideration. Despite the developer’s biologist admitting the site contained multiple of the criteria, which would disqualify the project for SB 9 processed, City staff dismissed the neighbors’ claims about the creek, without citing any specifics from the report, only explaining that a report by a “licensed biologist” must be accurate because such a professional would not want to run the risk of losing their license for producing a flawed report. The California License website reveals that “biologist” is not a professional category that holds a license to practice in the state. This situation presents a critical question: Will the city council require staff to comply with the City’s own law, or will the developer’s interests prevail? This question is increasingly important as the city expects to see an increasing number of SB 9 applications, which lowers the bar for developers and often more significant impacts on neighbors.
articles.title: Will the City Council hold its staff accountable to the law?

articles.text: Piedmont Police Department will host its 6th annual car show on September 21 in the center of town. Currently, 70 vehicles have registered for the popular event. It opens at 9:00 a.m. and runs until noon, with cars lined up on Magnolia Avenue near the Exedra. “I’m looking forward to this year’s turnout and our ability to continue to bond with the community through a common interest of beautiful vehicles,” said Officer Tyler Petit the event organizer. The event is not only a chance for the public to see some impres- 2024 Ray Bannister’s 1929 Ford Pickup in last year’s car show sive vehicles but it drives community connections between residents, neighbors, and the Piedmont police officers. “Creating a resilient bond between PPD and the community we serve is priceless and is the true definition of community service. This event is truly a blast. There are so many classic cars and exotic vehicles hidden in garages, and this is an opportunity for people to dust them off and share stories about their history,” said Petit. There will be free coffee at the event and a food truck with food for purchase on site. Cars from coveted Piedmont collections will be on display. Piedmont residents interested in participating are asked to contact Officer Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont.ca.gov. Include name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of the car. September 21, 2024 9 AM - 12 PM 800 MAGNOLIA AVE. PIEDMONT, CA RSVP: coffeecarscops@piedmont.ca.gov

articles.text: Meet Donna, a Rottie mama who just finished caring for her 10 pups and is now hoping someone will give her a forever home. Oakland Animal Services staff report she is low to medium energy, easy to handle, walks well on leash, and has an independent and gentle nature. Donna is available to meet you Thursday from 12 noon- 7 p.m., or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between noon and 3 p.m. or by appointment. articles.text: A look at the possible future of housing in Piedmont is not pretty The developers’ previous involvement in a housing project in San Francisco has residents worried that something similar could happen in Piedmont. A new housing project on Wistaria Way, located at 77 Wistaria Way, has sparked resident concerns that unchecked development could harm their neighborhoods in the near future. Using the framework of SB9 to justify housing projects does not bode well for the city according to nearby residents and a growing chorus of opponents. Residents have repeatedly expressed dissatisfaction with the city government for a lack of transparency during the planning phase and raised questions about what the future of Piedmont will look like under recently passed California housing laws. What happened? The construction project at 77 Wistaria Way aims to divide a vacant lot into two parcels. Property owners Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead, the developers, propose to build a new home on each parcel, as well as a third house as an accessory dwelling unit (ADU). The project’s application was approved by Piedmont’s Planning Department on December 27, 2023. On July 16 this summer- contractors from Gregorio Tree Service began cutting down trees on the property in the heavily wooded cul-de-sac of Wistaria. Controversial new state law SB9 (Senate Bill 9), also known as the California Housing Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act, continues to be a contentious issue in Piedmont. Beginning on January 1, 2022, the state decreed that homeowners can build up to four homes on an existing parcel. According to UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation, this state law effectively eliminates single-family zoning. The law allows the owner to “split” their lot, making it easier to sell or finance additional homes on the same parcel. While supporters believe the law will help address California’s current housing crisis by creating new opportunities for small-scale home building, opponents of SB9 are concerned that it will lead to speculation and unchecked growth at the expense of a community’s character and traditions. Many members of the community have expressed outrage over the plans for the Wistaria Way project. “When I bought my home, I had the guarantee of a single-family-zoned lot. I never anticipated high-density housing Photo by Staff Photos A portion of the creek runs through the properties around Wistaria Way. City officials and residents disagree on whether it qualifies as protected wetlands. A 3D rendering of what the project at 77 Wistaria Way may look like. in my backyard. And now, that’s what I’m getting,” said David Ashton, a third-generation Piedmont resident whose property borders the project. Residents have also complained that the Wistaria project’s three additional homes show no plans for a built-in garage, a move that will make parking scarce on an already narrow 14-foot wide road. “I don’t feel like City Council and staff appreciate that SB9 lot splits are not a desired outcome to the current residents and citizens,” said Rich Latvala, who also lives near the project. Possible wetlands on property Residents and city officials also disagree over the presence of protected wetlands on the property. Residents contend that the construction site at 77 Wistaria Way contains a section of Wildwood Creek which flows through many of their yards and that construction would interfere with the creek. Protected wetlands are considered an exception to SB9, and many residents insist that this should have precluded the Wistaria project’s application from approval. The Planning Department disagrees. “The project was found to be compliant with all state and city regulations under SB9 and our own city code,” said Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “These findings were based on the information provided, which included a report from a licensed biologist that determined that there were no wetlands on the site.” The biologist, he confirmed was hired by the property owners of 77 Wistaria Way. Lack of transparency City officials have said at several public meetings that the owners’ application for a lot split was approved via “ministerial approval,” meaning there was no public review of the building design. This has upset many residents, who believe it is a move away from the city’s usually transparent review practices. “This revised project seems to have avoided the obligatory planning review process that all residents live by under the pretense that it qualifies for SB9. This project will set a precedent for the misuse or application of SB9 in Piedmont that will open the door for unchecked and unreviewed development, degrading the character and standards that make Piedmont the city that it is today,” said Latvala. Some residents also believe that SB9, as it is currently being enforced, lacks refinement. For example, SB9 requires owner occupancy for all lot split developments. The owner must sign an affidavit stating they intend to live in one of the units as their primary residence for at least three years after approval. This requirement is intended to prevent developers from buying lots and splitting them and to maintain affordable housing options for the public. articles.text: The deadline to file nomination papers to run for the office of school board was extended until today, Wednesday, August 14, at 5:00 p.m. after no incumbents eligible to run again submitted papers by the original deadline Friday, August 9. As of Tuesday, August 14 at 7 p.m. six candidates have taken out paperwork, but only Michael Malione has officially qualified by turning in papers, and having signatures verified by the city. The extended deadline applies to non-incumbents only – current Board members are no longer eligible to file. Cory Smegal terms out after 8 years on the school board. Board president Veronica Anderson Thigpen and board member Hilary Cooper did not seek reelection. If there are fewer candidates than open seats, the current school board would turn to appointing members to fill the available seats. Five Piedmont residents initially took out the requisite school board candidate papers by the original August 9 deadline. One additional candidate, Max Roman, took out papers during the deadline’s extension. Roman has notified the Post that he turned in his nomination paperwork on August 13 and awaits the city to confirm his qualification. Piedmont Communications Manager Echa Schneider has informed the Post, that two candidates made appointments to file their paperwork on August 13. The list of candidates that have pulled or filed nomination papers is updated at the end of the day at Piedmont.ca.gov/vote2024 . Three seats will be open this election period, the term of service for the volunteer position is four years and the deadline to file papers is Wednesday, August 14 at 5:00 p.m. Susy Struble August 2 Emily Gorin August 5 Dai Meagher August 6 Victoria Rosenbaum August 6 Max Roman August 12

articles.text: For many children, the journey through school is a time of discovery, learning, and growth. However, for those with speech and language disorders, this journey can be fraught with challenges that impact their academic performance and overall school experience. Understanding the profound effects these disorders have on a child’s educational journey is crucial for parents, educators and policymakers. Speech and language disorders encompass a range of issues, including difficulties with articulation, fluency, voice and the ability to understand and use language effectively. These disorders can significantly affect a child’s ability to engage in the classroom. For instance, a child with a language disorder may struggle to follow verbal instructions, understand complex sentences or grasp new vocabulary. This can lead to difficulties in reading comprehension, writing, and participating in class discussions. Articulation disorders, where children have trouble pronouncing sounds correctly, can make their speech difficult to understand. This often results in children feeling self-conscious, leading to reduced participation in classroom activities and discussions. Fluency disorders, such as stuttering, can cause interruptions in the flow of speech, making it challenging for children to express their thoughts clearly and confidently. One of the most significant impacts of speech and language disorders is on literacy development. Reading and writing are foundational skills for academic success, and children with speech and language disorders often find these areas particularly challenging. Difficulty with phonological awareness – the ability to recognize and manipulate sounds in words – can hinder reading development. Children may struggle with decoding words, leading to poor reading fluency and comprehension. Writing can also be problematic. Children with language disorders may have trouble organizing their thoughts and using appropriate vocabulary and grammar. This can result in written work that is unclear and lacks detail, affecting their performance in assignments and exams. The academic struggles faced by children with speech and language disorders often extend beyond academics, affecting their social and emotional well-being. Communication is key to forming and maintaining relationships, and children who struggle to express themselves or understand others may experience social isolation. They may find it hard to make friends, join in play, or participate in group activities, leading to feelings of frustration, anxiety and low self-esteem. Early identification and intervention are critical in helping children with speech and language disorders succeed academically. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) play a vital role in assessing and treating these disorders. They work with children to improve their speech and language skills through targeted therapy, helping them to communicate more effectively. In the classroom, teachers can support these children by using clear and simple instructions, visual aids, and providing additional time for tasks. Collaborative efforts between SLPs, teachers and parents are essential to create individualized education plans (IEPs) that address the specific needs of each child. These plans may include accommodations such as speech therapy sessions, modified assignments and alternative communication methods. Schools and communities must work together to provide a supportive environment for children with speech and language disorders. Training teachers to recognize the signs of these disorders and implement effective strategies in the classroom is vital. Additionally, raising awareness among peers about the challenges their classmates face can foster a more inclusive and understanding school culture. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

articles.text: With the new school year starting, the Class of 2025 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as seniors. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. JULIANA THORNBORROW Soccer Staff Photos Will Parker led Piedmont’s baseball team with a .375 batting average. Juliana Thornborrow is one of Dan Chubbock’s most versatile players on the lacrosse team, contributing as a ball-handling midfielder and as a playmaker, a passer and a shooter. She earned an honorable mention for AllLeague honors last winter. The girls’ soccer team finished its season with a 12-2-4 (W-T-L) record, reaching the Division 3 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 7 before losing 2-0 to No. 2 Cardinal Newman on February 16. They beat No. 10 Albany 6-0 in the opening round three days prior and finished second in the Foothill Division. Both the girls’ and boys’ soccer teams were displaced for the entire season due to delays in construction at Witter Field. The girls returned to Witter in triumphant manner on February 6 when they beat rival Bishop O’Dowd 2- 1 on Senor Night. WILL PARKER Baseball Will Parker is a big hitter on the baseball team and often lines up as their starting catcher. Last spring, the Highlanders had one of its best seasons in coach Eric Olson’s 12 years at the school, winning the WACC regular season and advancing to the finals of the North Coast section in the post-season playoffs. They also qualified for the first time in the CIF NorCal tournament. Parker earned first-team AllLeague honors as one of its most productive batters. In 2024, Will led the team with a .375 batting average, recording 33 hits with eight doubles, He picked up 24 RBIs and scored 22 runs. PHS finished with a 19-10 record and won the Foothill regular season first-place banner with a 7-3 league record. PHS battled to the D4 NCS Championship as the No. 2 seed, losing to No. 4 Justin-Siena 11-1 on May 25. Earning the No. 1 seed on the Northern California playoffs, PHS beat No. 8 Capuchino 13-1, won 5-0 over No. 4 Colusa, but lost 6-0 to No. 2 Bradshaw Christian in the championship game on June 1. Miguel Long competes in football as a defensive back and is a long jumper in track. MIGUEL LONG Football, Track & Field Juliana Thornborrow is a versatile midfielder for the Highlander lacrosse team. Miguel Long is a two-sport athlete in football along with track and field. On the football gridiron he is a defensive back and a receiver. In track, Long predominantly competes as a long jumper. In football team he will be a three-year starter after earning second-team All-League honors as a defensive back last season. The team went 7-4 and received the No. 5 seed as a Division 5 team (small school enrollment) in North Coast Section. It won the WACC Shoreline Division title by defeating Newark Memorial in a heated 29-26 battle. Long was crucial in Piedmont’s win over the Cougars with two interceptions during Newark’s final two offensive drives. In track, Long reached the NCS Meet of Champions in the triple jump, finishing 13th of 23 with a distance of 42 feet, 1 inch. In the North Coast Section Bayshore meet he was fourth of 21 athletes with a leap of 43 feet, 1 inch.
articles.title: A look ahead at the Class of 2025

articles.text: The 2024 Summer Olympics have officially concluded in Paris, France with the United States claiming the most gold medals and an overall medal count with 40 gold, 44 silver, and 42 bronze. China finished second with 40 gold, 27 silver, and 24 bronze, while England had the third-most medals with 14 gold, 22 silver, and 28 bronze. Last week we reported on some highlights; • Katie Ledecky became the country’s most decorated swimmer ever, • The men’s gymnastics team surprised more than a few people by winning a bronze medal, • Noah Lyles’ 100-meter win in track • Julien Alfred of tiny St. Lucia won the women’s 100 meters • A pair of sharpshooters whose video went viral. Here’s a rundown of The Posts favorite moments from this year’s Olympic Games. Stephen Curry shines in semifinals, finals Stephen Curry showed the world just how significant a basketball star he is with big performances in the Olympic semifinals and finals. He scored 36 points with nine 3-pointers in the United States’ comeback 95-91 win over Serbia, then had 24 points in the 98-87 win over France for a gold medal. It was his first Olympics appearance. Perhaps his most stunning show came with 35 seconds left in the game, hurling a shot above two pursuing defenders, then hitting his memorable ‘Night, Night’ celebration. French broadcasters were calling him “the Devil named Curry.” U.S. Women’s soccer team is back on top The United States Women’s National soccer team won the gold medal for the first time since 2012 in a heated 1-nil win over Brazil. Since failing to advance to the knockout stage for the first time in 20 years one year ago, the U.S. took an early exit from the World Cup. The U.S. dynasty was in peril without a clear path forward. But with the hiring of Emma Hayes as new head coach less than six months ago and a lineup with a half dozen new players, the U.S. won all three of its knockout stages at the Olympics with1- nil victories. They beat Japan in extra time in the quarterfinals with a spectacular goal by Trinity Rodman, then followed with another overtime win over Germany on a sweet goal by Sophia Smith. In the gold medal game, Mallory Swanson, one third of the U.S. front line put away the second half winner in the 57th minute. It was a gutsy tournament by USWNT manager Emma Hayes, who opted to go without legendary women’s striker Alex Morgan. Perhaps Morgan could’ve given them more firepower, but the new forward combination of Smith, Rodman. Swanson was enough to get it done. Sha’Carri Richardson wins gold As the anchor of the women’s 4x100 relay team, Sha’Carri Richardson helped propel Team USA to the top by storming past the competition under a rainy sky. She even had time to look back at her competition as she approached the finish line. Lyles wins gold, bronze Although Noah Lyles couldn’t follow up his gold medal in the 100 meter dash with another top spot to his claim, he still made headlines by taking bronze under difficult circumstances. Lyles tested positive for COVID prior to the race and still ran, clocking a time of 19.70 to earn a medal. Gasping for breath at the end of the race, it was a moment that showed the sprinter’s prowess on the track despite placing third. Biles & Chiles celebrate Brazil’s Andrade With gymnast Simone Biles taking silver in the floor exercise and her United States’ teammate Jordan Chiles earning bronze, the pair took a respectful to Brazil’s gold medal winner, Rebeca Andrade. After the United States’ duo received their medals, the two turned to Andrade to celebrate her moment. It marked the first all-Black podium in Olympics women’s history. Break Dancing This year’s Olympic Games brought along many viral moments, but perhaps one not as funny (or embarrassing) as the Breaker (break dancing) competition. In particular, Australia’s Rachael Gunn made headlines for not being the most fleet-footed or flashy on the dance floor, instead showing off some wacky moves—like pretending to be a kangaroo, among other not so flattering moves. Perhaps it’s best we leave Break Dancing off the Olympic stage going forward. Photo courtesy of Yahoo Sports Sha’Carri Richardson takes a look at her competition as she sprints to her first gold medal. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

What is your workout program this summer? This summer was very eventful, busy with soccer and traveling. I spent most of my summer on the East Coast in the Boston and New York area, mainly for soccer but also some family vacation time. I made sure there was some level of soccer games/training/ practice, at least 4-5 days per week. I attended multiple camps, played lots of 11 v 11 games, and met many amazing players from all over the country. What are your fitness goals for the summer? As a forward, it is important to have the ability to convert goal-scoring opportunities into goals, which requires speed and strong technical ability. While I am pretty explosive, I need to continue working on my speed as well as technical aspects in front of the goal. How are you measuring your development? Over the last couple of years I have become more aware of development. While step-change in an athlete’s performance is very exciting, most progress is reflected as small incremental steps. articles.text: It has nearly been a full month since the Park Fire erupted on July 24 in Butte County outside of Chico. It has burned 429,263 acres as of Tuesday, August 13, and is the fourth largest wildfire in California history. The Park Fire was classified as arson after 42-year-old Ronnie Dean Stout II pushed his burning car into a ravine. He was sentenced to 25 years to life after starting the blaze. It is the largest fire caused by arson in state history. A press release issued by Cal Fire officials stated, “As the fire was starting, an unknown male was seen pushing a car that was on fire into a gulley near Alligator Hole in upper Bidwell Park. The car went approximately 60 feet down an embankment near Chico Creek, burning completely and spreading the flames that became the Park Fire.” Wind and dry conditions helped propel the fire exponentially over the first week. The blaze picked up 124,948 acres over the first 24 hours, then exploded to 239,152 over another 24 hours. So far, Tehama County has suffered the brunt of damage with 376,322 acres, while Butte County has had 52,937 acres destroyed. Lassen National ForPhotos courtesy of CalFire The Park Fire is now the fourth largest wildfire in California history. est has lost 113,736 acres to the fire. Butte County has taken most of the property damage with 428 destroyed structures and 47 damaged. “Firefighters continued to patrol the Park Fire overnight. With no additional growth, increased containment, and improving weather conditions, the amount of remaining hot spots along the fire’s edge and potential for additional growth will continue to decrease. Firefighters on the ground continue to be assisted by the infrared capabilities of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) and aircraft to locate remaining hot spots and extinguish them. Today, firefighting resources are focused on hazard tree removal along roadways and the fire perimeter, suppression repair efforts, strengthening existing fire line, and patrol of the entire fire perimeter,” a Lassen National Forest spokesperson said, via CalFire.com. The fire had no containment from July 24-26, and is now 39 percent contained. There have even been reports of rare pyrocumulonimbus clouds, thunderclouds produced by smoke and high heat. The Park Fire has called for 5,638 personnel members, 18 helicopters, 407 fire engines, 108 bulldozers, 216 water tenders, and 128 fire crews. A total of 5,638 fire personnel have been deployed to combat the Park Fire. The Park Fire is considered arson by Ronnie Dean Stout II after pushing his burning car into a gulley.

articles.text: [Originally printed in the Post in August 2022] Hola! Lisbon, Portugal is considered a great city for walking and hiking. The streets are tightly packed and have rolling hills similar to San Francisco. It’s a city where you can find great food, culture, warm weather, and a lot of history. Should you ever find yourself in Lisboa, an easy walk for all ages goes through the heart of the city from Parque Eduardo VII, down Avenida da Liberdade and Rau Augusta to the historic Praça do Comércio pm the edge of the Tagus River in just 2.1 miles of walking. The route from Praça do Comércio, or Commerce Square, goes slightly uphill on its way to Park Eduardo VII, so we start our venture at the top at the park for an easy walk. Parque Eduardo VII is 64 acres and just north of Avenida da Liberdad. The park is named after King Edward VII of Great Britain after he visited Portugal in 1903 to strengthen the relationship between the two countries and reaffirm their alliance. The park has a central strip of grass and an intricate hedge work, flanked by long walkways to the left and right. At the observation deck at the top of the park, you will see a statue of Marquês de Pombal and the Tagus River off in the distance. Praça do Marquês de Pombal is a roundabout and square dedicated to the Portuguese statesman and diplomat who effectively ruled the Portuguese Empire from 1750 to 1777 as chief minister to King Joseph I. From there, you venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon that could draw comparisons to the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. The largest monument is dedicated to the fallen soldiers in World War I. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores which was made to memorialize Portugal’s victory in the Portuguese Restoration War of 1640-1668 and erected in 1886. The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. From there, you venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon that could draw comparisons to the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. The largest monument is dedicated to the fallen soldiers in World War I. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores which was made to memorialize Portugal’s victory in the Portuguese Restoration War of 1640-1668 and erected in 1886. The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. articles.text: All summer performances at Filoli House are held outside during the summer. Beginning this Friday, August 16, Filoli House and Garden will host a series of outdoor performances called Summer Stage. The vibrant live performances feature everything from mariachi to jazz and take place against the backdrop of the historic Filoli House in Woodside. Guests are invited to relax in the meadow with a drink and food and enjoy the variety of performers coming to Filoli this summer. Performances begin at 5:30 p.m. each night with shows running from 6:30 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. VIP ticket-holders enjoy free wine, beer, canned cocktails, non-alcoholic drinks, and snacks throughout the evening. Every VIP ticket includes access to an Adirondack chair with a great view of the stage. For more information, visit https://filoli.org/summer-stage/.

articles.text: Louisiana-born singer-songwriter and solo guitarist Lucinda Williams performs this weekend, Sunday, August 18, at Stern Grove Festival in San Francisco. The 87th season of Stern Grove Festival, the country’s oldest nonprofit music festival, continues through August 25. Williams, originally from Lake Charles, Louisiana, has a long discography which includes elements of folk, rock, and country with a bayou twang. In 1988, Williams released her third, self-entitled album to wide acclaim. Williams’ biggest commercial successes were earned by her songwriting abilities. The 71-year-old’s first two albums, Ramblin’ on My Mind and Happy Woman Blues, incorporated a traditional country and blues style that received widespread critical praise. The amphitheater at Sigmund Stern Grove hosts ten weeks of admission-free concerts June through August. Concerts are free and on a reservation basis, but picnic tables are available to purchase. Visit https://www.sterngrove. org to reserve tickets. articles.text: Exhibition ends this Sunday The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s Art of Noise exhibition ends this Sunday, August 18. The exhibit includes more than 800 artworks largely from the SFMOMA collection including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that combine design and audio. The exhibition covers more than 100 years of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibition are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org. Selected pieces from SFMOMA’s newest exhibition, Art of Noise, are on view through August 18.
articles.title: Last chance to see SF MOMA’s Art of Noise

articles.text: Tickets now on sale for shows at the Piedmont Center for the Arts Festival Opera’s 33rd season will continue into autumn with a trio of Sunday afternoon artist recitals at the intimate Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series will launch on Sunday, September 22, at 4 p.m. with Lucky in Love presenting mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and Piedmont favorite, pianist Jeffrey LaDeur, founder of San Francisco International Piano Festival. The series will continue on Sunday, October 27, at 4 p.m. with Nothing to Fear featuring contralto Sara Couden and pianist Derek Tam. The final recital will be on Sunday, November 17 at 4 p.m. with Muses and Musings of an Impresario – a birthday celebration with special guest artists to be announced – showcasing Festival Opera General Director and baritone Zachary Gordin as well as pianist Daniel Lockert. Earlier in the company’s season, Festival Opera presented two annual Opera in the Park concerts at Orinda Community Park and Walnut Creek Civic Park, featuring beloved community park programs of grand opera and Broadway musical highlights. For the mainstage production at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin and guest stage director Céline Ricci presented a double bill of two one-act operas regarding love and betrayal: Francis Poulenc’s riveting mid-1950s monodrama La Voix humaine based on iconoclast Jean Cocteau’s play of the same name and Baroque masterpiece Dido and Aeneas by Henry Purcell, based on Virgil’s epic work, the Aeneid. Sunday, Sept. 22 at 4 p.m. Lucky in Love According to Kindra Scharich, “Lucky in Love celebrates the centennial anniversary of legendary French composer Gabriel Fauré by highlighting one of his most important song cycles: La Bonne Chanson. Inspired by his passionate love for soprano Emma Bardac and based on the exquisite poetry of Paul Verlaine, Fauré called La Bonne Chanson his “most exuberant writing.” Mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and pianist Jeffrey LaDeur present this work, alongside other beloved scores that explore l’amour! Sunday, Oct. 27 at 4 p.m. Nothing to Fear Contralto Sara Couden commented, “What do art, song and Halloween have in common? Well…monsters. Beasts without and within, love gone horribly wrong, generalized anxiety and existential crises, conversations with death… the world of classical music is rife with horrors, and I am excited to introduce as many of them as possible to the audience this October. I will be working with the fabulous and multi-talented pianist Derek Tam and presenting works by a list of composers including Schubert, Strauss, Wieck and Weill as well as modern composers Jordan Rutter-Covatto, Erika Oba and Chris Castro. Don’t worry, there’s nothing to fear… but fear (/love/ death/the beast within) itself.” Photos by Festival Opera Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin will be showcased in a concert in Piedmont on Sunday, November 17. Contralto Sara Couden will be featured at the PCA in Nothing to Fear on Sunday, October 27. Sunday, Nov. 17 at 4 p.m. Muses and Musings of an Impresario Baritone Zachary Gordin said, “I am honored to collaborate with this group of Bay Area treasures on this recital series and most especially to rekindle my work with the incomparable Daniel Lockert in a recital of repertoire and anecdotes that will tell a story of my journey and muses in this life of music. Songs of composers so very dear to me [will be featured]: Schumann, Mahler, Reynaldo Hahn and Jake Heggie mixed with a splash of early music and American Songbook classics.” Surprise guests are to be announced, and a birthday celebration reception including wine, bubbly and treats will follow the program. Festival Opera was founded in 1991 by Dr. Theodore Weis who twenty years earlier had helped create the Arizona Opera Company in Tucson. Past Festival Opera leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp and Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony. It is currently led by Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera is committed to presenting emerging and local artists in compelling and socially relevant productions of both new and classic repertoire. Festival Opera proudly gives emerging artists a venue to hone their craft in leading roles with the guidance and collaboration of established professionals - providing a vital launching pad for their professional future. Festival alums have gone on to perform in major opera houses and symphony halls around the globe. Tickets for the Festival Opera Artist Recital Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are $40 per person for each concert, or individuals may purchase all programs for the discounted price of $95. To purchase tickets online, visit www.festivalopera.org.
articles.title: Festival Opera announces a trio of recitals at PCA

articles.text: The Tony-award winning musical Evita is being performed on the San Francisco Playhouse stage now through September 7. Originally directed by Harold Prince with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, the award-winning Evita chronicles young and ambitious Eva Perón’s rise from poor illegitimate child to the most powerful woman in Latin America. The play is narrated through the lens of Marxist revolutionary Che Guevara and recounts the story of Argentina’s matriarch as she rallies the heart of a nation to bring about a new era in Argentine history. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English said he selected Evita for the 2023-24 season because he knew it was going to be an election year in the U.S. and that democracy was certain to be on the line. “I thought, wouldn’t it be interesting to look at another time and place where a very charismatic populist leader rose up with his incredibly charismatic, popular wife to be elected to office and then, at least as the musical and some historical narratives say, began to dismantle essential elements of democracy,” English said. Sophia Alawi is cast as Eva Peron, with supporting roles by Jurä Davis, Peter Gregus, Alex Rodriguez, Albert Hodge and Chanel Tilghman. Evita is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through September 7. The venue is located at 450 Post Street, in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. The show is on stage six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2023- 2024-season/evita/ or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. Sophia Alawi performs the title role in Evita at San Francisco Playhouse.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents Evita onstage now through Sept. 7

Sunday, Nov. 17 at 4 p.m. Muses and Musings of an Impresario Baritone Zachary Gordin said, “I am honored to collaborate with this group of Bay Area treasures on this recital series and most especially to rekindle my work with the incomparable Daniel Lockert in a recital of repertoire and anecdotes that will tell a story of my journey and muses in this life of music. Songs of composers so very dear to me [will be featured]: Schumann, Mahler, Reynaldo Hahn and Jake Heggie mixed with a splash of early music and American Songbook classics.” Surprise guests are to be announced, and a birthday celebration reception including wine, bubbly and treats will follow the program. Festival Opera was founded in 1991 by Dr. Theodore Weis who twenty years earlier had helped create the Arizona Opera Company in Tucson. Past Festival Opera leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp and Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony. It is currently led by Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera is committed to presenting emerging and local artists in compelling and socially relevant productions of both new and classic repertoire. Festival Opera proudly gives emerging artists a venue to hone their craft in leading roles with the guidance and collaboration of established professionals - providing a vital launching pad for their professional future. Festival alums have gone on to perform in major opera houses and symphony halls around the globe. articles.text: “Three-dimensionality has always interested me,” explained Paul Bartlett, whose art exhibit is currently on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “Before embarking on my exploration of the world of ‘Xtra-Dimensions,’” I was a professor of chemistry at UC Berkeley. I taught organic chemistry and my research focused on molecules involved in natural biological processes. Gaining an understanding of these processes required the invention of new reactions and the creation of new molecules, so “design” was always a key component of my research and what I tried to teach my graduate students. The chemistry and function of the molecules we designed depended on their structures and, most importantly, their shapes in three-dimensions. Thinking in three-dimensions was thus a central feature of my academic career. While the world we all experience is three-dimensional, the photographs we take and the paintings we create are invariably displayed in a flat, two-dimensional format. It is up to us, the viewer, to recognize the depth of a forest scene, to know that a water surface is rippled and moving, maybe even to imagine patterns that are not explicitly shown. It was an attempt to break out of the constraints of a flat world that led me to explore what I call Xtra-Dimensions. My first attempts were to capture the dynamic elements of the surface of Lake Tahoe - not just to imply the fluidity and movement of the water, but to actually show it. Presenting the image as separate components in a number of layers adds a third dimension to the piece. The layers overlap so that the complete image is recreated when viewed straight on. However, the shapes of the components and their overall pattern bring additional dimensions as well as a dynamic element, with reflections and perspectives that change with your angle of view – similar to the original scene. I found that this approach is effective for many other types of Artist Paul Bartlett images: forest scenes with overlapping foliage or trees, cityscapes or abstract images with underlying geometric patterns – in short, almost any image where additional dimensions stimulate closer inspection and the discovery of something that would be missed in a two-dimensional print. Although I’m not designing new molecules, each new image and each Xtra-Dimensions pattern is nonetheless an experiment, with all the accompanying anticipation and excitement for the outcome.”
articles.title: Paul Bartlett art exhibit currently at Center for the Arts

Music addresses this subject directly. Opera for example, arises from the contemplation of grief. Tragedy is when the good guy dies. Comedy is when the bad guy dies. Which emotion would you choose? Let’s have a look at levity in music. Variety abounds… from sophisticated to ribald and everything in between. Comedy in music developed after tragedy. During the Renaissance music was subtle and sophisticated. So was the humor. Then the Baroque composers got into the act with some outrageous antics. Being diplomatic, they let animals speak. Mozart came along and had us rolling in the aisles with pieces like “A Musical Joke.“ If any of you have ever played chamber music, you know what can go wrong and Mozart parodied every aspect of incompetent amateur musicians. Rossini wrote dramatic operas, but his success in comedy was what really established his success. When he retired from writing operas, he hosted lively parties in his Paris apartments. He wrote special pieces for these parties and entitled them “sins of my old age.” No one was safe from his jabs. One of his funniest pieces is the “comic duet of the two cats.” This piece, like Mozart’s “musical joke” needs to be the last piece of the program. Nothing could be a better conclusion to a concert. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The great violin virtuoso Paganini was another who let animals speak for him. His famous piece “Vagaries of the Barnyard” was one of his important improvisations. If he felt that his audience was not respectful, he would include a donkey imitation as the finale. The audience understood perfectly. So did Paganini, who exited the auditorium as quickly as he could with the audience in hot pursuit. Many composers have continued animal impersonations. One of the funniest and most memorable is “Five Humorous Pieces“ by the Belgian violin composer Hubert Leonard. Everybody knows St-Saens’ “Carnival of the Animals”, but almost no one knows Leonard’s “Five Humorous Pieces.” Some people ask who the worst singer of all time was. It was probably Florence Foster Jenkins, whose concerts from the 1920s to the 1940s were notorious. Listen to her recordings. I must be honest with you. Did she know how bad she was or was this merely a ploy? Jascha Heifetz was known for his perfection on the violin. He made recordings under the nom de plume Joseph Hague. I know for a fact that Heifetz and Hague were the same people. For some strange reason, a few people think otherwise. Two c ond uc t or s we r e famous for their humor. Eugene Ormandy was unwittingly funny. His musicians would often write down the silly things that he would say. The English conductor Sir Thomas Beecham could have been a professional comedian. A friend of mine was first violist in one of Sir Thomas’s orchestras. She kept a notebook of the funny things he said. During one rehearsal, he was not pleased with the way the orchestra sounded. He roared: “this sounds like hell.” Then under his breath, he said very softly: “I’ll know when I get there.” Comedy in music continues even today. Many times the joke is on the listener…but that’s a story for another day. articles.text: The title Brittany Runs a Marathon tells you all you need to know about the last twenty minutes of what proves to be a surprisingly nifty movie. But it’s what comes before the marathon that makes for a wickedly good character study of one Brittany Forgler (played with panache by Jillian Bell): New Yorker, late twenties, a bit chunky (well, maybe a lot), working as an usher at an off-Broadway theater, and living in a low rent apartment in Queens. Before there is even a hint that sweats and Converse tennies are in her future, however, there is a growing sense that she is fundamentally discontent with her life and its trajectory. She feels a bit adrift. Unmoored. And then there are her habits. If she does any serious walking, for example, it’s from the couch to the refrigerator, or to the pretzel guy who has a sidewalk cart near her digs. Weekends are for partying and casual, anonymous sex. What creates a kind of critical mass regarding her sense of ennui is when she visits her primary care doctor, complaining of an inability to focus. What she’s hoping for is a quick checkup and script for Adderall. Instead, the doc suggests that her weight just might be an issue bringing with it high blood pressure and a possible fatty liver. His prescription involves more than a pill and a glass of water; instead, he suggests a healthy diet and exercise. And, for good measure, trying to convince a nonplussed Brittany, he points to a body-mass index poster on his wall and tells her she is out of her healthy range. The idea that all body types are acceptable, given what’s at stake, is never mentioned. So, back home after a brief, tearful, sit-on-the-floor crisis, followed by a mild intervention by her landlord, Catherine (Michaela Watkins), who suggests Brit join her running group. Not going to happen, she says. Yet realizing she needs to do something, Brit grudgingly breaks out the sweats plus hightops and decides she’ll try jogging/walking around the block. That’s it. Know that Brittany Runs a Marathon is a story about running; but then it isn’t. Consider running down a nicely flat sidewalk or park path meant for walking to be the equivalent of jumping out of a plane. It’s all about the journey once you make the commitment. Like all stories that contain a physical challenge or an athletic hurdle to be overcome – the mountain to be climbed – there are elements of conditioning and endurance. It’s a no pain/no gain template allowing the individual to be fully revealed. For Rocky, it was preparing for the fight. For Brit, it is, amazingly, the N.Y. Marathon finish line. And thus begins her quest to transform not only her body but her life; a struggle that changes not only her self-image but provokes reactions from old friends, which prove just as interesting. She comes to realize that her roommate, Gretchen (Alice Lee), a self-absorbed Instagram maven, was fine with Brit being the fat sidekick, but strangely unhappy with her newly minted persona. This film is fresh and engaging, never overly sentimental and constantly surprising in its twists and turns. When Brit takes an animal housesitting job (shaggy dog in an uptown brownstone, owners on vacation), she meets Jern (Utkarsh Ambudkar), a twenty-something guy who is happily adrift and apparently has the dog sitting graveyard shift. Their interactions, oil and water, add another interesting dimension to Brit’s expanding life, disclosing her sharp wit and intelligence and how she uses her quick rejoinders as a way of remaining defended. She is also fragile and fearful and even suspicious of those who reach out. Recall that I mentioned that Brittany Runs a Marathon, while about running, is about much more. Such as how she comes to resolve that nugget of deep discontent and how these newly acquired insights seep into her daily life and impact her self-esteem. Ultimately, that’s a finish line she may never totally cross; but then who does? Brittany Runs a Marathon. Directed by Paul Downs Colaizzo. Starring Jillian Bell, Michaela Watkins, Micha Stock. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Now streaming on prime. Jillian Bell and Micah Stock in Brittany Runs a Marathon

articles.text: A scene from A Dog’s Way Home As far as the kids are concerned, A Dog’s Way Home finds the PG sweet spot and stays there. They’ll take to it like, well, ducks to water. But then, of course, it’s a story about a nifty dog named Bella and her owner, Lucas (Jonah Hauer King), a med student living with his mom, Teri Lucas and his fellow med student, Olivia (Alexandra Shipp), find Bella as a pup, living with cats and kittens under an abandoned wreck of a house, and it’s Lucas who takes the wiggly, excitable, playful pooch home. She is literally a rescue dog for the house is about to be bullA year goes by, Bella grows up, and is spotted by a villainous animal control guy, Chuck (John Cassini), who makes it his mission to catch her on the street, unleashed. He claims she’s a pit bull. Worried that Bella could be impounded and even put down, Teri and Lucas send her to stay, briefly, with relatives in Farmington, New Mexico, while they search for a place to live outside of the city limits and out of Bella is, of course, homesick, misses Lucas and Terri, and at the first opportunity makes a break for it, not realizing that she is 400 miles away from home. And so begins Bella’s great two-year adventure. It proves to be a mildly harrowing journey that involves humans, a pack of stalking wolves, two men who want to adopt her, an orphaned mountain lion cub that tags along, an avalanche, learning to survive on leftovers in garbage bins and other dicey moments. Meanwhile, Bella determinedly makes her way toward home and Lucas. Kids will love all of it. Plus the filmmakers, having adapted A Dog’s Way Home from the bestselling novel by Bruce Cameron, decide to give the film a Bella voice over (by Bryce Dallas Howard) allowing her to share her impressions of all that she encounters. No worries regarding animals talking. Kids are totally on board with anthropomorphizing animals, e.g. a Disneyesque small wooden boy and an iconic mouse. Plus humans talk to dogs all the time and swear they get an answer topped off with a wagging tail. Recall that this is a PG rated film, family friendly, with a great story. Bella meets lots of kind people along the way. Be prepared: if you don’t have a Bella at home, well, kids can be persistent. Okay, just think about. A Dog’s Way Home. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. Starring Ashley Judd, Jonah Hauer King, Edward James. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019. articles.text: It was a sunny, mild afternoon on August 5th when the First Mondays Reading Group met outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park for their monthly discussion. A good turnout of 18 readers came to enjoy it. The group was there to discuss Country Girl written in 2013 by Edna O’Brien. When O’Brien’s first novel, The Country Girls, was published in 1960, it so scandalized her local Irish priest that he burned it. That didn’t stop O’Brien. She went on to write books that some say are among the best writing of the 20th Century. Country Girl is the story of the events, people, emotions, and the world of an unusual and talented person. O’Brien’s memoir starts with her birth in a grand but deteriorating house in Ireland and moves through her experiences in convent school to eloping, divorce, single motherhood, wild 60’s parties in London, and her encounters with Hollywood, pop culture, and literary personalities. There is love and unrequited love, and trips to America as a celebrated writer and the guest of Jackie Onassis and Hillary Clinton. Victoria Glendinning of The Spectator wrote of O’Brien, “… She is brave, modest, bewildered.” National Public Radio’s review said, “Country Girl is Edna O’Brien’s exquisite account of her dashing, barrier-busting, up-and-down life.” Sadly, O’Brien died last month at the age of 93 while the group was reading this memoir. The group’s discussion of Country Girl clearly showed that it appealed to some but not others. The readers generally agreed on the quality of O’Brien’s writing. They appreciated her voice, courage, intelligence, style, and the book’s structure. Some liked how she closed chapters and often set up what came next. Some were deeply touched by O’Brien’s story. One reader was “gob smacked” by her life experience. This is a story of liberation for a beautiful, Irish firebrand, born in the 1930s, who escaped the control of her country’s societal and sexual norms, the dominance of the Catholic Church in her culture and a demanding husband who didn’t want her to write, but took her money when she achieved success. For these readers, O’Brien was fully alive and constantly thinking. However for other readers O’Brien’s story was depressing and tedious. Some did not know of her before they read Country Girl and found her obituary helpful in more fully understanding her and the life she led. The book seemed to assume that the reader knew who O’Brien was, but some didn’t. They did not have this frame of reference and wondered why they should be interested in her. These dissatisfied readers felt there was not enough self-reflection to fully understand who this writer really was. The story was “a slog” for them. They couldn’t get inside the person. They wanted more “meat” to understand her. O’Brien was a reluctant memoir writer, and some readers felt this may have resulted in her not providing this understanding. When O’Brien’s first novel, The Country Girls, was published in 1960, it so scandalized her local Irish priest that he burned it. That didn’t stop O’Brien. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had a great turnout of 48 walkers and three K-9 best friends for their official walk back to school on August 7. This was the last Wednesday this summer that the group could walk the three Piedmont elementary school campuses before classes began. The group was pleased Robert Lang brought Tom Bjornson to walk with them for the first time, and that Lori Rubens was back after a long absence. The walkers were also happy Judy Love invited her granddaughter, Emilia Razavi, to join them in advance of her first day as a first grader at Havens School on Monday, and the walk had some special relevance for her. The walkers went to Havens School and went into the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, where some history was shared. The City of Piedmont was incorporated in September 1907. Its population grew dramatically after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and city leaders decided to build two schools. The first school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. Havens School was expanded with Depression New Deal funds in the 1930s. A new five-classroom wing was built on the eastern edge of the grounds in 1937- 38 and an auditorium was added in 1940-42. The auditorium was named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, who was Havens’ first principal and taught at the school for 20 years. Students participated in painting the ceilings of all the Piedmont school auditoriums. The theme for Ellen Driscoll’s is California history. At Wildwood, it’s U.S. history; at Beach, it’s literature. Fifth and sixth graders painted the panels in a paint-bynumber fashion before they were applied to the ceilings. A new Havens School was built at the same site in 1955. The 1910 school, which faced Bonita Avenue, was torn down. The New Deal classrooms and auditorium in the back remained, but in 2010 the school was completely rebuilt, and the 1938 classrooms were demolished. The walkers exited the auditorium and stopped outside for a group photo with young Emi at her new school. They continued to Bonita and Oakland Avenues for a long walk down to Beach School on Lake Avenue. They entered the Linda Beach Playfield at Howard Avenue and made their way to the school playground. New play structures had been installed over the summer and many young people were enjoying them. “The Lake Avenue School” was built in 1913. There were four teachers and 100 students in six grades. In 1918, the school was renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in honor of Egbert William Beach, the first Piedmonter and California officer killed in France during World War I. The rapid growth of Piedmont from 1920 to 1930 created school facility needs. Beach students were taught in cramped, wooden portables. In 1933, the buildings were condemned as firetraps and an earthquake menace. They were torn down in 1934 and replaced in two Depression-era projects. The main wing was built in 1936, and an auditorium/classroom wing was added in 1940. As part of city-wide seismic facility upgrades, Beach hosted some Havens students for the 2009-10 school year while Havens was rebuilt, and Wildwood students in 2010-11. When Beach had its renovations in 2011-12, the school temporarily relocated to Emeryville with buses shuttling students there and back. In the fall of 2012, the school re-opened with two new classrooms and new playground facilities. The walkers exited the playground on Linda Avenue and went down to Grand Avenue. They crossed Grand at Ace Hardware and walked up Wildwood Avenue to Wildwood School, which opened in 1924 and expanded from 1936 to 1940 in four Depression-era projects with new classroom buildings and an auditorium. The walkers then got a look at the newly finished Witter Field track, climbed “PE Hill,” walked through the PHS campus, and returned to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. The week brought many clinics as well as courses (multi day clinics) to further build campers’ skills. The Old School Play Yard was a popular location for campers this week, with so many games to play it was impossible for campers to get bored. Camper favorite evening programs this week included Postal Apocalyptics, Adventures of the Last Light, and Ragnarok, a daytime programing of Caesar Augusta’s Coliseum (a Roman gladiator-themed camp Olympics), and first ever playing of the CIRCLERS’ “Lobsters: Garlic Side of the Moon”.
