The Indie Next List has fantastic summer reading recommendations, curated by independent book store owners and staff. This list for August focuses on the best new fiction titles out there, perfect for relaxing in the shade and whisking the imagination elsewhere. The Indie Next List consists of only the newest releases with reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small bookstore culture. A Sorceress Comes to Call Fantasy “In T. Kingfisher’s retelling of the Goose Girl fairytale, there’s an emphasis on found family, and finding strength in yourself that you didn’t know you had. I would like Hester and Cordelia to be my new best friends, please and thank you.” —Cora Kelly, Bear Pond Books, Montpelier, VT The Au Pair Affair “I am head over heels in love with Burgess and Tallulah! I mean, an overprotective hockey captain that falls first and falls hard, and nicknames her gorgeous? You can’t go wrong. Tessa Bailey knows how to bring the swooning full force.” —Mandy Harris, Angel Wings Bookstore, Oxford, NC The Dead Cat Tail Assassins Fantasy “When undead assassin Eveen is contracted to kill a person who appears to be her own younger self, forbidden magics and lethal shenanigans ensue. This is a delicious, funny, unexpectedly heartwarming story with just the right amount of viciousness.” —Milo Michels, University Book Store, Seattle, WA The Bright Sword: A Novel of King Arthur Fantasy “You know a book’s good when it starts with a quote from Monty Python. I utterly loved it from the first page to the last. Witty, serious, magical, and with an amazing cast of characters, this is everything an Arthurian epic should be.” —Emily Pate, Word After Word Books, Truckee, CA Slow Dance Morrow, Romance “Shiloh and Cary quickly became two of my favorite characters ever. Rowell uses dual POV and a non-linear timeline to explore a stunning relationship between two utterly flawed, brilliantly eccentric best friends.” —Ebani Filbert, The Bookworm of Omaha, Omaha, NE The Lost Boy of Santa Chionia “Set in an isolated Italian village, this is so rich in detail, so deep in characterization, that it’s like eating dessert in a fine restaurant: savoring each bite, letting it linger on the palette. Easily one of my favorite books of the year so far!” —Pete Mock, McIntyre’s Fine Books, Pittsboro, NC Pearl “A shatteringly beautiful story of a woman’s search for answers about her mother’s disappearance. Through shifting memories, the reader moves through Marianne’s trauma and changing understanding of her mother. This aches and amazes in equal measure.” —Allyson Howard, Invitation Bookshop, Gig Harbor, WA Lady Macbeth Fiction “Lady Macbeth is the gothic fantasy retelling of my dreams! Ava Reid stuns once again with their attention to historic detail as they maintain the magic of Macbeth. This book is dreamy, lush, and had me spiraling for days after reading it!” —Haley Calvin, The Novel Neighbor, Webster Groves, MO The Lost Story Books, Fantasy “Can you feel nostalgic about a book you just read? Apparently yes, if it reminds you of when you were a child who believed in magic. Like any fairy tale, there is darkness, but only enough to make the light more brilliant.” —Laura Kendall, Second Flight Books, Lafayette, IN Nicked Historical Fiction “A truly immersive, boisterous, playful, and earnest heist story from so far in the past it becomes magical. With a writing style as elusive as the plot twists, a colorful cast of thieves and priests, and a breathless romance, it’s not one to miss.” —Bridget Fenner, BookPeople, Austin, TX The Truth According to Ember Romance “Ember is tired of her deadend job, of being broke, and never getting ahead as a Chickasaw woman. So, she lies. As these lies pile up, how can Ember be real? Emotional, witty, and tender, this debut Native rom-com is a perfect workplace romance!” —Coco Zephir, Phoenix Books, Essex Junction, VT Five-Star Stranger “A completely modern look at the way we live, regarding hurt, protection, and connection. As the protagonist tries to make himself into a blank slate so he can rent himself to strangers, the faded outline of his real self keeps threatening to peek through.” —James Crossley, Leviathan Bookstore, St. Louis, MO Catalina One World, Fiction “Catalina is such a delightful book — funny and quick-witted, but also thoughtful and heart-rending. I loved Catalina’s smart, singular voice. This is a perfect read for lovers of Lily King’s Writers & Lovers, or fans of Sally Rooney’s work.” —Shannon Guinn-Collins, Bookworks, Albuquerque, NM The Ex Vows Romance “A swoony story about two best friends finding their way back to each other after breaking up five years ago. Georgia and Eli must work together for their best friend Adam’s wedding and realize they left a lot unsaid. I had butterflies the whole time!” —Claire McWhorter, River & Hill Books, Rome, GA The Horse Fiction “Al Ward is flawed – alcoholism, a never quite good enough country guitarist and song writer. When a blind horse shows up at his isolated shack on a snowy, freezing night, the best of Al comes out. Yes, Al is flawed, but you’ll root for him.” —Karen Emmerling, Beach Books, Seaside, OR I Was A Teenage Slasher Saga Press, Horror “My heart aches for the slasher? This cannot be right. Tolly, the slasher, tells his bloody, horrific story in a voice so real and raw that you can almost hear him, as though seated right beside you, and feel every detail of his inescapable pain.” —Nancy Sims-West, Raven Book Store, Lawrence, KS Burn “In the spirit of Station Eleven, there is only one thing humankind understands when it must survive: it cannot be done alone. You read this novel and wonder how such a painful book can be so damn beautiful. Gorgeous writing meets heart-pounding thriller.” —Jessilynn Norcross, McLean & Eakin Booksellers, Petoskey, MI The Unmothers Books, Horror “Anderson beautifully blends a small-town mystery with the supernatural (and a little feminist rage) to deliver this cathartic punch of a story. If you loved the what-the-hell-is-going-on energy of classic X-Files, then read this book.” —Jennifer Martin, Tattered Cover Book Store, Denver, CO Smothermoss Books, Thriller “Beautiful, surreal, and otherworldly, I fully fell into Alering’s supernatural mystery. Their use of sound grounds the reader in Sheila and Angie’s strange and difficult life on the margins of society in some of the best writing I’ve seen.” —Amanda Scroggins, Watermark Books & Café, Wichita, KS Banal Nightmare Fiction “Banal Nightmare crackles with humanity. You may hate these feckless and at times ugly characters, or recognize yourself in them. But it’ll thrill you in its fearlessness. Either way, this will leave a mark on you. It blisters.” —Matt Nixon, A Cappella Books, Atlanta, GA Mystery Lights: Stories Books, Short Stories “Mystery Lights is a collection of dark and beautiful short stories that will leave you breathless. A woven tapestry of women and girls living their lives amongst the desert and its mysteries.” —Elisa McIntosh, The Bookstore Plus Music & Art, Lake Placid, NY Charlotte Illes Is Not a Teacher Mystery “Siegel’s humor and heart shine as we follow Charlotte to her new job as a substitute teacher at her old middle school, where she helps her new colleagues solve a mystery. Fan favorites Lucy and Gabe are back to help and their banter remains delightful.” —Andi Richardson, Fountain Bookstore, Richmond, VA

These were huge milestones for me that I am very proud of. I have also seen my conditioning progress drastically with the help of all of our coaches. Each day they push every individual to get better, and over the entire summer everyone has seen lots of improvement. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? The two biggest pieces of advice I could give a young athlete is consistency is key. Even if you only have time for a shorter workout, do it. Every workout pays off in the long run and will help you get a little bit better each day. Second is recovery. Recovery is half the fight to becoming the best athlete you can be. Whether it’s stretching every morning and after workouts, or taking ice baths whenever you can. Both of these are key in developing your body and avoiding injuries.

But before you reach the column, take a tasty detour left after the Monumento aos Restauradores to A Ginjinha for a further dive into Portuguese culture. A Ginjinha is a historic bar that opened in 1840. There you can sip Portugal’s famous cherry liquor. The location was publicized by travel journalists Anthony Bordain and Rick Steves. From the Column of Pedro, head down R. Augusta avenue, where you can find several gift shops and restaurants on its way to the Arco da Rau Augusta and Commerce Square. In the center of Praça do Comércio is a monument to King José I, created in 1775. Your journey ends across the street from Commerce Square at Cais das Colunas, a pier named after the two columns on the edge of the Tagus River. The location was a a welcoming point for several prominent figures, including Queen Elizabeth II in 1957. From there you can see Ponte 25 de April, a bridge with a striking similarity to the Golden Gate Bridge, with Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left. Take off your shoes and dip your weary feet in the water after a day of walking around Lisbon. One of the most visited locations in Lisbon is Commerce Square with its large monument to King Jose I.

articles.text: Citizens dissatisfied with City’s handling of local statutes Tensions were high during a public discussion of the State Housing Accountability Act on Monday, August 5, hosted by city officials and held in the large performance space of the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. The meeting, which was intended to quell resident concerns over recent changes in land use laws and plans by a developer to build two large homes plus an ADU in a heavily wooded area with a creek on Wistaria Way. The meeting, led by Planning Director Kevin Jackson, seemed to only further expose the divisions between City Hall and community members, notably the 30 or so who attended. The meeting which the City named the “Housing Accountability Act Primer,” consisted of a presentation on the specifics of new state laws SB9, SB35, and the Housing Accountability Act followed by a Q&A session with city officials. A panel of city Staff Photos Planning Director Kevin Jackson answers questions from frustrated citizens.

Jim Hopkins I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues. It was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. In the biblical narrative, grief and gratitude frequently travel together. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. The first section (1-11) of complaint and grief is represented by words like “They set fire to your sanctuary, burned it to the ground” (7a). articles.text: Why should City rely solely on developer for all information? Editor: The following letter was sent on July 30 to members of Piedmont City Council. The recent dispute over the City’s grant of a lot-split and multiple-family development at 77 Wistaria way exposed several flaws in the City’s execution of the new state housing mandate known as “SB 9.” True, SB 9 places real constraints on local government zoning and land-use regulation. The City Council, however, has gratuitously embraced those constraints – and others – in an attempt to attract new housing that will increase the City’s tax base, subsidized school headcounts and the overly optimistic housing element plan. With nary a vote of the residents, Piedmont has opened a secretive fast-track highway to any developer who wants to tum a quick profit by building four dwellings on a property meant for one or two. The City Council added Division 17.54 to the City Code to administer the new constraints imposed by SB 9. But in its haste to embrace the new law, I believe the City Council has run roughshod over three core fairness principles that should govern its service on behalf of the citizens and voters of Piedmont: (1) Public transparency, notice and an opportunity to be heard, (2) administrative reasonableness and accountability and (3) the balancing of developers’ rights with the rights of our residents to avoid adverse impacts on their health, safety and environment. Why should a decision so consequential to our community take place in secret, without accountability? And why should the City rely solely on the developer for all of the information relevant to its decision? The recent Wistaria Way dispute has shown that Division 17.54 needs to be revised immediately in order to satisfy these three fairness principles. Accordingly, I respectfully request that the City Council amend Division 17.54 of the City Code to include the following elements, all of which are compliant with SB 9: 1. Upon receipt of an application under SB 9, the Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of the subject property. The notice shall include (a) a description of the application and proposed development, (b) the likely timetable for the City’s consideration/action, and (c) an invitation to provide facts relating to the qualification for SB 9 treatment and whether there would be any specific, adverse impact on health, safety or the environment by the proposed development. The notice shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 2. pages.text: Wednesday, August 7, 2024 3 EDITORIAL City council needs to change SB 9 application process Why should City rely solely on developer for all information? Editor: The following letter was sent on July 30 to members of Piedmont City Council. The recent dispute over the City’s grant of a lot-split and multiple-family development at 77 Wistaria way exposed several flaws in the City’s execution of the new state housing mandate known as “SB 9.” True, SB 9 places real constraints on local government zoning and land-use regulation. The City Council, however, has gratuitously embraced those constraints – and others – in an attempt to attract new housing that will increase the City’s tax base, subsidized school headcounts and the overly optimistic housing element plan. With nary a vote of the residents, Piedmont has opened a secretive fast-track highway to any developer who wants to tum a quick profit by building four dwellings on a property meant for one or two. The City Council added Division 17.54 to the City Code to administer the new constraints imposed by SB 9. But in its haste to embrace the new law, I believe the City Council has run roughshod over three core fairness principles that should govern its service on behalf of the citizens and voters of Piedmont: (1) Public transparency, notice and an opportunity to be heard, (2) administrative reasonableness and accountability and (3) the balancing of developers’ rights with the rights of our residents to avoid adverse impacts on their health, safety and environment. Why should a decision so consequential to our community take place in secret, without accountability? And why should the City rely solely on the developer for all of the information relevant to its decision? The recent Wistaria Way dispute has shown that Division 17.54 needs to be revised immediately in order to satisfy these three fairness principles. Accordingly, I respectfully request that the City Council amend Division 17.54 of the City Code to include the following elements, all of which are compliant with SB 9: 1. Upon receipt of an application under SB 9, the Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of the subject property. The notice shall include (a) a description of the application and proposed development, (b) the likely timetable for the City’s consideration/action, and (c) an invitation to provide facts relating to the qualification for SB 9 treatment and whether there would be any specific, adverse impact on health, safety or the environment by the proposed development. The notice shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 2. The Director shall consider all material received in connection with the application before rendering a decision on the application, as required by Code section 17.54.040.E. 3. The Director’s written decision under Code section 17.54.040 E. shall specifically address the “specific, adverse impacts” language of SB 9 and make specific findings thereon. The Director’s findings shall be based upon reasonable inquiry. 4. The Director may not delegate his/her responsibilities under section 17.54.040 to subordinate staff, although staff may provide support and resources to assist the Director’s determinations. 5. The Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of the approval or denial of the application following issuance of his/her written decision. The notice shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 6. The Director shall promptly notify nearby residents of any further permit applications being submitted following the approval of the SB 9 application. The notice(s) shall also be published in the next edition of the Piedmont Post newspaper. 7 The City Council reserves the right to review the Director’s decision on the application for compliance with administrative mandamus law, pursuant to City Charter section 2.09. (Ministerial administrative acts like those required by SB 9 still must pass the test that they are “neither arbitrary, capricious nor without reasonable evidentiary support.” When legitimate questions arise, the City Council must reserve its Charter authority under Sec. 2.09 to assure that the Director’s ministerial approval of an SB 9 application passes this test. 8 Current provisions of Division 17.54 that conflict with these provisions shall be amended to be consistent with these provisions. The citizens and voters of Piedmont deserve your endorsement of fundamental fairness, and your direction to City administrative staff to treat us with respect and due concern for our well-being. We will wait and see if you are willing to demonstrate your devotion to these core principles. Respectfully, –Harvey L. articles.text: Meet Neptune, a lively and treat-loving pup with a personality as big as his wagging tail. Neptune is four-years-old and weighs 80 pounds. Shelter staff report he already knows how to sit and shake and that he has strong recall off leash. Volunteers are helping him with his loose leash walking and he is excited to improve and learn more with positive reinforcement training. articles.text: Residents interested in running for City Council or Piedmont School Board can pick up nomination documents from the City Clerk. The deadline for all applicants is this Friday, August 9. On November 5, Piedmont voters will elect candidates to fill two City Council seats and three Board of Education seats. Councilmember Conna McCarthy and Board of Education members Hilary Cooper and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are eligible for re-election. Mayor Jen Cavenaugh and Board of Education member Cory Smegal will be termed out. The nomination process can be complicated, and filing deadlines are tight, so interested residents should begin as soon as possible. If you are interested in running: 1. Make an appointment with the City Clerk’s office at 420- 3040 or CityClerk@piedmont. ca.gov to obtain your candidate documents. At your appointment, the City Clerk will walk you through the nomination process, reviewing the different documents, deadlines and rules involved. Plan on spending 30-60 minutes. 2. Review the fundamentals of the process online. Prepare for your appointment by reading about running for office on the City website. This will give you an idea of what to expect and allow you to identify questions you may want to ask during your appointment. 3. Submit your nomination documents by Friday, August 9. Nomination documents must be filed in person at the City Clerk’s office. It is a good idea for candidates to file documents early so they can correct any errors that come up. A list of people who have filed nomination papers will be available at piedmont. ca.gov/vote2024. City Council and Board of Education are volunteer positions. As of Monday, August 5, only three city council candidates have submitted nomination paperwork, current Councilmember Conna McCarthy, Lorrel Plimier and James Green. McCarthy has served on the City Council since November 2020. Plimier is an attorney and data scientist who served as president of the Piedmont League of Women Voters from 2020 to 2024. Five candidates have taken out nomination paperwork for the school board: Michael Malione, Susy Struble, Emily Gorin Dai Meagher and Victoria Rosenbaum. For more information about Piedmont’s 2024 election or running for office, visit piedmont. ca.gov/elections, or contact City Clerk Anna Brown at 420-3040.

The law, effective January 1, 2022, allows homeowners to create up to four homes on an existing parcel. As UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation notes, this state law effectively eliminates single-family-only zoning. The law allows the owner to “split” its lot, which makes it easier to sell or finance additional homes on a single parcel. While proponents believe the law will help address the current housing crisis in California by opening new opportunities for small-scale homebuilding, critics of SB9 are concerned the law may lead to speculation and unchecked growth at the expense of a community’s character and traditions. Bayon Moore made it clear at the beginning of the night that officials would not be taking questions on specific projects and that the night was for general housing law questions only – a reference to the attention the City has received in recent weeks for allowing a controversial construction project on Wistaria Way, which was approved via an SB9 application and with little public input. The greatest point of contention between city officials and residents appears to be over how much the city government is allowed to do and its lack of transparency during this process. Throughout its presentation, the city argued that its hands are tied by limitations in SB9. “Cities must facilitate housing, and the state is requiring us to do that by adjusting local regulations consistent with state law, streamlining the process to process permits for housing development, and developing checklists and information for potential developers,” said Jackson. Jackson also laid out his understanding of the penalties for Piedmont at the state level for not complying with SB9, including the withholding of state funding and potential lawsuits from applicants and the Attorney General’s office. However, many residents remain outraged and believe City Hall should be doing more to defend the interests of its citizens and the character of its neighborhoods. “I don’t feel like City Council and staff appreciate that SB9 lot splits are not a desired outcome to the current residents and citizens,” said Rich Latvala, who lives near the city’s first SB9-approved project at 77 Wistaria Way. Many residents also believe that SB9, as it is currently being enforced, lacks refinement. One example they have cited is the city’s policy regarding moveins. SB9 is intended for use by homeowners, not institutional investors. As such, developers must sign an affidavit confirming they will live in the home they are building for at least three years. City officials admit there is no way of enforcing this, potentially opening neighborhoods to unchecked development. “When I bought my home, I had the guarantee of a single-family-zoned lot. I never anticipated high-density housing in my backyard. And now, that’s what I’m getting,” said David Ashton, a lifetime Piedmont resident who lives near Wistaria Way. Tensions were palpable during the one-hour meeting. “[The meeting] attempted to answer some questions, but basically presented even more questions about the implementation of SB9,” said Latvala. “I have lost faith in my local government. I can’t believe my city is doing this,” exclaimed Ashton, a third-generation resident. Bayon Moore urged concerned residents to contact their state representatives, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks and Senator Nancy Skinner, about “areas of concern” or “the changes that have taken place.” The meeting was attended by more than 30 people, who filed in gradually as the meeting got underway. READ IT IN THE POST Nominations for city, school elections close on Aug. 9 By Matt Simons Residents interested in running for City Council or Piedmont School Board can pick up nomination documents from the City Clerk. The deadline for all applicants is this Friday, August 9. On November 5, Piedmont voters will elect candidates to fill two City Council seats and three Board of Education seats. Councilmember Conna McCarthy and Board of Education members Hilary Cooper and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are eligible for re-election. Mayor Jen Cavenaugh and Board of Education member Cory Smegal will be termed out. The nomination process can be complicated, and filing deadlines are tight, so interested residents should begin as soon as possible. If you are interested in running: 1. Make an appointment with the City Clerk’s office at 420- 3040 or CityClerk@piedmont. ca.gov to obtain your candidate documents. At your appointment, the City Clerk will walk you through the nomination process, reviewing the different documents, deadlines and rules involved. Plan on spending 30-60 minutes. 2. Review the fundamentals of the process online. Prepare for your appointment by reading about running for office on the City website. This will give you an idea of what to expect and allow you to identify questions you may want to ask during your appointment. 3. Submit your nomination documents by Friday, August 9. Nomination documents must be filed in person at the City Clerk’s office. It is a good idea for candidates to file documents early so they can correct any errors that come up. A list of people who have filed nomination papers will be available at piedmont. ca.gov/vote2024. City Council and Board of Education are volunteer positions. articles.text: and Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 - Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble. Setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel?” Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: – “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” – “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 - Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: – “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” – “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 - Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes - congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s ok. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. This process of checking in with yourself is especially helpful during times of transition and can help you feel empowered to grow not only as a student but as a person! Emily Thompson is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel Rodriguez has worked in undergraduate admissions at public and private universities. Boot camp started with shoes, not boots, as students participated in a shoeless relay in the Buzz Redford Gym in socks. Students ran and slid to and from a large pile of everyone’s shoes. A total of 96 students signed up for a two-day 9:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. boot camp session this year, with more than three dozen kids in each. Like last year, an extra oneday condensed boot camp was offered for kids with conflicting schedules. Scherman, and retired teacher Penny Sullivan, started the orientation camp 10 years ago to ease the stress of incoming middle school students. “Number one, the kids are going to make new friends and meet new people. They will also get familiar with the campus,” Scherman explained. A id i ng Scher ma n a nd Wisniewski this year were Scherman’s three sons, Julian, 18, Quincy, 21, and Lucas, 24. The boys, along with the family labrador Josie, led a tour of the campus and a scavenger hunt. After slip-sliding on the polished gym floor, the campers put their shoes back on and turned to a group problem-solving game as teams attempted to scoot across a “hot lava river” running through the gym. By balancing on laminated paper, and making a human bridge, students used problem solving to transport their team in a race with the clock. “What is double compressed math?” asked one student, new to the district. Scherman took the opportunity to show the young scholar the location of the PMS office and how to talk to a counselor. On the first morning of the camp Scherman offered some organizational advice for students. “As soon as a teacher hands you a piece of paper, put your name on it,” he said Scherman. “A loose paper is a lost paper.” “Your grades will not be a surprise. You won’t suddenly get a D when expecting an A. Your teachers will give you opportunities to know where you stand, “he explained. After explaining the nuances of block scheduling, and the elective wheel, Scherman turned the floor over to 8th grader assistants Aava Lokre and Olivia Kan-Miller who offered student perspectives of what “Academy” period is like. Lokre explained she was volunteering her time to help, in part because she remembers meeting her first middle school friends in boot camp, two years ago. Having completed fifth grade, these students are now entering a world with increased consequences, and are given more freedoms as well. In place of recess, there is P.E., brunch, and seven minutes between class periods. Boot camp also included mind-bending math riddles, time to write and draw and creating questions for their next academic adventure. “We don’t want the new sixth graders to worry too much about school; have faith, it will be okay,” said Lokre. articles.text: On Monday, July 29, at approximately 6:15 a.m., Piedmont Police Dispatch received an ALPR alert regarding a stolen 2004 Chevy Suburban entering the city. Two officers quickly located the vehicle on Warfield Avenue and attempted a traffic stop. The driver raced away at high speed. As another officer arrived to assist, the suspect intentionally put the car in reverse and rammed his patrol car. This collision deployed the airbags, causing moderate injuries to the officer inside. The Chevy Suburban then pulled forward and rammed the other Piedmont patrol car, reversing several times and causing minor injuries to the officer. The suspect then sped up Wildwood Avenue where he later abandoned the car in the 300 block of Wildwood Avenue and fled on foot. One of the police cars suffered total damage, and the other sustained significant front-end damage. The officers injured have since been cleared for full duty. The suspect is described as a white or Hispanic male, approximately 5’6” tall, 160 lbs., with long hair. He was last seen wearing a black puffy hooded jacket with red lining and dark pants. Anyone with video surveillance or information is asked to contact Police Det. John Lagios at 420-3000. articles.text: Tennis Town, California appears to have another pupil on the rise. Isaac Milner, a fifth grader at Havens Elementary, brought home a trophy after winning the Little Mo West Regional Tennis Tournament at the Berkeley Tennis Club on July 22. The tournament is named after tennis great Maureen Connolly who died at age 35. The “Little Mo” began in 1976 in Dallas and expanded to a nationwide competition in 1998. It is considered one of the premier series of junior tournaments for girls and boys tennis stars. It is the only circuit of its kind for high-performance girls and boys in the United States. Competing in a field of 32 athletes, Milner squared off with Daniel Mac Sy of Rocklin in the Final. Milner dropped the first set 6-3, but powered back in the second set to claim a 6-4 victory and force a 10-point tiebreaker, which he won 10-6. “My instant reaction to winning was pure happiness because I won the whole thing!” Milner said ecstatically. Milner had some trouble finding his form in the first set, allowing Sy to claim the first set. But Milner altered his strategy to get on the offensive, slamming forehand and backhand winners to tie things up. In the tiebreaker, Milner got out to an early 5-1 lead and kept his foot on the gas pedal toward the victory. “In the final, I lost the first set because I was making more errors than normal. In the second set, I played better and more offensively. In the final tiebreaker I jumped to a 5-1 lead, then I tried to stay on offense and was able to win,” he said To get there, Milner had shutout victories in the Round of 32 and Round of 16 with a pair of dominant 6-0, 6-0 wins. In the Quarterfinals he continued his high execuIsaac Milner, 10, stands proudly with his first-place trophy after winning the Little Mo West Regional Tennis Tournament. tion with a 6-2, 6-0 win, following up with another dominant 6-3, 6-0 win in the semifinals. Milner is coached twice a week with Piedmont High tennis coach Jim Landes. Landes praised Isaac for his tenacity on the court, showing rare skill for someone his age. “What struck me when I first met Isaac was his drive and focus. When he practices, he concentrates from the first ball to the last—he ever wastes a moment. He runs for every ball and knows just what he wants to do with it, that’s very rare for someone his age. He is also very talented with great speed, timing and coordination,” Landes said. Milner has qualified for and will compete in the Little Mo Nationals in Austin, Texas on September 27-30. Isaac Milner (right) squared off with Daniel Mac Sy of Rocklin, winning in three sets. Milner will now compete in the Little Mo Nationals in Austin, Texas in September.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Spectrum News Katie Ledecky made history by winning her ninth Olympic gold medal, the most decorated women’s Olympics swimmer of all time. The 2024 Summer Olympics are underway in Paris, France and continue through August 11. As of August 6, the United States holds first place in the medal count with 23 golds, 31 silvers and 29 bronze medals. Host country France has the third most medals with 13 golds, 16 silvers, and 18 bronze medals through Day 12. Here’s a rundown of some of the best moments from this year’s Olympic Games. Katie Ledecky makes history U.S. swimmer Katie Ledecky made the history books as the most successful women’s swimmer to ever compete in the Olympics. Ledecky’s victory in the 800 meter freestyle with a time of 8:11.04 on August 3, marked the ninth gold medal of her career to overtake Jenny Thompson’s record set in 2004. It also marked Ledecky’s second gold medal at this year’s Olympic Games after winning the 1500 meter freestyle on July 31 with an Olympic record time of 15:30.02. Team USA Men’s Gymnastics wins first medal since 1998 On July 29, Team USA’s men’s gymnastics team won its first medal in 16 years after Brody Malone, Frederick Richard, Asher Hong, Paul Juda, and Stephen Nedoroscik took bronze (3rd place) in the artistic team allaround event. Nedoroscik had one of the most wholesome moments in an interview reflecting on the moments before dismounting from the pommel horse while re-watching his routine, knowing he just needed to get his job done to make history for the U.S. “Going up to pommel horse, I’m the last guy in the whole competition. I had a good feeling that our team was in a great spot, I just knew I had to go up there and do my job. I was super worried in my routine, I was thinking, ‘Let’s just get it done! Let’s go for it!’ Right here, I was like, ‘If I put this dismount up, Team USA gets a medal!’ You can see it right away when I land, I’m getting goosebumps right now, this is the best moment of my life,” Nedoroscik said. Noah Lyles wins Team USA’s first 100 meter since 2004 On August 4, Noah Lyles won the 100 meter dash with a time of 9.79 seconds to earn gold and tying the 12th fastest time in history set by American Maurice Green in 1999. Lyles becomes the first U.S. 100 meter sprinter to win Olympic gold since Justin Gatlin in 2004 in Athens, Greece. Simone Biles also makes history Simone Biles is back on top as the most decorated Olympic Gymnast to ever compete. She has secured three gold medals and one silver, her 11th medal and seventh gold. On July 30, she helped lead the U.S. to gold in the artistic team all-around event then put a stamp on the record by winning gold in women’s gymnastics all-around on August 1. Two days later, Biles also won the vault, and on August 5 she took silver in the women’s floor event. Sha’Carri Richardson wins first medal It may not have gone the way she envisioned, but track sprinter Sha’Carri Richardson claimed the first Olympic medal of her racing career after placing second in the 100 meter dash on August 3. After a slow start out of the blocks, Richardson stormed back to second place. But the event’s winner, Julien Alfred, made history for her country of St. Lucia, winning gold and becoming the only athlete to ever win a medal for the small East Caribbean island nation of just 180,857 people. Photo courtesy of USA Gymnastics Team USA’s men’s gymnastics team secured its first medal since 1998 by winning a Bronze medal in the artistic team all-around event.
articles.title: Top moments from first weeks of Olympic Games

What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goal is to be overall faster and stronger. How are you measuring your development? With a coach? A trainer? I do workouts specific to my body learned from past trainers. I also work with a hitting coach at least once a week. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I ran three miles in under 21 minutes What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Surround yourself with people who are supportive, competitive, and have similar aspirations as you. Being in a slump, mentally or on the field, is normal and can make you stronger by working to get out of it. LOUISA SYMKOWICK Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2025 Louisa Symkowick is a midfielder who enters her third year as a starter as a senior. She’s a key player in coach Dan Chubbock’s system, dictating the game with her controlling presence as a stout defender and playmaker on offense. She helped the soccer team go 12-2-4 (W-T-L) record and reaching the Division 3 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 7 before losing 2-0 to No. 2 Cardinal Newman on February 16. They beat No. 10 Albany 6-0 in the opening round three days prior and finished second in the Foothill Division. She earned second-team AllLeague honors last season and is working toward her collegiate decision. What is your workout program this summer? I have tournaments almost every other weekend this summer, which usually consist of 3-4 games. During the week, I have three training sessions with my team, De Anza Force SC, in the afternoon. I also lift 2-3 times per week depending on whether I have a tournament that weekend. I like to go to the field and train by doing sprint intervals, as well as getting touches with the soccer ball. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals are very soccer specific. I want to be able to play the 90-minute game at maximum effort with minimum fatigue. In soccer, one of the best workouts to do is game-realistic training, so games, scrimmages, pickup games, and things of that nature can be the best training for me to maintain my soccer fitness. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my development by timing each sprint and trying to improve every sprint. I also measure how much fatigue I feel during my games and focus on decreasing it. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I usually work out on my own, but I love to kick the ball around with my friends and family. I have a lifting coach who instructs me during my lifts. My soccer coach leads my team in fitness sessions as well. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I am lucky to be getting recruited to play soccer at the collegiate level. Right now, I am in the process to making the decision about which school I will choose to play at for the next four years. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? articles.text: With the new school year quickly approaching, the Piedmont High Class of 2025 looks ahead to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as seniors. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. Predominantly appearing as the leadoff hitter, Lagios finished with a .358 batting average. He was the team-leader in home runs with six, the most by a Piedmont player since Kyle Rolland hit six back in 2010, according to public records. Markos’ 34 hits, 28 RBIs, 30 runs scored, and 13 stolen bases also led the team. As the football team’s starting quarterback, Lagios led the Highlanders to a 7-4 record, a berth in the D5 NCS playoffs, and the school’s first Shoreline title since 2015. Lagios completed 62 percent of his passes for 1,941 yards, 22 touchdowns and three interceptions. He rushed for 788 yards and added 13 more touchdowns to his tally—giving him 35 total scores. articles.text: The Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat & Wat Phra That Doi Suthep [Reprinted from August 2023 Piedmont Post.] In our first international hiking story, we discover the wonders of Thailand. Welcome travelers, hikers, and traveling hikers. Thailand is home to some of the thickest jungles in the world. Luckily, the outskirts of Chiang Mai provides a scenic hike through a Thai jungle on its way to a pair of historic Buddhist temples. The Monk’s Trail, also known as the Wat Pha Lat Trail, takes hikers to a hidden temple, Wat Pha Lat, within the Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is just 0.8 of a mile but ascends a steep 550 feet in elevation gain. During the hike to Wat Pha Lat, you’ll pass under groves of bamboo with insects making noise around you, while also passing a small waterfall on your way to the temple. Wat Pha Lat translates to “Monastery at the Sloping Rock.” Created during the reign of King Kuena from 1355-1385, the monastery was originally used as a resting spot for people walking up to at Phra That Doi Suthep, the much famous and final location for our hike. Once the road leading to Doi Suthep was established in 1935, Wat Pha Lat became a residency for monks. You’re welcomed to the holy grounds by sculptures of Buddha with a cascading stream of water falling over the sloping Statues of Buddha greet you as you enter Wat Pha Lat. The glorious golden Chedi at Doi Suthep, standing 79 feet tall

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony opening gala is Wednesday, September 25 featuring Lang Lang and Gina Alice performing with the symphony. The internationally-renowned pianist couple take the stage with conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen and the San Francisco Symphony in a celebratory program featuring Saint-Saëns’s Piano Concerto No. 2 and Carnival of the Animals. Born in Liaoning, China in 1982, Lang Lang gained international fame as a pianist through the 1990’s. He has performed with major orchestras around the world and was the first Chinese pianist to be engaged with the Berlin Philharmonic, the Vienna Philharmonic and many of the top American orchestras. The superstar pianist will play alongside his wife, pianist Gina Alice, performing selections from Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/galalang-lang to purchase tickets. Ticket purchases and sponsors of the opening gala support the San Francisco Symphony’s artistic, education, and community programs. Pianist Lang Lang ®

articles.text: New Orleans’ famous Preservation Hall Jazz Band returns to San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz from Thursday to Sunday, August 15 to 18. The Preservation Hall Jazz Band is a Crescent City favorite founded by tuba player Allan Jaffe in the early 1960s. The band takes its name after the French Quarter art gallery and has been a fixture in the city for decades. They are regular performing guests at New Orleans’ JazzFest, the most-attended Jazz festival in the U.S., and has performed at San Francisco Jazz many times, including a series of concerts last summer. The big brass band is now run by Jaffe’s son, tuba player Ben Jaffe, and includes singer & instrumentalist Clint Maedgen, trumpeter Brandon Lewis, pianist Kyle Roussel, drummer Walter Harris, and trombonist Ronell Johnson. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/2024-summ e r - s e s s i o n s / p r e s e r v a - tion-hall-jazz-band/ to view showtimes and purchase tickets. articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco is exhibiting impressionist and realist artworks from 1848 to 1960 in an exhibition entitled “American Beauty” now on display through October 20. American art in the 19th and 20th centuries presents a variety of artistic responses during a complex period in US history. The artwork featured is borrowed from the collection of Bernard and Barbro Osher. The exhibition includes the first large-scale oil painting by Winslow Homer (The Angler, ca. 1874), the first genre picture by William Merritt Chase (Spanish Bric-à-Brac Shop, 1883), the first major George Bellows landscape (In Virginia, 1908), the first Georgia O’Keeffe images of the Southwest (Front of Ranchos Church, 1930 and The Patio, 1940), as well as 13 artists whose art is being shown at the museum for the first time. To learn more about the exhibition, visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/osher-american-art. The American Beauty exhibition is currently on display at de Young Museum in San Francisco.
articles.title: “American Beauty” exhibition at deYoung Museum through October

articles.text: Vallejo-based theater company to perform The Winter’s Tale Members of Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park performing Hamlet in Dracena Park in 2023 A free performance of Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale will take place in Dracena Park this Sunday afternoon, August 11, at 4 p.m., presented by Vallejo Shakespeare. The performance will take place in the quarry area. Seating is first come, first served and will be picnic-style on the lawn. Audiences are encouraged to bring a blanket or a low beach chair to enjoy the performance. Friendly, well-behaved dogs are welcome but must be on a leash. Attendees are encouraged to walk, bike, or carpool to the performance, as parking in the area is limited. This performance marks the third appearance of Vallejo Shakespeare at Dracena Park. Previously, the group staged performances of Henry V in 2019 and Hamlet in 2023. Established in 2010, Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park is a live theatre group that produces one live Shakespeare production each summer, with free performances in outdoor settings across the Bay Area. The troupe uses minimal sets and costumes, instead emphasizing the individual actors’ performances. “The most amazing thing about Shakespeare is how relevant it is to this day,” said Dalia Vidor, founder of Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park. “All of Shakespeare’s plays have a very simple storyline. People unnecessarily complicate it. And I think kids can really understand them.” In addition to producing and directing the plays, Vidor also plays several roles in each production. Although she now lives in Vallejo, Vidor grew up in the Trestle Glen neighborhood and attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School in her youth where she developed a life-long love of acting. Vidor said her favorite part of each performance is getting the chance to change people’s minds about the bard’s plays. “I find it most thrilling when after the show, people come up to me or to my actors and they say how much they disliked Shakespeare because of school, [...] and how surprised they were that they enjoyed the show. Specifically, how different it was from anything they were taught,” she explained. For more information about the performance, contact the City of Piedmont at 420-3040. Audiences look from their picnic blankets and lawn chairs in the quarry area of Dracena Park.
articles.title: Free Shakespeare in Dracena Park this Sunday

articles.text: Visit the Festival Pavilion at Fort Mason Center in San Francisco on August 24 for the 11tth anniversary of the West Coast Craft Fair. West Coast Craft was founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, which range from simple to craft to fine art and spans a variety of mediums. This year, artists are selling textiles, clothing, shoes, toiletries, jewelry, furniture and woodwork, and homemade libations. pages.text: Wednesday, August 7, 2024 17 Free Shakespeare in Dracena Park this Sunday Vallejo-based theater company to perform The Winter’s Tale Members of Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park performing Hamlet in Dracena Park in 2023 By Matt Simons A free performance of Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale will take place in Dracena Park this Sunday afternoon, August 11, at 4 p.m., presented by Vallejo Shakespeare. The performance will take place in the quarry area. Seating is first come, first served and will be picnic-style on the lawn. Audiences are encouraged to bring a blanket or a low beach chair to enjoy the performance. Friendly, well-behaved dogs are welcome but must be on a leash. Attendees are encouraged to walk, bike, or carpool to the performance, as parking in the area is limited. This performance marks the third appearance of Vallejo Shakespeare at Dracena Park. Previously, the group staged performances of Henry V in 2019 and Hamlet in 2023. Established in 2010, Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park is a live theatre group that produces one live Shakespeare production each summer, with free performances in outdoor settings across the Bay Area. The troupe uses minimal sets and costumes, instead emphasizing the individual actors’ performances. “The most amazing thing about Shakespeare is how relevant it is to this day,” said Dalia Vidor, founder of Vallejo Shakespeare in the Park. “All of Shakespeare’s plays have a very simple storyline. People unnecessarily complicate it. And I think kids can really understand them.” In addition to producing and directing the plays, Vidor also plays several roles in each production. Although she now lives in Vallejo, Vidor grew up in the Trestle Glen neighborhood and attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School in her youth where she developed a life-long love of acting. Vidor said her favorite part of each performance is getting the chance to change people’s minds about the bard’s plays. “I find it most thrilling when after the show, people come up to me or to my actors and they say how much they disliked Shakespeare because of school, [...] and how surprised they were that they enjoyed the show. Specifically, how different it was from anything they were taught,” she explained. For more information about the performance, contact the City of Piedmont at 420-3040. Audiences look from their picnic blankets and lawn chairs in the quarry area of Dracena Park. articles.text: Saturday, August 10, 11 a.m.–2 p.m. Xtra-Dimensions Art Exhibit A local artist and emeritus professor of chemistry at Cal, now living in Montclair, Paul Bartlett will open a threeweek exhibition of his work with a Meet-n-Greet Reception and refreshments for all! Bartlett has tried for years to find ways to think in three dimensions and has now developed techniques of layering images in ways that show the three-dimensional reality rather than just implying it in only two dimensions. His approach is effective for many types of images: forest scenes with overlapping foliage or trees, cityscapes or abstract images with under-lying geometric patterns – in short, any image where additional dimensions stimulate closer inspection and the discovery of something that would be missed in a 2-dimensional print. This special exhibition is free and open to the public from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through August 25. articles.text: The plot of The Wife is an elegant and intimate vehicle for the remarkable talent of Glenn Close as she portrays Joan Castleman, wife of Joe Castleman (impressively performed by Jonathan Pryce). For all 40 years of their marriage Joan has been content to walk in the literary shadow of Joe – college professor and accomplished novelist. However, it is at this point in their lives, the year is 1992, that the narrative hints, ever so subtly, that Joan is feeling that their relationship is becoming increasingly restrictive. The dormant emotions are triggered when Joe receives an early morning phone call at their Connecticut home, informing him that he has won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Joan is in the den, on the phone’s extension, and the camera lingers on her face as she hears this much hoped for news. Yet, briefly, the joy and excitement that she feels is eclipsed by something else, an enigmatic foreshadowing, yet to be revealed. And so, after several receptions and countless toasts and voiced congratulations, Joe and Joan and their son, David (Max Irons), leave on the Concorde for Stockholm for the Nobel awards ceremony. It is there that they step into a swirl of adulation, preparation, rehearsals and press photographs. Joe relishes and encourages the attention. What soon becomes obvious, expressed through the reactions of Joan, is that their marriage is unraveling and the honor bestowed on Joe is pushing fragile truths to the surface. Issues were once studiously buried beneath a patina of compromise and swallowed silence. Joan is growing increasingly impatient. Her signals of mounting discontent are at first discounted or simply ignored by Joe. This is his moment on the world stage. There is a something deeper at work and its import has yet to be fully revealed. The Nobel Prize is but a metaphor. Throughout the film, the camera caresses Close’s face, holds on her visage, the flash in her eyes, the set of her mouth, the tilt of her head, all silently speaking to the audience, all capturing one singular moment and then the next. It’s a master class in acting by Close, a consummate performer inhabiting a character. The Wife. Directed by Bjorn Runge. Starring Glenn Close, Jonathan Price, Christian Slater. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. Streaming on Fandango/ prime/apple tv. Glenn Close and Nick Fletcher in The Wife
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Wife a tour de force by Glenn Close

articles.text: Mark Rylance and Tom Hanks in Bridge of Spies In retrospect, the Soviet Union and the United States managed to navigate almost 50 years of adversarial encounters without a confrontation that would have taken us past the brink of the deterrence known as mutual assured destruction (aka MAD). Part of the kabuki dance that the two superpowers engaged in, however, was elaborate and the result of sustained spying. Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies, is a taut and well-made film, based on a true story. It begins in 1957 with the arrest by the FBI of Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel (Mark Ryance). The government, certain it had overwhelming evidence of his clandestine activity, decided to put him on trial. James Donovan (Tom Hanks), an insurance attorney, is selected to defend Abel who has stoically resisted all attempts by the CIA to extract information from him. What the government did not anticipate was that Donovan would mount a rigorous defense on Abel’s behalf, followed by an appeal of his conviction. Donovan was denigrated for carrying out what he felt was his constitutional obligation. He also suggested to the trial judge that Abel not be given the death penalty, arguing that should one of our spies be captured we just might need Abel should there be a proffered swap. So that’s the protracted set up. Written by Joel and Ethan Cohen, Bridge of Spies is actually a remarkable two-act story. Act one is the Abel capture and trial. Act two involves Donovan’s prescient statement about a possible trade at some point in the future – our guy for your guy. Our guy, as it turned out, was Francis Gary Powers, the U2 spy plane pilot, shot down in 1960 by the Russians. What could go wrong does go wrong and he’s captured and put on trial. The Soviets now have their spy. This is wonderful, spare, retro moviemaking, delivered as only Spielberg can. Act two is launched. Donovan is selected to negotiate the exchange and arrives in East Germany just after the Berlin wall was built (1961) to talk to the Soviets and the East Germans about how to achieve the grudgingly agreed upon trade. It’s winter, the skies are leaden, East German buildings and streets are awash in institutional blues and grays. Donovan, suffering from a tenacious cold, walks ever closer to a precipice, lost in a world of duplicity and obscure signals. He never knows if he is in discussion with the decision- makers or straw men. All that has occurred, from 1957 to 1962, leads to that intersection on a bridge which divides East from West. The outcome is always in doubt, the distrust between the players palpable. Tom Hanks gives a nuanced and spot-on performance, his portrayal worthy of awards. Ditto the movie. But not to forget Mark Ryance, accomplished stage actor, as Abel – his character is laconic in the extreme while laced with a humor so dry that it crackles. His scene-stealing is superb. As is this very entertaining film. Bridge of Spies. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Tom Hanks, Mark Rylance and Alan Alda. 2 hrs., 21 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2015. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/apple tv.
articles.title: Bridge of Spies one of Spielberg’s best

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Wind Rises The Wind Rises was intended to be Hayao Miyazaki’s final film. It would also serve as this intensely creative animator and storyteller’s tribute to Jiro Horikoshi, known in Japan as a master aeronautical engineer and a pioneer in aircraft design during the first half of the 20th century. Through Miyazaki’s prism, Jiro (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is portrayed as a bookish, bespectacled boy and young man (not dissimilar from Harry Potter) who possessed a dreamy, distracted manner, often lost in his imagination, his visions of airplanes filling his thoughts. Early on, Jiro so loved the idea of flight that he imagines meeting the Italian aeronautical engineer Giovanni Battista Caproni, who encourages him to pursue his love of airplanes and design. As it turns out Jiro cannot be a pilot himself because of his eyesight. And yet fly he does. As part of the story, Miyazaki includes a sad and tender romance between Jiro and a young woman, Naoko Satomi (Emily Blunt). They meet in Tokyo during Japan’s most devastating Great Kanto Earthquake in 1923, a natural disaster that all but leveled Tokyo and is grippingly captured in the film’s intense images. It is Naoko who quotes to Jiro the words of poet Paul Valéry, “The wind rises, we must try to live,” and is the source of the film’s title. In Jiro, Miyazaki creates a character of inherent idealism and innocence, qualities that thread their way through the wide spectrum of his own work. With insight and a languid beauty, using the resilient metaphor of wind, he involves, nay mesmerizes, those who gaze upon his wondrous animation, which never fails to transcend. Tweens and young teens will be enamored of Jiro and his personal quest to follow his dream. Others jaded by life and reality will recall that it was also Jiro Horikoshi who would one day design the Japanese Zero fighter aircraft used to deadly effect during WWII (Kamikaze meant “Divine Wind”). As a result, The Wind Rises opened worldwide to controversy. But it soon became Japan’s highest grossing film in 2013, was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, was awarded a Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and won the Japan Academy Prize for Animation of the Year. The Wind Rises, Animated from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Emily Blunt and Martin Short. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/MAX
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS The Wind Rises a beautiful film from Miyazaki

articles.text: Kodi Smit-McPhee in Alpha If you’re a parent of a tween or a newbie teen who may be feeling a bit anxious about the approaching first day of school, we suggest seeing the movie Alpha. It’s a wonderful merging of old-fashioned story-telling and state-ofthe art technology, creating a solidly engaging and riveting tale about a boy who out of kindness and then necessity befriends an injured wolf. But this narrative is not of the Lassie Come Home genre. The film is set in southwestern Europe, just as the Ice Age is coming to a close, meaning some 20,000 years ago. The story opens with Tau (Johannes Haukur Johannesson), the clan’s chief, leading a small cohort of hunters, to include his teenage son, Keda (Kodi Smit McPhee), on a bison hunt. Actually the strategy is to charge at the animals, herd them toward a cliff where some will drop to their deaths and can then be butchered and skinned later. During the stampede, Keda is thrown off the same cliff by a massive bison, falling onto a ledge some 20 feet below, knocked unconscious. His father is frantic but realizes that reaching his son is impossible and will risk his own death. Sadly, he is uncertain if Keda is still alive. Painfully, grief-stricken, the hunters leave Keda, stopping only to salvage the hides and meat of the bison deep in the gorge, and then start for home. And so begins the boy’s journey of survival. He is injured, his right ankle severely damaged from the fall. And he must find a way off the ledge. Remarkably, it begins to rain in torrents, and the deep canyon below is filled with flash flooding water. Having no choice, Keda drops down into the muddy waters, waking up on a muddy bank, the waters having receded. Placing his ankle between two rocks he snaps it back into place, fashions a splint with sticks and leather thongs, and slowly, awkwardly, limps toward the horizon. Soon he hears the howl of wolves. Terrified, he finds a gnarled and desiccated tree, and. with the wolves close behind, he clings to a wide branch as the wolves circle below. As the sun sets, Keda sees that one of the wolves has been injured and realizes that the wolf pack has left, leaving the wounded wolf below. His mother, Nu (Mercedes de Zerda), had counseled that Tau “leads with his heart, not his spear.” And so, at sunrise, Keda climbs down and begins to care for the wolf. And thus begins the story of a boy and a wolf and the start of a long, forced march toward the home of his clan. It is a precarious and perilous “walk about,” requiring that Keda and the wolf, eventually named Alpha, gradually learn to trust, then protect one another, as well as hunt as a team. As their journey continues, they are tested by predators and the elements. Alpha is gorgeous to look at, the landscapes breathtaking, the vastness of a deep blue sky, the distant horizons stunning. At night, in the heavens, the stars are a blanket of white and swirling pink. It is from that map of stars, marked on Keda’s hand by his father, which helps him find true north and the path leading home. As well, embedded in Alpha are countless questions about what life must have been like for a boy some 20,000 years ago. This is a classic, straightforward adventure film, as well as a rite of passage moment in Keda’s life. It’s compelling and thrilling, and a great end-of-summer movie. One tangential point: this story can be intense and has its harrowing moments. It may be more than some youngsters can handle. Alpha. Directed by Albert Hughes. Starring Kodi Smith, Jens Hulténm Natasha Malthe. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on prime/Fandango/apple tv.
articles.title: Alpha – a boy and a wolf during Ice Age

articles.text: Benji (2018) is a remake of the popular 1974 family-friendly film that focuses on the love of a stray dog by two latchkey kids, Carter and Frankie Hughes (Gabriel Bateman and Darby Camp) who recently lost their father, and live with their single mom, Whitney Hughes (Kiele Sanchez). The story opens when a mother canine and her small litter are taken to the animal shelter by a malevolent dogcatcher. Out of the shadows appears the face of a pint-sized pooch, watching as the family is carted off. He is a mixed-breed dog who lives on the street, searching for food wherever he can find it. In his travels, he meets up with Carter and Frankie. They try and feed him some strawberries, but he is cautious and timid; however, he quickly realizes that the kids will not hurt him and follows them home. Carter spots the little guy outside, and they decide to bring him inside. Uncertain of their mom’s reaction they hide him under a pile of stuffed animals. Frankie wants to name him after Benjamin Franklin, which naturally gets shortened to Benji. When mom discovers Benji, she insists that the kids take the stray back where they found him. With regret they obey, and leaving Benji to fend for himself they stop off at Mr. Sam’s Pawn Shop (Gralen Bryant Banks). Without their knowing, Benji follows them. To their surprise, they walk into the middle of a robbery carried out by two thugs (Will Rothhaar and Angus Sampson). When one of their masks slips off, they realize that Carter and Frankie can identify them and so they kidnap the kids, forcing them into a van. Benji, who has been outside waiting, sees this taking place and chases after the van, all the way to the robbers’ hideout, a large, decaying plantation house. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, August 7, 2024 MOVIES FOR KIDS The Wind Rises a beautiful film from Miyazaki Alpha – a boy and a wolf during Ice Age A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Wind Rises By Chris Honoré The Wind Rises was intended to be Hayao Miyazaki’s final film. It would also serve as this intensely creative animator and storyteller’s tribute to Jiro Horikoshi, known in Japan as a master aeronautical engineer and a pioneer in aircraft design during the first half of the 20th century. Through Miyazaki’s prism, Jiro (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is portrayed as a bookish, bespectacled boy and young man (not dissimilar from Harry Potter) who possessed a dreamy, distracted manner, often lost in his imagination, his visions of airplanes filling his thoughts. Early on, Jiro so loved the idea of flight that he imagines meeting the Italian aeronautical engineer Giovanni Battista Caproni, who encourages him to pursue his love of airplanes and design. As it turns out Jiro cannot be a pilot himself because of his eyesight. And yet fly he does. As part of the story, Miyazaki includes a sad and tender romance between Jiro and a young woman, Naoko Satomi (Emily Blunt). They meet in Tokyo during Japan’s most devastating Great Kanto Earthquake in 1923, a natural disaster that all but leveled Tokyo and is grippingly captured in the film’s intense images. It is Naoko who quotes to Jiro the words of poet Paul Valéry, “The wind rises, we must try to live,” and is the source of the film’s title. In Jiro, Miyazaki creates a character of inherent idealism and innocence, qualities that thread their way through the wide spectrum of his own work. With insight and a languid beauty, using the resilient metaphor of wind, he involves, nay mesmerizes, those who gaze upon his wondrous animation, which never fails to transcend. Tweens and young teens will be enamored of Jiro and his personal quest to follow his dream. Others jaded by life and reality will recall that it was also Jiro Horikoshi who would one day design the Japanese Zero fighter aircraft used to deadly effect during WWII (Kamikaze meant “Divine Wind”). As a result, The Wind Rises opened worldwide to controversy. But it soon became Japan’s highest grossing film in 2013, was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, was awarded a Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and won the Japan Academy Prize for Animation of the Year. The Wind Rises, Animated from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Emily Blunt and Martin Short. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/MAX Kids will love new version of Benji By Chris Honoré Benji (2018) is a remake of the popular 1974 family-friendly film that focuses on the love of a stray dog by two latchkey kids, Carter and Frankie Hughes (Gabriel Bateman and Darby Camp) who recently lost their father, and live with their single mom, Whitney Hughes (Kiele Sanchez). The story opens when a mother canine and her small litter are taken to the animal shelter by a malevolent dogcatcher. Out of the shadows appears the face of a pint-sized pooch, watching as the family is carted off. He is a mixed-breed dog who lives on the street, searching for food wherever he can find it. In his travels, he meets up with Carter and Frankie. They try and feed him some strawberries, but he is cautious and timid; however, he quickly realizes that the kids will not hurt him and follows them home. Carter spots the little guy outside, and they decide to bring him inside. Uncertain of their mom’s reaction they hide him under a pile of stuffed animals. Frankie wants to name him after Benjamin Franklin, which naturally gets shortened to Benji. When mom discovers Benji, she insists that the kids take the stray back where they found him. With regret they obey, and leaving Benji to fend for himself they stop off at Mr. Sam’s Pawn Shop (Gralen Bryant Banks). Without their knowing, Benji follows them. To their surprise, they walk into the middle of a robbery carried out by two thugs (Will Rothhaar and Angus Sampson). When one of their masks slips off, they realize that Carter and Frankie can identify them and so they kidnap the kids, forcing them into a van. Benji, who has been outside waiting, sees this taking place and chases after the van, all the way to the robbers’ hideout, a large, decaying plantation house. Watching the kids being taken into the house, and seeing that the men own a mean-looking Rottweiler, Benji hurries back to Grant and Frankie’s home where he tries to convince Whitney and a friendly cop, Lyle (Jerod Haynes), to follow him back to the hideout. Of course the children in the audience are rooting for Benji, and hoping that the adults will figure out what Benji is trying to say. Starring Gabriel Bateman, Darby Camp, Kiele Sanchez. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated G. Released 2018, Now streaming on Netflix Kodi Smit-McPhee in Alpha By Chris Honoré If you’re a parent of a tween or a newbie teen who may be feeling a bit anxious about the approaching first day of school, we suggest seeing the movie Alpha. It’s a wonderful merging of old-fashioned story-telling and state-ofthe art technology, creating a solidly engaging and riveting tale about a boy who out of kindness and then necessity befriends an injured wolf. But this narrative is not of the Lassie Come Home genre. The film is set in southwestern Europe, just as the Ice Age is coming to a close, meaning some 20,000 years ago. The story opens with Tau (Johannes Haukur Johannesson), the clan’s chief, leading a small cohort of hunters, to include his teenage son, Keda (Kodi Smit McPhee), on a bison hunt. Actually the strategy is to charge at the animals, herd them toward a cliff where some will drop to their deaths and can then be butchered and skinned later. During the stampede, Keda is thrown off the same cliff by a massive bison, falling onto a ledge some 20 feet below, knocked unconscious. His father is frantic but realizes that reaching his son is impossible and will risk his own death. Sadly, he is uncertain if Keda is still alive. Painfully, grief-stricken, the hunters leave Keda, stopping only to salvage the hides and meat of the bison deep in the gorge, and then start for home. And so begins the boy’s journey of survival. He is injured, his right ankle severely damaged from the fall. And he must find a way off the ledge. Remarkably, it begins to rain in torrents, and the deep canyon below is filled with flash flooding water. Having no choice, Keda drops down into the muddy waters, waking up on a muddy bank, the waters having receded. Placing his ankle between two rocks he snaps it back into place, fashions a splint with sticks and leather thongs, and slowly, awkwardly, limps toward the horizon. Soon he hears the howl of wolves. Terrified, he finds a gnarled and desiccated tree, and. with the wolves close behind, he clings to a wide branch as the wolves circle below. As the sun sets, Keda sees that one of the wolves has been injured and realizes that the wolf pack has left, leaving the wounded wolf below. His mother, Nu (Mercedes de Zerda), had counseled that Tau “leads with his heart, not his spear.” And so, at sunrise, Keda climbs down and begins to care for the wolf. And thus begins the story of a boy and a wolf and the start of a long, forced march toward the home of his clan. It is a precarious and perilous “walk about,” requiring that Keda and the wolf, eventually named Alpha, gradually learn to trust, then protect one another, as well as hunt as a team. As their journey continues, they are tested by predators and the elements. Alpha is gorgeous to look at, the landscapes breathtaking, the vastness of a deep blue sky, the distant horizons stunning. At night, in the heavens, the stars are a blanket of white and swirling pink. It is from that map of stars, marked on Keda’s hand by his father, which helps him find true north and the path leading home. As well, embedded in Alpha are countless questions about what life must have been like for a boy some 20,000 years ago. This is a classic, straightforward adventure film, as well as a rite of passage moment in Keda’s life. It’s compelling and thrilling, and a great end-of-summer movie. One tangential point: this story can be intense and has its harrowing moments. It may be more than some youngsters can handle. Alpha. Directed by Albert Hughes. Starring Kodi Smith, Jens Hulténm Natasha Malthe. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on prime/Fandango/apple tv.
