articles.text: Bonita Avenue School was Piedmont’s first public school, built in 1909 and designed by Albert Farr. The first order of business was to build a city hall and a school. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had eight classrooms for eight teachers who taught eight grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. An aerial photo in 1947 shows the original Bonita Avenue School with the 1938 classroom addition across the back, and the auditorium added in 1940.

articles.text: The April 18, 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire sent thousands of San Franciscans fleeing to the East Bay. The fires and smoke were visible for days from the Piedmont hills as over 15,000 lost their homes in the fire. While there were no reports of refugees camping in Piedmont Park, some refugees did stay with friends in Piedmont. As Oakland looked to the hills to annex more land for this influx of earthquake survivors, a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents did not want Piedmont to become part of Oakland. Hugh Craig and James Ballentine immediately began an effort to incorporate Piedmont as a city. They quickly drew up a map of Piedmont’s borders using an existing Piedmont Sanitary District map and filed the map in Sacramento. On January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate. The vote passed, and Piedmont officially became a municipality four days later, January 30, 1907. A photo from 1926 shows Ellen Driscoll, then the principal of Havens School, with her students. Under the guidance of Clara Crumpton, the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School, students recreated the Tower of Jewels, the centerpiece of the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 7, 2024 21 The History of Piedmont Piedmont’s first school: Bonita Avenue School By Gail G. Lombardi The April 18, 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire sent thousands of San Franciscans fleeing to the East Bay. The fires and smoke were visible for days from the Piedmont hills as over 15,000 lost their homes in the fire. While there were no reports of refugees camping in Piedmont Park, some refugees did stay with friends in Piedmont. As Oakland looked to the hills to annex more land for this influx of earthquake survivors, a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents did not want Piedmont to become part of Oakland. Hugh Craig and James Ballentine immediately began an effort to incorporate Piedmont as a city. They quickly drew up a map of Piedmont’s borders using an existing Piedmont Sanitary District map and filed the map in Sacramento. On January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate. The vote passed, and Piedmont officially became a municipality four days later, January 30, 1907. A photo from 1926 shows Ellen Driscoll, then the principal of Havens School, with her students. Bonita Avenue School was Piedmont’s first public school, built in 1909 and designed by Albert Farr. The first order of business was to build a city hall and a school. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had eight classrooms for eight teachers who taught eight grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. Hand-painted panels in the ceiling of all three school auditoriums were executed by 5th and 6th grade students in a paintby-number fashion. At the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, they depict California history. In 1953, the Piedmont Board of Education considered the 1909 Havens School to be inadequate to meet the school enrollment at the time. The number of students had grown to the point where some classrooms were in temporary buildings. A bond issue was passed, and the new Frank C. Havens School, designed by nationally recognized architects Miller-Warnecke, was completed in 1955 with 12 classrooms, a library, an administration office and cafeteria. By 2010 the sleek modern design of 1955 was considered an earthquake hazard and was replaced by the current Frank C. Havens School, designed by Mark Becker. For more on Piedmont’s history and the Piedmont Historical Society, visit the website: Piedmonthistorical.org. Previously published in the Post on April 25, 2018. Under the guidance of Clara Crumpton, the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School, students recreated the Tower of Jewels, the centerpiece of the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco. An aerial photo in 1947 shows the original Bonita Avenue School with the 1938 classroom addition across the back, and the auditorium added in 1940.

articles.text: A recent Post article reported that a Palm Drive home had won a landscape design award. Dick Carter thought it would be fun for the walkers to guess which home won. The group went through the Piedmont High campus, down its “PE Hill” to the under-construction Witter Field. At Witter they found workers were applying the top, burnt orange surface over a recently laid, black undersurface. In 1898 Piedmont real estate developer Frank C. Havens developed the Piedmont Springs Park attraction. It had a grand, palm-lined entrance that later became Palm Drive. One of the first improvements Havens made was the creation of a living hedge maze modeled after Hampton Court in England. The Maze was demolished when a new School Board purchased part of the park land in 1920 for its new high school and athletic field. The Maze was where Witter Field is today. The City also purchased Havens’ remaining park land for the current Piedmont Park. The original Witter Field surface was grass and the track around it was less than a quarter mile. The field was re-dedicated as the Witter Sports Complex in 1998 with a new synthetic turf field, a full quarter mile track, new baseball and softball fields, and a new field house. Witter Field’s original synthetic turf and track were replaced in 2007 because they were worn out. By the mid- 2010s they needed to be replaced again. Witter’s underground drainage system also needed to be replaced, as rain regularly flooded the field. The renovation was expected to be paid for with Measure H1 bond funds that Piedmont voters approved in 2016 for new high school facilities. However, construction costs exceeded estimates and the work at Witter was postponed. In February 2019, it was announced the project, which had been tentatively scheduled for that spring and summer, was being delayed for at least another year. It was determined that the costs for a new synthetic field and track surface could be paid for primarily with State facilities modernization and other funds, but the project was deferred again for at least another year until there was a clearer timeframe for disbursement of the State funds. The field renovation was budgeted for $3.6 million in 2019, but the estimated cost escalated to as much as $5.5 million. Construction finally began on June 6, 2023. The original timetable showed that the renovation could be fully completed in December 2023. However, many unforeseen surprises caused delays. EBMUD had to install a 54-inch aqueduct that runs under the field. The contractor discovered 60,000 square feet of substandard asphalt base needed to be removed and replaced before the track could be paved. In January 2024 change orders totaling a little over $155,000 were approved for this repair. The paving could start in February 2024, but the surfaces needed 30 days each to cure. To allow for high school spring sports, the track resurfacing was pushed back to June. The subsurface was prepared and ready for paving on June 17, and the final completion and reopening is scheduled for Friday, August 9. The first day of classes this year is August 12. The walkers continued to Palm Drive, where they came to the home of Karen and David Saenz. David came out and explained how his yard won the California Landscape Contractors Association’s 2024 Petite Residential Beautification Award. The group completed their walk of Palm and returned to the Exedra via Park View, Winsor, and Wildwood Avenues, and through what was once Havens’ Piedmont Springs Park. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu/. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 53 walkers and three K-9 best friends on July 24. Among those participating were: Melba Yee, Joanne Larson, Kat Lang, Linda Samuels, Sean Brient, Charlene Louie, Kathy Rolefson, Jeff Samuels, Helen Dong, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Stella Houston, Dave DeRoche, Tina Shum, Quincy Dong, Cherry Li, Jasmine Cai, Swee Ling Chen, Don Fones, Marianne Jakus, Silva Fones, Peggy Shultz, Bill Ahern, Jim Kellogg, Judy Love, Alicia Rivera, Joyce Ahern, Claudine Bach, Elane Rehr, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Sherry Jacobs, Jack Fischrup, Sharona Fischrup, Denny McGee, Brenda Fierro, Alan Goldhammer, Chuck Oraftik, Renee Goldhammer, Bob Wong, Jim Kuo, Phil Witte, Will Adams, Nadine Guffanti, Mary Carter, Sarah Johnson, Mari Negron with K-9 best friend Dakota, Mike Gallant, Rebecca Aldrich, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Dan Appelman, Carrie Weston, Kimberly Aumack-Yee, and Patsy Forsyth with K-9 best friend Chewy who were walking with the group for the first time.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Apricot and Almond Tea Cake is a sure-fire favorite for any occasion. This is a bonafide pantry cake! The opportunity for swaps is abundant in this simple cake, depending on what is available when the mood strikes to bake. Any variety of dried fruit should work, cherries, cranberries, dates, etc. Rehydrate accordingly to ensure a tender texture in the cake. If the dried fruit is soft and pliable, then skip the rehydration step. Either almond extract or vanilla extract will be delicious. If you don’t have either, try taking the melted butter to the next level and brown it slightly to impart its slightly nutty taste to the cake. The topping may be made with any nuts – finely chopped walnuts or pecans would be delicious. Or make a quick streusel, with or without nuts. Apricot and Almond Tea Cake Adapted from Food 52/Sarah Jampel Makes a shallow 10-inch cake INGREDIENTS • 1⁄2 cup unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 1⁄4 cup sour cream • 1 cup granulated sugar, divided 7⁄8 cup for the cake and 1⁄8 cup for the top of the cake • 2 eggs • 11⁄2 cup all-purpose flour • 1⁄2 teaspoon baking soda • 1⁄8 teaspoon salt • 1⁄3 cup dried apricots, diced into 1⁄4-inch pieces • 1 teaspoon fresh lemon zest • 1⁄2 teaspoon almond extract (substitute 1 teaspoon vanilla extract) • 3⁄4 cup sliced almonds INSTRUCTIONS 1. Position an oven rack in the middle position, and preheat oven to 350° F. Generously butter the bottom and sides of a 10-inch pie plate. 2. Rehydrate the diced apricots in a small bowl and cover with warm water. Let sit for 5-10 minutes, then drain the water and spread out on a clean towel to dry the pieces on all sides. You want to get them as dry as possible. This step is optional if your dried fruit is soft and pliable. 3. Combine the flour, baking soda salt in a small bowl. Whisk gently to blend thoroughly. 4. Combine the melted butter, sour cream and 7⁄8’s cup of sugar in a large bowl and mix well to combine. (Can be done either by hand with a sturdy whisk or a hand mixer.) 5. Add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each addition. Add the almond extract and lemon zest. 6. Add the flour mixture and mix gently until well incorporated but taking care to avoid over-mixing. Fold in the dried apricots. 7. Pour the batter into the prepared pie plate and smooth to level the surface. Sprinkle the sliced almonds atop in an even layer; then sprinkle on the remaining 1⁄8 cup of granulated sugar in a thin, even layer on top of the sliced almonds. 8. Bake for 30-35 minutes until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, and the cake and almonds are golden brown. 9. Cool completely before slicing. (The most difficult part of this recipe!) 10. Sit back and smile at what you have created.
articles.title: Apricot and Almond Tea Cake

Rehydrate the diced apricots in a small bowl and cover with warm water. Let sit for 5-10 minutes, then drain the water and spread out on a clean towel to dry the pieces on all sides. You want to get them as dry as possible. This step is optional if your dried fruit is soft and pliable. 3. Combine the flour, baking soda salt in a small bowl. Whisk gently to blend thoroughly. 4. Combine the melted butter, sour cream and 7⁄8’s cup of sugar in a large bowl and mix well to combine. (Can be done either by hand with a sturdy whisk or a hand mixer.) 5. Add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each addition. Add the almond extract and lemon zest. 6. Add the flour mixture and mix gently until well incorporated but taking care to avoid over-mixing. Fold in the dried apricots. 7. Pour the batter into the prepared pie plate and smooth to level the surface. Sprinkle the sliced almonds atop in an even layer; then sprinkle on the remaining 1⁄8 cup of granulated sugar in a thin, even layer on top of the sliced almonds. 8. Bake for 30-35 minutes until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, and the cake and almonds are golden brown. 9. Cool completely before slicing. (The most difficult part of this recipe!) 10. Sit back and smile at what you have created.

At 89, Kaz lived a full life. Born to Michael and Bertha Lawler, Kaz was raised in the Manayunk area of Philadelphia, PA and attended Villanova University where he studied Civil Engineering and was a part of the Navy ROTC program. During his commute to college Kaz met his future wife, Gloria. After graduation Kaz attended flight school with the US Navy and was assigned to be a transport pilot, moving men and materials around the world. In order to make it to his wedding, Kaz secured a special 24-hour pass to fly from Pensacola, Florida to Philadelphia, PA. Kaz later qualified to fly on aircraft carriers and served during the Cuban Missile Crisis on the USS Essex, the first US carrier to enforce the quarantine. During the Vietnam War Kaz flew the largest carrier plane, the A3 Skywarrior, from the smallest carrier, the USS Hancock, making over 150 carrier landings. From the USS Hancock, Kaz flew missions to refuel fighter jets in the air over the Gulf of Tonkin, as well as electronic counter-measure combat missions to protect the planes in flight and ships at sea. With the Navy, Kaz and Gloria moved many places around the country and raised a family of five children. They settled in Piedmont in 1967 when Kaz was assigned to the USS Hancock. In 1970, Kaz retired from Casimir “Kaz” Lawler of Piedmont died on July 14, 2024. He was 89. active duty to spend more time with his family. He worked as an engineer for the Naval Air Rework Facility in Alameda and retired as head of Quality Control for the Navy’s S3 Viking and the A3 Skywarrior aircraft. Kaz enjoyed traveling with Gloria throughout the world, visiting 35 countries. Kaz also loved traveling with the entire extended family, especially to Paris. Kaz is preceded in death by his beloved wife Gloria. He is survived by five children, nine grandchildren and one great-grandchild. He is additionally survived by a sister and brother. A memorial service will be held on August 23 at 11:00 a.m. in the Tower Chapel at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. Donations in Kaz’s name may be made to The American Cancer Society at www.cancer.org.

articles.text: In the midst of summer heat, it’s hard to think about the cool fall days ahead. For your garden, now is the ideal time to start sowing seeds for the next growing season. Fall gardening is one of the most underrated seasons; there are less weeds, fewer pests, and often more rain to help out with watering. Here are a few key takeaways to consider before planting for cool season harvests. As soon as your spring and summer crops stop producing, pull them to make room for all those delicious fall and winter crops. Start cool season vegetables in their place while we still have long days and warm soil. By the time brisk weather arrives, your plants will be strong, sturdy, and well established for whatever fall throws their way. Clean up garden beds by hoeing weeds, adding lots of compost, broadforking the soil to allow for air and moisture infiltration, and topping with mulch. Mulching in summer is key to moderating soil temperatures and keeping all that irrigation moisture in the ground. Watering is the most important task for your newly planted fall garden. High temperatures and low humidity mean that you’ll need to check the moisture of your seedlings often while they establish. If the heat of the sun is too intense, consider adding a lightweight shade cloth over your garden bed to keep things cool. Rita’s harvest of fall carrots Fall can really feel like a second spring. Here’s a selection of a few vegetables to plant in late summer to keep your garden growing through autumn. Broccoli and kale mature well in cool weather and will not be bothered by the cabbage moth as they are in spring weather. Root crops, like carrots and beets, will take longer but are worth the wait since they grow sweeter as the days get cooler. Snap and snow peas start producing in 60 days, and peas that mature in cold weather seem especially sweet and crisp. The real stars of the fall garden are Asian greens, like tatsoi, pak choi, mizuna, and napa cabbage. Quick-maturing varieties can even be harvested in 45 days. We are so lucky to be California gardeners with a long growing season. So, freshen up your empty beds with some compost and get ready to plant your second garden. articles.text: The dark clouds over Rajamangala Stadium in Bangkok led to monsoon rain, resulting in the Tottenham’s match being called off. It is considered the Crème-dela-crème of world football known in the U.S. as soccer. In 2019, Tottenham lost 2-0 in the finals to Liverpool, but stole hearts with its magical comeback victory against Ajax of the Netherlands when the Hotspur won with a second-half hat trick by Lucas Moura to beat Ajax on the away-goals rule in a 3-3 result. The Champions League knockout stages, other than the finals, are played in two legs. Tottenham lost the first leg 0-1 at its home stadium, but beat Ajax 3-2 on a magic night in Amsterdam—enabling the away-goal rule for outscoring an opponent in its home stadium. Moura, who came in as a second-half substitute when Tottenham trailed 0-3 scored goals in the 55th minute, 59th minute and then at the veryvery end at 90+6’ in the literal final seconds of the match. It would be comparable to a successful Hail Mary in American Football from your team’s own 40-yard line as the time expired. Watching Moura’s final shot in the waning seconds trickle across the line past Ajax’s Andre Onana’s dive birthed a new a fan thousands of miles away in California. In the time that followed, discovering the organization’s 140 years of tradition continued to gain my interest. The majority of European clubs have been around for well over 100 year and are steeped in traditions. Tottenham was a haven for England’s Jewish population in the 1930s. In the 1980’s Hotspur supporters reclaimed the slurs and have used them as a term of endearment ever since. Last year, Tottenham took its preseason tour to Bangkok, perfectly lining up with our vacation from The Post and a scheduled match between the Hotspur and Leicester City. The tour marked the final time for Hotspur supporters to watch England’s captain of its national team, Harry Kane, in person before he was traded to German superpower Bayern Munich. However, Tottenham scheduled the match during Thailand’s monsoon season. On Sunday, July 23, rain began to build an hour before kickoff, resulting in a waterlogged pitch that was unable to be safely played on, preventing balls from bouncing off of the ground, literally sticking like an arrow shot into the grass. articles.text: (12-17) of gratitude and confidence represented by words like “Yet God has been my king from ancient days” (12a). In the parables of Jesus, grief and gratitude are intermingled. An example is the Parable of the Lost Sheep. In this parable Jesus tells of a shepherd who must leave his flock in order to find one sheep who has wondered away. A lost sheep would have been an occasion for both fear and grief. A caring shepherd would not take such a loss easily or lightly. Jesus then speaks of the joy that comes when the lost is found and the terrified lamb is carried home. When the lost is found there is gratitude. One reason this parable continues to speak, even to those of us unfamiliar with sheep and shepherds, is that most us are well acquainted with loss and grief. We are also well acquainted with the gratitude that comes with restoration, recovery and remembering. Grief and gratitude travel together. They intersect. The prayer, the hope, of the great religious traditions, and my personal faith as well, is that at their point of intersection grace is born and that is grace which will lead us home. We do well to consider the ways in which these fellow travelers, grief and gratitude, travel with us. Rev. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue in Oakland. In the parables of Jesus, grief and gratitude are intermingled. An example is the Parable of the Lost Sheep. In this parable Jesus tells of a shepherd who must leave his flock in order to find one sheep who has wondered away. A lost sheep would have been an occasion for both fear and grief. A caring shepherd would not take such a loss easily or lightly. Jesus then speaks of the joy that comes when the lost is found and the terrified lamb is carried home. When the lost is found there is gratitude. One reason this parable continues to speak, even to those of us unfamiliar with sheep and shepherds, is that most us are well acquainted with loss and grief. We are also well acquainted with the gratitude that comes with restoration, recovery and remembering. Grief and gratitude travel together. They intersect. The prayer, the hope, of the great religious traditions, and my personal faith as well, is that at their point of intersection grace is born and that is grace which will lead us home. We do well to consider the ways in which these fellow travelers, grief and gratitude, travel with us. Rev. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue in Oakland. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on September 21, 2022. The dark clouds over Rajamangala Stadium in Bangkok led to monsoon rain, resulting in the Tottenham’s match being called off. It is considered the Crème-dela-crème of world football known in the U.S. as soccer. In 2019, Tottenham lost 2-0 in the finals to Liverpool, but stole hearts with its magical comeback victory against Ajax of the Netherlands when the Hotspur won with a second-half hat trick by Lucas Moura to beat Ajax on the away-goals rule in a 3-3 result. The Champions League knockout stages, other than the finals, are played in two legs. Tottenham lost the first leg 0-1 at its home stadium, but beat Ajax 3-2 on a magic night in Amsterdam—enabling the away-goal rule for outscoring an opponent in its home stadium. Moura, who came in as a second-half substitute when Tottenham trailed 0-3 scored goals in the 55th minute, 59th minute and then at the veryvery end at 90+6’ in the literal final seconds of the match. It would be comparable to a successful Hail Mary in American Football from your team’s own 40-yard line as the time expired. Watching Moura’s final shot in the waning seconds trickle across the line past Ajax’s Andre Onana’s dive birthed a new a fan thousands of miles away in California. In the time that followed, discovering the organization’s 140 years of tradition continued to gain my interest. The majority of European clubs have been around for well over 100 year and are steeped in traditions. Tottenham was a haven for England’s Jewish population in the 1930s. In the 1980’s Hotspur supporters reclaimed the slurs and have used them as a term of endearment ever since. Last year, Tottenham took its preseason tour to Bangkok, perfectly lining up with our vacation from The Post and a scheduled match between the Hotspur and Leicester City. The tour marked the final time for Hotspur supporters to watch England’s captain of its national team, Harry Kane, in person before he was traded to German superpower Bayern Munich. However, Tottenham scheduled the match during Thailand’s monsoon season. On Sunday, July 23, rain began to build an hour before kickoff, resulting in a waterlogged pitch that was unable to be safely played on, preventing balls from bouncing off of the ground, literally sticking like an arrow shot into the grass. As we watched the rain build on the field, there was little hope for the game to be played with a short-staffed crew working to re-line the field with chalk—only for it to disappear seconds later. With just six crew members working to clean the field, locals turned to me and laughed, saying: “Welcome to Thailand!” The match resulted in a cancelation, but it was a joy to sit with fellow Tottenham supporters and practice all the chants I’ve spent time learning over the years. And for a Hotspur supporter, any time is a good time to talk trash about Arsenal – our North London nemesis. Even with the match called off, hundreds of devout Thai fans stayed in the stands to chant the songs they’d been rehearsing in their homes. Though the match wasn’t played, it was an unforgettable experience to be huddled up in a hallway with people from Thailand, South Korea, and England. I was often asked mad this U.S. reporter from a small town in California a Spurs fan. I realized then that it’s not the pursuit of glory that makes a fan, but the passion and tradition. Khob khun krub (thank you), Thailand. A photo of the heavy rain pouring down at Rajamangala Stadium. The French refer to the resisters as les maquis (hiding in the brush). Resisters walked a dangerous tightrope continually at risk that a betrayal to the Gestapo could end their lives. Under Marshal Pétain’s Vichy regime, any neighbor could be a Nazi sympathizer or collaborator. One of the most respected Resistance leaders was Jean Moulin, and his story is told in one exhibition in the museum. His was a life dedicated to the Resistance, and he died for the cause before the German defeat. The Vichy government veered close to a police state. France, a democratic republic, to this day bears the stain of its wartime authoritarianism and anti-Semitism. The Vichy sought to blame France’s humiliating military defeat on the usual suspects – Communists, socialists and Jews. The Vichy cracked down on dissent, censored the press, and imprisoned critics. Their popularity diminished when the populace realized the depths of the deprivation of their authoritarian policies. Brutality and deaths at the hands of the Vichy piled up, and much public support was lost by the war’s end. Conversely and concurrently, the fight against Nazism was heightened as the Resistance gained momentum. The excitement of Liberation Day in Paris. Victory parade at Arc de Triomphe. When French Resistance troops battled to eject the German occupiers, it was not possible to tell who was French and who was American, because French soldiers wore U.S. uniforms, carried U.S.-made weapons, and drove U.S.-made tanks and jeeps, and were indistinguishable from the Americans – until they began to speak. The underground bunker circa 1938 is a featured exhibit in restored condition. Access is via this endless stairway down 100 steps followed by a return up the same 100 steps. General Charles de Gaulle had led a tank division against the Germans and when France surrendered in defeat, he left for England and publicly rejected the cease-fire agreement. Determined to keep fighting, de Gaulle worked with Winston Churchill who privately pressed the French to stay in the war. The General continually exhorting the resisters on the radio to never give up. Despite their considerable mutual dislike, Churchill and de Gaulle never wavered from the feat of stopping the Third Reich and Adolph Hitler. From London, de Gaulle ran the Free French forces and Resistance fighters to the war’s end, and de Gaulle was celebrated as a war hero. By 1944 Germany was weakened, the United States had joined the European front, and Free France fight was strengthened and ready to evict the occupiers. Resistance in Paris was led by Colonel Henri-Rol Tanguy from the bunker now on display at the museum. Tour of the Bunker A stairway descent appears endless, and the Liberation Museum’s bunker presents a 6-story climb back up that left me feeling a bit light-headed. It seems the air supply below may not be unlimited. Anyone with a respiratory or cardiac medical issue is not encouraged to climb. The bunker tour is strictly limited to a maximum of 30 minutes. Museum admission is free. The underground bunker tour is by special request. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and are celebrating springtime in Paris. The temple is a serene location in the middle of the bamboo forest; with ancient architecture to awe at. There is a Naga Staircase, two mythical serpent creatures down a stairwell. In Buddhist religion, the Nagas are known as protectors of the temple to ward off evil spirits. There are also three Chedis on the Wat Pha Lat grounds, which are large sacred structures that are known to house precious relics from Buddha or revered monks. There’s also a Viharn to worship Buddha. Stepping inside the building requires patrons to remove their shoes, like all temples in Thailand. Although I spotted many people in shorts, it’s not recommended to wear shorts or cutoff clothing on holy grounds in order to pay respect to Buddha. It’d be wise to keep light pants in your pack. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is a popular one, passing 46 hikers in the 0.8 mile span to the monastery before passing an uncountable amount of people walking around the temple grounds. Wat Pha Lat has a parking lot for those disinterested in putting on their hiking boots, while there are also taxis available for those wanting a short-cut to the renowned Wat Phra That Doi Suthep up the road. Venturing from Wat Pha Lat to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep by foot turns a moderate hike into a difficult one; it should only be traversed by skilled hikers ready to get their hands dirty. Although it adds just 1.4 miles of hiking to your day, you’ll pick up nearly 1,500 feet in elevation gain, requiring hikers to bring their knees all the way to your chest on some steep sections. Marching in humidity around 80 percent caused this Bay Area born-and-raised hiker to look like he jumped out of a pool when reaching Doi Suthep. But the path to Doi Suthep is extraordinary and cuts you away from the bounds of foot traffic on the Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat. After hiking up the remainder of the Monk’s Trail, you’ll intersect with Sriwichai Alley (route 1004), walking left to take the Pilgrim’s Path on the opposite side of the road. pages.text: Wednesday, August 7, 2024 31 Hiking with Jon Continued from page 15 One of the golden Buddha statues at Doi Suthep. rock that bears the monastery’s name. The temple is a serene location in the middle of the bamboo forest; with ancient architecture to awe at. There is a Naga Staircase, two mythical serpent creatures down a stairwell. In Buddhist religion, the Nagas are known as protectors of the temple to ward off evil spirits. There are also three Chedis on the Wat Pha Lat grounds, which are large sacred structures that are known to house precious relics from Buddha or revered monks. There’s also a Viharn to worship Buddha. Stepping inside the building requires patrons to remove their shoes, like all temples in Thailand. Although I spotted many people in shorts, it’s not recommended to wear shorts or cutoff clothing on holy grounds in order to pay respect to Buddha. It’d be wise to keep light pants in your pack. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is a popular one, passing 46 hikers in the 0.8 mile span to the monastery before passing an uncountable amount of people walking around the temple grounds. Wat Pha Lat has a parking lot for those disinterested in putting on their hiking boots, while there are also taxis available for those wanting a short-cut to the renowned Wat Phra That Doi Suthep up the road. Venturing from Wat Pha Lat to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep by foot turns a moderate hike into a difficult one; it should only be traversed by skilled hikers ready to get their hands dirty. Although it adds just 1.4 miles of hiking to your day, you’ll pick up nearly 1,500 feet in elevation gain, requiring hikers to bring their knees all the way to your chest on some steep sections. Marching in humidity around 80 percent caused this Bay Area born-and-raised hiker to look like he jumped out of a pool when reaching Doi Suthep. But the path to Doi Suthep is extraordinary and cuts you away from the bounds of foot traffic on the Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat. After hiking up the remainder of the Monk’s Trail, you’ll intersect with Sriwichai Alley (route 1004), walking left to take the Pilgrim’s Path on the opposite side of the road. The Pilgrim’s Path goes for 0.8 of a mile until greeting the road, once again, where you will follow the road up for the remaining half-mile up to Doi Suthep, where you will pass shops, restaurants, and taxi drivers at the bottom of the temple. Created in 1383, Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is named after the mountain which it is located and considered to be the most sacred temple in all of Thailand. There’s another magnificent Naga Staircase leading to the temple, this one much larger and colorful than the previous at Wat Pha Lat. Peer closely at the scales of the two serpents leading you towards Doi Suthep. Entrance to the monastery costs ฿100, which is just $2.85— it is also recommended to dress appropriately, so no tank tops. Some monasteries do not allow people wearing shorts as well, but if you’re traveling in July or August, some make exceptions like at Doi Suthep. You’ll find sweeping views of Chiang Mai from multiple overlooks on the grounds and several large statues of Buddha. You’ll also be required to take your shoes off when entering the primary section of the temple, where there’s a spectacular large golden Chedi, which towers 79 feet in height. Should hikers call it a day, you’ll end your hike at around 2.5 miles with over 2,000 feet in elevation gain. Taxis will be ready at the base of Doi Suthep to take your group back into town. Heading back down the road and onto the trails makes it a 4.5 mile day of hiking. Keep in mind some steep sections coupled with usual wet conditions in Thailand could make things difficult for a descent. Hikers should wear proper footgear for tackling the Monk’s Trail and Pilgrim’s Trail, along with packing mosquito repellent to keep away the pesky critters. articles.text: A dead bird found in Dracena Park has tested positive for West Nile Virus, according to the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District. On Friday, July 5, a dying crow reported near Ricardo Avenue was picked up by Community Service Officers (CSOs) from the Piedmont Police Department. “The bird was alive, but injured when [officers] arrived on the scene,” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “When a crow looks confused – they’re not walking quite right, they’re lethargic or if they don’t fight when someone tries to pick them up – that usually means they are dying pretty quickly,” said Judith Pierce, Public Outreach Coordinator for the Mosquito Abatement District. The crow was transported to the Lindsay Wildlife Experience in Walnut Creek, where it ultimately expired. The body was then sent to the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District for testing on July 5. On Tuesday, July 9, tests confirmed that the body was positive for West Nile Virus. articles.text: Residents interested in running for City Council or Piedmont School Board can pick up nomination documents from the City Clerk by appointment until Friday, August 9. On November 5, Piedmont voters will elect candidates to fill two City Council seats and three Board of Education seats. Councilmember Conna McCarthy and School Board members Hilary Cooper and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are eligible for re-election. Mayor Jen Cavenaugh and School Board member Cory Smegal will be termed out. The nomination process can be complicated, and filing deadlines are tight, so interested residents should begin as soon as possible. If you are interested in running: 1. Make an appointment with the City Clerk’s office at 420- 3040 or CityClerk@piedmont. ca.gov to obtain your candidate documents. At your appointment, the City Clerk will walk you through the nomination process, going over documents, deadlines, and rules. Plan on spending 30-60 minutes. 2. Review the fundamentals of the process online. Prepare for your appointment by reading about running for office on the City website. This will give you an idea of what to expect and allow you to identify questions you may want to ask during your appointment. 3. Submit your nomination documents by Friday, August 9. Nomination documents must be filed in person at the City Clerk’s office. It is a good idea for candidates to file documents early so they can correct any errors that come up. A list of people who have filed nomination papers will be available at piedmont.ca.gov/vote2024. City Council and Board of Education are volunteer positions. For more information about Piedmont’s 2024 election or running for office, visit piedmont. ca.gov/elections, or contact City Clerk Anna Brown at 420-3040.
articles.title: Interested residents have until August 9 to apply

Councilmember Conna McCarthy and School Board members Hilary Cooper and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are eligible for re-election. Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on July 6, 2023. ANNE BRYAN, Parkside Drive The antique cars are always fun. I remember riding in the parade as a kid with a sailor cap in a boat. By Pastor Jim Hopkins The following prayer was offered at the conclusion of worship at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church on July 21, 2024 upon learning thar President Joe Biden was withdrawing from the presidential race in November. Holy One: As we have celebrated today, you created us in your image, you created us for friendship with you and friendship with one another. On this Sunday, July 21, 2024, we acknowledge that we live in tumultuous times. It seems that our nation is careening from concern to concern, bumping from question to question, speeding from crisis to crisis. We pause to pray for President Joe, and First Lady Jill, Biden. We give thanks for the grace, wisdom and integrity that have marked his term in office and their stewardship of the White House. We respect their care for our nation and their patriotic values. We pray for their physical, mental and spiritual well-being. We pray for our nation, we pray for our planet, as we enter uncharted territory. We are facing questions both political and personal, we are facing questions of procedure, process and precedent. Here at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, on the corner of Lakeshore and Mandana in Oakland, California, we have spent the last week teaching our children that God is a friend who is real, God is a friend who loves, God is a friend who can be trusted, God is a friend forever, and God is a friend for everyone. In this moment, by faith, we claim these truths for ourselves. These truths celebrate the fact that you have been our help in ages past and are our hope for years to come. Apart from our questions, our confusion, our concerns and our uncertainties, there is our living hope that you will lead us relentlessly toward justice, toward gentleness and toward joy; there is our abiding trust that you will steer our nation towards the founding vision of each of us being created equal and all of us endowed by you with the rights of life, liberty and pursuit of happiness. In God we trust, Amen. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue in Oakland. articles.text: Photos by Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District A lab technician at the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District administers an oral swab to an expired crow. The lab uses two tests to confirm the presence of West Nile virus. which is measured on a scale of 0 to 640. “When the test returned, it had capped out at the highest possible test value, indicating the highest possible level of disease,” said Pierce. The department went into “instant response” mode on Wednesday, July 10. Lab technicians were dispatched to Dracena Park and set traps at likely mosquito centers within a one-mile radius of Dracena Park, including sewers and bodies of water. Areas where birds congregate were also investigated. An investigation by the Abatement District has not identified any West Nile-positive mosquitoes or West Nile-positive birds in the area. A second test confirmed the bird was positive for West Nile Virus on Tuesday, July 16. Pierce said that it is standard policy for her department to wait until this second test to make any announcements. The City of Piedmont was informed of the situation on Thursday, July 18, and issued a press release the following day. “Abatement District technicians have inspected the area where the bird was found, set mosquito traps, and searched for potential breeding grounds. Public Works staff will continue to coordinate with the Abatement District to review the park for areas of concern and take any recommended preventative actions,” reads the press release. Pierce added that the situation was “very unusual” for Piedmont and that West Nile-positive birds have not been discovered in neighboring towns of Berkeley, Oakland, Emeryville or Albany. The nearest positive case was reported earlier this year in Union City, over 25 miles to the south. This is the first positive bird detected in Piedmont in 2024. When a mosquito infects a bird with West Nile Virus, that bird can spread the disease to other mosquitos in its surrounding area. A second test confirmed the bird was positive for West Nile Virus on Tuesday, July 16. Pierce said that it is standard policy for her department to wait until this second test to make any announcements. The City of Piedmont was informed of the situation on Thursday, July 18, and issued a press release the following day. “Abatement District technicians have inspected the area where the bird was found, set mosquito traps, and searched for potential breeding grounds. Additionally, this is the 19th positive bird discovered in Alameda County this year and the 139th overall in California, a slight increase from the same time last year. In California, no humans have tested positive for West Nile virus this year. What you can do If you see a dead bird, call 1-877-WNV-BIRD or report it online at westnile.ca.gov. Birds are especially vulnerable to West Nile virus and can spread the disease over great distances because of their flight patterns. Mosquito districts throughout the state test dead birds for West Nile virus to track where the virus is spreading. If you have mosquito issues on your property, contact the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District for assistance by calling (510) 783-7744 or filling out an online service request. Be sure to check your backyard for standing water that may have been left by accident. Take precautions to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes. Avoid areas with mosquitoes during the early morning and dusk, when they are most active. Use an EPA-approved insect repellent. If possible, wear long sleeves and long pants to decrease areas where they can bite. West Nile virus is transmitted to people and animals through the bite of an infected mosquito. Most people infected with West Nile virus have no symptoms. Around one in five people infected will develop symptoms such as fever, headache, body aches, joint pains, vomiting, or rash. Less than 1% will develop serious illness. For more information about mosquitoes, West Nile virus or to request Abatement District services visit www.mosquitoes.org or call (510) 783-7744. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department will be participating in this year’s National Night Out on Tuesday, August 6, from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m. at several locations in town. National Night Out is an annual community-building event hosted by thousands of communities nationwide who join together with their local police departments to promote public safety. The event is designed to promote police-community partnerships and neighborhood camaraderie to make communities safer. Typically, neighbors spend the evening outside with their neighbors and members of the fire and police departments. Often it is a series of block parties. Three neighborhoods have already confirmed their participation: Glen Alpine-Sotelo, Huntleigh-Lexford, and Waldo and Blair. The Police Department, including Chief Jeremy Bowers and Capt. Chris Monahan will attend all three locations. “I always enjoy what I call ‘non-enforcement contact,’” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “This is an opportunity for us to get out and meet, discuss, share and communicate with people Photo by Piedmont Police Department Officer Jason Germano and Capt. Chris Monahan attend a National Night Out block party on Blair Avenue in 2023. in our community in a non-law enforcement scenario. This is not somebody calling because their car just got burglarized. It’s not somebody who’s getting a ticket for not wearing their seatbelt. These are events where neighbors come together and get the chance to talk to police and fire.” Monahan also extolled the virtues of getting neighbors to meet one another. “On any given shift, PPD has four officers on duty and eight firefighters. In case of a natural disaster where response times are heightened, those neighbors are going to be each others’ first line of support outside of their immediate families.” For more information about hosting or attending a block party, contact PPD Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo at ncasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: City Clerk Anna Brown (left) swears in new firefighter paramedics Viktoriya Franzen, Gary Randolph and Lucas Romero at a July 15 city council meeting. The Piedmont Fire Department welcomed three newly-minted firefighter paramedics at a badge-pinning ceremony during a city council meeting on Monday, July 15. Viktoriya Franzen, Gary Randolph and Lucas Romero completed their training at Las Positas College’s East Bay Regional Fire Academy in Livermore on Saturday, July 13. At the ceremony, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan spoke about the importance of the role. “Every shift, the firefighter paramedic is responsible for ensuring their readiness to respond in addition to that of their apparatus, equipment, and safety gear. You’ll see firefighter medics pulling hose, throwing ladders and providing advanced medical care whenever we respond to emergencies. Teamwork is essential and they need to fit into several roles that can change at any moment on any scene,” said Brannigan. The first to be pinned was Franzen. She and her family emigrated to the United States from Russia 20 years ago. She got her first job at Starbucks in high school, which she credits with developing skills in both teamwork and for making good coffee “which is critical in the firehouse,” joked Brannigan. Franzen spent four years delivering compassionate medical care in San Joaquin County before being hired in Piedmont. Franzen was pinned by her parents Andre and Svetlana Pakhamov. Gary Randolph, who was next to be pinned, was a paramedic for two years in Sonoma County. He worked for three and a half years with an ambulance company and served as a reserve firefighter for one year in Healdsburg. Randolph also earned his Bachelor of Arts degree in Kinesiology at California State University Stanislaus, where he was a three-time All-American in shot-put, discus and hammer throw. articles.text: For thousands of students that went through Piedmont schools since 1998, a formal and fascinating introduction to science was thanks to Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Greenebaum. He has retired after 31 years of teaching. Greenebaum’s love and enthusiasm for science and life in general will be greatly missed from the school district this fall. Students attending one of Greenebaum’s classes may remember him as a zany, high-energy teacher, always quick to recite a clever rhyme to help students recall a scientific principal. “I’m a musical guy. I’m always singing. I’ve got a song in my heart all the time,” said Greenebaum. “I found that singing classroom management expectations is better than harping on kids every day. ‘Sit down, get out your stuff.’ So then I developed these songs,” he said. Those daily expectation began with the backpack song. “Boom, boom, boom, boom, please put those backpacks...Under the tables, leaving the aisles clear.” To which students in class replied back “Cha, cha, cha.” Greenebaum underscored the importance of accurate data collection by starting every class off by also singing “Get that data, down!” He coined the phrase in his first teaching post in Minneapolis; data points for his eighth grade class included values for sunrise, sunset, temperature and phases of the moon. Ted Greenebaum’s teaching career: • 1993-1998 – Minneapolis Public School science • 1998-2024 – Piedmont Middle School science For many people, the middle school years are notoriously difficult and hard to understand, but Greenebaum’s enthusiasm and energy famously worked for students. His zeal for science and for the natural world provided comic relief without self-apprehension, a refreshing foil to the entropy and chaos underway during those formidable years. “I am fascinated by life. articles.text: Anybody at any age can be a scientist or an expert observer. Scientists make keen observations to help them understand why things are the way they are. This leads them to form and test educated guesses, paving the way for discoveries. It all starts with observation, a skill that we can practice in our everyday lives. Believe it or not, it’s easy and fun to do. One way to enjoy practicing observations is through nature journaling. It’s like keeping a journal, but instead of writing about your day, you use your senses to notice the amazing things around you. All you need is paper and something to write or draw with. Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you. Can you hear cars honking or the wind blowing? Jot down or sketch what you hear. Next, close your eyes, take a few deep breaths, and experience the scents around you, like trees or flowers. Then, write down your smell observations. Taste is closely tied to our sense of smell. Take a moment to notice any lingering tastes in your mouth, like breakfast or toothpaste. It’s worth journaling about. For touch, feel free to stand up and move around, exploring objects gently with your hands. Note the differences and use your nature journal to document your observations through writing or drawing. Finally, what can you see with your eyes? Humans depend greatly on our sense of sight, so this last section may bring you many things to write about. When you’ve finished, you will have a page of observations that paint a picture across all senses. When you try nature journaling again, you can look back, compare how each day looks different, and notice how each time you practice observations you get better at it, bit by bit. articles.text: A novel by Chris Honoré The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The excerpt is offered as a weekly series meant to encourage reading. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town called Watson in the mid-sixties. PART FIVE Though we didn’t advertise it, Jordie and I loved to read, and there was no place better for reading than the Watson library, a terrific old brick and timber building with lots of columns and wide concrete steps, leading up to tall oak doors with all this fancy glass that was so thick it looked like the bottom of a coke bottle. Just inside those doors sat Mrs. Hightower, the librarian. She was a straight-backed, serious lady who hardly ever smiled, just sort of puckered her lips like she was considering a smile and decided against it. Mrs. Hightower was usually seated at an elevated desk, her lookout post, and when we walked by she would watch us, her dark eyes flashing behind silver wire-rimmed glasses, like she was certain we had a bunch of overdue books hidden under our beds at home. Once, though, when I glanced back, I saw her smiling, sort of, and decided she was actually happy to see us. Jordie and I never really talked much about the books we read and no one ever asked. It was just something we did. But while the library was like our personal secret, going to the movies was just the opposite. Our house was only a short bike ride to the Vista Theater where every Saturday afternoon they had a special matinee. If Jordie and I could scrounge up a dollar between us, we’d take our favorite spot up in the balcony, front row, popcorn or Milk Duds in hand, counting the minutes, waiting for the next Republic adventure serial to begin. Like Don Winslow of the Navy. Don was always chasing men in baggy double-breasted suits, wearing fezzes and packing heat. You’d see Don, in a tux no less, hanging off the back of a racing speedboat with no one steering, slugging it out with two or three bad guys with thick, black mustaches, while this terrific looking woman with long silver-blonde hair, wearing a silky nightclub dress and lots of jewelry, is sitting up front, all terrified. Of course, she’s right next to the steering wheel, staring ahead at this approaching tanker, and then down at the wheel like she wasn’t sure what it was for. Meanwhile, Don’s getting punched pretty good and the kids in the theater are going crazy. There was always some kid down front who’d yell, “Grab the wheel, lady!” And everyone’d cheer. But just as the speedboat was about to crash into the tanker, the screen would flash the words: TO BE CONTINUED. And every kid in the theater would let out a groan and swear on a stack of bibles to be back next Saturday, same time, same seat. Of course, everyone knew that Don would escape; we just didn’t know how. While the Republic serials were exciting, there were some movies that turned the old Vista Theater into church, the squirming, squirrelly congregation suddenly quiet, no one wanting to get up for anything, not even more candy. Like The Thing, all about this ten-foot alien that had crashed in a flying saucer at the North Pole, and then escaped from the ice and was wandering around this scientific-military installation doing some serious damage. No one knew where the creature was or even what it was – except it was out there in the storm, killing men and sled dogs, then sucking out their blood, or standing behind some closed door that one of the research guys was trying to open. Lots of kids walked out of the Vista on those days covered with goose bumps, wondering how much furniture they could push in front of their closet doors when they hit the sack that night. Scary or not, the only thing that could keep Jordie and me out of a matinee on a Saturday was Howard, who would give himself a migraine trying to think up chores for us to do, saying how it built character, and how going to the movies was a waste of time and money. Howard Oakely was his full name and he’d come to live with us about a year after our father left. Jordie and I didn’t know what to make of him when our mom brought him home the first time. We stood awkwardly in the living room feeling pretty strange and a little embarrassed. He’d come right from work wearing a starched white shirt with a black leather clip-on bow tie. We learned later that he worked at Sid’s Tire and Motor. He was their window man, the guy who carried a clipboard and took down information and scheduled appointments for people when they called on the phone or brought in their cars. If you had a bad tire or your engine was barely running, Howard became this very important person in your life. PART SIX It didn’t take us long to understand that what kept Howard going were those moments of power. He was the guy. Jordie and me, we’d been down to Sid’s and seen people come in with this look on their faces, like Howard had one of their relatives locked up in a basement somewhere, and they’d just stopped in to drop off the ransom. See, Howard could keep the family Chevy for a couple more days or he could grant parole. You could tell: he loved every minute of it. Howard was a wiry guy with greasy, thinning brown hair that he continually pushed back off his forehead. He smelled of hair cream and cigarettes and usually had a matchstick wedged in the corner of his mouth. The day before he moved in with us, our mom explained how she’d worked out this living arrangement with Howard. One that would benefit everyone, meaning she would have help with the rent and Jordie and I would have a man around the house. Well, we understood the rent part. pages.text: Wednesday, July 24, 2024 11 The Journey of Max Braverman A novel by Chris Honoré The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The excerpt is offered as a weekly series meant to encourage reading. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town called Watson in the mid-sixties. PART FIVE Though we didn’t advertise it, Jordie and I loved to read, and there was no place better for reading than the Watson library, a terrific old brick and timber building with lots of columns and wide concrete steps, leading up to tall oak doors with all this fancy glass that was so thick it looked like the bottom of a coke bottle. Just inside those doors sat Mrs. Hightower, the librarian. She was a straight-backed, serious lady who hardly ever smiled, just sort of puckered her lips like she was considering a smile and decided against it. Mrs. Hightower was usually seated at an elevated desk, her lookout post, and when we walked by she would watch us, her dark eyes flashing behind silver wire-rimmed glasses, like she was certain we had a bunch of overdue books hidden under our beds at home. Once, though, when I glanced back, I saw her smiling, sort of, and decided she was actually happy to see us. Jordie and I never really talked much about the books we read and no one ever asked. It was just something we did. But while the library was like our personal secret, going to the movies was just the opposite. Our house was only a short bike ride to the Vista Theater where every Saturday afternoon they had a special matinee. If Jordie and I could scrounge up a dollar between us, we’d take our favorite spot up in the balcony, front row, popcorn or Milk Duds in hand, counting the minutes, waiting for the next Republic adventure serial to begin. Like Don Winslow of the Navy. Don was always chasing men in baggy double-breasted suits, wearing fezzes and packing heat. You’d see Don, in a tux no less, hanging off the back of a racing speedboat with no one steering, slugging it out with two or three bad guys with thick, black mustaches, while this terrific looking woman with long silver-blonde hair, wearing a silky nightclub dress and lots of jewelry, is sitting up front, all terrified. Of course, she’s right next to the steering wheel, staring ahead at this approaching tanker, and then down at the wheel like she wasn’t sure what it was for. Meanwhile, Don’s getting punched pretty good and the kids in the theater are going crazy. There was always some kid down front who’d yell, “Grab the wheel, lady!” And everyone’d cheer. But just as the speedboat was about to crash into the tanker, the screen would flash the words: TO BE CONTINUED. And every kid in the theater would let out a groan and swear on a stack of bibles to be back next Saturday, same time, same seat. Of course, everyone knew that Don would escape; we just didn’t know how. While the Republic serials were exciting, there were some movies that turned the old Vista Theater into church, the squirming, squirrelly congregation suddenly quiet, no one wanting to get up for anything, not even more candy. Like The Thing, all about this ten-foot alien that had crashed in a flying saucer at the North Pole, and then escaped from the ice and was wandering around this scientific-military installation doing some serious damage. No one knew where the creature was or even what it was – except it was out there in the storm, killing men and sled dogs, then sucking out their blood, or standing behind some closed door that one of the research guys was trying to open. Lots of kids walked out of the Vista on those days covered with goose bumps, wondering how much furniture they could push in front of their closet doors when they hit the sack that night. Scary or not, the only thing that could keep Jordie and me out of a matinee on a Saturday was Howard, who would give himself a migraine trying to think up chores for us to do, saying how it built character, and how going to the movies was a waste of time and money. Howard Oakely was his full name and he’d come to live with us about a year after our father left. Jordie and I didn’t know what to make of him when our mom brought him home the first time. We stood awkwardly in the living room feeling pretty strange and a little embarrassed. He’d come right from work wearing a starched white shirt with a black leather clip-on bow tie. We learned later that he worked at Sid’s Tire and Motor. He was their window man, the guy who carried a clipboard and took down information and scheduled appointments for people when they called on the phone or brought in their cars. If you had a bad tire or your engine was barely running, Howard became this very important person in your life. PART SIX It didn’t take us long to understand that what kept Howard going were those moments of power. He was the guy. Jordie and me, we’d been down to Sid’s and seen people come in with this look on their faces, like Howard had one of their relatives locked up in a basement somewhere, and they’d just stopped in to drop off the ransom. See, Howard could keep the family Chevy for a couple more days or he could grant parole. You could tell: he loved every minute of it. Howard was a wiry guy with greasy, thinning brown hair that he continually pushed back off his forehead. He smelled of hair cream and cigarettes and usually had a matchstick wedged in the corner of his mouth. The day before he moved in with us, our mom explained how she’d worked out this living arrangement with Howard. One that would benefit everyone, meaning she would have help with the rent and Jordie and I would have a man around the house. Well, we understood the rent part. Putting on a couple more pounds to defend bigger guards and excel athletically is a focus. How are you measuring your development? Stacking days — every day is an opportunity to get 1% better than yesterday whether on the court, weight room, track, or pool, there are always ways to improve and try new ways to push yourself harder, physically. Diet & Nutrition — maintaining a healthy balanced diet tracked on Cronometer, and being open to a new variety of foods. It helps being back home and have my mom make home-cooked meals that add 3,500 calories daily to my diet. Recovery — Ice bath, Stretch, Foam Roll, use a therapy gun. My parents also gave me a Norma-Techs Recovery system; daily use of these tools helps me limit inflammation and injuries, and helps with rapid recovery of my muscles and joints. Mentality — Log days and establish mini milestones inside of bigger goals within a certain time frame (days, weeks, months). Be a student of the game, and watch film on myself and others. I practice meditation, yoga, and composure of breath. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with several trainers in various locations around the Bay Area, The legendary PHS coach Bryan Gardere has helped me find different ways to improve each year. It is important to accumulate as much as I can when working with these specialists and incorporating what I have learned into my game. My father and I also work on the same routine that we have done every summer with some variations to make it more difficult. Individually, I will focus on my ball handling and footwork, while my dad will help rebound for me, as well as sharpening my shot and touch around the rim. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? My sophomore year at Chico State. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t overthink anything! Find what you love to do and work hard at it every single day, even if it is not basketball. Whatever sports or hobbies you participate in, I suggest you pursue it with everything you got! Surround yourself with people who support you and have similar interests that will push you to be a better athlete and person. Appreciate your parents for the time, money, and love that they always provide. They only want what is best for you and to see you grow. Photo courtesy of Cal Poly Parker Long, PHS Class of 2023, is currently training for the San Francisco Marathon on July 28. PARKER LONG Marathon Piedmont High Class of 2023 Cal Poly Class of 2027 Parker Long, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his freshman year at Cal Poly. He was the Post’s Athlete of the Year inn 2023 after finishing his time at Piedmont High among the best to ever run the 800 meters. He graduated as the third fastest runner in school history with a time of 1:53.25. As a freshman, Long competed in five events throughout the season. One of his best finishes was placing third of 17 runners in the 800 with a time of 1:52.07 at the Fresno State Invitational in April. The next month, Long ran in the 2024 Oxy Invitational at Occidental College, placing 15th of 47 in 1:52.90. During his senior year at Piedmont High, Long’s 1:53.25 in the 800 put him among the school’s best half milers of all time, behind Reece Proctor (1:52.64), and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer Gordon Johnson (1:51.10). Long won the NCS Meet of Champions’ 800 meter run with a time of 1:53.80 in a field of 12 finalists. He was also a member of Piedmont’s 4x400 relay team, helping the squad hit a season-best of 3:22.93 at the NCS Meet of Champions, which was— at least—the third fastest time in school history. It placed them narrowly behind 2022’s record-setting time of 3:21.77, set by Parker Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Long as the second leg. Piedmont High’s second-fastest time in the 4x400 was set in 1989 by a group led by Johnson. Long is no longer competing for Cal Poly, and is training for the San Francisco Marathon on July 28. What is your workout program this summer? I am training for the San Francisco Marathon on July 28th. I have been doing long runs to build my mileage. articles.text: Welcome to the second year of Piedmont High School’s girls’ flag football team. They are getting ready for the Fall season and their first official season on the new Witter Field. The coaches are looking forward to working with returning and new players to build upon what was started last year. If your daughter is interested in playing flag football this fall, come see the preseason conditioning and skills sessions starting Monday, July 29. Practices will occur July 29 to August 2 in the PHS weight room at Witter Field, and will include some light running, throwing, and receiving. From August 5-9 they will train on the outfield at Humphries Diamond, the baseball field and August 12 will be the first day of official practice on Witter Field. All skill levels are welcome. For questions contact Beth Black, the head coach at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us. JOJO MURPHY Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2022 Chico State Class of 2026 JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, just concluded his sophomore year at Chico State as a starter on the Wildcats basketball team. Chico State went 21-9 last season and qualified for the NCAA Regional tournament, defeating Montana State Billings 78-64 in the quarterfinals but lost a heated 75-73 game to Cal State Fullerton in the semifinals. In 2023/2024, Murphy missed just one game and started all 29 times, scoring 310 points by shooting 37 percent from the field and a sterling 40 percent from 3-pointers, including 26 steals and 52 assists. He earned an All-CCAA honorable mention. As a freshman, Murphy earned first-team All-CCAA honors and was selected as the conference 2022-23 Freshman of the Year. He led Chico State in several categories, including 456 points, 55 three-pointers, 173 field goals, and 960 minutes. He was also second on the team with 80 assists, second in steals with 37, and had 105 rebounds. The team finished with a 13-16 record. During his time at Piedmont High, Murphy earned Co-Player of the Year honors as a senior in 2022 and finished his career with 1,488 points scored. He was named Sophomore of the Year by the Post in 2020. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I have aimed to get the most exposure by playing against high-level elite talent with the San Francisco Pro-am Series held at Kezar Pavilion. This has been one of the best ways for me to evaluate my game while competing weekly against men who play at the professional level. I have been playing against Saint Mary’s Gaels players, which also helped me take steps forward in more of a fundamental college system along with on-court skill development. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Working out in the weight room has been a big emphasis in my preparation for heading back to school. Putting on a couple more pounds to defend bigger guards and excel athletically is a focus. How are you measuring your development? Stacking days — every day is an opportunity to get 1% better than yesterday whether on the court, weight room, track, or pool, there are always ways to improve and try new ways to push yourself harder, physically. Diet & Nutrition — maintaining a healthy balanced diet tracked on Cronometer, and being open to a new variety of foods. It helps being back home and have my mom make home-cooked meals that add 3,500 calories daily to my diet. Recovery — Ice bath, Stretch, Foam Roll, use a therapy gun. My parents also gave me a Norma-Techs Recovery system; daily use of these tools helps me limit inflammation and injuries, and helps with rapid recovery of my muscles and joints. Mentality — Log days and establish mini milestones inside of bigger goals within a certain time frame (days, weeks, months). Be a student of the game, and watch film on myself and others. I practice meditation, yoga, and composure of breath. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with several trainers in various locations around the Bay Area, The legendary PHS coach Bryan Gardere has helped me find different ways to improve each year. It is important to accumulate as much as I can when working with these specialists and incorporating what I have learned into my game. My father and I also work on the same routine that we have done every summer with some variations to make it more difficult. Individually, I will focus on my ball handling and footwork, while my dad will help rebound for me, as well as sharpening my shot and touch around the rim. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? My sophomore year at Chico State. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t overthink anything! Find what you love to do and work hard at it every single day, even if it is not basketball. Whatever sports or hobbies you participate in, I suggest you pursue it with everything you got! Surround yourself with people who support you and have similar interests that will push you to be a better athlete and person. Appreciate your parents for the time, money, and love that they always provide. They only want what is best for you and to see you grow. Photo courtesy of Cal Poly Parker Long, PHS Class of 2023, is currently training for the San Francisco Marathon on July 28. PARKER LONG Marathon Piedmont High Class of 2023 Cal Poly Class of 2027 Parker Long, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his freshman year at Cal Poly. He was the Post’s Athlete of the Year inn 2023 after finishing his time at Piedmont High among the best to ever run the 800 meters. He graduated as the third fastest runner in school history with a time of 1:53.25. As a freshman, Long competed in five events throughout the season. One of his best finishes was placing third of 17 runners in the 800 with a time of 1:52.07 at the Fresno State Invitational in April. The next month, Long ran in the 2024 Oxy Invitational at Occidental College, placing 15th of 47 in 1:52.90. During his senior year at Piedmont High, Long’s 1:53.25 in the 800 put him among the school’s best half milers of all time, behind Reece Proctor (1:52.64), and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer Gordon Johnson (1:51.10). Long won the NCS Meet of Champions’ 800 meter run with a time of 1:53.80 in a field of 12 finalists. He was also a member of Piedmont’s 4x400 relay team, helping the squad hit a season-best of 3:22.93 at the NCS Meet of Champions, which was— at least—the third fastest time in school history. It placed them narrowly behind 2022’s record-setting time of 3:21.77, set by Parker Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Long as the second leg. Piedmont High’s second-fastest time in the 4x400 was set in 1989 by a group led by Johnson. Long is no longer competing for Cal Poly, and is training for the San Francisco Marathon on July 28. What is your workout program this summer? I am training for the San Francisco Marathon on July 28th. I have been doing long runs to build my mileage. I enjoy the trail runs, so I’ve mainly been doing that. Also, some of my friends that are on the Cal Poly track team are training in altitude, and I went with them and did some of their runs. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Continue building my mileage. How are you measuring your development? The full marathon distance is 26.2 miles. If I can do a 16-18 mile run, then I have confidence that I could make it to 26. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working out on my own this summer. I’ve learned about running last year with Ryan Vanhoy, who is Cal Poly’s Director of Track & Field and Cross Country. I use his training to help with making my own regimen. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? On April 27 at the Fresno Invitational, I set a personal record in the 800 with a 1:52.07. It was good to get this PR, but I know I could do better. My plan for the future is to enjoy my time in college more now that I am not as focused on running, and maybe when I am older I will try again to beat my best time. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? How you train is important, but it is not as significant as being mentally strong. I’ve learned that when I am thinking about a race and I think about how fast I can do it, I usually end up running close to what I think. So, the most important thing is to be confident going into competition.
