articles.text: Photos courtesy of WeLoveCycling.com Tadej Pogačar has won his third Tour de France at just 25-years-old. Tadej Pogačar just put himself into the realm of legends as one of the greatest cyclists, winning the 2024 Tour de France. his third Yellow Jersey at age 25. He becomes the first threetime winner since Chris Froome accomplished the feat from 2015 to 2017. Pogačar, s now one victory away from matching Froome and France’s Jacques Anquetil (1957, 1961-1964), and two shy of Spain’s Miguel Indurain (1991- 1995), French great Bernard Hinault (1978-1979, 1981-1982, 1985), and Belgium legend Eddie Merckx (1969-1972, 1974). Stepping into the history books, Pogačar’s run has some similarities to Hinault’s threetour victories in 1981, 1982, and 1985. 1983 and 1984 were won by fellow Frenchman Laurent Fignon. Similarly, Pogačar won in 2020 and 2021 before Jonas Vingegaard won the next two years, This time, the Slovenian took the general classification lead on Stage 4 and never relinquished control, winning six of the race’s 21 stages. He won the final three stages of this year’s tour in miraculous fashion, including the critical Stage 21 time trial—clocking 45:24 on the 33.7 km course, one minute and three seconds ahead of second-place Vingegaard. Pogačar has now won 17 Tour de France stages already in his brief career. “I’m super happy. I cannot describe how happy I am after two hard years in the Tour de France. This year everything was perfection,” Pogačar said This year’s tour also meant history for Biniam Girmay, the first cyclist of African descent to win the points classification and the Green Jersey. Girmay won Stage 3 to become the first African rider to ever win a Tour de France stage, then followed up with wins in Stage 8 and Stage 12. With 387 points, Girmay finished 33 points ahead of second-place Jasper Philipsen who was hoping to win his second consecutive Green Jersey. “I feel like I’m floating through the sky. It’s super nice. I just want to say for the young kids, keep working hard and everything is possible,” Girmay said/ On the local level, Walnut Creek native and Team Visma rider, Matteo Jorgenson, finished in the top-10 of the general classification standings in 8th place. At 25-years-old, the Bay Area star still has years of opportunity ahead. The 112th edition of the Tour de France in 2025 is in development with the first three stages already announced, including the Grand Départ in Lille on July 5. Photo courtesy of Team Visma Walnut Creek’s Matteo Jorgenson finished 8th in this year’s Tour de France. He’s Jonas Vingegaard’s teammate on Team Visma.
articles.title: Tadej Pogacˇar wins third Tour de France

articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team is hosting tryouts on August 13-15 at the Montclair Swim Club in Oakland. Each swimmer will be given a 30-minute time slot and grouped by age over the 3-day session; swimmers will be given an individual starting time upon registering. Each athlete is expected to attend all three days. Please keep in mind that tryout expectations include the following: • • Swimmers age 8 and under: Tryout expectations include the ability to swim 25 yards of Freestyle (with side breath) and 25 yards of Backstroke. Legal Breaststroke and Butterfly are not required but are helpful. Swimmers age 9-11: Tryout expectations include the ability to swim a 50 Freestyle (with side breath), a 50 Backstroke, a 25 Breaststroke (with a legal kick), and a 25 Butterfly with basic stroke mechanics. • Swimmers age 12 and older: Legal 200 IM with proper breathing mechanics. Swimmers should be able to complete the 200 IM under 5 min. Interested athletes and parents can email joinpst@piedmontswimteam.org about registering. This week we feature one of the taller peaks in the Tahoe area, Washeshu Peak of Palisades Tahoe in Olympic Valley. If you are in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a worthy and achievable hike to Washeshu Peak at an elevation of over 8,000 feet. There are likely to be patches of snow still on the ground in July, but you’ll be OK with hiking shoes. Palisades Tahoe Olympic Valley is a popular destination for Piedmont residents during Ski Week in February, but during The view from Washeshu Peak looking toward Lake Tahoe. You’ll be standing at an elevation of over 8,800 feet. Staff Photos Take the tram to Palisades Tahoe High Camp to start your day of hiking. Return for the food, view, or even some skating. The resort formerly known as Squaw Valley was home of the1960 Olympic Games. The name was changed in 2021 to honor the history of the Washoe Tribe whose ancestral lands were in Olympic Valley. Our day starts by taking the aerial tram ride up to High Camp, which gives another incredible view from the viewing platform back towards Lake Tahoe, a popular restaurant, outdoor games, a skating rink, and Olympic museum dedicated to the 1960 Winter Games. The large-scale pool and hot tub, unfortunately, has remained closed for several years due to extensive repairs. articles.text: Oakland is getting its own ‘Walking on Wednesdays’ this week, hosted by the “Love our Lake” campaign. The starting point takes place at the Oakland Museum of California and Children’s Fairyland every Wednesday through Labor Day, beginning today, July 24. Oakland Walks Wednesdays is a series of lunchtime and after-work community walks that anyone can join. Walkers will take a stride along Lake Merritt this summer while getting to know their neighbors and the offerings of downtown Oakland. Anyone interested in joining can meet at the gate of Children’s Fairyland this Wednesday at 12 noon or at 5:30 p.m. at Oakland Museum at the front entrance steps on Oak Street. For more information about Oakland WALKS Wednesdays, visit https://www.oaklandcentral. com/oww/.
articles.title: Fairyland & Oakland Museum announce weekly walks

articles.text: Entry to the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) will be free to the public on August 1 during “Downtown First Thursdays,” a free monthly street party hosted in downtown San Francisco the first Thursday of the month. Currently on view at the museum is British visual artist and painter Rachel Jones’ exhibition !!!!!. Jones is known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. It is the first solo museum exhibition in the United States of Jones. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. The artist said she is “using motifs and color as a way to communicate ideas about the interiority of Black bodies and their lived experience.” To see all exhibitions on view, and to learn more about “Downtown First Thursdays,” visit https://www.moadsf.org/ event/free-admission-downtown-first-thursdays-2. ®
articles.title: MoAD offers free admission on August 1

articles.text: Visit the Festival Pavilion at Fort Mason Center in San Francisco on August 24 for the 11tth anniversary of the West Coast Craft Fair. They released their debut album in April of 2021 to rave reviews, and have since been performing all around the country. Juilliard School graduate Adam Moezinia on guitar, Ben Ring on drums, and Will Lyle on bass will appear as part of a five-week West Coast tour from Southern California to Vancouver and back. Tickets, $35, are available at www.bpt.me/6364033, and also at the door, $40 cash/check ONLY. Don’t miss this rare opportunity for a very special musical experience! Saturday, August 10, 11:00 a.m. Xtra-Dimensions Art Exhibit A local artist and emeritus professor of chemistry at Cal, now living in Montclair, Paul Bartlett has tried for years to find ways to think in three dimensions, and has now developed techniques of layering images in ways that show the three-dimensional reality rather than just implying it in only two dimensions. His approach is effective for many types of images: forest scenes with overlapping foliage or trees, cityscapes or abstract images with underlying geometric patterns – in short, any image where additional dimensions stimulate closer inspection and the discovery of something that would be missed in a 2-dimensional print. articles.text: California is famous worldwide for its beauty, romance, and history. The great travel writer Richard Halliburton extolled these in his book “Marvels of the World.” He noted our two great bridges in particular. He did not venture south to the Monterey Peninsula. We did it in order to attend some concerts at the Carmel Bach Festival. First, it’s an adventure just getting there. You can take the coast route or you can go through the mountains or you can go directly south through the farmlands of the Salinas Valley. These days, it’s a good idea to check what the traffic is like in advance. The best bet seems to be through Salinas Valley, but you guessed it. — the traffic was horrendous. We stopped off at the Jellyfish Restaurant in Gilroy for a marvelous lunch. The restaurant is owned by Chinese immigrants, but the restaurant specializes in Louisiana seafood, Our lunch consisted of a gigantic, softshell crab Poboy with French fries and a side order of fried okra. When the food arrived, it was enough for an army. And delicious too. Our friendly waiter advised us to proceed on the back roads and avoid the highway because of the bumper-to-bumper traffic. But the traffic was bad no matter where we went. Richard Halliburton would’ve found a beautiful way to describe an unfortunate situation. That was the beauty of his writing. We arrived in the sparkling gem of a city that is Carmel. There are colorful shops and good restaurants everywhere. There is not a traffic light anywhere in the city. Our first concert at the festival was devoted to the gospel of John as envisioned by Johann Sebastian Bach in his St. John’s Passion. It was first performed on Good Friday in the year 1724. What a coincidence that this is the 300th anniversary of that performance. This was as close to an opera as Johann Sebastian Bach ever got. It was his intention to get the audience emotionally involved. He was successful to say the least. This performance, as conducted by Grete Pedersen, with vocal soloists, chorus and orchestra featured a multilingual version of this masterpiece. This was logical because when God speaks to humanity it is through telepathy in any language the individual speaks. Some have criticized the St. John’s Passion because of its seeming antisemitism. While some people might see this as a fault, Bach handled it well, and the conclusion is that we shall have peace. The Bach Festival has been in Carmel since 1935 and has been successful over those many years. Music Directors are in place for long periods of time. Management is excellent, and all of the musicians are inspired. The conductor Grete Pederson is now in her second year as music Director. As a conductor, she has a clear, concise beat, and she communicates to all of the musicians in a superior manner. I spoke with some friends in the Orchestra, and they said they enjoy working with her. In addition to her high level of musicianship, she is also an excellent diplomat. The performance maintained a dynamic tension at all times. Photos by Joseph Gold Conductor Grete Pedersen speaks to the audience at the Carmel Bach Festival. the Carmel Bach Festival.
articles.title: Carmel Bach Festival – going strong after 87 years

He is a tall kid, thin of body, reminding me of a young Van Cliburn. The wonder of this pianist is that his tone is rich and round and full. His interpretations are very romantic and very nuanced. When I closed my eyes I was in a Time Machine, not listening to a contemporary pianist but a pianist of the distant past. Wild looks can be deceiving, but performance never is. There were no visual histrionics, just beautiful playing. It was a great pleasure to hear Eric Lu in concert. I took the opportunity to speak with him after his performance and can report that he is a delightful young man. Beethoven’s Ninth That same Sunday we attended a performance of the Beethoven Ninth Symphony in the evening. It is always interesting for me to watch how a conductor communicates with the orchestra. Conductor Pederson did not use a baton when she conducted the St. John’s Passion. That worked very well. For Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony, she used the conducting baton. Both ways produced excellent results. It was easy to see inspired discipline from everyone who participated in the concerts. The conductor achieved a high-level of musicality with diplomacy. There was respect on all sides. From a technical standpoint, the entire string section played on old-fashioned gut strings. articles.text: One of the many Paleolithic cave paintings found in the Chauvet cave in the Ardeche region of France In 1994, three spelunkers – Jean-Marie Chauvet, Eliette Deschamps and Christian Hillaire – were exploring cliffs in the Ardeche region of France. Feeling an air current, they dug and then crawled into what would become known as the Chauvet cave. Holding a lantern high above her head, and seeing the walls, we’re told, Dechamps yelled back, “They were here.” Who “they” were is soon made evident: cave artists, standing in the Chauvet cave 30,000 years ago, charcoal in hand, drawing some of the most astonishing images imaginable. Paintings that today would be judged remarkable. What the interior of the cave must have been like then can only be imagined: the floor covered with the detritus from cave bears, the walls illuminated by the dim light of fires. Cave of Forgotten Dreams, directed and narrated by Werner Herzog, reveals more than 100 paintings of lions, galloping horses, massive bears, wooly mammoths, a pride of lions, and red handprints on ethereal walls, all left behind by Paleolithic travelers, declarative images and an immortal record of their view of their world. When the discovery by the trio was made known, the French government closed the cave, fearful that even the exhalation of visitors would contaminate the treasures enclosed. Access to the cave is now limited to archeologists and curators, and, as we see, Werner Herzog, who, in 2010, received permission from the French government to film, for a limited time, using specially designed equipment, its interior. What is remarkable, and central to the meaning of this discovery, and to the film, is the quality of the paintings and the astonishing talent of the artists. It’s all but impossible to understand all those years ago, that Paleolithic man, who, we know to be not only prehistoric but primitive, was moved to create murals that are so clearly inspired, using the texture and shape of the walls in order to create a sense of animation. Is the impulse to create art so deeply embedded in the human condition that our antecedents were compelled to capture what they saw on the plains and in the forests that surrounded the Chauvet cave? Was it totemic? Or was it simply a wondrous flight of fancy? It’s impossible to know what the artists were thinking as they created these murals. We assume that every day of their lives was tentative, reduced to a fearful subsistence. And yet, there they stood, in the bowels of the earth, in this chapel-like place, and created. We will never know from whence this impulse came, for there is no written record left behind. And yet, yes, there they are: these drawings and paintings that are eternally captivating. Cave of Forgotten Dreams. Documentary. Directed, written, and narrated by Werner Herzog. Released 2011. 1hr 30min. Rated G. Streaming on apple tv. articles.text: Searching, uses a high risk, high gain stylized cinematic approach that results in a taut mystery-thriller, one that takes place almost entirely on a computer screen. What unfolds is a tension-building, well-crafted story that creates, initially, a sense of unease and foreboding and then gradually morphs into a worst-outcome fear that suggests it will not have a right ending. The premise is tantalizingly familiar: A single dad, David Kim (John Cho), discovers, inexplicably, that his 16-year-old daughter, Margot (Michelle La) has failed to return home from a biology study session with classmates (she tells him it will likely be an all-nighter). It’s only when he wakes the next morning that he realizes she has not come home. He also discovers that while asleep he missed three face-time messages from Margot during the night. These scenes are shown from the point of view of the computer, as if he’s Skyping. He waits, hours pass, the day slips away, no Margot. He calls around to those he assumes are her friends; no one has any information other than Margot left the study group around nine, the intended time to end and headed home. No mention is made of studying all night. Finally, growing seriously concerned for her safety (this is atypical behavior), perplexed, striving to tamp down his worst thoughts, he calls the police to report Margot missing. Sitting in her room, his sense of helplessness palpable, searching for any clue, he opens her computer, accessing social media. And thus begins an urgent journey through various platforms and apps. With each site he peels away a layer of Margot’s life, finding, to his chagrin, that the teenager he thought he knew is, in truth, a stranger. Her Internet world is a far-reaching web of contacts, countless footprints, constructed by an electronic cartographer with seemingly endless interconnecting strands. As time passes and David waits for the police to call, he tries to fit together the small pieces to what proves to be an expanding and increasingly complex puzzle. Where could she be? Why hasn’t she tried to contact him? Who is this random boy on Instagram? Why did Margot make monthly payments to a Venmo account, using her piano lessons money? To David it seems as if he is pulling on the loose strand of a sweater, and as it unravels it moves him closer to the truth, while simultaneously taking him farther away. He begins to realize that he is making countless assumptions about Margot and where she might be, confused about what is harmless or perhaps illicit, even unsavory. Becoming more frantic, he is beginning to feel a bit unhinged, all while scrolling ever downward on her screen. Finally, the police call. Margot’s case has been assigned to a detective Rosemary Vick (Debra Messing). She is tenacious and sympathetic and explains that together they will find Margot while trying to penetrate what can seem to be an impenetrable scrim of information. Again, this is all done on screen, texting, or via Skype. At no time are any of their encounters face to face. It’s at this point that this review should abandon all discussion of plot. Act two and three must be fresh (this is essential and it would be criticism malpractice to reveal more), for there are unexpected twists and turns that should be viewed absent even a hint or foreshadowing of what lies ahead. Throughout the film I awaited the moment of pull back, expecting sooner than later a wide shot of the characters taking stage center. But at no time does the director, Aneesh Chaganty, also the co-writer, release the audience from the screen format, even when using select television news clips of an anchor discussing Margot’s disappearance. To the filmmakers’ credit the sense of urgency inherent in every frame is sustained and proves to be not only engaging but completely credible. Like Jimmy Stewart, sitting looking out the rear window of his apartment, his leg in a cast, binoculars at the ready, David is equally compelled to peer at the screen of Margot’s computer. Each is searching for the answer to a mystery inside of a riddle, each is filled with a voyeuristic trepidation that this moment may not have a right ending. Searching. Directed by Aneesh Chaganty, Sev Ohanian. Starring John Cho, Debra Messing, Joseph Lee. 1 hr., 42 min. PG-13. John Cho stars in Searching

She is tenacious and sympathetic and explains that together they will find Margot while trying to penetrate what can seem to be an impenetrable scrim of information. Again, this is all done on screen, texting, or via Skype. At no time are any of their encounters face to face. It’s at this point that this review should abandon all discussion of plot. Act two and three must be fresh (this is essential and it would be criticism malpractice to reveal more), for there are unexpected twists and turns that should be viewed absent even a hint or foreshadowing of what lies ahead. Throughout the film I awaited the moment of pull back, expecting sooner than later a wide shot of the characters taking stage center. But at no time does the director, Aneesh Chaganty, also the co-writer, release the audience from the screen format, even when using select television news clips of an anchor discussing Margot’s disappearance. To the filmmakers’ credit the sense of urgency inherent in every frame is sustained and proves to be not only engaging but completely credible. Like Jimmy Stewart, sitting looking out the rear window of his apartment, his leg in a cast, binoculars at the ready, David is equally compelled to peer at the screen of Margot’s computer. Each is searching for the answer to a mystery inside of a riddle, each is filled with a voyeuristic trepidation that this moment may not have a right ending. Searching. Directed by Aneesh Chaganty, Sev Ohanian. Starring John Cho, Debra Messing, Joseph Lee. 1 hr., 42 min. PG-13. Cave of Forgotten Dreams One of the many Paleolithic cave paintings found in the Chauvet cave in the Ardeche region of France By Chris Honoré In 1994, three spelunkers – Jean-Marie Chauvet, Eliette Deschamps and Christian Hillaire – were exploring cliffs in the Ardeche region of France. Feeling an air current, they dug and then crawled into what would become known as the Chauvet cave. Holding a lantern high above her head, and seeing the walls, we’re told, Dechamps yelled back, “They were here.” Who “they” were is soon made evident: cave artists, standing in the Chauvet cave 30,000 years ago, charcoal in hand, drawing some of the most astonishing images imaginable. Paintings that today would be judged remarkable. What the interior of the cave must have been like then can only be imagined: the floor covered with the detritus from cave bears, the walls illuminated by the dim light of fires. Cave of Forgotten Dreams, directed and narrated by Werner Herzog, reveals more than 100 paintings of lions, galloping horses, massive bears, wooly mammoths, a pride of lions, and red handprints on ethereal walls, all left behind by Paleolithic travelers, declarative images and an immortal record of their view of their world. When the discovery by the trio was made known, the French government closed the cave, fearful that even the exhalation of visitors would contaminate the treasures enclosed. Access to the cave is now limited to archeologists and curators, and, as we see, Werner Herzog, who, in 2010, received permission from the French government to film, for a limited time, using specially designed equipment, its interior. What is remarkable, and central to the meaning of this discovery, and to the film, is the quality of the paintings and the astonishing talent of the artists. It’s all but impossible to understand all those years ago, that Paleolithic man, who, we know to be not only prehistoric but primitive, was moved to create murals that are so clearly inspired, using the texture and shape of the walls in order to create a sense of animation. Is the impulse to create art so deeply embedded in the human condition that our antecedents were compelled to capture what they saw on the plains and in the forests that surrounded the Chauvet cave? Was it totemic? Or was it simply a wondrous flight of fancy? It’s impossible to know what the artists were thinking as they created these murals. We assume that every day of their lives was tentative, reduced to a fearful subsistence. And yet, there they stood, in the bowels of the earth, in this chapel-like place, and created. We will never know from whence this impulse came, for there is no written record left behind. And yet, yes, there they are: these drawings and paintings that are eternally captivating. Cave of Forgotten Dreams. Documentary. Directed, written, and narrated by Werner Herzog. Released 2011. 1hr 30min. Rated G. Streaming on apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Migration Kids will find the family friendly, wonderfully animated Migration delightful. The tale is predicated on the journey that birds of all types make yearly in search of warmer climes. But there just might be a few exceptions, which brings us to Mark (Kumail Nanjiani) and his family of mallards: wife Pam (Elizabeth Banks), and kids Dax (Casper Jennings) and Gwen (Tresi Gazal). We soon come to understand that Mark is a riskaverse homebody, meaning he is content to remain in his safe, comfortable pond and whenever Pam or the kids point out that a frigid New England winter is on the way. Mark resists. Sure there are ducks that stop at his pond on their way south, heading to places where their tail feathers won’t get cold. But not Mark. Instead he recounts scary stories to the kids about what’s out there, far from the pond. But Pam, who is way more adventurous than her husband, with the help of the kids, finally convinces Dad to pack up their stuff and make the migratory journey. With a reluctant Mark, and the family grumpy Uncle Dan (Danny Devito), in tow, they leave the secluded pond and head for balmy Jamaica. Think of it as a road trip of sorts where we know for sure that they will have many unexpected encounters and meet a number of interesting if not ominous characters. articles.text: Planes: Fire & Rescue is a nice fit for kids 8-years-old and below and would be an ideal follow-up to Disney’s animated Planes. Both star Dusty Crophopper (Dane Cook). It was in Planes that Dusty realized his dream of becoming a world-class, hotdogging air racer and an international celebrity, basking in the continual attention of the cameras. But then, unexpectedly, as Planes: Fire & Rescue begins, Dusty discovers that his gearbox is failing, the parts he needs to fix it aren’t available, so he can’t reach those top speeds that have allow him to win races. An additional problem is that his much loved hometown airport, Propwash Junction, needs a serious updating. Its equipment is failing to meet compliance. But the situation gives Dusty something to do. He has been yearning to become an aerial firefighter, and so gets certified by the crusty, cranky Blade Ranger (Ed Harris) who is in charge of training. He finds Dusty a bit impulsive but approves him for the Piston Peak squadron. And so begins the story of planes zooming fire ravaged canyons, up into billowing clouds of smoke, swooping down to scoop up water from lakes and rivers, and dropping pink fire retardant. All of them are flying by the seat of their ailerons. Members of the Piston Peakers are risking their lives to protect those on the ground, which includes the ATV smoke jumpers, a courageous bunch who drop out of airplanes, parachute to the ground, and fight the raging fires. The hotshot crew of Piston Peak also includes military transport Cabbie (Dale Dye), and Lil’ Dipper (Julie Bowen), who has a crush on Dusty. And there’s May Day (Hal Holbrook), a dated fire and rescue truck, plus Windlifter (Wes Studi), whose helicopter blades are painted like feathers. One of the squadron’s missions turns out to be an all-handson-deck attempt to save the Grand Fusel Lodge and its guests. Dusty, of course, must overcome his fear as he confronts the ultimate villain in the story, the unforgiving forest fires wjhich are bearing down on the lodge. There’s lots of action, and Dusty manages to get out of some tight spots, as does the Piston Peak squadron. Sure there is peril, but parents shouldn’t be concerned. In spite of the close calls, no one gets hurt. And the little guys will love Dusty’s courageous antics. Planes: Fire & Rescue. Directed by Bob Gannaway. Disney Studios animation. Voiced by Dane Cook, Ed Harris, Dale Dye, Julie Bowen. 1 hr. 23 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Fandango, prime, Disney+/apple tv. A scene from Disney’s Planes: Fire & Rescue

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group was surprised on July 17th as it assembled at the Exedra for its weekly walk. A crew of tree removal workers with a tall crane were in the process of cutting down a big redwood tree behind City Hall. The walkers didn’t know why the tree was being removed. It turned out to be a harbinger of what they were going to see later. Real estate development has long been part of Piedmont’s history. Walter Blair built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 to attract potential residents. Early 20th Century developer Frank C. Havens created Piedmont Park to promote his Piedmont real estate, and currently there is a controversy regarding the development of a lot on Wistaria Way. Going to it would also let the walkers go through Havens’ beautiful neighborhood of Wildwood Gardens. This neighborhood was the site of Havens’ “Wildwood Estate.” He was born into a prominent New York family and after a year in the China shipping trade, he came to San Francisco in 1866 and worked in banking. In about 1880 he founded a stock brokerage before creating the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” in 1895 with F. M. “Borax” Smith. Havens became a major real estate developer in Oakland, Berkeley and Piedmont. Havens and Smith built the Claremont Hotel, and the Syndicate was originally the parent company of the Key System transit company. It also accumulated at least 13,000 acres of hilltop land that stretched from near Mills College to the boundary of North Berkeley. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road and built his “Wildwood” estate on it. The walkers made their way through the loops that make up Wildwood Gardens and found the back of 101 Wildwood Gardens, Havens’ mansion. Only a portion of it could be seen, but an “H” in the wrought iron gate indicated its origin. The group continued through the upper portion of Wildwood Gardens, past an impressive children’s treehouse with Wildwood Creek running nearby to the seldom-visited Wistaria Way. They made their way up the loop to the lot where another tree removal crew had just cut down many coastal oaks and other trees. This lot was once part of a home, but was donated to a local church after the owner’s death. The land was sold in 2022. The new owners twice submitted applications in 2022 to build a single family home on the lot, but were rejected both times after neighbors and the City objected to the size of the proposed project. The owners then developed a project to divide the lot into two parcels with a plan to construct two new homes on them with an ADU alongside one. This is allowed under a new California law based upon Senate Bill 9 (known as SB9). It went into effect on January 1, 2022, and is intended to address California’s housing shortage by allowing homeowners to divide their lots and build up to four houses on a single-family parcel. This Wistaria project’s application was approved by the Piedmont Planning and Building Department on December 27, 2023. Building permits were approved on July 2, and neighbors were notified of the construction by mail on July 5. A group of them is questioning the project’s legality. They maintain that the lot is protected wetland, as Wildwood Creek traverses it, and the project endangers the wetlands, so it should not be eligible to be split. The City disagrees. The neighbors met with City staff on July 5 and voiced their concerns to the Piedmont City Council at multiple Council meetings, but tree removal began on July 16. The walkers viewed the lot, took a group photo and finished the Wistaria loop. They continued on to Woodland Way, Lafayette and Crocker Avenues and returned to the Exedra with new knowledge of Frank C. Havens and California real estate law. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. and everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. Register at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. A large turnout of 47 walkers and two K-9 best friends participated in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays. Among those participating were: David Haecker, Edith Lee, Lee Hambrick, Helen Dong, Jim Kuo, Matt Gerhardt, Kat Lang, Mary Carter, Quincy Dong, Alan Goldhammer, Renee Goldhammer, Lori Austin, Janet Laurent, Elizabeth Richter, Ken Moy, June Yee, Judy Sokoloff, Martin Levy, Stella Houston, Phil Witte, Tina Shum, Adrienne Hamlin, Chuck Oraftik, Marianne Jakus, Gloria DaSilva, Peggy Shultz, Lois Price, Elane Rehr, Robert Lang, Sharona Fischrup, Leila Deacon, Jack Fischrup, Alissa Quan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kellogg, Denise Frankoff with K-9 best friend Chester, Rob Smith, Will Adams, Eric Behrens with k-9 best friend Mocha, Gary Meyers, Denny McGee, Alicia Rivera, Judy Love, Sherry Jacobs, Shirley Nakao and Dick Carter.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok This month’s favored recipe is for a tasty Apricot Vanilla Cobbler, perfect for warm summer nights. My neighbor’s apricot tree is having a bumper crop this year. And lucky for me, there are several large branches filled with fruit and growing on my side of our fence! They are just about ready to harvest, and even with sharing with our voracious Piedmont squirrels there will be enough to enjoy for our upcoming barbeque. This rustic dessert is a delightful way to highlight summer’s fresh fruit bounty. Here, we’re featuring apricots, but any stone fruit will be equally delicious. Bake this early in the day for your summer BBQ table. Apricot Vanilla Cobbler Makes one 9-inch pan A few advance tips • Make sure the butter and heavy cream are well chilled. You can also pre-chill the mixing bowl in the freezer if your kitchen is warm. • Warm kitchen hack: Place your working bowl in a larger one filled with an inch or two of iced water. This will help prevent the butter from melting. Soft/melty butter = flat, dense topping. • Avoid using really soft apricots as they will turn to mush during the 45 minutes of baking. • Keep the balls of dough on the smaller side, and don’t overcrowd them. This allows for steam to escape from the bubbling apricots and ensures the dough will bake thoroughly too. INGREDIENTS For the cobbles (topping) • 1½ cup all-purpose flour • ¼ cup granulated sugar • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1⁄8 teaspoon sea salt • 1 teaspoon Lafaza ground vanilla bean • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into ½-inch cubes, cold • 7⁄8 cup heavy cream, chilled • 1 tablespoon (scant) Turbinado sugar for topping For the fruit • 2 pounds firm-ripe apricots, pitted and halved • ¼ cup granulated sugar, to taste • 2 teaspoons quick cooking, granulated tapioca • ¼ teaspoon Lafaza ground vanilla beans INSTRUCTIONS Position an oven rack in the middle of the oven. Place a large flat baking sheet on it, for catching any bubbling juices as the cobbler bakes. Make sure your cobbler pan fits flat onto the baking sheet. Preheat the oven to 375°F. Gently toss the apricots, sugar, tapioca and vanilla in a shallow 1½ quart baking dish or 9-inch deep dish pie pan. Make sure all ingredients are well distributed. Set aside while you prepare the topping. Combine the flour, baking powder, salt, sugar and ground vanilla beans in a medium bowl. Cut in the cold butter using a pastry cutter or two knives. Mix until coarse crumbs are formed. Pour in the chilled heavy cream and stir until the dough barely sticks together. It will be a bit messy, and the flour will not be fully incorporated. Drop walnut-sized balls of dough (about 1½” rounds) over the apricot mixture, being careful to not overcrowd the pan. Sprinkle the Turbinado sugar over the dough. Bake until the apricots are bubbling and the top is deep golden brown, about 40-45 minutes. Serve with softly whipped cream, vanilla ice cream or all on its own. It’s all good. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on July 1, 2015.

INGREDIENTS For the cobbles (topping) • 1½ cup all-purpose flour • ¼ cup granulated sugar • 2 teaspoons baking powder • 1⁄8 teaspoon sea salt • 1 teaspoon Lafaza ground vanilla bean • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into ½-inch cubes, cold • 7⁄8 cup heavy cream, chilled • 1 tablespoon (scant) Turbinado sugar for topping For the fruit • 2 pounds firm-ripe apricots, pitted and halved • ¼ cup granulated sugar, to taste • 2 teaspoons quick cooking, granulated tapioca • ¼ teaspoon Lafaza ground vanilla beans INSTRUCTIONS Position an oven rack in the middle of the oven. Place a large flat baking sheet on it, for catching any bubbling juices as the cobbler bakes. Make sure your cobbler pan fits flat onto the baking sheet. Preheat the oven to 375°F. Gently toss the apricots, sugar, tapioca and vanilla in a shallow 1½ quart baking dish or 9-inch deep dish pie pan. Make sure all ingredients are well distributed. Set aside while you prepare the topping. Combine the flour, baking powder, salt, sugar and ground vanilla beans in a medium bowl. Cut in the cold butter using a pastry cutter or two knives. Mix until coarse crumbs are formed. Pour in the chilled heavy cream and stir until the dough barely sticks together. It will be a bit messy, and the flour will not be fully incorporated. Drop walnut-sized balls of dough (about 1½” rounds) over the apricot mixture, being careful to not overcrowd the pan. Sprinkle the Turbinado sugar over the dough. Bake until the apricots are bubbling and the top is deep golden brown, about 40-45 minutes. Serve with softly whipped cream, vanilla ice cream or all on its own. It’s all good. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on July 1, 2015.

articles.text: Piedmont native Evan Epstein contracted an aggressive and rare form of cancer and passed away just five weeks after being diagnosed at UCSF in San Francisco. He died on July 5, 2024 at age 42, one week before his 43rd birthday. Born Evan Joel Epstein on July 22, 1981, he was the son of Janet and George Epstein. He graduated from Piedmont High School in 2000, where he loved playing sports, including tennis, golf, swimming, and running cross-country. His two passions were basketball, which he was a member of the Piedmont High School varsity team, and later in his adult life, playing softball on Temple Isaiah’s team in the Sunday Jewish League. He loved fitness and cardio, and was unusually strong even at an early age. Evan graduated from the University of California at Santa Barbara with a Bachelor of Science degree. He did his post-graduate studies at Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo, where he received an MBA as well as a Master’s degree in Engineering Management. After college he was a Senior Manager Customer Success for five-plus years at Workday in Pleasanton. He touched countless lives with his easy-going nature and warmth. He had a sarcastic sense of humor to which people could relate. Evan met his lovely wife Katelyn as members of a coed softball league on the Peninsula. It was a good match, with Katelyn an extrovert and Evan’s quiet and Evan Epstein died on July 5, 2024. strong demeanor. They were married in 2016 in Pleasanton. They first lived in Redwood City, and after a few years decided to move to the East Bay. They chose the peaceful Town of Moraga to settle, where they raised two rambunctious boys, Drew and Aaron. Evan was a very “hands on” father, and when Katelyn traveled for work as a Clinical Account Manager for Insightec, he had no qualms about being a stay-at-home dad, while working remotely from home. Evan is survived by his wife Katelyn, his two sons Drew, age 5, and Aaron, age 3. He also leaves his mother, Janet, and father, George, along with sisters Alison Cohen (Eitan) of Los Angeles, and Leah Epstein of Oakland, in-laws Don and Shannon Mosbacher, and numerous other family members. When the cubs arrived in Oakland they weighed about five pounds and were visibly dehydrated. After being rehabilitated they were able to temporarily join the other mountain lions at Oakland Zoo on the California Trail. “Our current mountain lion habitat is full,“ said Marketing Manager Isabella Linares, “We still participate in the rehabilitation process for these cubs as part of our mission.” In 2012, the Oakland Zoo participated in a training session focused on resolving conflicts between humans and wildlife. This training led to the formation of BACAT (Bay Area Cougar Action Team). The alliance brings together various agencies, non-profit organizations, local parks, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, and mountain lion researchers. articles.text: In addition to the more prominent architectural styles we have been discussing during the last months, there are yet more to be seen walking through town. Some, like Victorian, are well known but not numerous here; others are hybrid, sometimes difficult to classify. But it also strikes me that every new building, or even every remodel, is necessarily advancing, albeit in small steps, the evolution of any and every base style employed. Looking back maybe 50 years from now, these incremental trends will probably be clearer and help describe how and why the future style came to be. To better understand the initial selection and continuing evolution of building styles it might be helpful to review the process architects normally employ in design. Based on my experience, there are three overriding considerations in the design of any building: the site, the building program, and the design style. 1. Any building site has a specific size, solar orientation, topography, along with existing amenities (like views, trees, rock outcroppings, or water features for example). Any site is also a part of a surrounding context – anything from vacant land to 2-story homes to 12-story office buildings. 2. The building program answers the questions: how big is the intended building? What types of uses and spaces are included? What service systems are included? While zoning regulations limit these options, there still are a wide range of choices based on user lifestyle preference, cost, and response to the site. 3. The design style chosen, no matter how closely or loosely followed, determines the aesthetic of both the building massing and details – inside and out. It influences materials, forms and siting. An intelligent response to and prioritization of each of these overlapping and integrated conThe paired ionic columns, classical detailing, beautiful ironwork, and Art Nouveau canopy are all indicators of French Colonial architecture of this truly exquisite Piedmont entry. Note the complementary light fixtures and potted landscaping – absolutely perfect. This fine Queen Anne Victorian home enhances the whole neighborhood with its eclectic and well-proportioned woodwork. The pleasing subtle color changes further accentuate the skilled detailing.

articles.text: it was a stretch for our mom each month. It was the man around the house part that we had a problem with. As far as we were concerned, there was only one man we wanted around the house and that was our dad and we said so. “Boys,” she said, taking a deep breath, “try and understand. Your father… he just can’t be with us right now. It’s been almost a year and…” Her eyes were welling up with tears and we knew it wasn’t easy for her, saying any of it. “He… well, he may not come back to us.” Jordie stood very still, listening, his body rigid, shaking his head back and forth, saying, “No way, mom. No way. Dad’s coming back. He is. It hasn’t been that long. It hasn’t.” His voice was trembling and he’d begun to cry, trying not to, rubbing his nose with the back of his hand, his cheeks wet, his lower lip quivering with feeling and hurt. I stood close to him, holding my breath, afraid if I said even one word I’d start crying, too, my chest tight and my throat feeling closed off. The thing of it was, Jordie and I had held onto the belief that our dad was coming back so tight our hearts ached, and the thought of having to let go was nearly impossible. Never theless, Howard Oakely arrived early the next morning, it was a Saturday, and he had barely unpacked his suitcase when he set up his tools in our garage along with this 1949 Ford which he made clear was one bang-up set of wheels, a classic, that he was in the process of restoring, “From the ground up,” as he liked to say. From the kitchen window we watched him back it down our driveway and into the garage and went out to see what was up. Howard was standing next to the car, holding a rag, rubbing the front fender with the kind of tenderness you reserved for newborn babies. The object of his affection was a black coupe convertible, one rear fender covered with gray primer, the paint faded on the hood, the chrome bumpers pitted and dull. “Fellas, this here is my pride and joy. This little sweetheart’s gonna be a showstopper when I’m through with ‘er.” Jordie said later that the only thing that wreck was going to stop was traffic when it stalled in an intersection. It was then that Howard declared the garage, meaning our garage, our dad’s garage, to be no-man’s land, and we were told, in what he referred to as “No uncertain terms,” to stay out. He even spelled the word, O-U-T. Very sharp, Howard. “See boys, this here is now my work space.” Emphasis on my. “And I need to know I can spread out and not worry my tools will get messed with. Can’t abide my tools being messed with. You both got the message?” He said all of this while he had one hand on the fender of the Ford, his voice flat, with Texas somewhere in it. “The tools, the car, everything’s off limits. Do not touch. I catch you foolin’ with my stuff, you and me, we’ll have words. We clear about this?” We could tell right away that Howard had a way with kids. Truly. So, having been evicted, we parked our bikes in the back yard and if it rained and we remembered, we put them in the small tool shed. Howard never asked us what we were doing or where we’d been. I don’t think he really cared, as long as we didn’t bother him. The deal with Howard, if he wasn’t in the garage breaking a sweat over the mysteries of the spark plug, he was in the family room slumped deep in his brown-green-yellow vinyl Barcalounger, a big easy chair that had arrived when he did. Jordie called it the barfolounger because of its pukey color. Howard would slump down deep, his feet on the raised foot-rest, watching television, mostly wrestling, drinking what he called the working man’s tranquilizer: a long neck bottle of beer and a shot glass filled with Wild Turkey. Neither of us could see what our mom saw in the guy, but then there are a lot of things that adults do that seem like this huge mystery to kids. What is occurring over time, however, is that each and every one of these three important considerations is in flux – they are always changing. Adjacent trees grow, neighboring buildings are built, and overhead utility lines are removed. Just accommodating current lifestyles, newer building methods, and improved material selections necessarily changes and advances any base architectural style initially chosen with every year that passes. A partial exception to this would be the case of strict historical renovations where exact themes and details are duplicated for historical accuracy. So, it is easy to see how all architectural styles can evolve. And with changes in the world occurring more rapidly, the style evolutions will also occur faster. Just think of the pandemic we were in. More time spent in the house with virtual activities has created in one year a whole new set of building program criteria to which architects, designers, engineers and their clients are already responding. articles.text: springs or “take the waters.” To get a feel for the importance of the hotel we must look a little further back. In 1852 Walter Blair bought much of the land in what is now the Piedmont area from the U.S. government. His 600-acre purchase cost him $1.25 per acre, meaning he bought nearly all of Piedmont for $750. The discovery of sulfur spring waters drew other investors towards the area. and they formed the Piedmont Land Company which purchased land around the springs. They sold bonds to build the Piedmont Springs Hotel, hoping to bring in visitors from San Francisco and Oakland. The springs contained sulphur, magnesia, iodine, and iron; bathing in them was (and still is) used to treat ailments such as rheumatism, poor circulation, pain and skin conditions. The hotel was a charming two-story Victorian building surrounded by a wide veranda and second floor balcony. In addition to 20 first-class bedrooms and two suites upstairs, four cottages were later added. The Piedmont Historical Society recalls the hotel’s “Five dining rooms offered the finest food. The main dining room had a crystal chandelier, fine china and velvet drapes and seated thirty-five. Paintings covered the walls.” The Grand Saloon, exclusively for men, featured a billiard table, sophisticated mahogany bar, spittoons and a pot-belly stove in the corner. The hotel drew affluent people from the area as the weather was more favorable to that of San Francisco. Visitors enjoyed the trails to the springs and fine dining coming from Blair’s local dairy and on-site garden. Equestrian enthusiasts frequented the hotel and helped develop a formidable stable across the street where The Piedmont Community Church now stands. The hotel was placed at the end of Piedmont’s main street, Vernal Avenue (now Highland), at the site of the Exedra (Blue Vase). Paintings covered the walls.” The Grand Saloon, exclusively for men, featured a billiard table, sophisticated mahogany bar, spittoons and a pot-belly stove in the corner. Blair co-owned a public transportation service of horses pulling railway cars from downtown Oakland to Broadway. He developed another horse line from Piedmont Avenue to the The Piedmont Springs Hotel was a tourist destination in the years before the city of Piedmont was incorporated. hotel. All were timed with the ferry crossings to San Francisco in the morning and evening. James Gamble served as proprietor of the Hotel and is credited in naming the region Piedmont. In an advertisement for the hotel, Gamble said, “carriages from San Francisco can make Piedmont, via the Oakland Ferry, in about an hour from Pacific Street wharf.” Travel times have not changed much in 150 years. Large “finger board” signs all along the carriage route marked the way to Piedmont around Lake Merritt. The hotel had a good run of 20 years and was instrumental in the development of Piedmont as a residential community, with guests being enticed to buy large estates up to 20 acres. In 1891 women of Piedmont led a prohibitionist movement to stop the sale of alcohol at the hotel with a petition to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors. The next year the hotel caught fire when sparks from the chimney lit the roof on fire. A fire engine coming from Oakland took two hours to get there, leaving residents and guests to sit and watch it burn down without their own fire department. articles.text: Piedmont police responded to a report of an armed robbery in the 300 block of Magnolia Avenue on Thursday, July 18, at 3:06 p.m. The victim was unloading his car when he was approached by three black males who wore black ski masks and demanded his wallet and watch. The victim said the suspects were armed with a pistol and two AR-15-style rifles. The victim complied and was not harmed, but the suspects stole his Vaer watch and a pair of Ray-Ban sunglasses. The suspects fled the scene in a silver Jeep Grand Cherokee with rear paper plate BU71K81. The victim called the Police Department immediately after the incident. The estimated loss was $200. PPD Police Captain Chris Monahan advised residents not to be lulled into a false sense of security by the city’s safe reputation and friendly culture. “Suspects often don’t even know what city they’re in,” said Monahan. “They’re just out driving around looking for somebody they can victimize. This plan by the city is clearly in response to the recent public outcry over a controversial new construction project at 77 Wistaria Way. The project seeks to divide the currently vacant lot at 67-77 Wistaria Way into two parcels on which the owners will construct a new large house on each parcel and a third house as an Auxiliary Dwelling Unit (ADU). The property owners Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead are not Piedmont residents. Using the recently passed California Housing Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act, also known as “Senate Bill 9 (SB9), the owners’ application for a lot split was approved via “ministerial approval,” meaning there was no public review for the building design. articles.text: Staff Photos Sam Shelby is entering his senior year at Piedmont on the football and track teams. SAM SHELBY Football, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2025 Sam Shelby is entering an important senior year on the football and track teams. He was named by the SF Chronicle as a candidate for Player of the Year in the East Bay region and to the All-Metro first-team. He was also named to The Mercury News’ All-Bay Area News Group second-team. He helped Piedmont’s football team compile a 7-4 record in the school’s full return to the WACC. He was named the Shoreline Division’s Player of the Year after recording 63 receptions, averaging an eye-popping 17.7 yards per catch for 1,117 yards and 14 touchdowns. He also had 403 rushing yards and averaged 12.2 yards per carry for eight more touchdowns. As the team’s kicker, he also converted 30 point after attempts. Shelby is entering the fall football season with a full head of steam after missing the track season last spring. What is your workout program this summer? I am training with the football team Monday–Thursday from 4:00 to 7 p.m. as well as doing my own personal workouts off the field on weekends. What are your fitness goals for the summer? This summer, I’m trying to get in good enough shape to play both offense and defense and gain weight. How are you measuring your development? I’m keeping track of my weight gain as well as watching my numbers grow in the weight room. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I occasionally work with trainers for recovery and workouts, but most of my workouts come from my football coaches and myself. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I reached 9 feet, 8 inches on my broad jump and clocked a 40-yard dash of 4.63 seconds. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Enjoy what you do and do it right.

SAM SHELBY Football, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2025 Sam Shelby is entering an important senior year on the football and track teams. He was named by the SF Chronicle as a candidate for Player of the Year in the East Bay region and to the All-Metro first-team. He was also named to The Mercury News’ All-Bay Area News Group second-team. He helped Piedmont’s football team compile a 7-4 record in the school’s full return to the WACC. He was named the Shoreline Division’s Player of the Year after recording 63 receptions, averaging an eye-popping 17.7 yards per catch for 1,117 yards and 14 touchdowns. He also had 403 rushing yards and averaged 12.2 yards per carry for eight more touchdowns. As the team’s kicker, he also converted 30 point after attempts. Shelby is entering the fall football season with a full head of steam after missing the track season last spring. What is your workout program this summer? I am training with the football team Monday–Thursday from 4:00 to 7 p.m. as well as doing my own personal workouts off the field on weekends. What are your fitness goals for the summer? This summer, I’m trying to get in good enough shape to play both offense and defense and gain weight. How are you measuring your development? I’m keeping track of my weight gain as well as watching my numbers grow in the weight room. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I occasionally work with trainers for recovery and workouts, but most of my workouts come from my football coaches and myself. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I reached 9 feet, 8 inches on my broad jump and clocked a 40-yard dash of 4.63 seconds. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Enjoy what you do and do it right. articles.text: Cost now estimated at $32 million; 1 year behind schedule The Piedmont City Council has confirmed that the latest cost estimate for the community pool will be $32,100,000, an increase of $2,132,450. Voters approved a bond of up to $19,500,000 in November 2020, three and a half years ago, with a target date of this summer, 2024, for families to swim in a new community pool. At a city council meeting on July 1 this summer, project leaders for the construction of the pool confirmed that although construction of the pool should be completed by January 2025, an official opening would not take place until Spring 2025. A prayer for America By Pastor Jim Hopkins The following is prayer was offered during the worship service at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland on July 14, the morning after an attempted assassination of former President Trump Loving God, Creator of All, from everlasting to everlasting you are God. In this space between everlasting and everlasting we are in a moment. A moment of fear, a moment of grief, a moment of shock, a moment of confusion, a moment of anger, a moment of desperation, a moment of very high anxiety. We are in a moment in which hope seems far, far away. In this moment help us to live humbly, to speak with quiet voices, to confess that we worship many false gods, gods named wealth, weaponry, party, nation and self. In this movement we pray for the grieving even as we give thanks for the brave. In this moment we would believe anew that you are a god of great transformations and magnificent reversals. We would trust afresh that you are able to take our sadness and make it joy, to take our doubt and make it hope and to take our fear and make it love. In this moment between everlasting and everlasting, you are God and we need you stay with us as, on this fresh morning, we do the serious work of living in a broken world. Amen. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. LUKA FABI, 7th grade I like running track so I will say the 400 meters. That’s one of the races I like running with the middle school track team. MASON MYERS, 8th grade I would have to say basketball would be the most fun. They will definitely win gold. articles.text: Editor: For 57 years Piedmonters have come together to celebrate our nation’s birthday as a community. Like most of our annual special events, the 4th of July parade and picnic grew out of a resident’s vision, Dick Johnson. It is brought to life year after year by a group of dedicated and hardworking volunteers. The Piedmont City Council would like to publicly extend our gratitude to the 4th of July Committee members and community volunteers who planned and executed the 57th annual Independence Day parade and picnic in the park. True to its theme, this year’s event showed our small town’s big spirit at its best. Thank you to volunteers: • Kathy Kelleher • Carla Betts • Roland Lazzarotto • John and Carolee Morrison • Michael and Carolyn Bruck • Gray Cathrall • Kimberly Gray • Marilyn Weber • Carrie McAllister • Paula Klein • Patty Edmonds This event would not be possible without countless hours of hard work from this team, with support from the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Chelle Putzer, Eva Phalen, and Cora Wood. They are an inspiration for us all. –Piedmont City Council Mayor Jen Cavenaugh Vice-Mayor Betsy Andersen Councilmember Conna McCarthy Councilmember Jennifer Long Councilmember Tom Ramsey

articles.text: Allen Carr leads Zenith New Orleans Parade Band in Piedmont parade for 15th year When Hollis Carr’s health began failing, the longtime Grand Marshal of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band asked his son, Allen Carr, to take up the mantle. “When my dad became sick with cancer, he wanted me to join the band. So, I said I’d gladly take it over,” recalled Allen Carr. For many years Hollis had brought his kids to see their dad march in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade. 2009 was the first year Allen Carr donned his father’s signature outfit – a magnificent tuxedo, black bow tie, red sash, dark shades and a red beaded necklace hanging down his chest with a crawdad. He completed his outfit with his father’s iconic parasol decorated with the colors of the Ghanaian flag. “The umbrella was a gift from a family friend, which my dad adopted for his wardrobe,” Alan explained. “There’s a straightthrough connection with New Orleans’s Line dance marching tradition and African celebrations. You’ll see umbrellas and parasols used heavily in both cultures.” The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band was founded in 1989 by local musician and bandleader Earl Scheelar (1929-2023). The band plays authentic New Orleans Jazz for dancers and music lovers alike and usually performs in two to three parades each year. Allen Carr, 62, grew up in a musical household. “I grew up playing jazz and classical. My dad played trombone, my mom played piano and sax, my brother played sax, I played sax and bass,” he said. His family attended the Monterey Jazz Festival each year. In high school Alan expanded his playing style to include Latin and choral influences. Today, Carr is the Director of Alternative Investments at FrankThe Zenith New Orleans Parade Band has performed authentic New Orleans Jazz to Bay Area audiences for 35 years. Allen Carr, 62, succeeded his father Hollis in 2010 as the Grand Marshal of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band. lin Templeton, a global investment firm. In 2009, Allen Carr and his father walked down Highland Avenue side-by-side to help Alan get used to the role. “We did it together that first year,” Alan said. However, by the next year, his father was too sick to march in the 4th of July parade. He watched proudly from the sidelines in 2010 as his son took charge of the band and its marching. Hollis passed away later that same year. Now Alan Carr carries on his father’s legacy by leading the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band down Highland Avenue each year. Although the band prides itself on playing authentic New Orleans Jazz, the man leading them is not from New Orleans. “It’s funny,” explained Alan. “My dad was from New Jersey, my mom was from Colorado, but Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Editor: Thank you for publishing Diane Prioleau’s letter criticizing John Solomon’s King Trump parody in the Independence Day parade, in which she asserts that Solomon should not have been allowed to participate. Publishing her views helps illustrate the broad viewpoint diversity of our community, an issue that she has previously celebrated, as should we all. (She spoke out against Piedmont School District’s DEI initiative because it didn’t sufficiently discuss viewpoint diversity.) But isn’t our celebration of our community’s diversity enhanced when views we disagree with are expressed? If I correctly understood Solomon’s point, his float was a celebration of Prioleau’s right to disagree, and of his concern that expression of diverse views might cease to be permitted under a Trump administration. –David Oppenheimer For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: New report suggests Piedmonters could be doing more The City of Piedmont Sustainability Division has released a new report on climate action in Piedmont, which suggests that the city’s greenhouse gas emissions have remained stable or even increased in recent years. “According to the Businessas-Usual Forecast, Piedmont is not on track to meet the 2030 emissions reduction goal. Rather, the City will have an estimated excess of over 5,000 [Metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent]” reads an informational report presented to City Council. For comparison, 5000 metric tons of CO2 is equal to 560,000 gallons of gasoline in vehicle emissions. In light of this new information, officials believe that new interventions will be required to meet the city’s current climate goals, which include halving greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and becoming carbon neutral by 2045. The Sustainability Division’s climate action update was delivered at a City Council meeting on July 1, 2024. “Together, transportation and building energy [sources] were responsible for over 96% of emissions in Piedmont,” stated Alyssa Romea, an AmeriCorps Climate Action Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. “We can also trace emissions to more specific subsectors,” they explained. “The first is passenger vehicles, which contributed 46.1% of total emissions. And then the second is residential natural gas, which contributed 41.6% of emissions.” She added that most homes rely on this form of energy by way of gas appliances like gas furnaces, gas water heaters and gas stoves. Romea identified these as “key areas” for the city’s attention. Romea also discussed the city’s plans to address these issues. When it comes to gas vehicles, “meeting these climate goals requires us to decarbonize transportation from gas passenger vehicles,” she said. This includes increasing support for the adoption of electric vehicles, lowering vehicle mileage and improving accessibility to alternative modes of transportation like public transit, biking and walking. The next part of the city’s plan is to reduce building emissions, which Romea said was mainly her department’s focus right now. To this end, the City plans to promote renewable electricity, source clean energy like wind and solar, reduce total energy use by increasing energy efficiency and “most importantly” promote the replacement of gas appliances with electric alternatives. As of May 2024, the City of Piedmont has issued 35 electrification rebates totaling almost $37,000 to encourage the adoption of heat pump hot water heaters, heat pump home heaters and electric panel upgrades. Piedmont has made significant growth in the last two decades in terms of sustainability. Since 2005, greenhouse gas emissions from activities within the City have fallen 33%. Currently, 24.7% of Piedmonters’ registered vehicles are electric or hybrid. The city adopted its first climate action plan in 2010. In 2018, the city released an updated second version called the Climate Action Plan 2.0. Both the first and second climate action plans included specific greenhouse gas emission targets. However, on July 17th, 2023, the city adopted a set of new goals to better match state and federal targets. Currently, they are to achieve municipal and community-scale carbon neutrality no later than 2045 as well as halving their total emissions by 2030. The city defines carbon neutrality as the point where all activities within city limits would generate zero emissions. The Piedmont Sustainability Division reports on the city’s climate action progress every year. The last update was given at a City Council meeting on July 17, 2023. articles.text: California’s upcoming November ballot will ask voters to fund schools with money from Proposition 2, a bond measure that would allow the state to borrow $10 billion to help with repairs and upgrades at public schools. If it passes, California schools TK-12 and community colleges across the state could receive matching funds for a wide range of projects by issuing their own bonds. A similar proposal for $15 billion was rejected by voters in November 2020. Only 47% of voters were in favor of giving public schools this economic pool during the uncertainty of the Covid pandemic. Proposition 2 needs a simple majority and would provide $8.5 billion in facility renovations and new construction for TK-12 schools. Community colleges would receive the final $1.5 billion. To receive bond money, school districts must have a local bond of their own and then apply to the State Facilities Program for a funding match on a sliding scale up to 65% for renovations and 55% for new construction. Some school districts, especially those in dire need of repair, are getting the ball rolling now by putting out their own bonds in this same election. Piedmont schools are focused on their own parcel tax increase and are finishing large facility projects, notably Witter Field “We are not currently contemplating a bond,” said School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “If and when we do, we would involve the community in such a decision.” The 2016 money from the last successful school bond, has long since been spent by the state, and the state’s school repair fund is expected to hit zero by 2025. “It’s been long in coming and desperately needed by many districts,” said Association of Piedmont Teachers President Elise Marks. “Keeping school buildings running, safe and healthy is expensive.” The local tax is on the ballot because there is no dedicated funding stream for school facilities in the state. California depends on raising money from bonds. Voter-approved ballot initiatives have raised $43 billion in bonds since 1998.

articles.text: Piedmont’s school board is calling upon residents to help support a parcel tax increase of Measure H, which will appear on ballots in the November 5 election. During a June 26 board meeting board members took the final opportunity to formerly advocate for the special tax measure. The ballot language is: “To attract and retain highly qualified teachers and educational support staff and continue funding advanced academic programs, shall Piedmont Unified School District’s measure renewing the school parcel tax for 8 years be adopted at the rate of 50 cents per square foot of building improvements, providing 5 million dollars in annual school funding that can’t be taken away by the State, with independent citizen oversight and all money locally controlled.” “We are excited to get this campaign started. We think this is going to be fun, we’ve had fun so far. The committee is looking very strong,” said school board member Lindsay Thomasson. articles.text: August is the optimal time to view the annual Perseid Meteor Shower, one of the most active seasonal meteor showers. this, the Perseids will have begun — they last from July 14 through August 24 this year. But the good news is that they will peak for best viewing between midnight August 11 and just before sunrise August 12. As with every year, hundreds of Bay Area astronomy enthusiasts are expected to flock to Chabot Space & Science Center to commune with fellow “shooting star” hunters and glean some insights from Chabot astronomers and scientists, including Gerald McKeegan and Ben Burress. “Meteor particles enter the atmosphere at about 40-60 kilometers per second, causing shock heating and friction that quickly burns up the particles and ionizes the air around them,” explained McKeegan. “This produces the long bright streaks that we see as ‘shooting stars.’” They are called Perseids for a reason. “The meteor streaks form lines that extend back to a radiant point in the constellation Perseus, which will be in the north-eastern sky at midnight,” he explained. “As Earth orbits the Sun, its direction of motion in mid-August is toward the constellation Perseus. That gives the illusion that the meteors come out of Perseus, when it is actually the Earth that is plowing into the particle stream from the comet.” According to Science.com, “The Perseids are caused by Earth passing through debris — bits of ice and rock — left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle which last passed close to Earth in 1992. The Perseids peak when Earth passes through the densest and dustiest area.” NASA predicts that viewers in dark sky locations this year can “expect to see up to 100 meteors per hour during the Perseid’s peak.” It’s interesting to note that Comet Swift-Tuttle takes 133 years to make one orbit of the Sun. It last reached perihelion (closest pass to the Sun) in 1992, so mark your calendars for its return in 2125. Last year was a good year to view the Perseids at their peak. This year, meteor-gazers will have to work a little harder, or at least stay up a little later, for best viewing to await the Moon’s setting to create less light interference. Other factors that affect viewing are the presence of clouds, fog and smoke in the air – all relatively unpredictable in the Bay Area. Plan to head up to Chabot Space & Science Center to view this year’s Perseid Meteor Shower between about 11 pm (PDT) Sunday, August 11, and 3 am Monday, August 12. Details: Perseids Meteor Shower Viewing at Chabot Space & Science Center, Adult $15, Youth $7, Free for Members. According to Chabot astronomers, the meteor showers are best viewed without telescopes or even binoculars, so plan to just sit or lay back, look up and enjoy the show!

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, July 17, 2024 SchOOLs School Board makes another push for Measure H By Jay Russell Piedmont’s school board is calling upon residents to help support a parcel tax increase of Measure H, which will appear on ballots in the November 5 election. PUSD will find out what letter of the alphabet their measure has been assigned, in August. School board member Ruchi Medhekar’s advice? “Vote yes on the parcel tax,” she said. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) hosted a Summer Adventures 2024 program in June thanks in large part to the dedication and creativity of the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) teachers. Erin Rivera, previously of Piedmont Rec Dept. was brought on to help the district rebuild the once popular Summer Adventures, which PUSD ran for 20 years before the pandemic. Eighty eager students participated in the PUSD Summer Adventures program session at Havens. The daily offerings included a blend of academic enrichment and enjoyable activities crafted by dedicated PUSD teachers. “The teachers are the true architects of this successful initiative, leaving a lasting impact on students and educators alike,” said Rivera. This year’s program was designed not just to engage, but to educate, ensuring a holistic approach to summer learning. Each teacher poured their expertise and passion into planning engaging activities that seamlessly integrated academics with fun, creating an enriching environment for all participants. Students, including many newcomers to the district, benefited greatly from this immersive experience, setting a positive tone for their upcoming transition into the fall semester. Additionally, the Welcome to TK/Kinder, and Welcome to 6th Grade programs were specially created to help those students feel more prepared for their transition to a new school and program in the fall. These initiatives provided a supportive environment for young learners, easing their adjustment and boosting their confidence. Another cornerstone of the program’s success was the Junior Counselors-in-Training (CITs), a dedicated group of middle school students. Trained in the mornings, these young leaders showcased their skills by organizing games and activities during recess and providing crucial support to teachers in classrooms, enhancing the overall program experience. In the initial planning, over 30 PUSD teachers and staff were interested in Summer Adventures. While enrollment limitations prevented all from joining, their enthusiasm and commitment underscored the program’s value and success. Looking ahead, PUSD is committed to building upon this year’s achievements. Plans are already in motion to expand and diversify future summer programs, with expanded summer school options for all grade levels. The impact of Summer Adventures extends beyond the classroom, fostering a community of lifelong learners and setting a benchmark for innovative educational initiatives. Look for Summer Adventures 2025 info in the late fall. Kids chase a Jr. CIT on the Havens playground during Summer Adventures 2024. Jr. CITs Margaret Eidt (standing) and Miles Hetherington show students the rules of a game in the Havens MPR during Summer Adventures at Havens. Jr. CITs create an obstacle course for Summer Adventure students.
