pages.text: 10 Wednesday, July 17, 2024 PEBCC performs to an audience at Llangollen Eisteddfod in Wales. PEBCC wins Continued from page 1 for their performances of “Salve Regina” and “Panda Chant II.” The title came with a 15-pound bronze trophy and total prize money of £1,150 (British pounds). “We didn’t expect to win,” admitted Eric Tuan, Artistic Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Tuan, formerly a member of the choir during his youth, was also its conductor for the award-winning performance. “The competition was really stiff. Before the event, we saw that we would be competing against some of the finest youth choirs in the world – choirs from Singapore, Thailand, Canada, England, Wales, the Czech Republic – some truly outstanding choirs. So, we thought, ‘we’re just going to give our very best performance and see how we do,’” he stated. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is a year-round music education and performance program for ages five through 18. It currently serves around 350 singers from the San Francisco Bay Area. In addition to competing at a high level, the choir places a special emphasis on international exchange and teaches its singers pieces from multiple countries in a variety of languages. Every summer since 1947, the Welsh town of Llangollen stages one of the world’s most inspirational and largest cultural festivals, the Llangollen Eisteddfod (literally translated to “a sitting”). Around 4,000 performers and as many as 35,000 visitors converge on this beautiful small town each year to sing and dance in a unique combination of competition, performance, and international peace and friendship. The competitions climax with the naming of the prestigious “Young Choir of the World” title, which determines the best overall choir of the event. Tensions were high before Piedmont took the stage. This was the first time Tuan had taken a team to a competition since he Photo courtesy of Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod The Llangollen Eisteddfod’s main competitions take place at the International Pavilion, which seats up to 4,000 people. became Artistic Director in 2019. Additionally, very few students had prior competition experience because of the pandemic. “It was pretty nerve-wracking for them because they’d worked all year to prepare this repertoire,” explained Tuan. Backstage, the students listened to the choir before them perform and their anxiety grew. “One kid actually came up to me and said ‘We’re cooked,’” laughed Tuan. But when the choir stepped onstage, a profound sense of connection took hold of them. “They rose to the occasion. They gave the finest performance, certainly, that they’ve delivered all year. We worked so hard on the technique that in the moment of competition we were able to let go and abandon ourselves to the meaning of the music and to the feeling of that special connection that you have when you’re singing with each other,” recalled Tuan. The choir began their set with “Salve Regina,” a beautiful, shimmering hymn to the Virgin Mary by contemporary Basque composer Javier Busto. The tones of the Piedmont choir brought a hush over an audience of more than 1000 people. They followed with a stunning performance of “Panda Chant II,” a contemporary piece by American composer Meredith Monk. Students moved side to side and belted out sounds akin to birds and howler monkeys as they sang. “They’re moving, they’re clapping, they’re making unusual sounds in this very complicated, rhythmic way [...] it’s a joyful, animal ritual,” explained Tuan. The judges seemed to respond to their beautiful mixture of ethereal and offbeat performances. The final score was 95 – the highest of any competitors in their division. The kids of the choir gasped, cheered and hugged one another. The festival included a Celebration of Nations, where each choir proudly carried its national flag through the audience and onto the stage. After winning their division, the choir performed later that evening in a sort of grand finale. The Piedmont choir went up against winners from two other youth divisions, champions in their own right, for the title of “Young Choir of the World.” They emerged victorious. The students of the choir celebrated with shouts of joy and took photos together. Many of them were interviewed by local UK and Welsh news organizations. At the end of the competition Tuan called his mentor Bob Geary, the founding director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, to tell him the good news. “He was very excited because he’s wanted us to win first place at this competition for many years, and we had finally done it. It was great to call him and acknowledge the legacy of this organization that he had created.” Tuan described the event as “one of our three greatest competitive achievements of the many competitions we’ve attended through the years.” For more information about the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir and its programs, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ programs or contact their Registrar Greg Rosas at grosas@ piedmontchoirs.org. Fall classes for the choir’s 2024-2025 season begin on September 5. Choir members are shown during an outdoor rehearsal ahead of the main stage concert.

articles.text: A novel by Chris Honoré The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The excerpt is offered as a weekly series meant to encourage reading. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town called Watson in the mid-sixties. The novel can be found online at Barnes & Nobel or Amazon. PART FOUR I guess you could say that what happened, at least the beginning of what happened, started just before school let out. Just before summer vacation. And even now, looking back, I can still remember everything. But then how could I forget? My life was changed forever. It had been more than a week since Howard left, and Jordie and I said as little as possible about his being gone, afraid we’d hex it. We both hoped with all our hearts he’d never come back. But we’d turned one brick into a castle before, only to come home from school to find old Howard sitting in the family room, just off the kitchen, watching television and acting like he owned the place. We lived in a small clapboard house on the edge of Watson, a dry, dusty town in Central California. Laurel and oak trees grew in the backyard, their limbs spreading out over our house like huge umbrellas, giving shade during the long, warm summers. We grew up climbing in the trees and playing “chase the bad guys” in an open field nearby, the dense grass tall enough to hide us as we crawled back and forth, stickers getting in our hair, catching in our socks. With Howard gone, the feeling in our house changed. Things were lighter, easier somehow. Maybe it was because summer wasn’t far off. But I think it was because Howard, cranky and whiney, had declared his intention to live somewhere else, and for sure nobody was sending out any patrols to beg him to return. Our mom played the radio and hummed along as she worked in the kitchen, while Jordie and I ran in and out of the house, the screen door banging behind us. pages.text: Wednesday, July 17, 2024 11 The Journey of Max Braverman A novel by Chris Honoré The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The excerpt is offered as a weekly series meant to encourage reading. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town called Watson in the mid-sixties. The novel can be found online at Barnes & Nobel or Amazon. And even now, looking back, I can still remember everything. But then how could I forget? My life was changed forever. It had been more than a week since Howard left, and Jordie and I said as little as possible about his being gone, afraid we’d hex it. We both hoped with all our hearts he’d never come back. But I think it was because Howard, cranky and whiney, had declared his intention to live somewhere else, and for sure nobody was sending out any patrols to beg him to return. Looking over at him, his face serious, wrestling with that old lumpy chair, I’d try not to laugh. “What the heck are you doing, Jord? It’s the middle of the damned night.” “Just give me a sec.” And saying that, he crawled into the chair, the back of it now hard up against the closet door. “Gees, Jord, you can’t sleep like that.” “Yes I can.” “Look, I can’t sleep with you sitting there like that. It’s weird. Move the chair back where it was and just get back in bed.” Jordie just sat there, his arms folded, looking at me, waiting. “Okay, fine,” I said, and got out of bed, walking over to him. “Get in bed, I’ll check the closet. Just to be on the safe side.” I slid the chair back and opened the closet door, turning on the interior light, making a show of pushing our clothes back and leaning deep inside. Then, hitting the light switch, I hustled back in bed. “Coast is clear,” I said, tunneling down under the covers. “Max, I swear, I heard something.” “It’s gone now, Jord. Could’ve been the wind. It’s blowing pretty good out there.” And it was, the leafy branches of the big tree near our bedroom window moving back and forth, brushing the side of the house. “Anyway, it’s time to get some Z’s.” And before I could even close my eyes I heard Jordie mumble, “Definitely,” already half asleep. When he slept, he was a log. We had single beds with identical blue and red-checkered bedspreads and a maple nightstand with a lamp on it in the shape of a western water pump. You moved the handle up and down to turn the light off and on. I know, pretty corny, but Jordie really liked it and always wanted to be the one to turn the light off at night, pulling down on the pump handle like he almost expected water to come shooting out of the spout. We shared one dresser, and Jordie carefully divided the drawers starting with the top one for me, alternating to the bottom. Sometimes he would just sit on his bed hitting his fist into the pocket until his knuckles were all dark and grimy, fiddling with the webbing and the lacing, all the while having this sad look in his eyes. articles.text: Piedmont Fencing Team qualified five team members to the U.S. National Championships, while three competed. Pictured are Sophie Choi (left), Teresa Mckay, Oliver Greenebaum, Maya Dvoiris, and Niko Kalamas. Members of the Piedmont Fencing team competed in the National Championships in Columbus, Ohio from June 30 through July 8. He prestigious event hosts more than 6,000 of the best junior fencers in the U.S. Representing Piedmont were Piedmont High School seniors Oliver Greenebaum and Teresa McKay, along with 8th grader Maya Dvoiris. Two other members, Sophie Choi and Niko Kalamas, qualified but did not compete. “U.S. Nationals is the largest fencing tournament in the world with 6,000+ athletes competing over two weeks. This year it was in Columbus, Ohio,” said coach David Sinkkonen. “We qualified five athletes and brought three this year. We didn’t achieve the greatest results, but it’s quite an achievement to even qualify for the National Championships.” Greenebaum competed in three events, Division 2 and 3 men’s foil and junior men’s foil. In the D2 foil event on July 7, he finished 126th of 259 athletes. He had six pool matches to start, winning two matches including one against a ‘hard’ rated opponent. Oliver won one match in the Direct Elimination round, defeating Ethan Capra, but lost to Brian Kim, who finished 13th overall. Greenebaum was 126th of 259 in the D3 category on July 8. He won two of six pool matches and lost his elimination round match against ‘hard’ rated Quinn Peck, who placed 103rd. Oliver also opened the tournament on June 30 in the junior men’s foil, placing 396 of 422 athletes. “Oliver competed in three categories in the extremely difficult Jr. Men’s Foil event. Unfortunately Oliver didn’t make it out of the preliminary rounds. In DIV2 and DV3 Men’s Foil Oliver made it out of the preliminary rounds but lost early in his Direct Elimination rounds and was eliminated,” Sinkkonen said. McKay competed in the Division 1-A and Division 2 women’s foil categories. On July 3 she was 88th of 110 contestants after competing in five pool matches against ‘very hard’ or ‘hard’ rated competitors, She defeated one opponent with a ‘hard’ rating, and lost in the elimination to Anika Breker, who went on to finish 27th. Competing on July 4 in the D2 event, McKay was 145th of 179 after winning one of five pool matches, including one against ‘hard’ rated competition. Maya Divoiris (right), an 8th grader, competed in the Y-12 category at National Championships.

articles.text: The Oakland Strokes recently returned from the prestigious Rowing BC Provincial Championship Regatta at Burnaby Lake in Burnaby, British Columbia on July 12-14. They took 26 athletes and 34 boats. Each boat competed in an Open division, in addition to U17, U19, U23, Lightweight, and U23 Lightweight. Girls Results The Strokes duo of PHS junior Geneva Johnson and PHS sophomore Sophia Brenner placed 2nd in the women’s coxless 2- boat in the Under-19 division, and 5th in the open division with a time of 8:48.806. The women’s 8+ boat was third of five in its race with a time of 7:46.76. The boat included Brenner and Johnson, and Piedmont juniors Laurel Minor and Claire von Metzsch. The women’s coxed four boat with Brenner and Von Metzsch finished second of seven boats with a time of 7:49.30. Placing fourth in 8:05.67 were Johnson and PHS senior Anna Lavin. Lavin also competed in the 4x quad scull, which placed fifth of 15 boats with a time of 7:59.963. They were also third in the U19 division. Brenner was also in the 2x double scull, which placed 11th of 34 boats in 8:57.06. They were fourth of 14 boats in the U17 category. Lavin’s boat was 16th overall in 9:06.72, while von Metszch double scull was 24th in 9:36.02. In the single scull, Lavin finished 16th of 34 boats with a time of 9:58.03. The boat also placed third in the U19 division. Boys Results The Strokes’ men’s 8+ boat finished fourth in 6:36.56. It included PHS juniors Senan Brodie and Evrim Duransoy. Brodie and Duransoy also competed in the 4x quad scull, finishing 10th in the Open Division and third in the U17 division. In the single scull, Brodie won the U17 race in a field of 16 boats. He placed 18th in the open division in a crowded field of 53 boats with a time of 8:25.89. The men’s double scull was fourth 7:51.77 with Nigel Willacy and Logan Raymond. They also were second of 12 boats in the U19 category. Raymond competed in the single scull race and placed seventh in 8:03.64. PHS juniors Geneva Johnson (back left), Laurel Minor (second from left), and sophomore Sophia Brenner (fourth from left) competed in multiple events in British Columbia. PHS junior Senan Brodie (third from left) won the single scull race in the U17 division in Canada.

Wednesday, July 17, 2024 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 17th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2023 Lewis & Clark College Class of 2027 Portland, Oregon Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his freshman season on Lewis & Clark’s baseball team where he earned a starting role. Aikawa finished his debut collegiate season with 35 appearances and 34 starts, recording a .214 batting average with 27 hits, 10 doubles, 23 runs scored, and 18 RBIs. His best performances include going 3-for-4 with a run scored against on Puget Sound on April 13, went 2-for-3 with two doubles and three runs scored against Pacific Lutheran on April 6, and he went 4-for-5 with two RBIs and a run scored versus George Fox on March 30. He was the Post’s 2021 Sophomore of the Year and an influential four-year starter with the Highlanders. He earned second-team All-League honors as a senior and was first- team in 2022. Aikawa contributed both as a shortstop and pitcher in 2023, closing the year as the team’s leading hitter with a .357 average, 25 hits, 12 doubles, one home run, 13 RBIs and 22 runs scored. As a pitcher, he led the way with 37 innings, a 4-2 record, 44 strikeouts and a sterling 1.32 ERA, despite being a pitcher for the first time. What is your workout program this summer? Currently, my workout program with my trainer is centered around increasing my speed and agility. For example, I do exercises with pulleys as resistance and follow a chaser for my reaction time. In addition, my trainer provided me with a running program, where I run four times a week with various exercises. On the side, I have push, pull, legs, and plyometric days from exercises I collected from college programs and previous workouts. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for the summer are to get stronger, faster, and quicker. How are you measuring your development? I can measure strength by being able to move weight faster and being able to lift heavier weight. For speed and quickness I use a timer to see my progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with a trainer, a hitting coach, and on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Leading Lewis & Clark in doubles my freshman year. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t work without a purpose. Believe in the work that you are putting in. Believe that it is going to pay off. There are many small things that make a difference. Recently I learned that a proper amount of sleep and the quality of food I eat have become a major focus. How you fuel your body, along with your physical and mental rest is key in an athlete’s development. NICO DEFAZIO Baseball Photo courtesy of Lewis & Clark Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, was a freshman starter at Lewis & Clark College in Portland. Piedmont High Class of 2022 University of the Pacific Class of 2026 Nico DeFazio, PHS Class of 2022, finished his redshirt freshman season at University of the Pacific in Stockton where he earned a starting role. In 2024, DeFazio finished with 29 appearances and started 21 times, recording a .210 batting average with 13 hits, four doubles, six runs scored, and four RBIs. He had a four-game hitting streak this season from March 26-30. Some of his best games include going 1-for-3 with an RBI double and a run against Seattle on February 19, 1-for-3 with an RBI and a run scored versus San Diego on March 28, and 1-for-4 with an RBI against San Diego on March 29. At Piedmont DeFazio was named the WACC Shoreline’s Player of the Year in 2022 with a .408 batting average with 29 hits, 10 doubles, three triples, and a home run. What is your workout program this summer? I am working out at Cal Strength in Danville, as well playing baseball for a summer competitive baseball team, the Walnut Creek Crawdads. What are your fitness goals for the summer? To gain strength and speed. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my development through consistency and following my specific development plan through the summer. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with both a trainer in the weight room and a hitting coach for development at the plate. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I played in the No. 2 collegiate summer ball league with the Rochester Honkers in Minnesota, competing in the Northwoods League. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Just to continue having fun every day and to always work hard. Keep it simple. PETER KRUMINS Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2024 Northern Kentucky Class of 2028 Peter Krumins just graduated from Piedmont High and was named the school’s Outstanding Senior Athlete for 2024. He was an influential member of the water polo team in the fall and baseball team in the spring. He is set to continue playing baseball at Northern Kentucky. He finished his time at Piedmont as a two-time Western Alameda County Conference champion in water polo and a member of the 2023 North Coast Section water polo championship team, He also helped this year’s baseball team win the WACC’s regular season title, reach this year’s North Coast Section championship, and helped the team qualify for the CIF NorCal tournament for the first time. He was also a member of the school’s league championship team in baseball in 2022. Krumins was primarily a shortstop and also appeared as a pitcher as a junior and senior. This year’s team finished with a 19-10 record, placed second in the North Coast playoffs, and advanced to the CIF NorCal tournament where it placed second. Krumins finished with a .275 batting average with 22 hits, nine doubles, one triple, one home run, 19 RBIs, 27 runs scored, and drew a team-leading 27 walks. Photo courtesy of University of the Pacific Nico DeFazio, PHS Class of 2022, just finished his redshirt freshman year at University of the Pacific in Stockton. What is your workout program this summer? I am following a training program that my coaches at Northern Kentucky University provided me. This includes weight training, diet guidance and speed exercises What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goal is to add weight and strength, but continue staying athletic by maintaining quickness and speed. How are you measuring your development? My workouts will help measure my development when I get to school and begin training with my team. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out alone in the weight room; I have a hitting coach and a, currently playing on my travel ball team. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? My travel ball team is playing games against D1 collegiate players. I am measuring myself against pitching and defense when we play games. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? My advice is to become comfortable doing uncomfortable things. Also to not force any unnatural body movement and use what your body gives you. articles.text: We’re entering the final five stages of the 2024 Tour de France with Tadej Pogačar extending his lead with the Yellow Jersey through Stage 16. Since our last coverage, Pogačar has added nearly three minutes of distance between him and second place/ He is three minutes and nine seconds ahead of back-to-back champion Jonas Vingegaard. Each day, it’s looking more like Pogačar is building toward his third victory of La Grande Boucle. It hasn’t surprised many that the Slovenian Pogačar has remained in first place. Perhaps the better race is for the Green Jersey for the lead in points between Biniam Girmay and Jasper Philipsen. The Green Jersey is reserved for sprints and stage victories. Girmay currently leads with 376 points to Philipsen’s 344, both with three stage victories after Philipsen won Tuesday’s Stage 16. For Girmay, the 24-year-old Eritrean became the first cyclist of African descent to win a Tour de France stage and would make history by claiming the Green Jersey following Stage 21. All will be said and done by the time the Post writes its final story of the race. Three of the final five stages are mountain classification rides during the next week, which could be pivotal toward Pogačar solidifying the Yellow Jersey or for Vingegaard to close the gap. Photo courtesy of BicyclingMagazine.com Tadej Pogačar continues to lead the Tour de France and wear the yellow jersey of the top rider through Stage 16. Stage 17 this morning was a 177.8 km mountain stage from Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux to SuperDévoluy. Stage 18’s 179.5 km hilly stage that could provide another close ending between Girmay and Philipsen, and then it’s followed by two more mountain stages. Stage 19 from Embrun to Isola Ski Resort has three steep climbs with a summit finish, while Stage 20 has four categorized and another summit finish up Col de la Couillole. The Stage 21 finale on July 21 is a time trial, marking the first time Le Tour has closed on with a time trial stage since 1989. It will be a 33.7 km ride from Monaco to Nice and could make an impact in the General Classification standings, but possibly a larger effect in the battle for the Green Jersey. articles.text: [Reprinted from August 2021] With the summer in full swing, we delve into our fourth of five features of trails near Lake Tahoe. This one is about the popular swimming hole of the Horsetail Falls Trail. For Bay Area residents, the welcome sight of Horsetail Falls’ gushing waters off in the distance of U.S. 50 means you’ve nearly arrived to South Lake Tahoe. In Twin Bridges between Strawberry and the Sierra at Tahoe Resort along the El Dorado Freeway is a magnificent 500 foot tall waterfall cascading down Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from Stateline, Nevada and a worthy visit should readers consider vacationing in the area. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip, while hiking beside The hike along Pyramid Creek is just as majestic as the reward of reaching Horsetail Falls. The trail continues over a vast rockface into the Desolation Wilderness towards Horsetail Falls.

articles.text: The Post offers a second batch of photos from Piedmont’s Fourth of July parade. After months of planning, it’s over in a flash. The classic cars and the bunting disappear into bins and garages for another year. For people who keep track, it was America’s 248th birthday. Photos by Matt Simons and Jay Russell A snapshot of automobiles by the decades includes a brown 1973 Plymouth Road Runner leading a 1976 Alfa Romeo, followed by a 1993 Lexus 400SC, a yellow 2000 Volvo S90, and a red 2007 Lotus Elyse. School Board Vice President Lindsay Thomasson rides shotgun with her family in the back of a 1915 Pierce Arrow owned by Dan Erceg. The Oakland Company custom vehicle had the chassis of a 1909 open air vehicle. Kids wave their flags and hands to Grand Marshal Gray Cathrall – also Editor of the Piedmont Post – leading the parade in a 1967 Ford Mustang, hopeful of securing a delivery paper route in the near future. City council Member Tom Ramsey rides in George Teebay’s gleaming 1930 Pierce Arrow Roadster. The scene from Vista and Highland after city council members Conna McCarthy and Tom Ramsey roll by in classic cars.

articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Symphony will perform the music of John Williams, responsible for some of the most epic film scores of all time, this Friday and Saturday, July 19 and 20. Originally from New York City, Williams’ career spanned seven decades as he composed some of the most popular, recognizable, and critically acclaimed film scores in cinema history. Edwin Outwater will lead the symphony through famous film scores, including Star Wars, Superman, Raiders of the Lost Arc, Jurassic Park and the Harry Potter film series. Both performances begin at 7:30 p.m. The Friday, July 19 concert will be at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco, and the Saturday concert at Stanford University’s outdoor Frost Amphitheater. Composer & conductor John Williams Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2023-24/ SWTS-JohnWilliams to purchase tickets or call the box office at 415-864-6000.
articles.title: SF Symphony performs music of John Williams July 19 & 20

articles.text: The Bear Valley Music Festival will open this Sunday, July 21, marking the 55th anniversary of the iconic outdoor music festival along Highway 4. All concerts are tucked inside a large tent that holds 500 guests in the outdoor wonderland of Bear Valley, California. The festival features an eclectic variety of music from 80s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy. We’ve been doing it for 55 years and are excited to celebrate that milestone this summer. From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone,” said Board of Directors president Julia Mee. Music Director Alexander Mickelthwate returns for his second year, and British band English Beat will open the festival with an energetic mix of musical styles, fronted by showman Dave Wakeling. English Beat fuses Latin, ska, pop, soul, reggae and punk rock and released three studio albums in the early 1980s, including I Just Can’t Stop It (1980), Wha’ppen? (1981) and Special Beat Service (1982), as well as a string of singles, including “Mirror in the Bathroom”, “Save It for Later”, “I Confess”, “Too Nice to Talk To”, “Can’t Get Used to Losing You“ and “Hands Off...She’s Mine.” Opening weekend will also include Steel ’n’ Chicago, a tribute to both Steely Dan and Chicago, and Deja Vu, a tribute to Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young. The Laurence Hobgood Trio, a Jazz ensemble, performs on Wednesday, July 26. The festival runs through Sunday, August 6. For the full festival lineup, a map and more information, visit www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org. Bear Valley Music Festival runs from July 21 to August 6. She has a very beautiful voice, which is rich and resonant. In addition, she presents a lovely and gracious image on stage. When she sings in Italian, I understand almost nothing. I got into a conversation with an Italian woman who was seated behind me. She claimed that she understood everything in Italian. I discovered that she was a very close friend of the singer. For the songs from various musicals Miss Zahra used a microphone. Her diction in English is quite a bit better than her diction in Italian. The unfortunate thing was that everything was so loud that I had to put my fingers in my ears to protect my hearing. The orchestra was billed as “The Dream Orchestra,” but I could not find any information about them. It seems it was a pickup orchestra and the players are drawn from the various Los Angeles studios. The conductor urged the musicians to play at a super loud level. The brass section was extremely large, and the string section was rather small which created the imbalance. I sat in the balcony for the first half of the concert. For the second half, I sat very close to the orchestra, just behind Miss Zahra’s parents and alongside her friends and neighbors. To be honest with you, the orchestra sounded better from afar. The Dream Orchestra was conducted by Daniel Suk who bills himself as Maestro Daniel Suk. His two-page biography was so loaded with superlatives I thought that I was in the presence of the greatest conductor of all time. He was competent but not nearly as good as his biography touted. After every number on the program, there were hugs galore. The audience loved everything.

Mostly French or French-inspired, the program includes works by Rimsky-Korsakov, Koechlin, Villa-Lobos, Poulenc, and Milhaud, performed by Martha Stoddard, flute; Jan Davis, oboe; Marcelo Meira, clarinet; Adam Williams, bassoon; Alex Stepans, horn; and Stanley Wolfersberger, piano. articles.text: “I am the greatest!” screamed Muhammad Ali. “I am the greatest!” Indeed. The great boxing champion Muhammad Ali certainly knew how to get publicity. For most of his career, he backed up his words. I think he admired PT Barnum, the ultimate master of publicity. But the ballyhoo wears quite thin when the talent cannot back up the publicity. That’s what I was thinking when I attended a concert in Santa Monica last weekend. The concert was a lovely homecoming for a local girl, soprano Golda Zahra, who has made good in Italy. The concert was Saturday night in a beautiful theater, the Broad Stage seating about 500. Almost everyone attending the concert was a friend of the soloist. I spoke with many of the people and learned they were neighbors as well as friends. Needless to say, she got a standing ovation for everything that she did. The concert reminded me of the concerts that the “three tenors” did some years ago ad nauseam but to great public acclaim and profit. In the first half, Miss Zahra sang a few famous Italian opera arias and in the second half a few songs from various American musicals. Golda Zahra

articles.text: Exhibition ends Monday Asian Art Museum in San Francisco’s exhibition Takashi Murakami: Unfamiliar People — Swelling of Monsterized Human Ego ends this Monday, July 22. Murakami: Monsterized is the first solo exhibition in San Francisco by Japanese artist Murakami, born in 1962. He is an internationally-recognized contemporary artist and major figure in global pop culture, whose influences draw from the aesthetic characteristics of the Japanese artistic tradition and the nature of postwar Japanese culture. Murakami’s influence in the contemporary art world makes his works highly sought-after in art trades and his vibrant prints maintain a consistently high value. In this exhibition, the artist’s larger-than-life paintings and sculptures use monsters, a common theme in his pieces, as a central motif. Senior Curator of Japanese Art Laura W. Allen said “the visual DNA of Murakami’s characters has origins in centuries-old styles in Japanese art, such as depicting Buddhist arhats and Daoist immortals as wizened beings with strange features, bulging eyes, and bared teeth.” Murakami adds “technicolor palette, goofy expressions, and eclectic mixture of motifs” that quickly became his trademark, Allen added. Visit https://asianart.org/ to learn more.

articles.text: Entry to the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) will be free to the public on August 1 during “Downtown First Thursdays,” a free monthly street party hosted in downtown San Francisco the first Thursday of the month. Currently on view at the museum is British visual artist and painter Rachel Jones’ exhibition !!!!!. Jones is known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. It is the first solo museum exhibition in the United States of Jones. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. The artist said she is “using motifs and color as a way to communicate ideas about the interiority of Black bodies and their lived experience.” To see all exhibitions on view, and to learn more about “Downtown First Thursdays,” visit https://www.moadsf.org/ event/free-admission-downtown-first-thursdays-2. ®

articles.text: Leonardo DiCaprio in Inception A remarkable revolution has taken place in filmmaking over the past two plus decades, one that has profoundly altered the moviegoing experience. What has occurred is the increasing use of CGI (computer generated imaging) in movies of all genres. The transformation has taken place with little fanfare, involving esoteric technology that is incorporated in even the most mundane movies without audiences taking particular note. Recent blockbusters as well as countless big tent comic book derivative films have all utilized state of the art advances in CGI hardware and software. It also has taken place with many of the recent children’s stories adapted for the screen such as “The Chronicles of Narnia,” and “Lord of the Rings.” Disney animation, where originally every frame was handdrawn and transferred to cels and then painted, is now done entirely with computers. The transition has been astonishing. What audiences see on the screen today is only limited by the imaginations of the writers, directors and cinematographers. No longer do they have to construct elaborate props, sets, handbuilt models or miniatures, or use stop-motion claymation. They can create set pieces that are mindbenders. Recall the impact of watching the groundbreaking Jurassic Park, one of the first films to effectively use CGI, replete with gripping set pieces that raised goose bumps on more than a few arms. If there’s a downside to the revolution in CGI (an estimated 50 percent of all films now use digital special effects), it has been the temptation to make special effects the main character, giving less thought to dialogue and narrative. This can turn films into carnival rides, absent of coherent stories. But when CGI is joined with exceptional storytelling, a new level of entertainment has arrived. Any discussion of CGI is mere prologue to the 2010 film Inception. Director Christopher Nolan (Dark Knight, Memento) has taken a spare story, a heist in reverse, and created a complex, visually stunning film. Set in the not too distant future, it involves a crew of corporate espionage specialists, led by Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio), who steal ideas from people’s minds while they are in a dream state. Cobb is hired for one final job by an energy mogul, Saito (Ken Wantanabe); however, instead of stealing an idea from the mind of the mark, Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), heir to a corporate empire, the objective will be to plant an idea in Fischer’s unconscious. If they succeed, he will decide (against his own best interest) to fragment his father’s global corporation and sell off the parts. The mission is high risk, high gain, the possibility of being lost in Fischer’s unconscious a distinct possibility. Travel into the unconscious and into a person’s dreams requires an elaborate construction of a new reality. An architect, Ariadne (Ellen Page), is brought on board to design the scenes and structure the journey. And it is in that construction that Nolan demonstrates his talent for consummate filmmaking. The movie is a labyrinth, a journey into a different world, across six countries, as the crew wends its way through multiple layers of Fisher’s unconscious, searching for the precise point where the idea can be planted (an inception as opposed to an extraction). When Fischer returns to consciousness, he will believe the suggestion is his own. Of course, the narrative, with film noir overtones, is convoluted and complicated. Despite his brilliance, Cobb has personal issues involving Mal (Marion Cotillard), his wife, and his absent children – issues which he takes along like so much personal luggage. The risk inherent in such films is that the emotional core of the movie will be lost as the special effects dazzle. And they do dazzle. But Nolan manages to sustain a coherent story throughout. It is necessary, however, to pay very close attention. Inception. Directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Ken Wantanabe, Marian Cotillard, Ellen Page, Cillian Murphy. 2 hrs., 28 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Inception a brilliant look into the future

articles.text: A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s The Boy and the Heron From the legendary Japanese Studio Ghibli comes the animated feature film The Boy and the Heron, written and directed by the iconic Japanese filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki. It won a 2024 Oscar, a BAFTA (British Academy of Film and Television Arts) and a Golden Globe Award. While the story is loosely based on the 1937 Japanese novel, How Do We Live, by Yoshino Genzabuno, in the main it thematically relies on the comingof-age memories of Miyazaki, as do many of his films. The story begins in Tokyo, the year is 1942, during the first months of the Pacific war. It focuses on an angry, but vulnerable 11-year-old boy, Mahito Mimaki (Luca Padovan). His mother is in a local hospital where she is killed in an allied bombing. Mahito is devastated. His father, Shoichi (Christian Bale), who works in an arms factory, makes the decision to marry his wife’s sister, Natsuko (Gemma Chan), and move the family to the countryside. Having lost his much loved mother, and weighted by grief, Mahito believes the marriage is a betrayal of his mother, and so feels a growing estrangement from his father. He also faces having to enroll in a new school where he is bullied. Unexpectedly, Mahito encounters a grey Heron (Robert Pattison) who has not only a mouth of teeth, but the ability to talk. The gravelly-voiced Heron lures Mahito to a strange, abandoned tower that is located on the estate’s property. The anthropomorphic bird claims that if Mahito goes with him, he will be reunited with his deceased mother. Of course, steeped in grief and loss, Mahito agrees, but quickly discovers that the Heron’s promise is only a mirage framed by an untruth. However, guided by the Heron, what Mahito discovers instead is that the tower has a portal to a parallel universe, one filled with strange, odd, fantastical creatures – a talking penguin (Willem Dafoe) and a parakeet king (Dave Bautista) who commands a ravenous avian army. Mahito also confronts danger, monsters and fanciful creatures. The film’s hand-drawn artistry is extraordinary and sumptuous, the tale told both tortured and whimsical, while offering a continuing contrast between the reality of loss, war and fantasy, the themes that frame The Boy and the Heron. The Boy and the Heron. Written and Directed by Hayao Miyazaki, Voiced by Mahaita Miaki, Christian Bale, Dave Bautsta, Gamma Chan. 2 hrs., 4 min. PG-13. Released in 2024. Now streaming on Fandango, apple tv, and appearing in theaters.

articles.text: Perhaps you have watched a television program titled McGyver. It was a series in which the hero, an incredibly resourceful and resilient young guy in a Indiana Jones leather coat and khakis, would invent his way out of impossible jams. It’s been some time since the show was on prime time television, but no matter. As it has turned out that McGyver’s name has become a verb, meaning if you can come up with a solution to a no-exit problem, fraught with clock-ticking danger, you have McGyvered it. It always involves using a combination of ad hoc stuff to include the ubiquitous duct tape. Dwayne Johnson’s most recent film Skyscraper, finds his character, Will Sawyer, in the opening scene suffering an injury that requires his retirement from the F.B.I.’s hostage rescue unit. He becomes a security specialist and has an opportunity to land a spectacular job He is able to travel with his wife, Sarah (Neve Campbell), and their two kids to Hong Kong where he will evaluate the security system of a 240- floor high-rise owned by a billionaire developer. Everything starts off peacefully until it’s not. Apparently there are some very bad people with foreign accents who, for reasons that are somewhat obscure, want to burn the building down. And so they try. It turns out that Will Sawyer’s family is staying there when the fire starts and it’s Will’s task to get inside the building – not out of the building – to rescue them. It’s something that proves to be no small thing. His situation defines high risk, high gain. Movies of this type may not be your first choice. But if you have time on a warm, slow moving day and the kids – newbie tweens, teens – are grumbling that there’s nothing to do, try the pure escapism found in Skyscraper. It’s the perfect choice. Kids love pulp cinema. Dwayne Johnson, aka The Rock, a fine specimen of a man and once an ex-wrestler, is perfectly cast. He’s managed to carve out a niche in action movies that call for brawn and good intentions. And in this film he actually pulls out a roll of duct tape and bandages a wound. McGyvered. It’s all a thrill, and the muscle-bound charisma of Johnson is evident in every frame. Skyscraper. Directed by Rawson Marshall Thurber. Starring Dwayne Johnson, Neve Campbell and Roland Moller. 1 hr., 43 min. PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ hulu/apple tv. Dwayne Johnson in Skyscraper
articles.title: Thrills and chills in Skyscraper

articles.text: A strong turnout of 54 walkers and three K-9 best friends was on hand for a special walk through the center of Piedmont on July 10. Architect and walker Jim Kellogg had agreed to lead the group in another discussion of Piedmont’s early 20th Century architectural development. Before they started off, thanks were given to Lois Price and Sherry Jacobs who organized the group’s participation in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, and the 25 walkers and K-9 who marched. The focus of Jim’s tour was the distinctive architectural character of early Piedmont. He noted that when the city was incorporated in 1907, it was a small community of only 1,700 residents and was thought of as “The Queen of the Hills.” It was a beautiful place to live and included homes with exceptional architectural character that are still appreciated today. The city’s architecture was influenced by many families from around the country who moved to Piedmont in early 1900 and wanted their new homes to recall the style from where they came. The city center provides examples of French Colonial, Victorian, English Tutor, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, Bungalow, and Craftsman styles. than doubled in size to 4,400 residents. During the “Roaring 20s” Piedmont was referred to as “The City of Millionaires” because it had the largest number of millionaire residents per square mile of any city in America. Many of the homes reflected the success of its residents. The planned walk was two miles and would go through parts of the early city center – Bonita, Park Way, Mesa, Highland, upper Oakland, Pacific, and Mountain Avenues. It started at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, which was built in 1926 and designed by Albert Farr, then past the Jesse Wetmore House for a view from the Bonita Avenue side of this beautiful French Colonial house built in 1878. pages.text: Wednesday, July 17, 2024 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers learn more about Piedmont’s architecture By Jim Kellogg A strong turnout of 54 walkers and three K-9 best friends was on hand for a special walk through the center of Piedmont on July 10. Architect and walker Jim Kellogg had agreed to lead the group in another discussion of Piedmont’s early 20th Century architectural development. Before they started off, thanks were given to Lois Price and Sherry Jacobs who organized the group’s participation in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, and the 25 walkers and K-9 who marched. The focus of Jim’s tour was the distinctive architectural character of early Piedmont. He noted that when the city was incorporated in 1907, it was a small community of only 1,700 residents and was thought of as “The Queen of the Hills.” It was a beautiful place to live and included homes with exceptional architectural character that are still appreciated today. The city’s architecture was influenced by many families from around the country who moved to Piedmont in early 1900 and wanted their new homes to recall the style from where they came. The city center provides examples of French Colonial, Victorian, English Tutor, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, Bungalow, and Craftsman styles. By 1920, Piedmont had more than doubled in size to 4,400 residents. During the “Roaring 20s” Piedmont was referred to as “The City of Millionaires” because it had the largest number of millionaire residents per square mile of any city in America. Many of the homes reflected the success of its residents. The planned walk was two miles and would go through parts of the early city center – Bonita, Park Way, Mesa, Highland, upper Oakland, Pacific, and Mountain Avenues. It started at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, which was built in 1926 and designed by Albert Farr, then past the Jesse Wetmore House for a view from the Bonita Avenue side of this beautiful French Colonial house built in 1878. This house was restored by Alice Erskine in the 1940s and listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. The Wetmore House is noted for its colonial wrap-around front porch and beautiful wood “fretwork” detailing. The tour continued on to the Rupert Whitehead House on Bonita Avenue, built in 1907. The group gathered for a photo in front of it and discussed the English Tutor style with unusual detailing which includes a stucco exterior finish and a unique double arched overhang at the front entry. Further up Bonita, the group visited several examples of houses built in a variety of styles. The first was a French-style bungalow with a pair of “oxeye windows” at the corner of Oakland Avenue, then the noteworthy Berkenfeld Victorian built in 1895, with extensive Bavarian style carved wood detailing, and the humble Craftsman shingle-style house built in the same year but with a completely different style than the Berkenfeld Victorian. The group walked to Mesa and stopped at the Lowell Hardy house, built in 1905. This house is an excellent example of Berkeley craftsman shingle-style influenced by Bernard Maybeck. The house includes a complex gable roof, projecting bay windows and sun porch, and handcrafted wood front entry. The next stop was the John Rackliffe house at the corner of Oakland and Highland Avenues, built in 1899. It is a distinctive Queen Anne shingle-style, designed with a steep multi-gable roof, distinctive “Witches Cap Turret,” wrap-around front porch, and whimsical shingle detailing. Many people do not know that an extensive second story addition was added to the house about 10 years ago, designed by Greer Graff. The scale and workmanship of the addition fits perfectly with the original house and received a Piedmont Planning Design Award. The walking group then moved on to the house next door on Oakland Avenue. This is a great example of a mid-century International Style. It was built in 1952 and is completely different from Queen Anne Victorian. The style is quiet, restrained, with an open plan layout focused on a large private backyard atrium. The architectural detailing includes full height expansive glass walls, low-slope hip roof with a raised interior ceiling below and no-frills detailing using natural materials. Which house was more appealing was left up to each member of the group to decide. The final stop on the tour was the Hugh Craig House, built in 1879. It is an excellent example of Victorian Stick Italianate, designed by Charles L. Bugbee who was a partner in San Francisco with his father, S.C. Bugbee. They had many notable clients, including Leland Stanford, Charles Crocker, Richard Tobin, and David Colton. They were the architects for Mills Hall at Mills College. The Hugh Craig House was thought to be Charles L. Bugbee’s last work, because he died in January 1880, just after the Craig House was completed. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Among those participating on July 10 were: Joyce Ahern, Nancy Henn, Albert Chen, Dave DeRoche, Robert Lang, Chuck Oraftik, Lois Price, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Denny McGee, Lee Hambrick, Alicia Rivera, Leila Deacon, Bob Wong, Marion Lim Yankowitz, David Haecker, Dana Shultz, Sharona Fischrup, Jack Fischrup, Gary Meyer, Matt Gerhardt, Peggy Shultz, Charlene Louie, Janet Laurent, Jim Kellogg, Judy Love, Elizabeth Richter, Quincy Dong, Lori Austin, Noemi Alvarado, Mark Davis, Betsy Lim, Helen Dong, Swee Ling Chen, Melba Yee, Paul Silberstein, Karen Glasser, Judy Sokoloff, Mark Laurent, Stella Houston, Adrienne Hamlin, Sherry Jacobs, Bill Ahern, Claudia Bach, Jim Kuo, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper Kathy Rolefson, Ken Hubbert, Joanne Larson, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Avelina Buijs, and Mary Carter. articles.text: Part 2 For the second year in a row, I was delighted to attend the “Taste of Sonoma” event put on by the Sonoma County Vintners Association. Just like last year this was one of the best organized and most impressive wine tastings I have ever attended. Everything was top-notch – the food trucks were amazing and varied – tacos, pizza, paella, BBQ. There were numerous comfortable seating areas where guests could relax under the shade of the trees or tents. The event was held at Kendall-Jackson Winery in Santa Rosa and over 100 wineries filled three giant tents with tables pouring their current vintages. One thing that was evident from this tasting is that Pinot Noir has hit it it big. The grape was everywhere with most regions of the county producing it extensively. Pinot was closely followed by Chardonnay by far the most popular white grape. Throw in some fine Zinfandels, Cabernets and Syrahs and the result was an exceptional and varied day of tasting. The following wines and the ones I will be reviewing in Part Two represent the best of the tasting and even more, represent the best of Sonoma County. • 2021 Fort Ross Pinot Noir The Terraces The mountaintop Fort Ross Vineyard is at 1700 feet elevation overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The Terraces bottling is introduced by a smoky savory nose with notes of plum, black cherry, sage and tobacco. The palate is silky and focused, leading to a bright, delicate, nuanced finish that expands with time. Energetic and delightful out of the gate, this should gain further dimension over the next 8 to 10 years. Very impressive. • 2021 Auteur Pinot Noir Gap’s Crown Vineyard The Auteur Pinot has a nose that is fragrant and perfumed, with aromas of black cherries, lilacs, tobacco and turned earth. Silky, seamless and medium-bodied, the palate explodes with decadent fruit, high-toned acidity and tight, fine-grained tannins. The wine is drinking beautifully now but has the structure to last for 7 or 8 years in the cellar. • 2022 Head High Skin Contact White Wine Made in the “Orange Wine” style of leaving the grape juice in contact with the skins for a period of time to extract more flavor this wine was both unusual and enchanting. It smells of peaches and oranges, and in the mouth it is bursting with melon and citrus fruit flavors. There is good weight and body for a white wine and the finish is long and intense. This wine would be amazing with roast chicken. • 2020 Bederra Malbec Coming from Alexander Valley grapes, the Bedarra Malbec exudes broad-shouldered and focused aromas of juicy plums, violets and baking spices. Full-bodied and rich, the wine reveals flavors of blackberry and cassis on the palate and maintains focus and firmness with pronounced food-friendly tannins delivering a fruit-forward and bold drinking experience. Built to last many years in the cellar. • 2021 Tongue Dancer Chardonnay Bacigalupi Vineyard The wine leads with peach and ginger, spring florals and jasmine. On the palate, it has good acidity with creamy, delicate apple and pear fruit. The wine is balanced and well-structured with a long savory finish. Bonus points for a beautiful and whimsical label. • 2021 Merry Edwards Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast The Sonoma Coast bottling from Merry Edwards has a hightoned, floral nose with aromas of cherries, hibiscus, honeysuckle and fresh herbs. The palate carries this energy forward with a delicate, polished texture and lively, fresh finish with good length and structure. Perfect with a fillet of grilled salmon. • 2021 La Crema Pinot Noir Saralee’s Vineyard The Saralee Pinot opens with a deep, elegant and generous aroma of dark berries and cherries intertwined with oriental spices on the nose. articles.text: Myra Elizabeth Dickson, known as Liz Dickson to friends and colleagues, a well-respected realtor in Piedmont and the surrounding area, passed quietly in her home in Walnut Creek on June 9, 2024. She was 86. Born on December 10, 1938, she grew up in a small farming community with two siblings. As time went on neither of them wanted to continue farming. Liz went on to the University of Iowa and after graduating dreamed of seeing far off places. She became a flight attendant for four years with United Airlines. Jim Dickson saw her picture on the front page of the United Airlines magazine and quickly wanted to meet her. Meeting her went extremely well and six months later he proposed to her. They got married and moved to Oakland. Liz got a job in a well-known travel agency and Jim took a position with his uncle in a real estate business selling land to developers of apartment buildings. They had two boys and as time went on they joined Claremont Country Club for their youth programs and for senior tennis and golf. They enjoyed spending weekends with friends playing golf. Jim started to build apartment buildings and Liz raised their two boys. They lived in a two-story house in Oakland. Liz became interested in having a more fulfilling job and Jim arranged an appointment for Liz to join the Grubb Company, the top real estate firm at that time headed by DJ Grubb. For 30 years Liz enjoyed success as a real estate agent. As time passed and for health Well-respected realtor Liz Dickson died on June 9. reasons, they moved to a one-story home in Rossmoor Village in Walnut Creek. Liz got terminally ill due to chronic pneumonia. Liz lived a good life. She loved to read books, play golf, exercise, take walks and watch sports on tv. She was known as a strongwilled woman. She was so loved by her family and will be greatly missed. Her husband is thankful for almost 62 years of marriage and a beautiful life together and for the enduring love of their family. Jim wishes to thank his son Jay Douglas for assisting his mom with her health issues, and all her caregivers who gave attention to her needs day and night. Exceptional care was provided by John Muir Hospital. She is survived by her husband James Dickson and sons James Jeffrey Dickson and wife Tarasha, and Jay Douglas Dickson and wife Lorena Dickson.

articles.text: Oakland Zoo prepares for moving beloved male African Elephant to Tennessee Osh during a pool day. After 20 years at the Oakland Zoo, Osh is moving to a new home at The Elephant Sanctuary in Tennessee in the fall, allowing him to be with other African elephants. Donna, the last female African elephant at the Zoo moved to the same location last September. The decision to move Osh to the Sanctuary was made after careful consideration and consultation with the AZA’s African Elephant Taxon Advisory Group (TAG). After more than a year of discussions, it was agreed that while difficult and heartbreaking, this was the best decision for the wellbeing of Osh. As an AZA-accredited facility that ensures the same gold standard of care, the availability of other possible social companions, and the decades-long relationship with Oakland Zoo, the Sanctuary provides the most suitable home for Osh for the rest of his life. “Although it’s difficult to say farewell to Osh, we’re filled with joy knowing he’s found a new home at The Sanctuary. He will have the opportunity to socialize and develop relationships with many other elephants over his lifetime. It is something that we could not offer him here. Those of us who know and love him, including our Oakland Zoo community, will miss him terribly,” said Colleen Kinzley, VP of Animal Care, Conservation and Research at the zoo. For the past year, the Zoo has worked with AZA in a nationwide Photos by Melinda Bartlett-Blante search, yet no compatible African elephants in protected care were available now or anytime soon to join Osh at Oakland Zoo. Upon his arrival in Tennessee in the fall Osh will immediately be able to communicate with and smell other elephants. Elephants often communicate using low-frequency vocalizations over many miles. Two new 3,000-square-foot bull barns are under construction for Artie, an African elephant male aged 41, and Osh at The Elephant Sanctuary. Osh will have the opportunity to get to know Artie across fence lines. After settling into the new barns and habitats, and with the care staff at The Sanctuary, Osh will also have the opportunity for introductions to African female elephants. We are hopeful that Osh and Donna will have the opportunity to reunite. Moving Osh, who weighs 15,000 pounds and stands 11 feet 2 inches tall, requires significant time and preparation to ensure his comfort during transit. He will be transported in a specially designed, air-conditioned trailer, providing enough space for the 40-hour journey to Tennessee. In the upcoming months, the Animal Care team at Oakland Zoo will hold voluntary training sessions to prepare Osh for the journey. Members of The Sanctuary’s animal care and veterinary staff will also visit Oakland Zoo to connect with his current staff and begin building their relationships with Osh. The Zoo will also Osh, the 30-year-old African elephant, will be leaving Oakland Zoo for a sanctuary in Tennessee.

Upon his arrival in Tennessee in the fall Osh will immediately be able to communicate with and smell other elephants. Elephants often communicate using low-frequency vocalizations over many miles. After settling into the new barns and habitats, and with the care staff at The Sanctuary, Osh will also have the opportunity for introductions to African female elephants. We are hopeful that Osh and Donna will have the opportunity to reunite. In the upcoming months, the Animal Care team at Oakland Zoo will hold voluntary training sessions to prepare Osh for the journey. Members of The Sanctuary’s animal care and veterinary staff will also visit Oakland Zoo to connect with his current staff and begin building their relationships with Osh. The Zoo will also launch a half-million-dollar campaign to support this transition and its commitment to conservation for one year. With Osh’s departure, the Zoo can explore different options for Osh’s current habitat, including bringing in a new species to take residence. The Zoo must invest significantly in renovating the 35-year-old habitat (including the barn and behind-the-scenes areas) and evaluate the long-term wellbeing of whichever species it commits to. Envisioning a new, state-of-the-art facility will allow the Zoo to provide the highest level of care to any species it chooses to commit to. This endeavor may take at least 18 months to complete. Oakland Zoo has maintained an elephant program for 75 years, which has evolved into and industry leading program. With a 35-year commitment to elephant conservation in the wild and advocating for elephant welfare under human care, the Zoo sees this move as a pivotal moment to reaffirm its commitment to elephants. “Oakland Zoo’s ‘elephant program of the future’ requires much more than our habitat and facilities can provide today for this species to thrive in human care. Our commitment to supporting the success of elephants remains unwavering, although our participation in their success may need to evolve,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Zoo will continue to support its elephant partners who combat poaching, collaborate with communities to launch initiatives that stop the illegal wildlife trade and promote coexistence with this iconic endangered species. Osh has lived at the Oakland Zoo for 20 years. Throughout different stages of life, from field trips to family vacations and engagements, Osh and other African elephants have called the Zoo home and have been a part of Zoo community members’ lives, creating strong bonds with the elephants at Oakland Zoo. The Zoo wants to honor the bonds people have formed with Osh by announcing his move early. This early announcement of his departure provides ample time for those who wish to say goodbye before he moves to Tennessee. Guests are encouraged to visit Osh before he leaves this fall. The Zoo urges guests and followers to submit their Oakland Zoo Elephant Memories by emailing photos and videos of the elephants throughout the years to web@oaklandzoo.org The Zoo is accepting donations for its elephant campaign at www.oaklandzoo.org/elephantfund. articles.text: Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com or visit her website at www.themacmama.com

articles.text: On Wednesday, June 19, fashion-minded Piedmont Seniors got a closeup experience wearing a few couture fashions at the De Young Museum in San Francisco through the use of interactive reality technology. Each of the Seniors simply stepped to a designated spot in front of the gowns, and the gowns magically appeared on them. There were three gowns available: a 1955 gown by Yves Saint Laurent, an evening ensemble with a plunging neckline by San Francisco designer Kaisik Wong and a 1987 print gown by Valentino. This was a rare opportunity for the group to envision themselves in a Valentino or other gowns by famous designers. Even the men in the group enjoyed trying them on. The current exhibition, entitled “Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style,” showcased a variety of gowns by designers including Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, and John Rogers. The collection also includes designs from French couturiers, Japanese avant-garde designers, and other pillars from the fashion industry. The gowns ranged from timeless classics that are perfect for today, to those which were beautiful but more like costumes of a bygone era. Some of the gowns being exhibited have never been on display before. The exhibit includes designer shoes. The gowns are placed at different levels throughout the galleries, which give the exhibit an interesting touch. You can see how fashion evolved, starting from the 1906 earthquake, to the 21st century. There are several “basic black” dresses on display, which are still popular today, and to more formal gowns that could be worn to the San Francisco Opera or Symphony, For an extra touch, the Seniors had an audio tour so they could listen to the stories behind the exquisite gowns and move through the galleries at their own pace. The exhibit will be open to the public through August 11. To complete their outing, the Seniors ventured to the De Young Tower on the 8th floor to enjoy a fabulous panoramic view of San Francisco and the Golden Gate Bridge. And no excursion by the group would be complete without lunch, so the group enjoyed a delicious meal in the De Young Café before heading home. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors and their activities, including monthly meetings or to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: “We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy.” – Joseph Campbel As seniors get older, they may face many challenges in life. Loss of health or loved ones can affect them deeply. While life is filled with ups and downs for all of us and we will not be happy at every moment, it is important to try and help seniors when they are experiencing sadness. Caregivers can play a crucial role in spreading joy to those in their care. Here are four ideas to assist you in bringing happiness to a senior. Encourage the use of assistive devices to maximize independence As people age, they may become less mobile and experience difficulty performing daily tasks. They might not know how to ask for help but there are many products they can use to make their life simpler and more comfortable. Reach out to your healthcare provider for a PT/OT consultation to ensure that you are using the correct devices for your particular needs. If your senior loved one is having a hard time walking, they can use a scooter or walker to help them get around. It may also be helpful to have a shower seat or grab-bars installed in their bathroom, to assist them in safely moving around the room. Seniors experiencing dexterity issues can also utilize products to make their life easier, such as an electric toothbrush. Ask for their stories Just like all of us, older adults want to know that their life has meaning. Ask them to tell you about one of their favorite memories – for example, “What did you enjoy doing most as a kid?” “Did you have a favorite pet when you were growing up?” “What has brought you the most joy in life?” It’s important to listen closely and ask relevant questions as they share details from their life. Many seniors feel like no one remembers them or that they are a burden to their loved ones. You can counteract these feelings by asking to know more about them and their past. They will feel fulfilled in sharing the favorite parts of their life journey with you. Just keep in mind that seniors may not always feel like talking and that’s okay too. Give them a chance to share if they are comfortable but don’t pressure them to have a conversation if they are not in the mood. Find classes that align with their interests Boredom is a very common occurrence amongst older adults. There are lots of classes they can take to help fill their time with enjoyable activities. Here is a list of a few that they can try: Activities for Seniors • Yoga: There are many yoga classes designed specifically for seniors. Yoga can help calm the mind and body, especially yoga exercises that are slow and gentle. Seniors with limited mobility can try doing chair yoga which will allow them to increase strength, f lexibility and breath awareness, all from a seated position. • Painting: Art is an excellent form of self-expression and a great outlet for seniors to share their experiences with the world. Studies have shown that art therapy has many benefits, both physical and mental, for seniors. Picking up a paintbrush can help seniors keep their motor skills sharp and improve hand-eye coordination. The bright, vibrant colors • can boost their mood and help reduce depression or anxiety. Painting can also assist seniors with concentration skills and memory, all while improving confidence and giving them a sense of control. Cooking: There are many cooking classes geared towards seniors which may offer advice regarding specific diets, such as making nutritious meals or meals with low salt content. These classes can be taken in-person which allows seniors to make social connections and establish friendships. Or, for the senior who has a hard time getting out or who prefers to take classes from the comfort of home, there are online options as well. Treat them with compassion When interacting with parents, grandparents and other loved ones, it’s important to remember to speak with compassion. Seniors want to know that their voice matters and that they will be treated with dignity. We should strive to always speak to seniors with care, patience, and respect, being mindful of any physical or mental challenges they are experiencing. If you can do this, you will see that your efforts go a long way in bringing joy to seniors and making them feel appreciated.
