pages.text: Wednesday, July 17, 2024 29 Wisteria Way Continued from page 1 owners’ application for a lot split was approved by way of ministerial approval. There was no public review process for the building design. SB 9 was passed and signed by Governor Newsom in 2021. This bill went into effect on January 1, 2022. Neighbors living nearby have taken issue with this lack of public review, criticizing what they see as a lack of transparency by the City of Piedmont and in particular a distrust of the Piedmont Planning and Building Department and its director Kevin Jackson. Neighbors insist that the project endangers protected wetlands, as defined by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, which should Contractors begin cutting down trees from a wooded area on Wistaria Way. Photo by Diane Prioleau Staff photos Harvey Lederman, a concerned citizen who lives on Wistaria Way, speaks to City Council about possible actions they could take before construction begins. Staff photos Teddy McWilliams, whose family has lived in Piedmont for over 80 years, attended the City Council meeting on Monday, July 15, in opposition to the project on Wistaria Way. Staff photos Resident David Ashton is worried about how the project will affect his property. Staff photos Councilman Tom Ramsey questions City Attorney Michelle Kenyon about whether the City can start notifying residents about SB9 applications. Photo by Diane Prioleau Workers at 77 Wistaria Way took down 14 trees on the first day of construction, according to eyewitnesses. have made the project ineligible for SB9 approval in the first place. The City and the Planning Department claim that there are no wetlands on the lot. A photo with this article shows running water in an area that feeds into Wildwood Creek. “We’re not saying they shouldn’t build. Just that they should build within what’s appropriate for our city,” said David Ashton, who lives downstream from the project. Ashton fears how the new construction will affect his own property. “Our house on Woodland Way backs right up against the property,” he explained. When Ashton became curious about how the project would affect his home, he made a public records request for the developers’ hydrology report of the area. “The report indicated that this project is going to increase runoff to downhill properties by 18%. They have no easement to import wastewater onto any downhill property,” he asserted. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore has said that although the SB9 process is less transparent than what citizens are used to, City Hall is compelled to follow state law. “The Wistaria project is the first SB9 project in the City. SB9 overrides conventional local authority. The ministerial pathway intentionally removes local discretion, public noticing and participation from the equation. It is a major shift away from our approach to design review projects that involve neighborhood notification, engagement and oftentimes, compromise. Conformance with State law is the City’s obligation and we are actively seeking ways to improve community understanding of this new State framework,” she said. Members of the neighborhood voiced their opposition to the project at a City Council meeting on Monday, July 15. Nearly 30 residents attended the heated council meeting. “We’re here because the irreversible destruction of the property at 77 Wistaria Way is scheduled to start tomorrow if you do nothing,” began Harvey Lederman. “We’ve appeared now three times before you. Each time you’ve remained silent. We’ve had no reaction from this council.” Lederman also pushed back against the assertion that City Council’s hands were tied in the matter, adding that under section 54954.2A3 the Brown Act, City Council could direct their staff to suspend construction on Wistaria Way to give them more time to investigate the matter. That is, “if you had the will to do it,” he said. In addition to citizen comments, lawyer Rachel Doughty appeared via Zoom to represent a “group of neighbors who live nearby and in the general vicinity of this project.” “What we’re asking you to do tonight is something within your power,” she affirmed. The residents seemed to receive a show of empathy from Councilman Tom Ramsey, a former member of the Planning Commission, after public comment closed. “Can the city notify neighbors of SB9 applications?” he asked City Attorney Michelle Kenyon, who responded that the notification would serve “no purpose,” but that there is “nothing legally preventing the city from notifying residents about SB9 applications.” A brief set of questions and answers followed between council members Betsy Andersen, Ramsey, Conna McCarthy and Kenyon. Diane Prioleau, who has lived next door to the property since 1968, said she is worried about the precedent the action will set for nature and wildlife in Piedmont. “When they said there’s no creek on the property, I remembered my kids damming the stream when they were little and having a swimming hole,” she laughed. “It is a stream, and it is a creek. However, Prioleau took council members’ questions after the forum as a good sign for their cause. “It means we’re getting too big to be ignored.” For more information about the project on Wistaria Way, contact Planning Director Kevin Jackson in City Hall at 420-3050.

articles.text: The Troop 1 burger stand is a yearly tradition for nearly 30 years. Every Fourth of July, Troop 1 Scouts and their parents volunteer to run the stand. Some Scouts grill the burgers, others wrap them and the younger Scouts take orders from customers and work the registers. This is a good learning experience for the Scouting kids. Some of these Scouts only set foot in the kitchen at their homes to eat (me). Eagle Scouts Tobin and Alexander Cantrill stay busy at the Troop 1 burger stand grill. Scout Ayaan Jajodia cooking burgers. Scouts Sasha Liu and Ciaran Gallagher on July 4th. Scouts Theo Cost, Sammy Donnelly, and Susannah Cantrill helping customers at the Troop 1 Burger Stand. Now they can learn how to cook. Hopefully the burger stand will inspire them to cook more on their own. Scouts working at the Troop 1 burger stand get service hours while also helping the community. Piedmont Grocery has been the principal donor for many years, and The Grubb Co. has quietly helped fund the Scouts’ efforts. The food is also sourced from donations from Trader Joe’s, and Costco. Burgers were sold for $10 each, and this year there were four types – cheeseburger, regular burger, the impossible burger, and the impossible burger with cheese. The menu did not consist only of burgers. They also had watermelon slices and sparkling water. After getting a burger yummy condiments were are on the side of the stand, including lettuce, tomatoes, onions, ketchup, mustard, and pickles. articles.text: There may not have been record breaking attendance at Piedmont’s July 4 parade, but even in the middle of a heat wave, the 57th annual parade still showed why it is one of the best (and oldest) parades in the Bay Area. While the casual observer may have just seen red, white, and blue, subtle changes and adaptations made this year’s parade unlike the previous 56 years. Last year’s parade, 2023, fell on a Tuesday and the parade had a turnout of over 3,500 bystanders and parade entries. This year, a Thursday, saw a high number of parade viewers who were absent apparently all getting a jump on a four-day weekend. Similarly the number of parade entries was noticeably smaller. The presence of excessive heat, with Piedmont temperatures in the 80s, could have also kept parade goers at home just blocks away. For decades, compulsive Piedmonters would place lawn chairs along the parade route as early as 10 days in advance of the parade. Not so this year. True to tradition, some important people led the parade, including Smokey the Bear with Piedmont firefighters, and Piedmont’s police on motorcycles. From there, the fun began with the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band making way for Grand Marshal Gray Cathrall. Grand Marshal Gray Cathrall in Martin Falarski’s 1967 Ford Mustang with Cici Hoover.

articles.text: – David Ashton Imagine that the home next door to you is sold, a developer demolishes the existing structure, and then builds two new homes on the lot. Each home is larger than all other homes on the street, doesn’t conform with city codes, and violates environmental regulations. It seems that shouldn’t be able to happen in Piedmont, right? As it turns out, it can. In December 2023, the city of Piedmont quietly changed the city code, making this scenario possible. In fact, a project very similar to this has just received building permits from the city. A developer from out of the area purchased an empty lot and quietly applied to build two homes on what was once a single-family home lot. These two homes, plus an ADU, appear certainly to fail to comply with numerous city codes, and apparently will be built in a stream setback, likely violating state and city environmental regulations. Residents believe that this project also poses numerous health and safety risks for the community. There are concerns about increased fire risk by nearly doubling the density of homes on a one-way street as narrow as 13 feet wide, which is not up to state fire code standards and is at the top of a wooded canyon. Additionally, there are concerns about hillside stability and streambed erosion given the project’s scope and proximity to the streambed. This new development approval process, called SB9, has been codified by the city of Piedmont to be even more lenient than state standards require. SB9 forces the local city to fast-track multiple family residential development, bypassing the usual public notice and review process. As a result, this project was approved by city planning staff ministerially, and neighbor concerns for health and safety have thus far been dismissed by Piedmont’s’ Planning Department. Lots with certain environmental features are protected by state law and are exempted from fast-tracking under SB9. The lot in issue has such a feature, a stream, in fact one of Piedmont’s protected streams. However, the city has accepted the developer’s assertion that no stream exists, and has ignored evidence presented by the community to the contrary. When city staff were asked if they would consider evidence in order to enable them to work from facts and find the truth, their response was equivocal. If a project which does not qualify for SB9, proceeds under SB9 review without transparency to the community nonetheless, it signals to developers that environmental and safety standards and compliance with even the most basic aspects of city code can be bypassed with little consequence in Piedmont. This is a dangerous precedent to set. articles.text: Major controversy erupts over plans on dead-end street Piedmont City staff members met with a group of concerned neighbors on Friday, July 5, over concerns about a controversial proposed housing project located at 67-77 Wistaria Way. The project, started by property owners Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead, seeks to divide the currently vacant lot at 67-77 Wistaria Way into two parcels where the owners will construct a new home on one parcel and a new home as well as an Auxiliary Dwelling Unit (ADU) on the other. Neighbors close to the project claim that the project fails to meet the law’s site eligibility requirements, lot split requirements, non-compliance with objective standards as well as health and safety concerns of neighbors covered by California’s protective easement statutes. The most serious of these accusations is the assertion that the project endangers protected wetlands, as defined by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and thus should not be eligible for a lot split under state law. The project’s application was approved by the Planning and Building Department on December 27, 2023. Building permits for the project were approved one week ago on July 2, 2024. Neighbors were notified of the construction by mail on Friday, July 5. Construction is expected to begin on Tuesday, July 16. Neighbors close to the project insist that the lot at Wistaria Way meets the state’s criteria of a wetland. They allege that Wildwood Creek and its headwaters traverse this property, a fact they insist is well known to Piedmont residents and public officials, including members of the Planning Department. According to the United States Fish and Wildlife Service, a wetland is defined as “lands transitional between terrestrial Water flowing down Wildwood Creek headwaters during the wet season at 77 Wistaria Way. Neighbors say that the presence of hydrophyte vegetation is a clear indicator of the property’s status as a protected wetland. and aquatic systems where the water table is usually at or near the surface or the land is covered by shallow water.” Additionally, a wetland must have at least one of the following qualities: 1. At least periodically, the land supports predominantly hydrophytes (plants specifically adapted to live in wetlands) 2. The substrate (the surface or material on or from which an organism lives, grows, or obtains its nourishment) is predominantly undrained hydric (wetland) soil 3. The substrate is non-soil and is saturated with water or covered by shallow water at some time during the growing season of each year. Observers of the proposed Wistaria Way project claim that the lot qualifies on all three counts. The City’s first offer to engage with residents on this topic came on Wednesday of last week, July 3, the day of the Piedmont Post’s first article on this topic. A meeting between city staff and concerned neighbors took place on Friday, July 5, in a conference room at City Hall. “We sat down and expressed that it was really important for us that the process and the city comply with state and local law,” said Jeff Olson, a neighbor present at the meeting. “We were clear that we wanted no favorable treatment beyond what would be required in state and local law nor to assert our opinion beyond what would be required by state and local law.” The City disagrees that wetlands exist on the property. According to Kevin Jackson, Director of the Planning Department, a “licensed biologist” hired by the property owners has evaluated the site and has concluded it is not a wetland. Jackson said that his department required an extra investigation from the developers after they received arguments of the neighbors in August 2023. “What we required was the analysis of the site by a professional with expertise in the area. pages.text: Wednesday, July 10, 2024 3 Tensions arise on city’s stance on Wistaria Way project Major controversy erupts over plans on dead-end street By Matt Simons Piedmont City staff members met with a group of concerned neighbors on Friday, July 5, over concerns about a controversial proposed housing project located at 67-77 Wistaria Way. The project, started by property owners Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead, seeks to divide the currently vacant lot at 67-77 Wistaria Way into two parcels where the owners will construct a new home on one parcel and a new home as well as an Auxiliary Dwelling Unit (ADU) on the other. Neighbors close to the project claim that the project fails to meet the law’s site eligibility requirements, lot split requirements, non-compliance with objective standards as well as health and safety concerns of neighbors covered by California’s protective easement statutes. The most serious of these accusations is the assertion that the project endangers protected wetlands, as defined by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and thus should not be eligible for a lot split under state law. The project’s application was approved by the Planning and Building Department on December 27, 2023. Building permits for the project were approved one week ago on July 2, 2024. Neighbors were notified of the construction by mail on Friday, July 5. Construction is expected to begin on Tuesday, July 16. Neighbors close to the project insist that the lot at Wistaria Way meets the state’s criteria of a wetland. They allege that Wildwood Creek and its headwaters traverse this property, a fact they insist is well known to Piedmont residents and public officials, including members of the Planning Department. articles.text: Book celebrates what makes great cartoons great The book Funny Stuff: How Great Cartoonists Make Great Cartoons, co-authored by Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte and former Piedmont resident Rex Hesner, will be released nationally in hardcover this month on July 16. The book is a 135-page exploration of comics and cartoons with a particular emphasis on the art form of the single-panel cartoon. The pages contain over 100 cartoons which the authors use to spark discussions about process, inspiration, art and diversity in the world of cartooning. The book is now available for pre-order online and has already received endorsements from wellknown cartoonists. Witte’s single-panel cartoon FLIP appears weekly in the Piedmont Post. “Funny Stuff is a must-read for cartoon fans who wonder about the strange process of turning life inside-out, twisting and combining unrelated topics and creating a mental story that makes us laugh at ourselves,” said Dan Piraro, creator of the comic strip Bizarro, which appeared for years in the San Francisco Chronicle. “If you only buy Funny Stuff for the 100 great cartoons, you’d be getting your money’s worth. But the real bang for the yuck comes from what cartoonist Phil Witte and cartoon afficionado Rex Hesner have to say about them,” said Bob Mankoff, former cartoon editor of the New Yorker, who suggested the idea for the book to Witte and Hesner. Witte and Hesner were previously the creators of Cartoon Companion, arguably the world’s first website dedicated to reviewing and rating single-panel cartoons. They also produced “AnatLong-time Piedmont resident Phil Witte and former resident Rex Hesner met in the early 2000s but didn’t begin collaborating until 2016. Funny Stuff is currently available for pre-order via Amazon as well as Barnes & Noble and will be available at local bookstores starting July 16. Two book launches are scheduled in the next week and a half. • Book Passage will host a launch party for Funny Stuff at their store in the Ferry Building in San Francisco on Tuesday, July 16 at 5:30 p.m. • A book launch closer to home will be held on Tuesday, July 23 at 7 p.m. at Montclair Presbyterian Church in partnership with A Great Good Place for Books bookstore in Montclair. The authors will be present at both locations to read excerpts from their book as well as sign copies of their book.

He is still learning the ropes, but has mastered basic commands like sit. articles.text: The salon series at Pardee Family Museum in Oakland continues with a talk by author Aleta George this Sunday, July 14 at 4 p.m. It will be held in the Pardee Family Museum gardens at 672 11th Street, Oakland (enter on Castro Street). The lecture and reception is $25 per person. Aleta George writes about the nature, history, and culture of California. She is the author of the award-winning biography “Ina Coolbrith: The Bittersweet Song of California’s First Poet Laureate” and is currently working on a new book about long time valet to Jack London, Yoshimatsu Nakata. Nakata is a primary character in her biography about London’s formative and lifelong relationship with the San Francisco Bay. Nakata kept journals in 1909 and 1914. Her hope is that Nakata’s 1914 diary will help tell the story of London’s last, four-month cruise on the San Francisco Bay less than two years before his death. The lecture will include stories of the history of the Bay Area literati scene and should be interesting, educational and fun. After the talk, a champagne reception will be presented with sweets and savories. Please reserve your seat as soon as possible on Eventbrite or call Richelle Lieberman at 510.381.1973

articles.text: PIEDMONT UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT GENERAL FUND EXPENDITURES 2024-25 BUDGET - PUBLIC HEARING Classified (nonAdmin) Salaries & Benefits 21% In the final school board meeting of the 2023-24 year on June 26, the Piedmont School Board adopted a budget for next year. Two weeks prior, Business Officer Ruth Alahydoian presented the board with a detailed report of the general fund budget and all other budgets associated with the school district. A board background document summarizes the defining features of these budgets. “For [PUSD], the budget is impacted by the three-year [salary] settlements with employee groups, the reductions to staffing, and the increase in enrollment to ensure classes are near capacity. The District will meet the 3% reserve requirement, but will have no other funds available for unexpected or increased costs,” she said. An increase in enrollment of approximately 100 students will help with increased revenue. School districts are funded based on average daily attendance. A steady decline in enrollment for Piedmont is being counteracted by an increase in out of district transfers. “It’s going to adjust,” Alahydoian said of the 2,410 enrollment number. “We are kind of taking as many interdistrict, [and] any students we can, within our existing footprint of classes. So we are not looking to expand [by classes] but looking to utilizing our resources maximally,” said Alahydoain. In addition to the General Fund, the District also maintains eight other funds to track restricted revenues and the associated expenses, such as budgets for the high school cafeteria and student government. In comparison to the district’s budget last year, Alahydoian made candid remarks which bode well for the district’s new Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. “I feel comfortable with all these numbers,” Alahydoian said of the newest budget. “Last year, we kind of took out more than we really felt was right, just to get to the bottom line,” she said of the previous budget. articles.text: Photo by Jonah Pagenhart Sophia Gilbert as Maria in YMTC’s production of The Sound of Music Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) concludes its 19th season with the Rodgers and Hammerstein classic The Sound of Music, running July 19-28 at El Cerrito High School’s Performing Arts Theater. Based on the real-life story of the irrepressible would-be nun Maria and the Von Trapp Family Singers, The Sound of Music is one of the most beloved musicals of all time and has been entertaining and inspiring audiences for over 60 years. The story of love and art prevailing in the face of fear and hatred features music by Richard Rodgers, lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II, and a libretto by Howard Lindsay and Russell Crouse. The show features a cast of 29 student performers and six student creative apprentices from cities all over the Bay Area. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, headed by Co-Directors Jennifer Boesing and Celeste Kamiya, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Pam Crane. The production features a 30-piece live orchestra, including three student orchestra musicians, playing Robert Russell Bennett’s original Broadway orchestrations. Piedmont High School senior Danielle Zaroukian plays the role of Berthe, one of the girls in the Trapp family. The Sound of Music opens Friday July 19. Performances run for two weekends at El Cerrito High School’s Performing Arts Theater, 540 Ashbury Avenue, El Cerrito. The run includes evening performances at 7:30 p.m. on July 19 and 20 and July 26 and 27, and matinees at 2 p.m. on July 21 and 28. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Tickets are $17-$38, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. A talk with local theater artist Becky Potter will be held on Saturday, July 20, at 6:30 pm in the theater lobby. Potter is an expert on Trude Rittmann, a long-time collaborator of Rodgers and Hammerstein, and arranger of the extended vocal sequence in “Do Re Mi.” Piedmont High School senior Danielle Zaroukian.
articles.title: YMTC’s Sound of Music opens July 19

articles.text: Creativity always involves risk. At some point, you have to take the leap and trust that things will work out. Most of us aren’t naturally inclined to enjoy risk; it feels scary and unpredictable. We like to be in control, but creativity requires stepping into the unknown. Creativity means bringing something new into the world. You might have an idea – a cake, a painting, a robot, an app – but you can’t predict the exact outcome. The cake might flop, the painting might change colors, the robot might malfunction, and the app might solve a different problem than intended. You just don’t know. To embark on any creative act, or to encourage your children to be creative, you have to get comfortable with risk and make it a normal part of life. Some of you may remember the days before cell phones? We used to take risks regularly. I recall planning to meet a friend in London during a study abroad program in my twenties. We had one overlapping night and planned to meet in a specific park at lunchtime. With no contact in between – no cell phones, no regular email – we still managed to meet up. articles.text: Instead of eating to live, Malaysians like to flip the script and live to eat. However. most of that eating is done in humble hawker stalls or centers, places that serve cheap, handmade food in a casual setting. Serving favorites such as satay, chicken rice, rojak, roti, and char kway teow, these family-run stalls have earned the honor as being one of the most popular places to grab a quick bite. Prominent in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia, food hawkers earned their name in the early 1800s, called “street peddling hawkers.” Many people who were left unemployed after WWII began hawking to make ends meet, occasionally roping in children to help. Nowadays, Malaysians will argue tirelessly over their favorite stalls, keeping the rich hawker culture alive. Hawker stalls are much more than a place to grab a quick bite – they are a rich pillar of Malaysian culture. Unfortunately, by the 1960’s hawker stalls fell under continuous scrutinization from the government, with unlicensed hawkers seen as nothing more than a nuisance and a source of traffic congestion. The Municipal Health Officer saw hawker stalls as a health hazard due to often unsanitary conditions in which food was prepared. This led to a large number of bowel complications, further leading to diseases or death. When local law enforcement tried Nonya kueh purchased from a hawker stall in Malacca Chicken rice is an addictive local favorite. taking action by forking out fines and imprisoning hawkers for short periods of time, this did nothing to solve the problems; hawkers went right back to business. A more effective solution needed to be taken and In 1967, two multi-story hawker centers (no longer stalls) were constructed, paving the way for a new era of hawkers. A significant upgrade from the dusty carts on the streets, the centers offered more stability and more space for hawkers. One of the tings my family loves to joke about is that “Malaysian food is the best Singaporean street food.” In recent years, Singapore has become a popular foodie destination for their “diverse range of international delicacies.” While Singapore is often noticed for its “unique hawker culture”, Malaysia and other South-East Asian countries also deserve this recognition. As Malaysians continue their passionate debates over their favorite hawker stalls, they not only honor the rich history and cultural significance of these establishments but also ensure their enduring presence in the modern culinary landscape. The evolution of Malay hawker culture from its early origins to the present day serves as a testament to the resilience, adaptability, and creativity of diverse hawkers who have preserved and enriched Malaysia’s culinary tapestry. While inarguably producing delicious food, hawker stalls deserve to be recognized for the backbreaking work behind the stall. Whether it’s waking up at four a.m. to make popiah skin (a spring roll with both cooked and fresh ingredients), or standing over an enormous wok to fry goreng pisang (fried banana) all day every day in Malaysia’s back-breaking heat, hawkers deserve praise for their work ethic and contribution to the very fabric of Malaysia. The moral of the story is when you find yourself in Malaysia, instead of heading to the Banyan Tree, make your way down to Petaling Street. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen that enjoys writing for The Post. She also wishes her brother would share his goreng pisang. A traditional hawker stall, selling wonton soup and noodles

At some point, you have to take the leap and trust that things will work out. Most of us aren’t naturally inclined to enjoy risk; it feels scary and unpredictable. We like to be in control, but creativity requires stepping into the unknown. Creativity means bringing something new into the world. You might have an idea – a cake, a painting, a robot, an app – but you can’t predict the exact outcome. The cake might flop, the painting might change colors, the robot might malfunction, and the app might solve a different problem than intended. You just don’t know. To embark on any creative act, or to encourage your children to be creative, you have to get comfortable with risk and make it a normal part of life. Some of you may remember the days before cell phones? We used to take risks regularly. I recall planning to meet a friend in London during a study abroad program in my twenties. We had one overlapping night and planned to meet in a specific park at lunchtime. With no contact in between – no cell phones, no regular email – we still managed to meet up. It was a huge risk, but back then, we took risks like this all the time. Today, everything is preplanned and controlled. To spark creativity, we need to practice taking risks. Here are some simple ways to get started: 1. Take a Leap: Jump off a diving board, dock, or boat into a pool, lake, or river. Feel the thrill of the jump. 2. Learn a New Skill: Be a beginner at something new— try a sport or new artistic medium and embrace the learning process. 3. Try New Food: Order something unfamiliar at a restaurant or try a recipe with a new fruit or vegetable 4. Speak Your Mind: At your next social gathering, share your thoughts and opinions, even if it feels uncomfortable. The more that you can practice taking these kinds of small actions that feel slightly risky, the more your nervous system will be prepared for the larger risks required to embark on the creative path. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) has returned from a 10-day summer service trip in Lucca, Italy, where the youth-led organization sent 10 Piedmont students and five adult chaperones to serve the local community. While in Italy, crew members volunteered in agricultural co-ops, sewing garments for nonprofit organizations, braiding garlic, and picking rosemary in the fields for prison rehabilitation centers. The service trip took place from Sunday, June 16, to Wednesday, June 26. “I think it was very eye-opening to be able to have this opportunity. I think it inspired how I look at poverty as a whole,” said Samantha Huynh, a youth leader on the trip along with co-leader Olive Reining. Originally, the service trip’s mission looked quite different. “The original plan was for us to be working with a host family to help local migrant workers,” said Reining. Reining has family in Lucca and often spends her summers in the small Italian city. Through her local connections, the Community Service Crew was able to find a suitable organization to partner with: Caritas Internationalis, an outreach division of the Catholic Church with strong ties in Lucca. “Caritas helped us set up many events that let us get to know the community in Lucca and broaden our horizons on what service and poverty means around the world,” said Huynh. Of the group’s activities, the most interesting was surely the days they spent working in local rosemary fields alongside prisoners at the end of their sentences. “It was kind of like a halfway PCSC members meet with their partner organization Caritas on their first day. It’s something the prisoners do as a job and it helps them receive some form of purpose in life again.” Reining said that she particularly enjoyed eating lunch with the prisoners after working together in the fields. “It was fascinating to hear their life stories, how they came to Italy and to just talk to them. They were people with interesting lives. In general, I think food brings people together a lot – especially in Italy,” she remarked. In the evenings, crew members stayed at a pair of modest, three-bedroom apartments on the fringes of town, which they rented. articles.text: Recent Piedmont High graduate Jackson Violich has a chance to represent his country on the main stage. After helping the Oakland Strokes Youth 8 boat finish third at the National Championship in Sarasota, Florida, Violich received an invitation to the U.S. Junior National Team as they train for the 2024 World Rowing Under 19 Championships in St. Catharines, Canada from August 18-25. Violich received invitations for both the Youth 8 and Youth 4 boats. “I was elated. It’s definitely a huge opportunity and something I’ve been working toward for a long time,” Violich said. Violich recently competed in Florida at the U.S. Rowing Junior National Championship against hundreds of other athletes, becoming a member of one of the best teams in the country. “It was such an accomplishment. I’m just super proud of everyone at Oakland Strokes; it’s really been my home. There are so many amazing people and friends I’ve met there. It’s a life-changing program and experience as a rowing coming through Oakland Strokes. It was great to show our speed and the work we’ve been putting in,” Violich said. The World Rowing Championships is one of the most prestigious events in the sport. It includes athletes from all over the world, giving youth rowers at a step above their usual competition on the local scale. “It’s super big. Countries from around the world send their top athletes through their own rigorous selection process. It’s international competition, so it’s a cut above some of the racing I’ve been used to. It’s a huge competition,” Violich said. Getting invited to training Jackson Violich will have a chance to earn a spot on a United States boat for the 2024 World Rowing Under 19 Championships. Jackson Violich, PHS Class of 2024, recently received an invitation to train with the U.S. Junior National Team. meant Jackson turned heads in racing events but also during individual workouts. “I think a lot of it comes down to race results and boat-moving scale. Another contributor is speed on the rowing machine, I think my power to weight ratio is pretty good as a lightweight, so I have a lot of potential to move the boat really well,” Violich described. Violich now travels to Chula Vista in Southern California for the start of training. “We’re looking at rowing as much as possible. We’ll be doing a 20-25k row in the morning, a lifting and core session in the afternoon, and probably more rowing on the machine in the evening,” Violich said. Still looking to bring his rowing talents to a college campus, Violich is taking his time on college decisions. Now earning a U.S. Junior National Team invitation, it’s clear any college would hit a jackpot by winning the sweepstakes for his services. Jackson Violich (second from right) helped Oakland Strokes’ Youth 8 boat take third at the U.S. Rowing Junior National Championship.

articles.text: Tryouts for Piedmont Swim Team, Piedmont’s year round swim team, will take place on August 13-15 at Montclair Swim Club in Oakland. This will be a 3-day tryout, where each swimmer will be given a 30-minute time slot and grouped by age. The expectation is that everyone who tries out will attend all three days. Tryout expectations include the following: Swimmers age 8 and under Swim 25 yards of Freestyle (with side breath) and 25 yards of Backstroke. Legal Breaststroke and Butterfly are not required but are helpful. Swimmers age 9-11 Swim a 50 Freestyle (with side breath), a 50 Backstroke, a 25 Breaststroke (with a legal kick), and a 25 Butterfly with basic stroke mechanics. Swimmers age 12 and older Swim a legal 200 IM with proper breathing mechanics. Swimmers should be able to complete the 200 IM in under 5 minutes. If interested and for more information email joinpst@ piedmontswimteam.org.
articles.title: Piedmont Swim Team tryouts open to all youth in August

Wednesday, July 10, 2024 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 17th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Jack Stein is set to start his junior year at Pomona-Pitzer, whose team won last year’s Div. 3 NCAA cross country championship. He was the Post’s 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year. JACK STEIN Cross County, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2022 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2026 Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, just concluded his sophomore season on Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams. Last November, Stein helped the Sagehens defeat Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159, to claim the Division 3 NCAA National Championship. The former Highlander star finished as Pitzer’s fifth-best runner. His time of 25:49.3 ultimately was what they needed to win the title. He traveled home to Piedmont for Thanksgiving break to run in the 2023 Piedmont Turkey Trot, a 5k street race, and won with a time of 15:30, a course record. In track, Stein closed the season by finishing 50th of 104 in the Occidental Invitational on May 4 with a time of 15:01.20 on a 5k course. He was also seventh of 16 in the 3,000 meter Steeplechase at the 2024 SCIAC Championships on April 27-28. Stein graduated from Piedmont as the school’s all-time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 meters with respective times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. He also won the WACC Cross Country championship with a time of 15:34.76, was second of 144 in the NCS Championship in 15:29.4 and placed 12th of 209 at the CIF Championship, clocking a 15:43.4. What is your workout program this summer? I am currently going into my junior cross country season for Pomona-Pitzer. For distance runners, training is measured in miles. Summer training usually includes a slow build in “weekly mileage” until said runner returns to school in the fall where they will have reached “peak mileage”, a weekly mileage that they can maintain throughout the school year and competition. The characteristics of this are specialized to each runner’s goals, injury history, and physiology. For me, I have slowly been building my mileage with the goal of peaking around 85 miles a week in early August. This mileage is primarily done at “easy pace” or a pace that one could hold a conversation at while running. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goal for this summer is to build what runners call a strong “base”. Fall victories are won on fitness built during the summer, and if you can stay consistent and put in the mileage during the summer, you are setting yourself up for success during the regular season. How are you measuring your development? For distance running, measuring development is easy as you have numbers like weekly mileage and race times to refer to. While this is useful, listening to how my body is feeling is an even better indicator of fitness for me. Numbers are useful, but if relied on too heavily, it can lead to injury. Taking breaks and resting when I feel tired or beat down is super important in ensuring that I don’t burn out on training during the summer. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am currently working with my coach, Emma Delira, to keep in touch about how my training is going. She was recently named USTFCCCA Men’s West Region Outdoor Track & Field Assistant Coach of the Year. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? In fall 2023, I competed at Division 3 Cross Country Nationals and helped win an NCAA National Championship with Pomona-Pitzer. This spring, I set a personal record in the 5k, running 14:26 at the Occidental Distance Carnival. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? As an athlete at PHS, the best piece of advice I received was “consistency is key”, a phrase that my coach Jeanine Holmlund (Coach B) always emphasized. Especially in distance running, if an athlete can be consistent with their training and set goals, they will improve regardless of their starting point or athletic background. Another piece of advice I would give is to have fun; training is so much easier when you don’t make it a chore, so make sure you are enjoying it. Piedmont High Class of 2024 San Diego State Class of 2028 Natalia Martinez recently graduated from Piedmont High and is embarking on her freshman year on San Diego State’s women’s basketball team. We named Martinez The Posts’ Athletes of the Year in 2024 and 2023, becoming our publication’s first-ever candidate to receive back-to-back Athlete of the Year awards. Martinez led the PHS women’s basketball team to a 20-8 overall record and 7-1 league record to split this year’s WACC title with Bishop O’Dowd, marking Piedmont’s second consecutive league banner. PHS received the No. 6 seed in the NCS Open Division and automatically qualified for the D1 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed. Martinez put up record scoring numbers throughout the 2023-24 season, concluding her high school career with 2,272 total points, including the school-record for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28. In a 40-point performance against San Leandro, Natalia also set a school record by scoring 10 3-point shots without missing. Natalia won her second straight WACC Player of the Year award and was elected to the SF Chronicle’s All-Metro first-team for the second time. CalHiSports named her to the second-team Open Division. She is one of Piedmont’s highest scorers of all time alongside Courtney Paris, Ashley Paris, Casey Morris, and Trinity Zamora. She concluded her high school career as a four-year starter and never missed a game since coming to Piedmont in 2020. She received our end-of-year awards in each year of her high school career; winning our 2021 Freshman of the Year, 2022 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Athlete of the Year as a junior. What is your workout program this summer? Here’s my workout program: 5:00 a.m.; individual shooting workout, make 250 shots. 9:00 – 10:20 a.m.; Team workouts. 10:30 – 11:30 a.m.; Weight Lift. 11:35 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.; Recovery stretching/ice baths. 3:00 – 4:00 p.m.; Individual dribbling and finishing workouts. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for this summer are to get stronger and maintaining muscle throughout the season. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development by keeping track of the weight I use every time to squat and bench. Typically each week I try to add a little more weight than the week before. Staff Photos Natalia Martinez was the Posts’ first-ever back-to-back Athlete of the Year award winner. She embarks on her freshman year at San Diego State. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I left to college on June 14 to start team workouts but I still try to find the time to try to get individual workouts and work with one of the school’s trainers. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished is getting my first college practice done. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Find a routine that works for you and stick to it every day. Also, prioritize recovery. JULIEN LEE Cross Country, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2024 Colorado College Class of 2028 Julien Lee, PHS Class of 2024, was a four-year varsity member of the school’s cross country and track teams. He’s set to continue his running career at Colorado College in Colorado Springs. Most recently, Lee wrapped up his track and field season by finishing eighth of 24 in the 3200 at the NCS Meet of Champions in 9:55.89. He recorded a personal record of 9:40.94 in the prestigious Sacramento Meet of Champions earlier in the season, finishing 11th of 24. Last fall Lee finished the NCS Championship 27th of 140 runners in 16:57.2. What is your workout program this summer? I have a program from my college coach detailing running and strength workouts. I’m running six days a week and lift three days a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I’m just trying to have a solid base for cross country in the fall, so I’m focused on slowly increasing my mileage and strength. How are you measuring your development? I’m not measuring any specifics in these workouts, but I’m doing similar work to previous summers so I know I will be where I need to be by the end of the summer. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m getting my workouts from my coach through a spreadsheet but I’m mostly running on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I had a good track season in which I ran 4:29 in the 1600 and 9:40 in the 3200. Since then, I’ve mostly been training but I did run a trail race and. placed third. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Be patient. Whatever sport you participate in, you have a long season and hopefully a long career. It’s easy to get frustrated if you’re not hitting your goals right away, but you have to stay consistent and the results will come eventually. articles.text: Mark Cavendish breaks record for stage wins Photo courtesy of Bicycling.com Tadej Pogačar continues on top with the Yellow Jersey through Stage 10. Reaching the halfway mark of the 2024 Tour de France, twotime champion Tadej Pogačar continues to wear the Yellow Jersey as the leader in the General Classification standings through Stage 10. Pogačar has a 33-second advantage over Remco Evenepoel while back-to-back champion Jonas Vingegaard of Team Visma remains in third place, one minute and 15 seconds back. Aside from Pogačar staying in first, the largest headline of the past week came at the end of Stage 5. Veteran Mark Cavendish, 39, came across the line in first place, marking the 35th stage win of his nearly 20-year career. He broke Eddie Merckx’s 34-year-old record. “I’m in a bit of disbelief. My team took a big gamble letting me come in to try and win one stage. You have to go all in and we’ve done it. We did exactly what we wanted to do, every little detail has been put toward specifically today. We’re not going to be at the top of the rankings, but the Tour de France is bigger than cycling,” Cavendish said following the historic moment. Another bit of exciting news is Walnut Creek native Matteo Jorgenson has entered the top-10 of the general classification standings in 10th place. He’s a teammate of Vingegaard and will likely be pushing the Dane to the finish. It’ll be interesting to see how their team’s strategy develops. This morning, Stage 11 marks a critical day on a 211 km mountain course from Évaux-les-Bains to Le Lioran with six categorized mountains. By the time we return, Le Tour will pass through flat courses in Stages 12-13 of 204 km and 171 km before taking a turn up the Pyrenees to Pau. Stages 14-15 provide 350 km of mountain riding. Stage 14 has three steep climbs, including 19 km up Col du Tourmalet which will have a pair of 9 percent gradient climbs. Stage 15 comes on Bastille Day, July 14 and has five mountain climbs and a 15.8km summit finish up Plateau de Beille. When we return on Wednesday, July 17, things won’t let up with a 177.8 km mountain stage from Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux to SuperDévoluy. It features three consecutive categorized mountains including a summit finish. She should walk in as the favorite, no surprise. Cary also won the 2020 Olympics. In the vault, Biles took silver at the World Championships. Carey took first in the Olympic Trials and will also represent the States. But it’ll be Brazil’s Andrade as the one to watch after winning the 2020 games and the 2023 World Championships. For the men, the United States will be represented by Donnell Whittenburg, who won the U.S. National Championship. In the balance beam, Biles took third at the 2020 Olympics, but took fourth at the Olympic Trials. articles.text: [Updated from August 2021] With the summer in full swing, we delve into our third of five features of trails near Lake Tahoe. This one is about the lengthy but awe-striking Rubicon Trail around Emerald Bay. There is currently a fire near Truckee. The Royal Fire at 168 is about 45 miles away from the Rubicon Trail. Be sure to always be aware of your surroundings and remember your way back to your car. The Rubicon Trail is a 5.9 mile out-and-back (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation gain) trail that stretches around Emerald Bay with a 360-degree view of Fannette Island, enabling hikers to see the historic Vikingsholm mansion through the quant and quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp, with countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. Starting from the parking lot in the Upper Eagle Point Campground, the Rubicon Trail goes 1.6 miles beside Lake Tahoe with before reaching Vikingsholm – a 38-room mansion built in 1929 on the shores of Emerald Bay. It was the summer home of Mrs. Lora Josephine Knight. She inherited her fortune from the passing of her former husband William Henry Moore, whose law firm had controlling interests in United States Steel, Union Pacific, Rock Island Railroad and the National Biscuit Company (later named Nabisco). She was among the primary financial backers of Charles Lindbergh’s trans-Atlantic flight in 1927. Resting on top of Fannette Island is the famous Tea House Knight had constructed when her mansion was finished. The trail continues beside the white sandy beach along Emerald Bay to the northern portion of the Rubicon Trail. It means you’re finally past the exhaustive foot traffic you’re bound to encounter around Vikingsholm. The northern section of the Emerald Bay gives visitors a much more private look of Fannette Island with spots along the shoreline to cool off on a hot day. It leads to the Emerald Bay Boat Camp a mile from the mansion, a secluded $30 per night boat-in campground. Less than a mile from the Emerald Bay Boat Camp entrance is another private unnamed cove with crystal blue water after you The Rubicon Trail walks past the Vikingsholm mansion, created in 1929 by Lora Josephine Knight, who also arranged the construction of her personal Tea House on Fannett Island.

Ups and Downs Continued from page 16 It was only their second time in the parade and first since 2015. They got to show off their prize winning robot, Banshee, as it hurled 12-inch rubber rings on the parade route, then quickly recovered them. “It was fun to see so many kids interacting with 8033’s robot as it tossed rings in the air — catching them and throwing them back down on Highland Ave for Banshee to pick up again,” said Ragones. “We wanted to make our parade entry memorable so we packed a lot in with go-karts, Makey the giant inflatable robot, t-shirt slingshots, LEGO giveaways, and LEGO robots.” The Makers addition to the parade this year was timely considering their meteoric rise in popularity in town in the last decade. And their prize-winning performance at the World Championships. Also new was a large entry by the Oakland Strokes junior rowing program. Piedmont resident and Director of Women’s Rowing Allison Ray organized the rowers for their first entry in the parade. “The kids had a blast and enjoyed passing out flyers, seeing people they knew and greeting the little kids on the parade route,” said Ray. The Strokes’ parade float was one of the tallest, almost scraping the stoplight at Oakland Avenue with a 4-oar scull on top of their trailer. Rowers holding oars with the Stokes’ trademark orange and green colors hung off the trailer every which way to the excitement of the crowd. This week the Strokes took the trailer loaded with boats to Canada for the BC Provincial Championships Regatta. Also changing in identity each year, but not in significance is the Grand Marshal. Cathrall, who has published the town’s only local newspaper for the last 26 years, rode in Martin Falarski’s 1967 Ford Mustang along with Cici Hoover while holding the high honor. articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s next free family day is this Sunday, July 14, in conjunction with the museum’s newest exhibition, “Art of Noise.” The exhibit features over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that marry design and audio. Between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m., families can explore the ways music and visual art come together with interactive art activities. It is a sound-based scavenger hunt, and performances and story time with the San Francisco Public Library. Up to four adults get in free when accompanied by a child. Visit www.sfmoma.org to learn more. Visit SF MOMA this Sunday for a range of family-friendly activities centered around exhibitions currently on view.

articles.text: The 30th annual Sculpture in the Garden is underway at Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek with a range of returning local artists and newcomers. Sculpture in the Garden is the annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural art with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features art installations and sculptures by local craftspeople, ranging in design and materials used. The event also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Sculpture in the Garden is on view through August 11 and is open to the public during regular garden hours. The event is free This year’s Sculpture exhibit at Ruth Bancroft Gardens will feature over a dozen local artists. with regular Garden admission. articles.text: The 11tth annual West Coast Craft Fair will take place on August 24 in the Festival Pavilion at Fort Mason Center in San Francisco. West Coast Craft was founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, which range from simple to craft to fine art and spans a variety of mediums. This year, artists are selling textiles, clothing, shoes, toiletries, jewelry, furniture and woodwork, and homemade libations. It is considered one of the largest of its kind in the country. The free-to-attend outdoor market happens on Saturday, August 24 from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. Refreshments are available for purchase and food trucks will be onsite. articles.text: Festival Napa Valley The iconic symphonic and orchestral Festival Napa Valley is underway, and tickets are still on sale for individual nights through July 21. The summer festival pairs innovative classical, jazz, contemporary, opera, and dance productions with Napa Valley’s unparalleled food and wine scene. “We present dazzling talent on spectacular stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” said Festival President and CEO Richard Walker. “It’s a one-of-a-kind experience and a highlight of the year for guests and artists, both returning and new.” Performances take place on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Ecolab Theatre and Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at CIA at Copia in Napa, Nickel & Nickel in Oakville, and at wineries, resorts, and estates throughout Napa Valley. Now in its 18th season, the festival began on July 6 with a concert by musicians from The Frost School at Festival Napa Valley’s Blackburn Music Academy. The Academy is an immersive summer conservatory for emerging professional instrumentalists in the idyllic setting of Napa Valley, and is led by a distinguished core faculty of musicians from The Frost School of Music at the University of Miami and leading orchestras and institutions. “We welcome locals and visitors to enjoy the best days of summer,” said Robin Baggett, Chairman of the Festival’s Board of Directors. “We are thrilled to provide exceptional programming and food and wine events that showcase the very best of Napa Valley.” Visit ht t ps://festivalnapavalley.org/calendar/festival-live-frost-recital-0706/ for full programming and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Jan Bijvoet in Embrace of the Serpent Know first that Embrace of the Serpent was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language film from Colombia. Written and directed by David Gallego and filmed in black and white, it is set in the heart of Colombia’s Amazon rainforest. Its images are luminous, the scale of its expansive beauty breathtaking. As well, it possesses a depth of melancholy that is unrelenting, for above all it is an allegory. It is also a tribute to the indigenous people of the Amazon whose voices are now silent and whose cultures have vanished like so much mist on the swirling jungle rivers. The film opens in 1909 on a German ethnographer, Theo (based on the diaries of real life explorer Theodor Koch-Grunberg), portrayed by Jan Bijovet. Deathly ill, he convinces a young shaman, Karamakate (Nibio Torres), to take him up river in search of a plant, the yakruna, which is thought to have healing properties. Karamakate is at first reluctant for inside he rages at the rubber barons who have decimated his tribe and the ecosystem of the forest. Theo convinces him that if he will act as their guide he will show him where his people, called the Cohiuano, are, insisting they still exist. Karamakate agrees, and so with Theo’s river Sherpa, the three men begin their journey in a dugout canoe in search of the sacred plant. It is a trip that takes them into Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness. One of the most unsettling moments of the film occurs at a mission where a priest has taken in a group of orphan boys, their parents killed in the rubber plant wars. But Theo finds that the father is physically abusive and regards his charges as pagans, beating them remorselessly. Running parallel to the story of Theo is that of Evan (Brionne Davis), based on the American botanist Richard Evans Schultes, who, using Theo’s diary and sketches, is also in search of the elusive plant, interested in its medicinal properties. The time is 40 years later; and the guide is a now aged Karamakate who agrees

articles.text: Concerts in the old wild West were a popular form of entertainment. One of the most important concert promoters was PT Barnum, a master of ballyhoo. Whether it was the circus or serious music…it didn’t matter to him. Our scene is a dusty frontier town of the old wild West. A cowboy goes into his favorite saloon, expecting to hear some honky-tonk piano and enjoy some liquid refreshment. He goes through the swinging doors and sees a sight that he has never seen before. There are rows of chairs set up theater style. The audience is sedate and dressed in their Sunday best. The cowboy is confused, but he pretends otherwise. He is told that he has to pay for the concert. This is OK with him. The concert is produced by PT Barnum, so it must be a good show, he figures. The first thing that the cowboy sees is a shiny concert grand piano rather than a honky-tonk upright piano. The show appears to be some type of a variety show. There’s an actor who introduces the musical acts. A European opera star, a world famous pianist, and the “world’s greatest violinist.” Sounds really interesting. That was the scene throughout the west from about 1840 until the first world war in 1917. PT Barnum knew how to sell concert music. The other promoters followed the same scheme. Ballyhoo always worked. The earliest music in America from 1500 until 1840 was confined to church music. There were musicales in the homes of wealthy and educated people. Did you know that Benjamin Franklin was a composer and also the inventor of a famous musical instrument of the time? President George Washington and Thomas Jefferson were Composer-pianist Louis Moreau Gottschalk very avid violin players. Both of them hosted regular musical gatherings in their homes. The general public was interested in all of these things, but there was no real concert activity. That changed in about 1840. American concert promoters brought the most famous European musicians to perform in America. In 1836, they tried to get Paganini. It was not possible because Paganini was too ill to travel. But they got his successor, Ole Bull. He was an impressive man to look at. Think of Arnold Schwarzenegger playing the violin. Ole was a brilliant performer. All imported artists catered to the American taste by writing catchy American musical numbers. Sensational stories were the order of the day. One of the greatest stories about Ole Bull tells us that he was having a smoke while on a Mississippi riverboat. A robber came up to Bull, pulled a gun and said, “Give me your money.” Bull calmly looked the robber over and then picked him up and threw him into the Mississippi river. I believe this story is absolutely true. At about the same time that Bull was making musical history, in the United States another violinist came along as a competitor. articles.text: Coco Chanel created a worldwide brand to include haute couture, perfume and simple black dresses. She resided at the apex of a fashion pyramid, her sense of style and elegance unassailable for decades. Born in 1883 as Gabrielle Chanel and raised by nuns in an orphanage, she managed to overcome the prevailing culture of the time that dictated that women must be linked to men as a mistress or a wife if they were to survive. Unattached women, regardless of their intelligence or abilities, if they were without income, found themselves adrift and at the mercy of harsh economic forces. The film Coco Before Chanel follows Chanel from her very early years to that defining moment when a long line of elegantly dressed women walk down a long staircase wearing her designs as those in attendance applaud. While Chanel’s rags to riches story may be of interest to those following fashion, a more general audience will find her story only mildly compelling. To be sure, Audrey Tatou is perfectly cast as Chanel, the ingenue, and later as the very individualistic woman who would become a hugely successful designer. And Benoit Poelvoorde is remarkable as Etienne Balsan, rich, prone to decadent largesse, and the man who takes Chanel into his home on a sprawling horse farm just outside of Paris. The most interesting and complex aspects of Chanel’s story reside with the emergence of her creative vision – from the tentative design of women’s hats, clothing, and later high fashion. Unfortunately, that period of her life is taken up far too close to the end of the film. Just when Chanel begins to explore her passion for style and her completely revolutionary view of women’s fashion, the film ends. For reasons that are not obvious, the filmmakers spend an inordinate amount of time focusing on her relationship with Etienne and later Arthur Capel, portrayed by Alessandro Nivola, an English industrialist. These are two men with whom she was involved, though neither lends much heat to the story. For Chanel, the heat was in her keen eye for innovation and design. She was an artist, but her art is given short shrift; it should have been the essence of Coco Before Chanel. Coco Before Cha ne l , Directed by Anne Fontaine. Starring Audrey Tauto, Benoit Poelvoorde, Marie Gillain and Alessandro Nivola. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Audrey Tautou in Coco Before Chanel
articles.title: Coco Before Chanel – the story of Chanel fashions

articles.text: Princess Mononoke, the magnificent 1997 feature length animated film by Japan’s Studio Ghibli, is an epic story set in Medieval Japan during its ironage period. A world order, so to speak, is in transition: the balance between the forces of nature and those trying to bend the natural world to their own purpose is in conflict. However, animator/ director/storyteller Miyazaki often blurs the lines between good and evil, creating a sense of compelling ambiguity. In this narrative humans, forest animals and nature gods struggle for their share of the changing order. The film opens with a watchtower guard spotting “something wrong in the forest.” Out of this disturbance leaps a remarkable creature, a kind of boar-monster with flesh made of snakes. It attacks the villagers. Riding to their defense comes Ashitaka (Billy Crudup), a young prince of an isolated people. He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try to discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. It is then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. The story includes a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that for many young viewers, Princess Mononoke is not only complex, but one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated films. It may not be accessible or suitable for the little guys. While it is mythical history, to be sure, it also engages, using action and melodrama which will enthrall. The artistry is magical and masterful, qualities that define all of the films of Hayao Miyazaki. Princess Mononoke. Animé by Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Gillian Anderson and Minnie Driver. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2019. Now streaming on prime/Fandango/ MAX/apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Princess Mononoke a magical masterpiece from Studio Ghibli

articles.text: By Chris Honoré Hayao Miyazaki is regarded as one of the most accomplished and award-winning filmmakers in the history of animation. He founded the internationally acclaimed Studio Ghibli in 1985, whose work is revered internationally, most especially in Japan. He won two Academy Awards, and has been the recipient of two nominations, and in 2015 he was awarded a lifetime achievement Oscar. He has also won a BAFTA, A Golden Lion Award for lifetime-achievement, a Kinema Jumpo Award and a Japanese Academy Film Prize. Miyazaki’s filmography is extraordinary and his handdrawn animated films have grossed millions. Princess Mononoke, made in 1999, was outsold at the worldwide box office only by Titanic. Many of his films are considered to be artistic masterpieces while displaying a genius for imaginative storytelling. Born in Tokyo in 1941, he took an early interest in the creation of manga (Japanese comic books and graphic novels) and later animé (Japanese animated shorts and feature films). Miyazaki is today revered in Japan, and coming out of retirement his work continues to be remarkable, as is demonstrated in the recently released, Oscar-winning The Boy and the Heron, now streaming. It will be reviewed in next week’s edition of The Post. Japanese animated film director Hayao Miyazaki, founder of Studio Ghibli
articles.title: The wonderful world of film director Hayao Miyazaki

articles.text: Peter Rabbit is based loosely based on the iconic book by Beatrix Potter. This incarnation is a fast-paced, frenetic comedy starring, of course, Peter (James Corden), dressed in his familiar blue coat, always mischievous, who resides on a bucolic farm in the English countryside. He lives a relatively carefree life along with his siblings Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki) and Cotton-tail (Daisy Ridley). This cohort also includes cousin Benjamin Bunny (Colin Moody) and is looked after by the kindly painter, Bea (Rose Byrn). Meanwhile, the denizens of the warren do clash with farmer McGregor (Sam Neil) whenever they raid his vegetable garden. On one particular veggie raid, with Mr. McGregor in hot pursuit, he unexpectedly collapses and fails to get up. It is, of course an unexpected moment; and it sets in motion the essence of the story. Now, in the absence of old Mr. McG, the clan discovers it has the run of the farm, all happily gorging on rows and rows of vegetables. That is until Mr. McGregor’s great-nephew, Thomas (Domhnall Gleeson), moves from London to take over the farm, rehab the aging cottage, all in preparation for a quick sale. Feeling out of his element, he plans a quick return to the city where he will open a toy store. But Peter, of course, has other plans, and so he and his rabbit tribe set out to obstruct Thomas at every turn, intending to sabotage this city slicker’s efforts. Unexpectedly for Peter and crew, Thomas doesn’t retreat but decides that he’s all-in despite the fact that he doesn’t know a rake from a hoe. And thus begins the rabbit vs. city boy scrum over the rights to feed on the veggie garden whenever they please. As it turns out, it was old man McGregor who had captured Peter’s father and alas turned him into a stew. So with a score to settle, and a carrot in hand, Peter, becomes a committed rebel, leaning into battle against another McGregor. Meanwhile, Thomas confides in Bea, telling her he has a “rabbit problem.” Bea in contrast is on the side of the rabbits insisting they are harmless and just part of the local color. But no matter their viewpoints, Thomas does find Bea to be very charming. And so the story goes, riotous at times, and rarely slowing down. Kids will definitely be entertained. Peter Rabbit. Directed by Will Glick. Live action and with CGI. Voiced by James Corden, Faysai Bazzi, Rose Byrn, Doomhnall Gleeson. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Streaming on Fandango/ptime/apple tv. A scene from Peter Rabbit
articles.title: Peter Rabbit a fast-paced comedy

articles.text: Sunday, July 21, 4 p.m. PCO Sextet Chamber Concert In a lovely homage to early summer, a skilled sextet of Piedmont Chamber Orchestra musicians will perform a concert called Concentric Circles with music for winds and piano spanning three-quarters of a century. Mostly French or French-inspired, the program includes works by Rimsky-Korsakov, Koechlin, Villa-Lobos, Poulenc, and Milhaud, performed by Martha Stoddard, flute; Jan Davis, oboe; Marcelo Meira, clarinet; Adam Williams, bassoon; Alex Stepans, horn; and Stanley Wolfersberger, piano. The variety of music and combinations of players make this a memorable musical experience. It is free; donations are welcome. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up-to-date vaccinations. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.
articles.title: Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts

He has also won a BAFTA, A Golden Lion Award for lifetime-achievement, a Kinema Jumpo Award and a Japanese Academy Film Prize. Miyazaki’s filmography is extraordinary and his handdrawn animated films have grossed millions. Princess Mononoke, made in 1999, was outsold at the worldwide box office only by Titanic. Many of his films are considered to be artistic masterpieces while displaying a genius for imaginative storytelling. Born in Tokyo in 1941, he took an early interest in the creation of manga (Japanese comic books and graphic novels) and later animé (Japanese animated shorts and feature films). Miyazaki is today revered in Japan, and coming out of retirement his work continues to be remarkable, as is demonstrated in the recently released, Oscar-winning The Boy and the Heron, now streaming. It will be reviewed in next week’s edition of The Post. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. It is then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. The story includes a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that for many young viewers, Princess Mononoke is not only complex, but one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated films. It may not be accessible or suitable for the little guys. While it is mythical history, to be sure, it also engages, using action and melodrama which will enthrall. The artistry is magical and masterful, qualities that define all of the films of Hayao Miyazaki. Princess Mononoke. Animé by Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Gillian Anderson and Minnie Driver. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2019. Now streaming on prime/Fandango/ MAX/apple tv. Peter Rabbit a fast-paced comedy By Chris Honoré Peter Rabbit is based loosely based on the iconic book by Beatrix Potter. This incarnation is a fast-paced, frenetic comedy starring, of course, Peter (James Corden), dressed in his familiar blue coat, always mischievous, who resides on a bucolic farm in the English countryside. He lives a relatively carefree life along with his siblings Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki) and Cotton-tail (Daisy Ridley). This cohort also includes cousin Benjamin Bunny (Colin Moody) and is looked after by the kindly painter, Bea (Rose Byrn). Meanwhile, the denizens of the warren do clash with farmer McGregor (Sam Neil) whenever they raid his vegetable garden. On one particular veggie raid, with Mr. McGregor in hot pursuit, he unexpectedly collapses and fails to get up. It is, of course an unexpected moment; and it sets in motion the essence of the story. Now, in the absence of old Mr. McG, the clan discovers it has the run of the farm, all happily gorging on rows and rows of vegetables. That is until Mr. McGregor’s great-nephew, Thomas (Domhnall Gleeson), moves from London to take over the farm, rehab the aging cottage, all in preparation for a quick sale. Feeling out of his element, he plans a quick return to the city where he will open a toy store. But Peter, of course, has other plans, and so he and his rabbit tribe set out to obstruct Thomas at every turn, intending to sabotage this city slicker’s efforts. Unexpectedly for Peter and crew, Thomas doesn’t retreat but decides that he’s all-in despite the fact that he doesn’t know a rake from a hoe. And thus begins the rabbit vs. city boy scrum over the rights to feed on the veggie garden whenever they please. As it turns out, it was old man McGregor who had captured Peter’s father and alas turned him into a stew. So with a score to settle, and a carrot in hand, Peter, becomes a committed rebel, leaning into battle against another McGregor. Meanwhile, Thomas confides in Bea, telling her he has a “rabbit problem.” Bea in contrast is on the side of the rabbits insisting they are harmless and just part of the local color. But no matter their viewpoints, Thomas does find Bea to be very charming. And so the story goes, riotous at times, and rarely slowing down. Kids will definitely be entertained. Peter Rabbit. Directed by Will Glick. Live action and with CGI. Voiced by James Corden, Faysai Bazzi, Rose Byrn, Doomhnall Gleeson. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Streaming on Fandango/ptime/apple tv. articles.text: Dear Abby: You won’t believe it but we saw a scruffy coyote come out of a driveway on our walk last week. It was around 4 pm and the coyote was cruising down Sea View, not the least bit afraid of my big Lab. Fortunately, a woman came by and clapped loudly and the coyote scrammed. Just wanted you and everyone to know. –Cindy and Bad Boy the Lab Dear Cindy and BB: Grrrracious. What’s next? I called Piedmont Animal Services, and they said that because Piedmont is so woodsy, coyotes like it here. They aren’t able to trap coyotes because of Fish & Game’s laws so it’s important to be careful with your cats, dogs, guinea pigs, marmots, parrots or any other creature you love. They did say there’s one coyote that roams around our town that has mange. Be doubly careful around that one. I’ve seen them near Reservoir #2 on Blair and also near Village Market but not in town yet. Animal Services said that coyotes don’t like loud noises or bright lights. They do tend to come out around sunset so consider putting on some lights on the driveway or backyard or any dark areas. Feeling Coyote Ugly (remember that movie?). Thanks for the alert. –Abby Dear Abby: What is up with the locked dog bag dispensers at Crocker Park? The rolls seem to get twisted in the dispenser and you can’t pull them out even if you lift weights. There must be another solution. –Amelia and Tuxe the Golden Doodle Dear Amelia and Tuxe: It seems the City did this so people wouldn’t take entire rolls of bags from our Dispenser Stations but it isn’t working so well. I have definitely wrangled with the dispensers in various parks, including Crocker. At the far end of Bear Park (Crocker) near the intersection of Crocker and Hampton, the bags do come out. However, the dispenser near the Bear statue is impossible. If our lovely City wants owners to use bags, they need to be certain that they’re easy to get. Bag headaches. Thanks for woofing. –Abby If you have any sweet ideas to make our City more animal friendly, please send a note to: Melandogs@gmail.com.
