articles.text: It was a sunny, mild afternoon on July 1 for the First Mondays Reading Group. They met outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park with a good turnout of 19 readers. Phil Witte had been at an event promoting his new book, Funny Stuff, How Great Cartoonists Make Great Cartoons. The group wanted to know more, so Phil told them how the book came to be and about the promotional events that are happening. The group was there to discuss Australian author Jane Harper’s 2016 murder mystery, The Dry. It won numerous international awards, has sold more than one million copies worldwide and was the first book in Harper’s Aaron Falk trilogy. A film adaptation of The Dry was released in January 2021 and was one of the highest grossing Australian film opening weekends ever. The novel tells the story of Australian Federal Police investigator Aaron Falk reluctantly returning to his hometown, the struggling farming community of Kiewarra, for the funeral of his childhood best friend, Luke Hadler. The worst drought in a century has created extreme pressure in the community, and it is shocked when the Hadler family is found dead in their farmhouse. Falk and Luke had shared a teenage secret regarding the death of a young friend 20 years earlier, and Luke’s death threatens to bring it back to the surface. The community suspected Falk then, and he doesn’t want to re-engage the townspeople. However, the circumstances around the Hadlers’ deaths, which appear bogged down some readers. They wanted more sustained action and a better understanding of the characters. The inclusion of the long-ago death of Falk and Luke’s friend seemed unnecessary for them, while other readers felt it was a key element of the story. Some members of the group said they weren’t mystery readers, and they don’t enjoy the formulaic complexity of the genre where lots of different possible motives are floated. The reader has to identify which clues are the keys to solving the murder. Other readers liked the twist in the identification of the murderer, but some found it to be a bit of a stretch. One reader regretted there wasn’t complete justice for all the guilty parties, but maybe that’s the way life is too. The Dry may not have satisfied everyone, but the majority of the readers found it a fun, enjoyable summer read. They also said they like the group’s schedule of alternating fiction and non-fiction books. It has expanded the books they read and their reading enjoyment. The group had previously selected Country Girl by Edna O’Brien for August and The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store by James McBride for September. After Lois Price presented reviews of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell for their October book. The next discussion will be on August 5 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. to be a murder/suicide, force him to stay, investigate, and ultimately solve the murder. Most readers enjoyed Harper’s style and particularly the depth of description she provides. Descriptions of things like flies on rotting corpses certainly provided vivid images for the readers, but this depth of description was also true of Harper’s character development and the story’s setting. The readers agreed the remote geography of Kiewarra and the Australian Outback is a character in the novel. So is the rural, insular, community of Kiewarra’s residents. The draught is central to the story. It is like a vise squeezing the characters and affects what happens. It is a harsh environment in terms of climate, culture, and people. Like Aaron Falk, the group said they wouldn’t want to live in Kiewarra. Some readers did have issues with the book. They found Harper’s storytelling slow and, like Kiewarra, dry. The back and forth of Harper’s flashbacks Participating in the First Monday Reading group last week were Lisa Euphrat, Gerry Gregg, Adrienne Hamlin, Bella Almanzan, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Peggy Shultz, Claudine Bach, Darby Gregg, Phil Witte, Lois Price, Ken Young, Hilary Honore, Melba Yee, Nancy and Mike Henn, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Dick Carter and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus.

articles.text: Part 1 The tasting was hosted by the Sonoma County Vintners Association For the second year in a row I was delighted to attend the “Taste of Sonoma” event put on by the Sonoma County Vintners Association. Just like last year this was one of the best organized, most impressive wine tastings I have ever attended. Everything was top-notch; the food trucks were amazing and varied with tacos, pizza, paella, and BBQ. There were numerous comfortable seating areas where guests could relax under the shade of trees or tents. The event was held at Kendall-Jackson Winery in Santa Rosa and more than 100 wineries filled three giant tents with tables pouring their current vintages. One thing that was evident from this tasting: Pinot Noir has hit it Big. The grape was everywhere with most regions of the county producing it extensively. Pinot was closely followed by Chardonnay, by far the most popular white grape. Throw in some fine Zinfandels, Cabernets and Syrahs and the result was an exceptional and varied day of tasting. The following wines and the ones I will be reviewing in Part Two represent the best of the tasting and represent the best of Sonoma County. • 2021 Siduri Pinot Noir Van der Kamp Vineyard This wine hails from the Sonoma Mountain AVA and the high elevation gives it great acidity and structure. The nose is high-toned, with aromas of cherries, earth and leather. The palate is medium-bodied and grippy, with an upright, sturdy finish perfectly showing off the terroir of this region. • 2022 Croix Estate Pinot Noir West Pyramid Originating in the Russian River Valley and the iconic Westside Road region, this is a big voluptuous Pinot not for the timid. It gives off aromas of red fruits and herbs and in the mouth, it provides a massive blast of luscious plum, cherry and strawberry fruit that lingers on the long, savory finish. Delicious. • 2019 Ramey Cabernet Franc Grown in the Alexander Valley, these Cab Franc grapes show scents of tobacco, blackberries and cassis. It’s full-bodied and firm but silky and ripe with hints of licorice and supple tannins on the lingering finish. Would be great with a grilled ribeye steak. • 2021 Acta Deeds This is a Bordeaux blend of Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Petite Verdot from the Alexander Valley. Scents of raspberries and plums are joined by hints of roses, dried herbs, earth and leather on the nose, while the palate is medium to full-bodied and framed by soft tannins yet with some mouthwatering ripeness on the long finish. • 2021 Brick & Mortar Chardonnay Skin Fermented I am a big fan of the new wave of “orange wines” that ferment the white grape juice along with the skins for an extended period. The color of this wine is truly orange and it leads with peach Food trucks were a bit hit.

The color of this wine is truly orange and it leads with peach Food trucks were a bit hit. The VIP section of the Taste of Sonoma event at Kendall-Jackson winery and ginger, tea and orange peel. On the palate the acidity is piercing but very fine and ensconced within the creamy, delicate fruit. There is white pepper and almonds in the mix of this balanced, pretty wine. • 2021 Limerick Lane Zinfandel Russian River Valley Limerick Lane has long been one of the country’s finest Zinfandel producers and this bottle is no exception. It offers aromas of blueberry, floral perfume and botanical nuances with hints of mushrooms and earth. The palate is medium-bodied with a graceful, delicate texture that shows layers of ripe, floral plummy fruit wrapped in a silky frame of refined tannins. • 2019 Patz & Hall Pinot Noir Jenkins Ranch The Jenkins Ranch Pinot Noir leads with strawberries and blueberries, cherry and cranberry in the mouth, the wine is layered with red berries and shaped by fine silky tannins. It is tight, tangy, light and alluring. Each sip makes you want another one. • 2022 Stressed Vines Pinot Noir Eden Vineyard This winery is based on the notion that stressed vines make the best wines. This bottle is pure, very fine yet intense and clear on the nose, with beautiful cherry and spicy aromas. Very elegant and aromatic on the palate and quite seductive with refreshing tannins this is a complex and layered Pinot that would make a great partner to grilled salmon. • 2023 Pride Mountain Viognier This unique winery sits at the crest of the Mayacamas The Brick & Mortar Winery table Mountains and the vineyards are planted in both Sonoma and Napa Counties. This bottle delivers a boatload of spring flowers, peaches, apricots a hint of lychee and citrus notes. In the mouth the wine is big and viscose and a little oily as Viognier should be. The fruit flavors explode on the tongue and are long lasting. For my money this is the best Viognier this side of Condrieu, France. • 2017 Comstock Cabernet Sauvignon Crafted by the talented winemaker Chris Russi, this wine is brimming with sophisticated aromas of blackberries, licorice, dried spices and earth. It’s full-bodied, packed with rich and concentrated black fruits with a long, velvety finish. While drinking well now, it will improve with time in the cellar. • 2021 Emeritus Vineyards Pinot Noir Hallberg Ranch The Hallberg Ranch Pinot presents a sultry, smooth, terroir-driven profile, offering hints of wild brush alongside juicy cherry accents. The wine features succulent acidity and a fresh, Three big tents contained over 100 winery tables. spicy mouthfeel that will pair well with duck and salmon. It has a clean flinty finish that enhances its food-friendly appeal. • 2022 Mascarin Red Field Blend Angelo Vineyard This intriguing wine is made of 85% Syrah and the rest is a field blend of 8 different grapes from the Loire Valley, including obscure varietals like Romorantin and Pineau d’Aunis. The inclusion of 11% white varietals gives the wine the finesse and aromatic complexity of a fine Cote Rotie. It is opulent with luscious plum and blueberry fruit undergirded by a firm structure with great balance. Crack it open with a hearty beef stew or Provencal daube. • 2019 Gary Farrell Pinot Noir Bacigalupi Vineyard The Gary Farrell Pinot offers a fascinating deep, pure, savory ethereal bouquet of dark berries and cherries. Remarkably pure yet intense on the palate, this is a dense, lush and spicy Pinot with fine tannins and a beautiful tartness on the finish. This elegant, finessed Pinot has great intensity and an opulent mouthfeel.

articles.text: Rita Liston, a longtime resident of Piedmont passed away on June 19, 2024. She was 78. Born on a small farm in Mentor, Ohio on May 16, 1946, she was the youngest child and the only daughter of Anna and Frank Juska. Her two older brothers successfully lobbied their parents to name her Rita after watching a film starring Rita Hayworth. Three years later her family moved to Cleveland where Rita graduated from high school in 1964. She attended Ohio University and received her bachelor’s degree in education in 1968. After teaching in Cleveland for a year, she moved to San Francisco where her two brothers were living. Rita’s first and last job in California was at Corvallis Elementary School in the San Lorenzo School District where she taught for over 30 years. Loved and admired by students, staff and parents, Rita taught with humor, enthusiasm and a genuine concern for every student. After retiring in 2008, she was invited to join two honorary societies for educators: Delta Kappa Gamma and Alpha Delta Kappa. She served as an officer in both organizations. Rita was generous in volunteering her time with numerous charities and was passionate about helping children and people in need. Two charities she was especially devoted to were cuddling premature and drug addicted babies at Alta Bates Hospital, and helping Piedmont Community Church settle the Yosufzai refugee family from Afghanistan. Rita formed a close relationship with the mother, Nargis, and was devoted to the Yosufzai children. Rita continued her friendship and support of the family long after they moved from Oakland. In 2007 Rita met Bob Livsey while playing bridge. They fell in love and became life partners in 2008. They both enjoyed traveling and took many wonderful trips together. One highlight of their travels was attending the Democratic National Convention and dancing at one of the Convention Balls while Barack and Michelle Obama were dancing on stage. One lowlight was a bike and barge trip in France. On one very rainy bike day, Bob, the navigator, took a wrong turn despite being in possession of a map and detailed directions to the next barge stop. Rita finally figured out they were on the wrong road, but getting back on track took over two hours in the dark and driving rain. They were the last bikers to arrive at the barge, exhausted and soaking wet. But Rita Liston, a longtime Piedmont resident, died on June 19 at age 78. after changing her clothes and having a stiff drink, Rita (kind of) forgave Bob. Rita had a great sense of adventure and loved to hike with Bob and her beloved dog Molly. During the Covid years Rita discovered a new way to enjoy the outdoors when she came across a book titled “Secret Stairs of the East Bay.” Rita, Bob and Molly completed all 38 walks described in the book, and then moved on to conquer all 21 walks from the “Berkeley Walks” book. This spring she took on the challenge of “Stairway Walks in San Francisco.” Rita’s favorite walk in San Francisco was the beautiful Moraga Stairway in the Golden Gate district which had a special serendipity for her and Bob. But her all-time favorite walk was always Dracena Park where she walked Molly every day. Rita was an avid bridge player and for many years played in two weekly bridge groups. Many lifelong friendships were made over afternoon bridge games and an occasional glass of wine. She also enjoyed her book group, her yoga group, Motown music, crossword puzzles, jigsaw puzzles, and lunch with friends. Rita is survived by her life partner Bob Livsey, her brother Frank Juska and his wife Candace, nephew Andy Juska and his wife Mary, nephew Gabriel Juska, niece Carrie Juska, and two grandnieces Chancey Juska and Maude Juska. She is also survived by loving members of Bob’s family, Scott Livsey, Rachel Livsey and her husband Jeff, Daniel Livsey and his wife Mary, Ben Livsey, and four grandchildren. A Celebration of Rita’s life will be held on Saturday, July 20, 2024 at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. In lieu of flowers please consider donating to The Sierra Club Foundation, Feeding America or your favorite charity.
articles.title: Rita Liston dies on June 19

articles.text: A heat wave arrived just before the 4th of July. so the inaugural appearance of the Walking on Wednesdays group in the city’s 4th of July Parade was a hot one. A good holiday week turnout of 34 heat-resistant walkers and one K-9 best friend were on hand for the July 3 walk. Jim Kellogg will lead the walk the following week, and will complete his tour of architectural styles in Piedmont that he started last month. It was hot, so the group planned to stay in the central part of Piedmont to preview the parade route and see their Mesa Avenue assemby spot for the parade. This was going to be the 57th Annual Piedmont Parade, but it was noted that residents of El Cerrito Avenue had mini 4th of July parades during the late 1950s and early 1960s. They were under the leadership of Mary Ellen Sherry and Dorothy Carter, Dick Carter’s mother. Dick and current Piedmont Parade Mistress of the Microphone Patty Edmonds were kid participants in them. The walk began with a look at the Police Department in the lower level of the Veterans Memorial Building where construction had started the prior week on a new dispatch center with the demolition of the old one. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers gave the walkers a report saying that he began advocating for a new dispatch center three years ago. The old one was small and inadequate for the city’s current needs. Piedmont voters approved Measure F this March to increase staffing support, and Piedmont’s share of fund from the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 is being used for the construction. The project is scheduled to be completed in March 2025. Walkers were told that the area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Jack London lived there, but before him land developer Frank C. Havens was a resident in the area in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries. The house at the corner was built in 1898 and might have been an early office for Havens. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake inn 1906. After Piedmont became a city in 1907 home construction boomed. These streets were part of Wickham Havens’ (Frank C.’s son) Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development. The walkers went on Highland to Moraga Avenue and up to Mesa Avenue, the deignated assembly area for the group’s parade entry. They continued on Mesa to Pala Avenue, and back to Oakland Avenue for their return to the Exedra. Some walkers continued on a loop on Highland to Sheridan and Caperton Avenues, and to a hidden path to Guilford Road. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join. and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration can be done at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Among those participating with the Walking on Wednesdays group last week were Karin Fetherston, Bob Wong, Peggy Shultz, Jim Kellogg, Ken Hubbert, Chuck Oraftik, Garrett Clifford, Sherry Jacobs (holding the Piedmont Post), Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado, Avelina Buijs, Albert Chen, Bill Ahern, Pat Keller, Claudine Bach, Dave DeRoche, Greg Slatoff, Lori Austin, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Alicia Rivera, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Melba Yee, Eric Behrens, Kat Lang, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Larry Olsen, Elizabeth Richter, Mary Carter, Lois Price, Nancy Olsen, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Kathi Roisen who was walking with them for the first time.

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, July 10, 2024 Obituary Walking on Wednesday Rita Liston dies on June 19 Rita Liston, a longtime resident of Piedmont passed away on June 19, 2024. She was 78. Born on a small farm in Mentor, Ohio on May 16, 1946, she was the youngest child and the only daughter of Anna and Frank Juska. Her two older brothers successfully lobbied their parents to name her Rita after watching a film starring Rita Hayworth. Three years later her family moved to Cleveland where Rita graduated from high school in 1964. She attended Ohio University and received her bachelor’s degree in education in 1968. After teaching in Cleveland for a year, she moved to San Francisco where her two brothers were living. Rita’s first and last job in California was at Corvallis Elementary School in the San Lorenzo School District where she taught for over 30 years. Loved and admired by students, staff and parents, Rita taught with humor, enthusiasm and a genuine concern for every student. After retiring in 2008, she was invited to join two honorary societies for educators: Delta Kappa Gamma and Alpha Delta Kappa. She served as an officer in both organizations. Rita was generous in volunteering her time with numerous charities and was passionate about helping children and people in need. Two charities she was especially devoted to were cuddling premature and drug addicted babies at Alta Bates Hospital, and helping Piedmont Community Church settle the Yosufzai refugee family from Afghanistan. Rita formed a close relationship with the mother, Nargis, and was devoted to the Yosufzai children. Rita continued her friendship and support of the family long after they moved from Oakland. In 2007 Rita met Bob Livsey while playing bridge. They fell in love and became life partners in 2008. They both enjoyed traveling and took many wonderful trips together. One highlight of their travels was attending the Democratic National Convention and dancing at one of the Convention Balls while Barack and Michelle Obama were dancing on stage. One lowlight was a bike and barge trip in France. On one very rainy bike day, Bob, the navigator, took a wrong turn despite being in possession of a map and detailed directions to the next barge stop. Rita finally figured out they were on the wrong road, but getting back on track took over two hours in the dark and driving rain. They were the last bikers to arrive at the barge, exhausted and soaking wet. But Rita Liston, a longtime Piedmont resident, died on June 19 at age 78. after changing her clothes and having a stiff drink, Rita (kind of) forgave Bob. Rita had a great sense of adventure and loved to hike with Bob and her beloved dog Molly. During the Covid years Rita discovered a new way to enjoy the outdoors when she came across a book titled “Secret Stairs of the East Bay.” Rita, Bob and Molly completed all 38 walks described in the book, and then moved on to conquer all 21 walks from the “Berkeley Walks” book. This spring she took on the challenge of “Stairway Walks in San Francisco.” Rita’s favorite walk in San Francisco was the beautiful Moraga Stairway in the Golden Gate district which had a special serendipity for her and Bob. But her all-time favorite walk was always Dracena Park where she walked Molly every day. Rita was an avid bridge player and for many years played in two weekly bridge groups. Many lifelong friendships were made over afternoon bridge games and an occasional glass of wine. She also enjoyed her book group, her yoga group, Motown music, crossword puzzles, jigsaw puzzles, and lunch with friends. Rita is survived by her life partner Bob Livsey, her brother Frank Juska and his wife Candace, nephew Andy Juska and his wife Mary, nephew Gabriel Juska, niece Carrie Juska, and two grandnieces Chancey Juska and Maude Juska. She is also survived by loving members of Bob’s family, Scott Livsey, Rachel Livsey and her husband Jeff, Daniel Livsey and his wife Mary, Ben Livsey, and four grandchildren. A Celebration of Rita’s life will be held on Saturday, July 20, 2024 at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. In lieu of flowers please consider donating to The Sierra Club Foundation, Feeding America or your favorite charity. Wed. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, July 10, 2024 Selling the Best in Rossmoor Selling the Best in Rossmoor PCSC in Italy Continued from page 7 gelato and a nightly gelato run. “I think those were good for the group, not only to understand another culture but to bond with each other on this trip.” The crew also visited some famous travel sites near Lucca, including Cinque Terre (the iconic five seaside villages), the Leaning Tower of Pisa, as well as the nearby Tuscan cities of Siena and San Gimignano. PCSC members also visited the famous art museums of the Uffizi Galleries and the Academia before stopping by the famous Ponte Vecchio arched bridge. “I felt very inspired that our work could make a difference,” said Huynh. “The work that we do here in the States is so different compared to what we were able to do in Italy.” Reining agreed. “I’ve lived here (in Lucca) a lot, but this is the first time I was able to connect with other kids my age here. I think it was really interesting to see how I can help my Italian community by incorporating people from different sides of my life into my service.” The Community Service Crew’s service trip in Italy came on the heels of an earlier 10-day service trip in Medford, Oregon, where crew members spent their time building tiny homes for the houseless community of Southern Oregon, doing trail maintenance work and cooking largescale meals for those in need. The Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-led venturing crew under the Piedmont Scout Council that inspires teenage crew members to actively uplift the broader community through service events. For more information and to learn how you can help or join, visit pcservicecrew.org/new-member and contact crew advisor Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net. Letters sent home from kids at Camp Augusta Another beautiful week with fabulous weather; fabulous campers, so much whimsy and creativity beyond the clinics. We are grateful to have experienced it, and to you for showing it in the Post. The first half of Camp Augusta’s third summer session drew to a close this past weekend. Monday’s August Glade evening program brought campers into a woodland world run by counselor-sized critters. Campers solved See Postcards from Camp on page 28 Oak Four’s Camille doing an aerial silk performance at the Camper Talent Showcase Counselor Danny swapping stories with Cedar campers Sam and Austin at Evening Storytelling Campers enjoying seeing their friends perform at Showcase Lukas and Sawyer admiring their pictures from their Secret Pool scuba diving afternoon. The week was also chock-full of arts & crafts, campers diving into evening games, and getting hands-on learning in clinics. See Postcards from Camp on page 29 Ethan firing away at the mixed skill clinic of Horse Archery Austin happy with his three shot round at Horse Archery Lauren full focus with her clout arrow drawn at Horse Archery

Wednesday, July 10, 2024 29 POSTCARDS FROM CAMP - CONT 2 Postcards from Camp Postcards from Camp Manzi Three and Albert showing off their new puppet masterpieces thanks to Puppet Making clinic Pine Two’s Connor and Ilan entering the level one platform on the brand new Pole Course Continued from page 28 Lathe, blacksmithing, and stained glass were popular this week, with sessions filling up several times. Campers crafted pens and assembled glass, creating pieces from scratch in only a couple of hours. Campers also took time to cool down in Lake Vera on the inflatable Iceberg and with water guns and soaked sponges. Throughout the summer, the Piedmont Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. articles.text: The Fourth of July Parade Committee announced that this year’s Grand Marshal will be Gray Cathrall, Editor and Publisher of the Piedmont Post, the city’s weekly newspaper for 26 years. “He’s the only guy I know who can write 32 pages of news about a town that’s only three square miles,” joked Kathy Kelleher, Chair of the Fourth of July Parade Committee. “Gray is such an amazing part of our community and cares deeply about it. We are thrilled to have him,” said Kelleher. Cathrall found out about his selection in a phone call from Carla Betts, head of the parade committee for the past 23 years. “It was classic Carla Betts.“ he laughed. “She started by telling me, ‘Now, we don’t accept ‘no’ for an answer.’” Fortunately, he was wise enough to accept. “Nobody says no to Carla,” Cathrall explained. The Grand Marshal is an honorary title given each year to a person of significance in the community. Those selected ride in a parade car as part of the Fourth of July Parade festivities and join members of the Fourth of July Committee on the reviewing stand in front of the police station. “I’ve been on the reviewing stand as a photographer of the parade for close to 25 years, so to be to be on the reviewing stand officially is a big change,” said Staff photo Gray Cathrall, Editor and Publisher of the Piedmont Post, has been named Grand Marshal of this year’s Fourth of July parade.

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) will host its annual pancake breakfast tomorrow morning, July 4, from 8:00 - 10:30 a.m., complete with pancakes, sausages, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee for all hungry attendees. Adult tickets are $15 (ages 15+) and youth tickets will be $10 (ages 3-14). Children under three can eat for free. The Pancake Breakfast is a decades-old Fourth of July tradition in the city. The event was hosted by the Piedmont-Montclair Rotary Club for many years ago until it was run by the Piedmont Recreation Department. The Recreation Department passed the tradition on in 2015 to the Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit of Piedmont Scouts uynder the leadership of Ken Li. This will be the PCSC’s sixth year in charge of the event. “One of the really fun things about the breakfast is seeing old friends show up. We often get lots of ‘community vibes’ where people run into their old friends at this event. There’s nothing quite like catching up with people over a nice, hot stack of pancakes,” said Li with a grin. In addition to its popularity, the Pancake Breakfast is one of the PCSC’s largest fundraising events. Every year, crew members sign up to volunteer at the breakfast, set up the dining area, cook, prep-cook (including slicing fruit and making pancake batter), serve food and drinks, keep the dining area clean during operations and finally store the organization’s kitchen supplies until the following year. All proceeds from the pancake breakfast are used by the PCSC to fund their service projects in the coming year, projects that include renovating homes in Oakland, cooking and feeding the food insecure, building tiny houses for the homeless, hosting tutoring sessions at Bridge Academy and building planter boxes at elderly homes. “Now that we’re a few years 4th of July preview. ........... 1 Viewpoint. ...................... 2 Goats are back. ................ 4 Wistaria Way project......... 5 Schools......................... 6 Postcards from Camp . ....... 8 Travels with Daisy .......... 10 PPD Blue...................... 11 Sports. ......................... 12 Theater, Music............... 16 Glass exhibit at PCA......... 18 Movies. ........................ 19 Indie Book List. ............... 21 Piedmont Pantry............. 22 Ace of Spades................ 23 Wine Corner.................. 24 Real Estate. ................... 25 Max Braverman . ............. 27 Classifieds.................... 30 Where in the World.......... 32

articles.text: U.S. Surgeon General’s report What follows below is based on the recently published U.S. Surgeon General Advisory (a public statement that calls the American people’s attention to an urgent public health issue and provides recommendations), and is directed most particularly at parents of children or adolescents. It summarizes, paraphrases, or quotes the most relevant and applicable information from the Advisory, which is available online in full, or as a summary of its main points. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, after an examination of the still ongoing research regarding the impact of social media on children and adolescents, concluded that platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube should come with a warning label stating they are associated with significant mental health harm for children and adolescents. In a sense, the Advisory is a cautionary tale, part of a suggested national dialogue, which informs us that 95% of teenagers, ages 13-17, use social media daily (the average is 3.5 hours), with more than a third saying they use social media “almost constantly.” One in three adolescents report using such sites until midnight or beyond. One-in-four teens spend 5+ hours per day online, and one in seven spend 7+ hours. Onethird or more girls, ages 11-15, say they feel “addicted” to certain social media platforms, and over half of all teenagers indicate it would be “hard to give up.” The Advisory goes on to affirm that research has revealed that there are ample indicators that social media can have a profound risk of harm to the mental health and well-being of children and adolescents during critical stages of their lives. Youth, ages 10-19, are undergoing a highly sensitive period of brain development. This is a stage in life when change, both physically and mentally, is the constant. High risk-taking behaviors reach their peak, and well-being experiences reach their greatest fluctuations. Mental health challenges emerge, such as identity, sense of self-worth, susceptibility to peer pressures, as well as peer opinions and comparisons, impulse control, plus the challenges of moderating social behavior. Teens also experience an increasing sensitivity to social rewards and punishment, thus intensifying their responses to social media. Research has also found that among youth there is a relationship between excessive social media use and poor sleep quality, reduced sleep duration, sleep difficulties and depression. And there is the chilling fact that harmful content continues to be easily accessible by children and adolescents on social media. While platforms can be hubs used for the sharing of ideas, nurturing and sustaining communication with friends and family, they also can possess a dark curtain of anonymity. Social media sites can embody a cartography of predatory behavior and interactions perpetrated by malicious actors whose intent is to target vulnerable young people. Hiding in the darkest corners online are individuals/ adults seeking to exploit or extort risk-taking children and adolescents sexually (using intimate images) or financially. Nearly six out of ten adolescent girls say they have been contacted by strangers in ways that make them feel uncomfortable. Some social media platforms, targeting adolescent girls, show depictions of self-harm acts such as partial asphyxiation, cutting leading to excessive bleeding, suicide pacts, images of disordered eating habits, and ever present is potential tragedy. Some 64% of adolescents are “often” or “sometimes” exposed to hate-based content, and one third of girls of color report exposure to racist language or content. Cyber-bullying has been linked to depression among children and adolescents causing negative social comparisons, especially among girls and sexual minorities (LGBTQ+). Advance float judging will take place on the evening of July 3 for three awards that will be publicly displayed during the parade: Most Artistic, Most Consistent with Theme and Best Spirit. This year, the parade Grand Marshal will be Gray Cathrall, founder 26 years ago of the Piedmont Post, the community’s weekly print newspaper. As is tradition, Cathrall will be featured as a prominent rider near the front of the parade in one of the parade’s dignitary cars. The parade will once again host a diverse lineup of classic cars ranging from turn-of-thecentury model T’s and boxy 1960s Thunderbirds to the sleekThe Art Deco Society rides in their classic car as part of last year’s Fourth of July parade. er-looking Volvos and Jaguars of the mid-90s. “A lot of this is because of the memories,” said Roland Lazzarotto, the parade’s official starter, who stations himself at the corner of Highland Avenue and Park Way dressed in a tuxedo. “People will say, ‘Oh, my dad had one of those’ or ‘Oh, my grandfather had one of those.’ People will remember these cars from their childhood.” Lazzarotto believes that this familiarity lends the event a unique, nostalgic quality. The Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that can claim a single rehearsal during the year, will celebrate its 40th anniversary as part of the city’s 4th of July parade this year. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – who can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led each year by Ken Kawaichi, who has the distinction of being the only person to march the length of the parade route backwards. Parade Committee Chair Kathy Kelleher wanted to give a special thanks to the committee members who volunteered to put on the parade this year. “It takes the entire committee’s hard work and dedication to get the parade to where it is. And we have an amazing committee that I need to thank for that,” she said. In 2020, the parade was canceled because of COVID-19 concerns, and returned in 2022 with a mix of eagerness and cautious hesitancy. This will be the parade’s third year back since it was canceled, and the event is poised to be the parade’s first full-fledged return, according to organizers. The Piedmont Post will provide free programs for all attendees at the parade, with newspaper delivery kids handing out the programs along the parade route. The Highland Cup (left), Highland Saucer and Highland Spoon are presented each year to the best entries in the 4th of July Parade. He comes to the meetings, he has great ideas, and he’s always willing to help,” said Betts. Betts also mentioned that Cathrall’s paper, the Piedmont Post, played an important role in keeping the parade non-commercial year after year. Every year, the newspaper prints announcements about the parade and posts advertisements to attract entrants to the parade, a process she said has helped keep them independent of corporate influence. In addition, the Post produces a glossy 32-page program each year which is handed out free to everyone on the parade route by Piedmont Post delivery kids. Over the years, it has become a staple of celebrating the Fourth of July in Piedmont. “He’s very generous about taking a backseat and not promoting himself. But that’s not going to happen this year,” said Betts emphatically. “This year, he’s the main man.” In addition to creating the city’s weekly paper, he is a founding member of the Piedmont Center of the Arts and for 10 years had a band, Shades of Gray, that played in the local area. The Fourth of July Parade is the city’s largest public event of the year. Planning the event begins in February by the Fourth of July Parade Committee. articles.text: Keeping with tradition, the City of Piedmont has hired a herd of nearly 200 goats to control the weeds in Moraga Canyon ahead of the upcoming fire season. At 6:15 a.m. last Wednesday, June 26, the goats rushed out of their trailer in a flurry of black, white and brown fur as they filed onto the hillside behind the Corporation Yard. The four-legged grazers will be working in this area for approximately two weeks, according to the Piedmont Public Works Department. After their task is complete, the pack of furry lawncare advocates will be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park where they will continue their work. “It is kind of a common practice for managing open spaces, but it’s for good reason. It’s a great practice,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works for the City of Piedmont. Each year, the City of Piedmont competitively bids on the services of these goats in the employ of Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company. “The goats are very much in high demand for the same reasons we like them,” said Gonzales. “They’re very inexpensive. Ecologically, they’re One of the goats takes a break after a long day at work. Photos by Jesse Rosenberg A brown goat from Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company, scales a hill above Coaches Field with his herd. much better for the environment. They also do a lot of the things that you would otherwise have to do with mechanical equipment in areas that are very challenging to get into.” Ecosystem Concepts has set up a trailer where the goat herder will stay for the duration of the work. Additionally, a herding dog will also be present on-site to corral the goats when necessary. The herd’s vegetation-eating efforts are crucial to fire prevention, especially in the hot summer months. In the coming weeks, goats will chew their way through the overgrown brush, weeds and the lower limbs of trees behind the Corporation Yard to create a “fuel break” through which wildfires are less likely to burn. Officials hope that this effort will provide a critical buffer for homes up the hill in the event of a fire. “Our goal is to prevent fire from being able to spread from point A to point B around the City,” explained Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The Fire Department has been working with the Public Works since April to prepare this area for several different vegetation management projects that will mitigate fire risk, including the arrival of the goats. “In this case, we don’t want the uphill travel of fire from a lower area in this topography up to the higher levels where there are residents and houses.” Gonzales estimates that the annual grazing will take between two to three weeks. Residents who want to see the herd are being advised to not park on dry grasses, block traffic or touch the goats. For more information about the goats and where to see them, please contact the Public Works Department at 420-3050. Goats team up to take down a bush.

articles.text: Looking for a mellow, low-maintenance canine companion to brighten up your holiday weekend? Look no further than Tarzan, a chill 48-pound three-year-old Bulldog. Oakland Animal Service staff describe Tarzan as laidback, noting he likes to walk at a leisurely pace. When off leash at dog playdates, Tarzan prefers to stay by the gate and observe rather than cavorting with other dogs. While not overly affectionate, he enjoys pettings and quiet companionship. If you’re looking for a relaxed, easygoing and adorable companion, adopt Tarzan and let his calm presence bring tranquility to your life. Tarzan would do well as an only dog or in a multi-dog home. He is available to meet you this weekend on Friday, Saturday, or Sunday Meet Tarzan, a laid-back threeyear-old Bulldog. between 12 and 3 pm, or by appointment. Put in an application online for faster service. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Tarzan must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

By Matt Simons Keeping with tradition, the City of Piedmont has hired a herd of nearly 200 goats to control the weeds in Moraga Canyon ahead of the upcoming fire season. At 6:15 a.m. last Wednesday, June 26, the goats rushed out of their trailer in a flurry of black, white and brown fur as they filed onto the hillside behind the Corporation Yard. The four-legged grazers will be working in this area for approximately two weeks, according to the Piedmont Public Works Department. After their task is complete, the pack of furry lawncare advocates will be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park where they will continue their work. “It is kind of a common practice for managing open spaces, but it’s for good reason. It’s a great practice,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works for the City of Piedmont. Each year, the City of Piedmont competitively bids on the services of these goats in the employ of Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company. “The goats are very much in high demand for the same reasons we like them,” said Gonzales. “They’re very inexpensive. Ecologically, they’re One of the goats takes a break after a long day at work. Photos by Jesse Rosenberg A brown goat from Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company, scales a hill above Coaches Field with his herd. much better for the environment. They also do a lot of the things that you would otherwise have to do with mechanical equipment in areas that are very challenging to get into.” Ecosystem Concepts has set up a trailer where the goat herder will stay for the duration of the work. Additionally, a herding dog will also be present on-site to corral the goats when necessary. The herd’s vegetation-eating efforts are crucial to fire prevention, especially in the hot summer months. In the coming weeks, goats will chew their way through the overgrown brush, weeds and the lower limbs of trees behind the Corporation Yard to create a “fuel break” through which wildfires are less likely to burn. Officials hope that this effort will provide a critical buffer for homes up the hill in the event of a fire. “Our goal is to prevent fire from being able to spread from point A to point B around the City,” explained Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The Fire Department has been working with the Public Works since April to prepare this area for several different vegetation management projects that will mitigate fire risk, including the arrival of the goats. “In this case, we don’t want the uphill travel of fire from a lower area in this topography up to the higher levels where there are residents and houses.” Gonzales estimates that the annual grazing will take between two to three weeks. Residents who want to see the herd are being advised to not park on dry grasses, block traffic or touch the goats. For more information about the goats and where to see them, please contact the Public Works Department at 420-3050. articles.text: Lawyer representing neighbors receives no response from the city A group of homeowners is questioning the legality of a construction project on their street approved by the City of Piedmont’s Planning and Building Department. The project, located at 67-77 Wistaria Way, seeks to divide the vacant lot into two parcels, and its property owners will construct a new home on each parcel alongside a single auxiliary dwelling unit (ADU) on the property. Citizens residing adjacent to the property are being represented by Piedmont resident and lawyer Kurt Peterson of the law firm Peterson Martin Reynolds LLP. Peterson said he took the case because of the new legal challenge posed by the law related to the project — the California Housing Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act, also known as “SB9” after its designation before signing, “Senate Bill 9.” “I do a fair amount of real A photo of the wetlands located at Wistaria Way which flow into Wildwood Creek. Neighbors are concerned this new housing project could disrupt local flora. estate property work, and this sounded like an interesting legal project,” said Peterson. “SB 9 is a fairly new law. It hasn’t really Water flows down Wildwood Creek during the wet season and under a long-standing permanent bridge on the Wistaria Way property. been tested [...] And so whenever you see a new statutory scheme coming about, lawyers like to try to understand if it really meets the policy objectives that the law was intended to meet. And I don’t think this one does.” SB 9 was passed and signed by Governor Newsom in 2021. This bill went into effect on January 1, 2022. According to the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley, the law aims to address California’s housing crisis by allowing homeowners to divide their lot and construct up to four houses on a single-family parcel. When the legislation was passed, some heralded it as a significant win for zoning reform, paving the way for smallscale homebuilding in previously exclusionary areas. Others worried that the law would encourage speculation and unbridled expansion at the price of the character of the neighborhood and vulnerable residents. In a letter to the city dated August 23, 2023, Peterson outlined a four-pronged argument for why the city should reject the project’s application for a lot split, claiming that the project fails to meet the law’s site eligibility requirements, lot split requirements, non-compliance with objective standards as well as health and safety concerns of neighbors covered by California’s protective easement statutes.
articles.title: Residents challenge legality of project on Wistaria Way

articles.text: On May 16, Dress Best for Less Board Member Nagisa Yamamoto, a new member of the Piedmont Education Foundation board, presented a check for $35,000 to PEF Board as an addition to the $15,000 contribution made last October. “I am honored to be joining the PEF board as the DBFL representative. I am looking forward to working together to support the children of Piedmont,” said Yamamoto. “We are thrilled with this incredible contribution from Dress Best for Less,” said outgoing PEF Board Chair Tonya Antonucci. “This has been an important partnership for over 40 years and we look forward to continuing to strengthen it.” Earlier this year, Chad Olcott, a new member of the PEF Board and owner of Mulberry’s Market, added a Dress Best for Less dropoff bin in front of the store. “Clothing donations had dropped off since the city closed the Carriage House,” said Olcott, “I wanted to make sure Piedmonters could easily keep DBFL well stocked with designer duds.” DBFL volunteers report a significant increase in quality contributions since the drop-off point was installed. DBFL, now located at First Congregational Church, 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland and with a retail store on Piedmont Avenue is a nonprofit whose mission is to support the children of Piedmont, which it does by regularly donating to Piedmont School District. DBFL also supports the Turkey Trot and Wellness Center. DBFL is now located at First Congregational Church, 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, and with a retail store on Piedmont Avenue

articles.text: The popular First Fridays return to Chabot Space & Science Center just in time for summer. Beginning Friday, July 5, from 6 to 10 p.m. Chabot will be transformed on the first Friday of every month into a fun, interactive, science-filled playground for learners and weekend revelers of all ages to come together and discover, dance and dream. First Fridays have become a habit for families with K-12 children and toddlers, a popular date night for singles and couples, and a hangout for friends and colleagues. Visitors can surf through the stars in Chabot’s newly renovated Planetarium, strap in for some seriously exciting hands-on science, and be a part of the most stellar block party in the Galaxy. In addition to a wealth of regular exhibits and things to see and do, First Fridays includes DJs, food and beverages, and is open from 6-10 p.m. Admission is $10 adults, $5 kids/seniors and free for Chabot members. For more information and advance tickets, visit www.ChabotSpace.org. First Fridays at Chabot GLOW This month, First Fridays at Chabot promises a bright and electrifying evening of neon nebulae and glowing galaxies. Visitors will explore the mysteries of the universe through interactive exhibits including the all-new NASA Ames Visitor Center, hands on activities and mesmerizing glowin-the-dark displays revealing the illuminating science behind why things glow. Guests can make and keep DIY glow-in-the-dark jewelry. Adults can enjoy a relaxing experience at Cosmos & Cocktails in the Courtyard.
articles.title: First Friday events return to Chabot

articles.text: A recent Piedmont Middle School graduate, Gracey Ann Hatchell, will return to her old campus this summer to paint a mural with a marine conservation theme. Hatchell described her project to members of the Piedmont School Board on June 26, to get board approval for her project. The mural will meet the requirement for her to earn a Girl Scout Silver Award. Speaking remotely to the school board from Camp Augusta near Nevada City, Hatchell said, “This has been three years in the making, so it feels really good to present it to the board.” The goal of this project is to educate middle schoolers about making sustainable choices regarding the ocean and to promote overall ocean conservation. The mural will bring attention to the website seafoodwatch.com. Some of the criteria for earning a Girls Scout Silver Award are that a project must involve 50 hours of community service and make a lasting difference in the community. “One of the things that came up at the middle school site council was how to beautify the campus, and I think having a mural would fit that bill perfectly,” said A sketch of Hatchell’s mural design containing a shark, an octopus and a dolphin. “Greeting from the woodchips!” Hatchell addressed the school board, while connected to Camp Augusta’s WIFI. board member Cory Smegal. The mural will be located on the first floor of the school. The project is expected to take two weekends to clean and map out the mural, then to paint it onto the wall in layers. Hatchell received coaching from PMS Green Team teacher, John White, and more general support from science teacher, Laura Archer. She received approval from PMS administrators before taking the idea to the school board. “When I was a tiny four-yearold, with a pink bow on my head, I would drag my parents to the Monterey Bay Aquarium to see the Giant Pacific octopus and other creatures that were there,” said Hatchell. “My love of the ocean has very much defined me as a person,” she added.

articles.text: “Look out the window; everything’s different here,” my dad excitedly told me on the drive to my aunt’s house. This line was a favorite of my dad, an avid traveler. Anywhere we went, he encouraged me to look for the differences, and in doing so see what remains the same, what connects us. (Dad, I take credit for that last line but only because you never said it out loud. I’m just informing our audience.) Malaysia is a unique country by many measures, and it’s always incredible to visit, even if I’d rather stuff my face with kueh than pay attention to my surroundings. This time however, I kept my eyes open extra wide, just in case a global pandemic hit again and my next visit wouldn’t be for five years. One thing I noticed more than ever was the nature and atmosphere. Being a Californian, I thought I’d seen some pretty complex ecosystems. Imagine my shock when I saw monkeys playing near my grandfather’s memorial, or when I saw exotic fruits whose names were a mystery casually displayed at a local market, as well as fruits we rarely get treated to in the U.S. Everywhere I turn it is green. The natural beauty is so vibrant, enhanced by nearly 100 inches of rain each year, allowing an abundance of plants and animals to thrive. Coupled with the consistent 80°F heat year round, a trait almost exclusive to the equator, the variety of wildlife in Malaysia is unlike anywhere else in the world. The lush rainforests are home to an unparalleled array of biodiversity and complex ecosystems. From the proboscis monkey – the world’s largest – an almost extinct species that resides mostly in Malaysia, to the Hibiscus, its national flower, Malaysia is brimming with species unlike anything in California. Orchids, one of the most complex flowers in the world, have unique species in Malaysia, in sharp contrast to its four-foot Raffia Arnoli, nicknamed the ‘corpse flower’ due to the fact that besides being the largest flower in the world, it stinks of rotting flesh. Back in Kuala Lumpur, daily wet market vendors unload their goods. From fresh magosteen and custard apples to crisp greens, the wet market is a reflection of the connection to nature. And, who would I be if I didn’t mention the durian, king of fruits? Notoriously smelly and a dividing point between many Malaysians, durian is an integral part of our culture, from the No Durian signs on trains to durian dodol, a gluttonous candy made with the fleshy fruit. Late at night, the large, prickly fruits are bought, then brought home and broken apart with a knife. The fruits crack naturally, and the family swarms to get their hands on the fleshy, fragrant pods that encase large seeds, the aroma holding still in the air for time long after the last stone has been licked clean. Gathering around durian should be a family tradition. There is always an abundance of fresh vegetables at wet markets. In embracing the differences, I not only witnessed the striking contrasts between Malaysia and my home in California but also discovered the underlying threads that connect us all. Adopting my father’s frame of mind as I explored Malaysia not only broadened my horizons but also deepened my appreciation for the diversity of our world. As I carry these memories with me, I am reminded that in embracing the differences, we uncover the profound similarities that unite us all. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen fascinated by the gecko outside of her window. She is a regular contributor with the Piedmont Post. Monkeys play in the grass. Skyscrapers and foliage blend in harmony in Kuala Lumpur, the Capital of Malaysia.

articles.text: Emily Thompson School is out, the days are longer, and (hopefully) we are all enjoying some much-deserved rest. Summer is a time to decompress from the school year but it can also be a great time for academic enrichment. Finding balance is important, and by building some structure into the summer, students can rest and recuperate while also exploring interests, shoring up academic foundations, and preparing for the future. Our top recommendation is to use the summertime to read! Reading has numerous benefits, including increased comprehension, reduced stress levels, more vivid imagination, and higher levels of concentration. Students who already enjoy reading might use the summer to explore new or more challenging material. If reading isn’t your student’s favorite activity, set a small but consistent goal, such as 15 minutes or one chapter per day. Making reading a family activity can also be helpful. Try family reading time, where everyone sits down at the same time and reads a text of their choosing. Or, pick an op-ed for everyone to read and then discuss over dinner. Turning “reading time” into “family time” helps students create a positive association with a task that can feel like a chore. Practicing math over the summer will make the transition back into school smoother. Unlike most other classes, math builds on itself each year. If a student has missed or forgotten concepts, learning new concepts may feel more challenging. Summer is a great time to make sure prior content is secure. Myriad resources exist for practicing math, such as workbooks, online tutorials and drills, and math games. For many high school students, especially rising juniors and seniors, summer is the right time to take on more responsibility and start planning ahead. That may look like a summer job, a volunteer program, or taking some community college classes. Summer is a good time to assess how the SAT or ACT may fit into a student’s college application plan. Rising seniors can use the summer to start work on their college essays, which will help alleviate stress in the fall. If you use your time wisely, the summer can be fun, relaxing, and productive! Ariel is the Director of College Counseling and Emily is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel has worked in undergraduate admissions at both public and private universities. For more information, please visit www.studysmarter.com, email info@studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center celebrated International Asteroid Day on Saturday, June 29, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Chabot and B612 Foundation scheduled a full day of presentations and activities marking the ninth annual event. Featured guests included three NASA astronauts, Rusty Schweickart, Steve Smith and Nicole Stott, who gave illustrated talks and signed books. The astronauts were joined by other experts and scientists, including astronomer and YouTuber Scott Manley and Chabot astronomer Gerald McKeegan. The program aims to highlight the importance and impact of space on Earth and attract a wide audience to learn about asteroids and the science and business of space. Presentations by NASA astronauts and scientists, family activities, photo opp and announcement of the Schweickart Prize mark ninth annual International Asteroid Day observance A schedule of Asteroid Day events and activities may be found at www.ChabotSpace.org. Asteroid Day activities are included with regular Chabot admission and tickets may be purchased in advance at www.ChabotSpace. org. Asteroid Day is a United Nations-sanctioned global awareness campaign participated annually on 30 June, the anniversary of the 1908 Tunguska meteor airburst event. Co-founded in 2014 by astrophysicist and Queen guitarist Dr Brian May, Apollo 9 astronaut Rusty Schweickart, filmmaker Grig Richters, and B612 Foundation President Danica Remy. As part of the day, the B612 Foundation, in partnership with Chabot, will present the first winner of the Schweickart Prize. The winner, alongside astronauts, will receive the prize and a $10,000 check. The Schweickart Prize honors graduate students with innovative ideas and leadership potential in planetary defense fields. Photo courtesy of the B612 Foundation. All Rights Reserved. articles.text: Layth Haddawy with his silver medal at the USPA National Championship in Las Vegas. Piedmont High junior Layth Haddawy continues his ascent as a talented power lifter, recently competing in the United States Powerlifting Association National Championships in Las Vegas on June 24-28. In the Age 16-17 category at 132 pounds, Haddaway finished second of 10 athletes by hitting 309 pounds in the squat, 204 pounds on the bench press, a 419 pound dead lift, and the combined total of 932 pounds. Haddawy last competed in the USPA 2024 Spring Break back in April, increasing his squat 29 pounds, his dead lift nearly 50 pounds, and his combined weight up 73 pounds. “Since then, I’ve been sticking to a similar program. But this time, I was able to shoot my attempts at a higher weight. I was definitely happy to shoot what I wanted to and it was a good learning experience. I wish I could have lifted a higher total. The person who beat me was 11 and a half months older than me,” Haddawy added. The only category Haddawy was unable to improve with his bench press. He thinks the toll of pushing his 132-pound weight limit had something to do with it. Some of the common rigors for athletes like weight-lifters, wrestlers, and those in fighting sports are facing a difficult weight-cut down to a specific target. Leading up to his second official event ever, Haddawy had to drop pounds before weigh-ins. “I think I could’ve increased my total if I didn’t have a super harsh water-cut. On the final day, I had to sweat out two pounds of water the day before,” Haddawy said. He’s now focused on bumping up a weight class to the 148- pound category, giving him an opportunity to build more muscle after dealing with the constraint of competing at 132. “I’m going up a weight category. I haven’t really been able to put on much size over the last couple of months because of having to cut down to 132,” Haddawy said. With the National Championships being the second competitive event of his power lifting career, Haddawy knows he is learning a lot as he continues. “I think one thing that held me back was on my bench was figuring out a consistent technique. I feel my numbers didn’t go up because I got a bit stuck on trying to figure out my technique to a consistent level,” Haddawy. Layth found power lifting after competing on Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team last year. Instead of standing out on the field, he found he was always lifting more weight than his football teammates – leading him to Get Bent Gym in Oakland. “I’ve been lifting for a while, but I began taking powerlifting very seriously in November when the football season ended,” Haddawy said in April. “Throughout my life, I played all the team sports you can think of, but I never was great at any of them. But I realized, especially at football, I wasn’t ever the best guy on the field but I was always the strongest player on the team. I thought, if I’m too undersized for football, I should find something that fits me.” He looks ahead to the Iron Built Games on September 14 in Concord.

articles.text: Now getting through the first week of the 2024 Tour de France, the peloton has a familiar person wearing the Yellow Jersey, Slovenian superstar Tadej Pogačar. In the very first mountain stage of the La Grande Boucle, two-time champion Pogačar won the stage by 35 seconds over Remco Evenepoel to give himself a 45 second advantage over everyone in the General Classification standings. He also picked up an 18-second time bonus. It’s been a difficult opening week for defending champion Jonas Vingegaard of Team Visma, yet he’s still in third place, 50 seconds back. Going into Le Tour, Vingegaard crashed in the Itzulia in April and sustained a punctured lung. Following Stage 2, Vingegaard admitted he expected to lose time in the early part of the tour. “We expected to be 3-0 behind, so maybe that’s a small victory. We came here believing we’d lose time in three of the first four stages, so to lose time on just one is pretty good in my opinion. We thought we might lose two minutes or more, so only 50 seconds behind is quite good. Our time will come,” Vingegaard told reporters. be passing the midway mark. It’s going to be a long stretch for the sprinters before reaching the next mountain classification on Stage 11 on Wednesday, July 10. Stages 5-6 provides a collective 376 km of flat riding, including individual intermediate sprints in each stage, while Stage 7 is another speed-demon Photos courtesy of CyclingWeekly Tadej Pogačar won Stage 4 and catapulted to the top of the General Classification standings. He’s looking to win his third Tour de France. After suffering a punctured lung in April, Jonas Vingegaard is back in action and is in third place day with an individual time trial. Stage 8 continues the sprinting on a 183.4 km flat stage from Semur-en-Auxois to Colombeyles-Deux-Églises, which will feature relentless up-and-down movement with five different categorized climbs – giving the mountain climbers like Vingegaard and Pogačar a chance to pick up seconds. Stage 9 in Troyes is a 199 km hilly stage has four categorized mountains for the Polka Dot jersey, while it will also include 14 gravel-road sections called “White Roads,” making it a possible hazardous section. July 9’s Stage 10 is a 187.3 km flat course from Orléans to Saint-AmandMontrond, including one intermediate sprint. Stage 11 will be a critical day for the climbers with a 211 km mountain course from Évaux-lesBains to Le Lioran. It will have six categorized mountains and a grueling 4,350 meters of elevation gain. articles.text: Perhaps the lasting memory for the U.S. in the 2024 Copa América was manager Gregg Berhalter signaling to his team that Panama and Bolivia, teams in the same group as the U.S., were tied 1-1. Seconds later Uruguay scored to beat the U.S. The CONMEBOL Copa América group stage played out exactly how United States Men’s National Team fans were dreading. After opening the tournament with an expected 2-0 win over Bolivia, the Americans fell apart in a 2-1 loss to Panama, and then closed with an ugly 1-0 loss to No. 15 Uruguay on Monday, July 1. They finished third in the group and out of competition. The United States became the first host nation in Copa América’s 108-year history to get knocked out in the Group Stage. Photo courtesy of Sporting News Is it time to turn the page on United States manager Gregg Berhalter? Against Panama, the U.S. entered as the undoubted favorite but a red card on Tim Weah in the 18th minute was the start of the letdown. Although Folarin Balogun scored to put the U.S. ahead in the 22nd minute, they conceded to Cesar Blackman just four minutes later. Panama finished the night with a dominant 74 percent of possession, notching 13 shot attempts to the States’ six. While one man down, the Stars and Stripes never figured out a way to deal with the disadvantage. It led to a do-or-die game on Monday with Uruguay. With everything on the line, the United States continued its lackluster ways with just three shots going on target for a second-consecutive game. Mathias Olivera’s game-winning goal in the 66th was a questionable non-offside call, but it wouldn’t have mattered. With Panama beating Bolivia 3-1, the United States would have needed three goals to achieve second place in Group C. Perhaps the most embarrassing moment was manager Gregg Berhalter signaling to his team that Bolivia and Panama were tied 1-1—meaning the U.S. briefly held second-place. But just seconds after the camera cut away from Berhalter, Olivera put in the winner. The United States’ inability to win big games and get out of Group C was a strong indictment on Berhalter and the roster dubbed, “the Golden Generation.” The question remains: Is the problem the U.S. coaching leadership, or is it a lineup that has failed to take the next step with its development. Aside from being successful in their confederation’s tournaments, like the CONCACAF Nations League and Gold Cup, the United States has routinely struggled to pull off wins against teams outside its confederation. In the 2022 World Cup, the U.S. drew 1-1 with Wales and tied England 0-0 before getting dominated 3-1 by the Netherlands in the Round of 16. It was a tournament marred with controversy after Gio Reyna was benched, leading to a rift in the locker room. Despite the situation with Reyna, the United States Soccer Federation elected to extend Berhalter’s contract as head coach. The goal since the World Cup was to show improvement with a roster filled with talent playing in Europe, like Christian Pulisic, Tyler Adams, Gio Reyna, Weston McKennie, and Tim Weah, But

articles.text: This spring, I went to the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation umpire training. It was 3 hours long! It taught how to become an umpire. For example it taught where to be when you make a call, what the calls look like and how to manage a baseball game. PBSF is the Piedmont baseball and softball little league. A little league is a league for youth baseball and softball players. PBSF also brings more youth into their baseball and softball games, umpires. Umpires are like referees for baseball and softball. Now, PBSF has made it so kids as young as 10 can umpire the age division below them. After the training I soon got to umpire my first baseball game (I only umpire baseball) . It was very fun making the calls, like if a runner made it to first base in time or not in time. At the time of publishing I have umpired 4 games. Umpiring has its upside and downside. An upside is that you make money. $30 is not that much for adults but, for kids that is a lot. Plus, it is a great way to make friends. The other umpires that you work with normally are pretty similar to you. It’s a great way to join the baseball community. Also, your decisions stand and the players have to follow it. So you do not have to argue, which saves you a lot of effort. The downside is that umpiring is pretty exhausting. You have to stand for 90 minutes and you have to pay attention for 90 minutes. Also, sometimes the coaches and players get mad at you. One reason they get mad at you is when they think you called something wrong. Another reason they get mad is when a rule is broken and the coach and players don’t know that rule. They get mad because they think what just happened is normal and you called it out or safe differently then normal. Overall, I think umpiring is an awesome experience. It is so fun. I would recommend umpiring if you are a sporty kid who wants to make some money. Jonah Kerr is a 5th grader at Havens Elementary School.
articles.title: Baseball umpiring a great Piedmont sporty kid job

articles.text: Our second of five features of trails around Lake Tahoe continues with the Five Lakes Trail in Olympic Valley near Alpine Meadows on the northern side of Lake Tahoe. Some back country hikers will try to get to this location quickly in the morning to camp out next to three swimmable lakes. You’ll require just over an hour worth of hiking to reach one of the most picturesque dayhikes in California. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.8 mile hike in total and provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain in Tahoe National Forest’s Granite Chief Wilderness. It’s a good location to get accustomed with hiking in high elevation. Our day starts at 6,450 feet of altitude, topping out at near 7,600 feet. It also connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Washeshu mountain peaks. To your left will be views of the pine-treed strewed mountains of Scott Peak and the mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak. This location is surrounded by resorts and the tourist towns of Truckee, Tahoe City, Kings Beach and other North Lake Tahoe destinations, so the hike can be a traffic jam. We passed 105 other hikers in the trek toward the summit and another 51 on the way back to the car. You’ll to have patience while passing others. . Long portions of the trail are less than six-feet wide, requiring you to step aside for groups. I passed at least three groups of 10 or more people and many families. Faster hikers may find themselves behind slower traffic without a clear pathway around. But at the summit, a group of five alpine lakes awaiting. Despite the foot traffic, you can easily find your own area on one of the three swimmable lakes. This lake is more marshy but equally as picturesque. Another of the three swimmable lakes You’ll pass under a tramway toward the summit of KT-22 Mountain peak

articles.text: By Allyson Aleksey Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Lifespan of a Fact, written by Jeremy Kareken, David Murrel and Gordon Ferrell, will be performed through July 21. The critically acclaimed 2018 Broadway play follows the demanding and high-stakes world of publishing. Magazine editor Emily Penrose hires a young, determined fact-checker named Jim Fingal to work on a groundbreaking essay written by the famous author John D’Agata. Based on the true story of D’Agata’s essay What Happens There, the show blurs the lines between fact and fiction as young reporter Jim finds that the the legendary essayist bends the truth in his own writing. The cast includes Hernán Angulo as Jim and Carrie Paff as Emily. The production is directed by Jessica Holt in her Aurora Theatre directing debut Post-show discussions of Aurora’s production of Lifespan of a Fact will be led by Aurora staff and members of the creative team, joined by the actors on July 2, 10 and 18. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024-season/the-lifespan-of-a-fact. articles.text: Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 21, marking the 55th anniversary of the iconic outdoor music festival along Highway 4. All concerts are tucked inside a large tent that holds 500 guests in the outdoor wonderland of Bear Valley, California. The festival features an eclectic variety of music from 80’s tribute bands to classic Jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy. We’ve been doing it for 55 years and are excited to celebrate that milestone this summer. From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone,” said Board of Directors president Julia Mee. Music Director Alexander Mickelthwate returns for his second year. The British band English Beat will open the festival with an energetic mix of musical styles, fronted by showman Dave Wakeling. English Beat fuses Latin, ska, pop, soul, reggae and punk rock and released three studio albums in the early 1980s, including I Just Can’t Stop It (1980), Wha’ppen? (1981) and Special Beat Service (1982), as well as a string of singles, including “Mirror in the Bathroom”, “Save It for Later”, “I Confess”, “Too Nice to Talk To”, “Can’t Get Used to Losing You“ and “Hands Off...She’s Mine.” Opening weekend will also include Steel ’n’ Chicago, a tribute to both Steely Dan and Chicago, and Deja Vu, a tribute to Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young. The Laurence Hobgood Trio, a Jazz ensemble, performs on Wednesday, July 26. The festival runs through Sunday, August 6. For the full festival lineup and tickets. visit www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org.
articles.title: Bear Valley Music Festival opens July 21

articles.text: Organist Jonathan Dimmock performs every Saturday at the Legion of Honor. Visit the Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturday afternoons and enjoy a free organ concert by Jonathan Dimmock or Angela Kraft Cross. Residents of all nine Bay Area counties, including Alameda, receive free admission to Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturdays. Visit the museum during operating hours and view its permanent collection galleries. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. Included with free admission is an organ concert every Saturday at 4 p.m. Dimmock is a graduate of Oberlin and Yale, and the first American to hold the prestigious position of organ scholar of Westminster Abbey. He was resident organist at St. John the Divine in New York City, St. Mark’s in Minneapolis, and Grace Cathedral in San Francisco. Dimmock is principal organist at the Legion of Honor, organist for the San Francisco Symphony, and director of music at Congregation Sherith Israel. He has recorded a Grammy-winning record with the San Francisco Symphony. Cross is a local organist, pianist and composer.
