articles.text: Review by Paul Hertelendy In writing a symphony, composers are like architects designing a new city. But not Gustav Mahler. In his Symphony No. 3 he created a musical metropolis of 100 minutes, running the length of two or three others’ symphonies. The oversize orchestra, with doubled winds and harps, a paired set of timpani within a seven-member augmented percussion group, plus singers, add up to a bulging score more like four symphonies in one. The extravagance was unprecedented, with no regard for production costs. At the end, like the cherry on the sundae, three percussionists haul out oversize cymbals two feet in diameter for a single, colossal crash. Created mostly in summer “holidays” of 1895-96, the work had Mahler in an unparalleled burst of inspiration, wherein parts of the resultant score actually had to be siphoned off to enter his next (fourth) symphony. Holed up in a small summer cabin by the Salzburg-region’s lakes, Mahler required absolute silence, with helpers chasing away birds and noisy children. Mahler’s musical metropolis was above all pastoral, with subtitles alluding to summer, flowers, animals, love, even angels. And yet the five-movement opus is bursting with passion and drama, even providing funeral marches. The emotional extremes of late romanticism were never more expansively spelled out. I’d propose that Mahler was consciously or unconsciously also plumbing human emotions in their many extremes, so artfully alluded to in his orchestra and singers. Why else, in Part I alone, San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen the sequence of assertive horns, funeral march, sunny trombone solo, dissonance, upbeat march (a la ”Star Wars”), total exuberance, tempo shifts, and a murky, pensive transition toward marches both depressing and upbeat? For this grandest of season finales however, it finished with sheer bliss June 28, Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen dashing upstage and hugging his soloists on trumpet (Aaron Schuman) and trombone (Timothy Higgins), who both came through splendiferously. The trumpeter had a dual role, also playing a cornet offstage to simulate the post horn. Part Two is a four-movement smorgasbord. It ranged from the mezzo Kelley O’Connor’s interpretation of an ultra-soft Nietzsche midnight poem to an exuberant 50-member women’s and youth chorus, combined, for the crowning Angels’ Song. By then, if the Gates of Heaven don’t actually open up, at the very least Mahler had completed his biggest composition ever, presumably heralding enough income to pay for those bucolic and inspiring lakeside summers near Salzburg. MUSIC NOTES The financial plight of the debt-ravaged SF Symphony, had the musicians once again leafletting patrons as they arrived. While voicing their strong support of Salonen, hoping that he will delay his announced 2025 departure, they also deplore the program cutbacks at SFS, done to reduce the growing deficits. The SFS debts, prompting Salonen’s 2025 departure, has gotten media attention as far away as New York City….The oddity of conductor Salonen’s sitting down for a five-minute break between parts one and two were not due to fatigue, but rather a specification in the score – perhaps more motivated for the perspiring musicians than the conductor. S.F. SYMPHONY and choruses under Salonen in Symphony No. 3 of Mahler June 28-30, Davies Hall, San Francisco. SFS season finale. For SFS info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www. sfsymphony.org .

From July 19 to August 10, Music@Menlo’s 22nd season celebrates French chamber music and its impact across the globe, featuring 44 artists including 13 festival debuts and music spanning 300 years. articles.text: Marion Cotillard and Owen Wilson in Midnight in Paris Woody Allen is a serial monogamist when it comes to world-class cities. He fell in love with New York, then London, briefly Spain, and now Paris. Ah, Paris. Allen caresses its wide boulevards and avenues, reveals skylines under a startling blue sky, captures the wide sidewalks, damp from rain, the busy outdoor cafes, the lovely restaurants and grand lobbies of hotels. From the first frame of Midnight in Paris, photographed by the gifted cinematographer Darius Khondji, Allen gives the city of lights a lingering embrace that ripples throughout the film. Gil Pender (Owen Wilson) and his fiancée, Inez (Rachel McAdams), have joined her parents (Kurt Fuller and Mimi Kennedy) in Paris. Gil is enchanted by the city, wants to walk the streets in the rain – especially the rain – and waxes nostalgic about what he believes were the glorious 1920s, the golden age when writers and artists, known as the Lost Generation, took up residence. A screenwriter in Hollywood, Gil tells Inez that he would love to move to Paris, find inspiration, and work on his novel – his protagonist owns a nostalgia shop filled with memorabilia. Inez, a lovely, mercenary young woman with the heart of a philistine, doesn’t grasp anything that Gil is attempting to convey, nor do her suspicious, judgmental parents. So instead of spending time going to clubs with Inez, he wanders the streets of Paris into the midnight hours. And it’s on one such late night peregrination, feeling lost, literally and figuratively, that a classic Peugeot town car stops and a couple, formally dressed, insist that he join them. And so begins Gil’s journey back to that period about which he has romanticized, meeting a host of writers and artists to include Gertrude Stein (Kathy Bates), Ernest Hemingway (Corey Stoll) and the Fitzgeralds, F. Scott (Tom Hiddleston) and Zelda (Alison Pill). These moments are wonderfully rendered, Gil’s jaw constantly dropping in astonishment, his heart given a tumble when he meets the lovely Adriana (Marion Cottillard), current girlfriend of Pablo Picasso (Marcial Di Fonzo Bo). It’s all pretty heady stuff with background music by Cole Porter. But there is a nugget of Woody Allen wisdom tucked into this engaging narrative, and it has to do with the nudging belief that plagues us all – well, perhaps many of us – that the past is always qualitatively better than the present. For Gil it’s Paris of the 20s. For others, it might be pre-industrial America, or the early 40s when America was on the cusp of World War II. Some have referred to those who stepped forward during this period as the “greatest generation.” A nice bit of nostalgia. This slim but important insight offered up by Midnight in Paris – which is seamlessly presented with laugh-out-loud moments – is that we have but one life to live and if it’s going to be lived fully it’s best to live it in the present. A nice thought that resonates, offered up by Gil, who is an uncanny doppelganger for Woody in mannerisms and pacing, conveying just a hint of Allen’s signature nebbish uncertainty. This film is one of Allen’s best since Match Point. It’s richly put together, with a strong sense that the auteur is back on his game. Which is all to the good. Midnight in Paris. Written and directed by Woody Allen. Starring Owen Wilson, Rachel McAdams, Marion Cotillard. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Fandango/Prime.

articles.text: Let’s get a round-trip ticket from Heaven to Hell. Sounds like a great adventure, doesn’t it? That is what happened at a concert on Sunday in San Francisco. I neglected to realize that Sunday was Pride Day in San Francisco. “The City” loves its rainbow-hued celebration. It was a red- flag day for sigalerts. The streets were clogged with idling cars. As the traffic stalled, we heard Bronx cheers from snails as they sped past the halted cars. Traffic was at a standstill. You could see the smoke coming from the ears of the drivers. There was a very interesting concert at St. Mary’s Cathedral which was scheduled to begin at 4 p.m. We finally arrived, albeit late, for the concert’s opening. Frustration was the most appropriate word. The concert was in progress. My first thought was: “this sounds like hell!“ I looked at the program and sure enough the first piece was “Hell” from Three Symphonic Chorales by Sigfrid Karg-Elert (1877-1933). Seated at the grand console of the organ was St. Mary’s outstanding organist, Christoph Tietze. There was a small audience in St. Mary’s spacious Cathedral. The absentees missed an outstanding concert. As Tieze continued his program, I began to realize that we were listening to imaginative tonal colors and dramatic dynamics. Just as a fine orchestra needs a great conductor to inspire it, so does a grand organ need an imaginative organist. That’s what we got on Sunday. The German composer Sigfrid Karg-Elert is not a famous name. I cannot say that he is one of my favorite composers, but he certainly is imaginative. The entire concert was dedicated to works by this German composer with his Swedish-spelled name. As for the music, it ranged from heavenly to hellish, soloistic to cacophonic – and everything in between…often taking the listener into the beyond. The final composition of the concert featured violin soloist Philip Santos and a four-member chorus. I have heard Phillip Santos perform in the past. His playing is always artistically beautiful. I wonder why he is not engaged as the featured violin soloist with one of our big-time orchestras. Next week, let’s go back to the wild West. Concerts were in saloons as well as churches. If the audience liked the concert, they would throw Gold nuggets onto the stage. If they didn’t like the concert, they might take out their guns and begin shooting. Photo courtesy of Cathedral of St. Mary of the Assumption St. Mary’s Cathedral organist Christoph Tietze.

articles.text: Kyle Chandler, Joel Courtney, Elle Fanning and Ron Eldard in Super 8 Super 8 is a great movie. What makes it great is the story, a solid coming of age tale of four boys and a girl, all on the cusp of adolescence, all set free from school, eager to begin their summer project: the shooting of a super 8 monster movie. And so, on a balmy night at midnight, having snuck out of their respective houses, they drive (don’t ask) to the local railroad station and under a canopy of stars, the camera on a tripod, begin shooting their film. That is until they hear a train in the distance. Charley (Riley Griffith), the director, tells his crew to wait. He wants the train for background. And so the kids wait, the light of the train growing larger, the noise of the locomotive reaching them. And it’s at that moment something happens that sends the narrative in a profoundly different direction. It’s a huge shift, delivered with a riveting crash. The movie quote that comes to mind is from Jaws, when Roy Scheider, small town sheriff, standing on the stern of a trawler, sees the enormous shark for the first time. Eyes wide, he backs toward the wheel house and says, “I think we’re going to need a bigger boat.” Super 8 is set in 1979 in a small Ohio town. At the center of the kids’ adventure is Joe Lamb (Joel Courtney), 12-years-old. He has recently lost his mother in an accident at the steel mill. His father, town deputy Jack Lamb (Kyle Chandler), is remote and, like Joe, still grieving. Joe finds solace with his friends; the prospect of spending the summer making a monster movie offers a way to escape the wrenching loss he has experienced. It also helps that Charley has asked Alice Dainard (Elle Fanning) to act in the film, Alice being a girl that Joe has admired from afar but never dared speak to. For Super 8 to work, Abrams has to get the story and the kids just right. And he does, which is no small thing. The tale is compelling and the kids are wonderful, each delivering an excellent performance, led by Fanning and newcomer Courtney. The young filmmakers soon learn that they are caught up in circumstances they never could have foreseen and realize that they must rely on one another to survive. Their fear and sense of urgency has an overwhelming sense of verisimilitude, conveyed nicely to the audience. Their dilemma is our dilemma. If this all sounds a bit vague, well, Super 8 is a movie that must be seen fresh, with as little information as possible. Of course, reviews and comments, even the trailer, will conspire to be too informative. But resist. As an aside, the second half of the film proves to be the most difficult. It’s in act three that Abrams must decide how to reveal what is behind the phenomenon that is impacting everyone in town. He handles this moment as well as can be expected. articles.text: When I saw the trailer for The Aeronauts I was immediately taken. What denotes adventure more than a massively tall, colorful balloon (or better, a sky full of balloons) floating into the distance on unseen currents of wind? And there was the cast, almost exclusively of Felicity Jones as Amelia Wren, balloon pilot, and Eddie Redmayne portraying James Glaisher, a wannabe meteorologist. The year is 1862, so, naturally, pretty much what is known about the weather is gleaned by stepping outside. Jones and Redmayne were wonderful in The Theory of Everything, that wonderful story about Stephen Hawking. They are about to join forces in a great adventure, meaning an attempt to go higher than anyone has before (above 23,000 feet). Their vehicle, so to speak, is a spectacular red and white gas balloon, some 80 feet tall and 55 feet wide (actually made for the production), with a good-sized rectangular wicker basket hanging below, its interior filled with ropes and bags of sand and James’ weather measuring instruments. At the outset of their journey, they bicker; as a team they’re oil and water. James is a bit of a rigid fussbudget. Amelia is an unwilling pilot, disinterested in the techie stuff that is scattered about. After a brief prologue, up they go – but directly into a storm that buffets them about, reminding them and the audience that they are incredibly vulnerable, a mere speck in a sky that is endlessly unpredictable. As they reach the higher elevations, well above 23,000 feet, the air becomes frigidly cold and the air perilously thin. Something they could not have fully anticipated since no one had ever been this high above the earth. But know that for drama, it is the weather and not much more that creates tension. We watch them cope with the unknown as they near the farthest reaches of the atmosphere, while all they have is each other and the confines of the basket, meaning there are long stretches in the tale that feel benign. Benign that is until the moment they realize that they must descend or die. It’s then that they discover that the opening to the balloon, designed to spill the gas, has been frozen shut. And thus begins a nicely riveting ending to act three. But it’s a bit of a wait. The Aeronauts. Directed by Tom Harper. Starring Felicity Jones, Eddie Redmayne, Tom Courtney. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2019. Now streaming on Fandango, Prime / Apple TV. Felicity Jones and Eddie Redmayne in The Aeronauts

articles.text: Chocolate Chip Cookie Cake When my latest edition of Bake from Scratch magazine arrived, this was the first recipe I wanted to bake as it is exactly the kind of sweet treat we enjoy. It is such a hit that I’ve baked it several times, making a few adaptations along the way. This will make frequent appearances over the summer as it both keeps and travels well for picnics, barbeques, block parties, you name it. The texture is firmer than a typical cake but less dense than a brownie. Its crispy edges and softer center mean plenty of texture for all tastes. Chocolate Chip Cookie Cake Adapted from Bake from Scratch, May/June 2024 INGREDIENTS • ½ cup unsalted butter • 1 tablespoon heavy whipping cream • 1⁄3 cup granulated sugar • ¾ cup light brown sugar, lightly packed • 1 large egg, room temperature • 1 large egg yolk, room temperature • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract • 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour • ½ teaspoon sea salt • ½ teaspoon espresso powder • ½ teaspoon baking powder • ¼ teaspoon baking soda • 1 cup chocolate chips, preferably dark, but a mix of dark and semi-sweet works too • Garnish: ¼ cup chocolate chips, melted INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 9-inch springform pan by cutting a round of parchment paper to fit the bottom. Butter the sides. Set aside. Melt butter over medium heat in a small, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Cook until the butter foams and the milk solids turn golden brown. Stir occasionally and do not leave unattended. This takes about 5 minutes. Transfer to a 3-quart, heatproof mixing bowl to cool slightly. Add the heavy cream and cool completely. Photos by Deborah Quok Meanwhile whisk together the flour, salt, espresso powder, baking powder, and baking soda in a small bowl and set aside. When the butter mixture is cooled, add the granulated sugar and beat with a handheld mixer, or in a stand mixer, on medium-high speed. When the granulated sugar is incorporated, add the brown sugar and continue beating on medium-high speed until the mixture is light, fluffy. Stop to scrape the sides of the bowl as needed. Add egg and egg yolk one at a time, beating until combined after each addition. Beat in vanilla extract. The mixture should have at least doubled in volume from the beginning. Add the flour mixture, beating on low speed until just combined. Finish stirring by hand using a spatula as needed to incorporate the flour fully, but don’t overmix. Fold in the chocolate chips to disperse evenly. Transfer the dough into the prepared baking pan and gently pat into an even layer. Cover with cling wrap and refrigerate overnight or up to 3 days. Position an oven rack to the middle oven position. Preheat to 350° F. Bake until the edges of the cake are golden brown and top looks dry, about 40 – 45 minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool for 10 minutes, at which time remove the sides from the springform pan. Cool completely before garnishing and serving. Garnish: Optional as the cookie cake looks appealing as is. But to fancy it up, melt ¼ cup of chocolate chips in a small, heatproof ramekin (a few short bursts in the microwave works here). Use a small spoon, knife tip or wooden skewer to dip into the melted chocolate and spread onto the cookie cake as desired. Store in an airtight container for up to 3 days. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers take a group photo at the intersection of Mountain and Bellevue Avenue, where a live oak has been planted to replace an historic Sequoia tree that was dying. Participating in last week’s walk were: Avelina Buijs, Karen Glasser, Alicia Rivera, Dave DeRoche, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Denny McGee, Kat Lang, Elizabeth Richter, Carolyn George, Jackie Leventhal, Tina Shum, Stella Houston, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Greg Slatoff, Joyce Ahern, Jack Fischrup, Sharona Fischrup, Judy Sokoloff, Kat Kewley, Rick Eigenbrode, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Gloria DaSilva, Bob Wong, Bill Ahern, Peggy Shultz, Sean Brient, Janet Laurent, Priscilla Wanerus, Jim Kellogg, Mark Laurent, Claudine Bach, Marianne Jakus, Albert Chen, Chuck Oraftik, Mark Davis, Nancy Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Mary Carter, Charlene Louie, Elane Rehr, Sherry Jacobs, Greg Meyer with K-9 best friend Rumi, Robert Lang, Noemi Alvarado, Lois Price, Brenda Ferrero and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Kathleen Parkerton, a first-time walker. The Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a strong turnout of 50 walkers and three K-9 best friends last week. Lois Price and Sherry Jacobs reminded the group that they are an official entry in this year’s 4th of July Parade. The City has completed a public tree inventory to catalog the many different species of trees in Piedmont. Dozens of trees were identified that are either failing or have died because of the increasingly harsher climate. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation has begun a campaign to support replacing these trees with species that are native, or compatible to California, and more likely to thrive. The Reforestation Project started in Dracena Park with the removal of more than 30 dead trees. The City’s arborist thinks they died because of the prolonged drought, warmer summers with less fog, and changing climate conditions. The project also included replacing the tall Sequoia in the Mountain-Bellevue circle. The walkers hadn’t been to the circle for a while, so it was the destination this week. The group headed off going through Piedmont Park and stopped by the Japanese Tea House to look at a redwood tree that is clearly not in good health. The walkers went up Sierra Avenue to a hidden path to the Mountain-Bellevue circle where more information was shared. Cameron Wolfe had written that the Sequoia stood high in this intersection for generations, even serving as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 20s and 30s but stopped at the onset of World War II. Last fall, there was an immediate danger of the tree toppling and it was thus removed. The Park Commission and the Beautification Foundation approved replacing the Sequoia with an Island Oak. This species is native to California, especially the Channel Islands. The tree is likely to thrive in this small traffic island that has no regular source of water. PBF raised $8,000 from neighbors and the new tree was planted in the circle on June 10. These funds will also cover additional planting, and care for the tree for at least two years. Some walkers went down Sea View, but the rest of the group continued up the steep Mountain Avenue. They enjoyed the beautiful homes along the way, and crossed Blair Avenue to see the wonderful view of San Francisco from Bell Avenue. Peggy Shultz, who lives on Bell, said the street was once the continuation of Mountain Avenue, but someone named Bell wanted the road’s name changed. The group continued down Scenic Avenue to a public stairway 281 feet long and emerged on Blair Avenue, where they saw the house where Jack London wrote The Call of the Wild in 1903. Going up Hardwick Avenue took the walkers to Oakland Avenue and then back to Highland Avenue and the Exedra. It was a two mile walk with trees, elevation, hidden paths, history, views, fun, and friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Chocolate Chip Cookie Cake By Deborah Quok When my latest edition of Bake from Scratch magazine arrived, this was the first recipe I wanted to bake as it is exactly the kind of sweet treat we enjoy. It is such a hit that I’ve baked it several times, making a few adaptations along the way. This will make frequent appearances over the summer as it both keeps and travels well for picnics, barbeques, block parties, you name it. The texture is firmer than a typical cake but less dense than a brownie. Its crispy edges and softer center mean plenty of texture for all tastes. Chocolate Chip Cookie Cake Adapted from Bake from Scratch, May/June 2024 INGREDIENTS • ½ cup unsalted butter • 1 tablespoon heavy whipping cream • 1⁄3 cup granulated sugar • ¾ cup light brown sugar, lightly packed • 1 large egg, room temperature • 1 large egg yolk, room temperature • 2 teaspoons vanilla extract • 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour • ½ teaspoon sea salt • ½ teaspoon espresso powder • ½ teaspoon baking powder • ¼ teaspoon baking soda • 1 cup chocolate chips, preferably dark, but a mix of dark and semi-sweet works too • Garnish: ¼ cup chocolate chips, melted INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 9-inch springform pan by cutting a round of parchment paper to fit the bottom. Butter the sides. Set aside. Melt butter over medium heat in a small, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Cook until the butter foams and the milk solids turn golden brown. Stir occasionally and do not leave unattended. This takes about 5 minutes. Transfer to a 3-quart, heatproof mixing bowl to cool slightly. Add the heavy cream and cool completely. Photos by Deborah Quok Meanwhile whisk together the flour, salt, espresso powder, baking powder, and baking soda in a small bowl and set aside. When the butter mixture is cooled, add the granulated sugar and beat with a handheld mixer, or in a stand mixer, on medium-high speed. When the granulated sugar is incorporated, add the brown sugar and continue beating on medium-high speed until the mixture is light, fluffy. Stop to scrape the sides of the bowl as needed. Add egg and egg yolk one at a time, beating until combined after each addition. Beat in vanilla extract. The mixture should have at least doubled in volume from the beginning. Add the flour mixture, beating on low speed until just combined. Finish stirring by hand using a spatula as needed to incorporate the flour fully, but don’t overmix. Fold in the chocolate chips to disperse evenly. Transfer the dough into the prepared baking pan and gently pat into an even layer. Cover with cling wrap and refrigerate overnight or up to 3 days. Position an oven rack to the middle oven position. Preheat to 350° F. Bake until the edges of the cake are golden brown and top looks dry, about 40 – 45 minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool for 10 minutes, at which time remove the sides from the springform pan. Cool completely before garnishing and serving. Garnish: Optional as the cookie cake looks appealing as is. But to fancy it up, melt ¼ cup of chocolate chips in a small, heatproof ramekin (a few short bursts in the microwave works here). Use a small spoon, knife tip or wooden skewer to dip into the melted chocolate and spread onto the cookie cake as desired. Store in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: The state motto of New Hampshire is also my philosophy for raising chickens. Backyard chicken husbandry has been gaining in popularity for years, driven in part by a backlash against industrial agriculture. Now kept by 10 percent of American households, chickens have become the country’s third most popular pets after dogs and cats. But most of these pet chickens live in backyard cages, even though their owners would probably choose to buy “free range” eggs at the grocery store. Cages aren’t fun for the chickens or their owners, who must clean them out constantly. So when my wife and I bought our first chickens a decade ago, she suggested having them bed down in a small coop at night and during the day roam free all over the backyard. It seemed like a reasonable idea – until the chickens shredded up the flower beds and pooped all over the patio. It turns out that people keep chickens in cages for a reason. A great deal of discussion ensued, with aesthetics at the fore. We finally agreed to relegate the chickens to the rear portion of the forested backyard, where the mix of Algerian ivy, mock orange, and oak trees was chicken proof. We didn’t want to install an unsightly fence, however, so we chose a green wire fence that was less than 3 feet tall and blended in with the foliage. This worked fantastically – for a couple of days. Chickens are ground birds but they actually do fly. Once they figured out how to jump the fence, we were back to where we’d started. Next, I clipped the feathers on the chickens’ wings, to the great consternation of my wife, who did not understand that it’s a painless procedure akin to trimming one’s fingernails. This prevented some of the chickens from hopping the fence. And that’s when I learned certain Our free-range kiddo several years ago with one of our first free-range chickens. You’ll need to cage baby chickens until they’re nearly full-sized. We lost many to hawks. chicken breeds are known to be “flighty,” meaning that even with clipped wings they can get up high in the air. My wife loved the Ameraucanas, a flighty breed that comes from Chile and lays beautiful eggs ranging from green to turquoise. But she didn’t want to herd them back across the fence every day. “Fine,” I told her. “I guess that means I’ll have to eat them.” She promptly enlisted our kids in a campaign to “save the chickens.” I felt a little bad researching how to kill and pluck animals that the kids thought of as pets. Fortunately, the problem worked itself out. The Ameraucanas got eaten by raccoons. I quietly celebrated our loss, but not for long. The raccoons’ welltimed coup de grace marked the beginning of an onslaught against all of the chickens. Though chickens will reliably roost in their coop every night, we’d forget to close the coop door and the next morning find our flock reduced from, My son pictured with our small coop, now controlled by an automatic door. The chickens forage in this area during the day.

articles.text: One of the keen pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it afterward. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting and then a discussion of it afterward. This month’s film is the sizzling 1959 American comedy, Some Like It Hot, directed by Billy Wilder and starring Marilyn Monroe, Jack Lemmon and Tony Curtis. Adding to the fun are two stars who came out of retirement to lend their talents: George Raft as the bad guy and the great Joe E. Brown. The tale starts off with a bang: machine gun fire in 1920s Chicago. After accidentally witnessing a Mafia massacre, saxophone player Joe (Tony Curtis) and his long-suffering buddy, Jerry (Jack Lemmon), improvise a quick plan to escape town with their lives. Disguising themselves as women, they join an all-female band and hop a train bound for sunny Florida. While Joe pretends to be a millionaire to win the band’s sexy singer, Sugar (Marilyn Monroe), Jerry finds himself pursued by a real millionaire (Joe E. Brown) as things heat up and the mobsters, headed by the snake-eyed Spats (George Raft) close in. Nominated for seven Academy Awards, Some Like It Hot received widespread acclaim from critics and audiences alike, and is considered among the best films of all time. Roger Ebert said of it, “Wilder’s comedy is one of the enduring treasures of the movies, a film of inspiration and meticulous craft.” In 1989, the movie became one of the first 25 inducted into the U.S. National Film Registry. In 1999, Entertainment Weekly voted it number nine on their list of “100 Greatest Movies.” It was voted the top comedy movie ever by the American Film Institute. Some Like It Hot offers many pleasures, among them the best and funniest closing line of any movie: “Nobody’s perfect,” uttered with a smile of heavenly silliness by Joe E. Brown on a racing speedboat. This is not a spoiler. You have to see the movie to understand how funny the line is. Some Like It Hot will be screened on Thursday, July 11th, at a one-time Flix Fest starting time of 3:30. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the event takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors for this showing will open at 3:00. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration may be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is Chinese director Zhang Zimou’s much honored 1994 drama, To Live. It will be shown on August 8th, at the usual time of 1:00 p.m. Movie poster from Some Like It Hot

articles.text: Preserving the Summer Harvest Preserved summer flowers crafted into framed art Now that it’s officially summer, the best part of gardening is here - harvesting. From tomatoes to corn, summer brings the freshest crops from a home garden and the farmers market. Here are a few fun ways I like to preserve the taste of the season. We’re lucky enough to have both a plum and apricot tree in our yard that produce generously each season. While fresh fruit from the tree is incredible, my favorite way to preserve stone fruit and berries from our garden is by canning a fresh fruit jam. For the best tasting jams, I use the ripest fruit and find a recipe from a reputable source. Depending on what fruit you’re working with, canning recipes require the correct PH levels and processing times in order to preserve safely. Check out the National Center for Home Food Preservation website for a wide selection of trusted recipes. I believe you truly haven’t tasted jam until you’ve harvested and canned the fruit yourself. If you open my fridge in peak summer, you’ll find mason jars full of cucumbers, beans, and peppers all pickled and ready for a quick snack. Unlike canning jam, quick pickling isn’t a labor-intensive project. With a mason jar full of hot vinegar, water, a little honey for sweetness, a pinch of salt, and your fresh vegetables, you can have delicious pickled snacks in just 30 minutes. These won’t last as long as shelf stable pickles, but it’s a great method to extend peak harvest vegetables. My other go-to preserving method is simply freezing produce. I hate to waste a perfectly ripe heirloom tomato, so into the freezer it goes. Later in the year it’ll be perfect to make a sauce or incorporate into a stew. Some vegetables will taste better postfreeze after a quick blanch, like beans, carrots, and leafy greens. Summer flowers have a special kind of magic that feels so fleeting, but there’s an easy way to preserve that summer beauty. Many flowers can be dried upside down to create everlasting bouquets. While most flowers won’t maintain their original color this way, pressing flowers to dry is an excellent method to save the true colors of summer. I’ll be hosting a class on this very topic in my home garden on Sunday, July 28th. We’ll create framed flower art from dried flowers to preserve the beauty of summer. Sign up on hotplate.com/girlandherdogfarm.

articles.text: A few months back, I decided to do an article on an obscure grape variety that I happen to be a big fan of. I collected about 15 samples of Alicante Bouschet from around the country and did a blind tasting with a couple of wine friends. The results were very illuminating, and the majority of wines were well made and very interesting, making it hard to understand how this once widely grown grape had fallen so low in popularity. The other interesting thing about the tasting was that the winner of the tasting, Spangler Vineyards, hailed from the most obscure location of all the entries. Most were from Sonoma or Mendocino County but Spangler was from Roseburg, Oregon. We all know Oregon’s Willamette Valley has skyrocketed to fame based on the quality of their Pinot Noirs, but Spangler hails from the much warmer Southern Oregon region of Roseburg and the main grapes there have nothing to do with Pinot Noir. The success of their Alicante Bouschet made me want to look into the other Spangler wines. In an earlier life, Pat Spangler was a floor trader on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange when he decided to set out on a whole new adventure. He came to California hoping to purchase a winery and start a new career as a wine maker. He did become a wine maker, but instead of California he ended up buying a property in Roseburg, Oregon and founded Spangler Vineyards in 2004. Over the years, the winery has grown to about 2500 cases production per year. The impressive thing about Spangler Vineyards is the amazing number of cuvees they produce for a small winery. This year they have produced 14 different wines. Pat Spangler has an affinity for unusual and little-known grapes, and he isn’t afraid to take a chance on making a wine few people have heard of. That’s why his offerings include Dolcetto, Malbec, Carmenere, Grenache Blanc and Tempranillo. If you are ever driving through Roseburg while cruising up Interstate 5, stop in at their friendly tasting room. Failing that, the best way to buy Spangler wines is through their website www.spanglervineyards.com. • 2022 Spangler Grenache Blanc Made from Grapes grown in Washington’s Columbia Valley, the Spangler Grenache shows aromas of citrus, apple and pear leading to peach and apricot flavors in the mouth. Light to medium-bodied and lively on the tongue, it’s very minerally with tangy acidity and a clean finish. Great aperitif wine. • 2019 Spangler Carmenere Griffin Creek Vineyard Originally from Bordeaux, the Carmenere grape is now mostly grown in Chile and rarely seen in North America. This wine opens with a dark core of bold red fruits and generous black fruit essence. Aromas of blackberries, dark chocolate, tobacco and just a touch of vanilla oak are pleasing. Medium to full bodied on the palate, it offers good structure with juicy tannins in a lush, fruit-forward style that ends with baking spices over the long savory finish. • 2019 Spangler Petite Sirah Southern Oregon The Terraces Spangler has won multiple awards over the years for their Pat Spangler, founder of Spangler Vineyards Spangler Vineyards tasting room

We all know Oregon’s Willamette Valley has skyrocketed to fame based on the quality of their Pinot Noirs, but Spangler hails from the much warmer Southern Oregon region of Roseburg and the main grapes there have nothing to do with Pinot Noir. The success of their Alicante Bouschet made me want to look into the other Spangler wines. In an earlier life, Pat Spangler was a floor trader on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange when he decided to set out on a whole new adventure. He came to California hoping to purchase a winery and start a new career as a wine maker. He did become a wine maker, but instead of California he ended up buying a property in Roseburg, Oregon and founded Spangler Vineyards in 2004. Over the years, the winery has grown to about 2500 cases production per year. The impressive thing about Spangler Vineyards is the amazing number of cuvees they produce for a small winery. This year they have produced 14 different wines. Pat Spangler has an affinity for unusual and little-known grapes, and he isn’t afraid to take a chance on making a wine few people have heard of. That’s why his offerings include Dolcetto, Malbec, Carmenere, Grenache Blanc and Tempranillo. If you are ever driving through Roseburg while cruising up Interstate 5, stop in at their friendly tasting room. Failing that, the best way to buy Spangler wines is through their website www.spanglervineyards.com. • 2022 Spangler Grenache Blanc Made from Grapes grown in Washington’s Columbia Valley, the Spangler Grenache shows aromas of citrus, apple and pear leading to peach and apricot flavors in the mouth. Light to medium-bodied and lively on the tongue, it’s very minerally with tangy acidity and a clean finish. Great aperitif wine. • 2019 Spangler Carmenere Griffin Creek Vineyard Originally from Bordeaux, the Carmenere grape is now mostly grown in Chile and rarely seen in North America. This wine opens with a dark core of bold red fruits and generous black fruit essence. Aromas of blackberries, dark chocolate, tobacco and just a touch of vanilla oak are pleasing. Medium to full bodied on the palate, it offers good structure with juicy tannins in a lush, fruit-forward style that ends with baking spices over the long savory finish. • 2019 Spangler Petite Sirah Southern Oregon The Terraces Spangler has won multiple awards over the years for their Pat Spangler, founder of Spangler Vineyards Spangler Vineyards tasting room Petite Sirahs and this bottle shows why. This P.S. is made in an accessible style without the harsh tannins some Petites show. Blackberries, chocolate and tobacco appear on the nose while the palate is full-bodied, opulent and lush. Drinking beautifully now, this will last at least a decade in the cellar. • 2020 Spangler Petite Verdot I am always glad to see this underappreciated Bordeaux variety bottled on its own as it often has a lot to offer. The Spangler P.V. has layers of fresh dark fruit with violet/floral notes on the nose. Medium bodied, it is focused and balanced, with a firm, fresh structure and succulent acidity. The wine is bold without being overly ripe and maintains a dense chewy character perfect for grilled ribs or burgers. • 2018 Spangler Cabernet Franc This wine totally avoids the unpleasant bell pepper scents this variety sometimes shows in colder climates. The wine is pleasantly floral on the nose with aromas of black cherries, and vanilla oak. In the mouth, it explodes with a burst of ripe raspberry and currant fruit with a touch of earth. The tannins are smooth on the long, satisfying finish. Nicely done. • 2021 Spangler Merlot The Spangler Merlot is a beauty, marked by scents of mocha, cherries, cola spice and vanilla. In the mouth, it shows tons of cherry, cassis and plum fruit. Its’s medium-bodied, rich and velvety, already approachable, supple and mouthwatering on the finish. Would be a great partner to beef bourguignon or other hearty stews.

articles.text: A novel by Chris Honoré INTRODUCTION The intended audience for the novel The Journey of Max Braverman, written by Chris Honoré, is preteens and early adolescents. The Piedmont Post is providing weekly installments of the book to encourage reading by young people. Hopefully, young readers will embrace the story, which focuses on the close relationship between two young brothers, Max and Jordie. The setting is a central California town in the mid-sixties. The novel is available through Barnes & Noble and Amazon. PART 1 - Jordie Jordie believed he could fly. I’d just come home from Marty’s and walked down the driveway into the backyard and saw him standing on the roof of the garage, his arms forward, feet together like he was balancing on the edge of a diving board. “Jordie,” I yelled. “Don’t you move. Don’t you do anything. I’m not kidding.” “Watch this, Max,” he called down, his reedy voice excited, his eyes looking straight ahead, already seeing himself in full flight, buzzing treetops. “Watch nothing, Jordie. You listen to me. I’m not kidding around. There is no way.” Jordie stood very still, his face scrunched in concentration, his skinny legs bent at the knees, every muscle tight, committed, ready to go airborne. The problem started when our mom made him this terrific orange cape with a silver lightning bolt down the back. It looked exactly like the one that Captain Marvel wore, a comic book superhero that Jordie couldn’t stop talking about. She’d given it to him as a surprise and when he opened the box and took out that amazing cape, all silver and orange, flaring wide at the bottom, well, she and I realized right then that maybe it hadn’t been such a good idea. See, Jordie got this look in his eyes, like all he had to do was put that cape on and he could levitate. Leap tall buildings. Run around the block faster than a speeding bullet. Or launch himself off the garage roof. And when our mom draped it over his shoulders and buttoned the strap, I had this feeling that Jordie was already planning his first flight. “Jordie, here’s the deal,” I yelled up at him. “If you don’t get down off that roof right now, I’m coming up there and throw you off and you’ll see that people can’t fly, no matter what they’re wearing. I mean, think about it. That’s why they take the damn bus to work. And if you jump, I’ll have to use that cape to wrap up your broken arm. I’m not fooling around. Swear. You will break something if you do this. Like a brick, Jord. Straight down.” Jordie stood there, weighing what I’d said, wanting with all his heart to give that cape a try, but the look on his face told me that he was starting to think about the role gravity played in our lives. Seeing an opening, I yelled, “I swear to God, Jord, this is no bull, you couldn’t fly a foot if you were wearing ten capes. Now will you please knock this off and get down.” Finally, muttering and complaining, he walked slowly to the back of the garage where he’d set up a ladder and crawled down, all the while telling me he could’ve done it. If I’d just keep my big nose out of stuff, it would’ve worked. I told Jordie to put a lid on it and how about starting with flying from our bedroom to the bathroom and back. If that worked, he could get back up on the garage and I’d even hold the ladder. Jordie was like no one else, I swear. Take his height. Weeks would go by and not a peep about it. Then, suddenly, it was a very big deal. More than once he’d refused to come in for dinner, and I’d find him sitting up in the huge oak tree in our backyard, his baseball cap on backwards, never a good sign, his thin body wedged between the branches, sulking. And Jordie could sulk like no one else. Though I have to say he didn’t hold a candle next to Howard, this guy who lived with us for a while. He was the sulking champ of the world, no contest. and sure enough, there he’d be. “Jord, mom wants you to come in for dinner.” “I’ve stopped growing, Max.” “What?” “I’m not getting any taller.” “Yes you are, Jord.” “I’m not. I swear. I can tell. Not an inch.” “Jordie, come on, just get down. You haven’t stopped growing. You’re growing every day. Really.” “How can you tell?” “Look, here’s how it works. The person growing? They can’t tell they’re growing. Other people, who’re watching, they can tell. Think about it. What does Aunt Celia say every time she sees you? She says, ‘Well, look at you, Jordan, look how much you’ve grown.’ Remember how she always says that? You think you’re not and she can tell you are. Celia’s watching. From the outside. You, the one growing, you’re watching from the inside. Inside doesn’t count. Now, will you get down outta that tree and come in and eat? Mom’s waiting for us.” “Fine. But after dinner, you have to measure me. And no mooshing down the hair this time. articles.text: Piedmont police noticed a vehicle driving in the middle of the night on Vista Avenue with a covered-up license plate on Monday, June 17. The vehicle, a 2001 blue Jaguar S-type, was being driven by a suspect known to the Piedmont Police. When officers pursued the vehicle, the suspect jumped out of the vehicle and fled on foot onto Bonita Avenue. Police were unable to locate the suspect, who had a $10,000 misdemeanor arrest warrant for narcotics out of Alameda County Sheriff’s Office. The vehicle was abandoned by the driver on Vista Ave, not far from the police station. Inside the vehicle was “a large volume of property.” Thirty-eight items in total were inside the vehicle; the items came from several stolen packages. Fifteen items were returned. The suspect’s vehicle was towed away and any other found property that could not be returned was booked as evidence at the Police Department. The suspect is still at large and charges are pending.
articles.title: Package thief abandons Jaguar full of packages

articles.text: The largest lake is off the main trail. Hugging its eastern shore brings you to another interconnecting swimmable lake. The most hidden lake is just east of there. Staying on its eastern shore takes you to an open ridgeline where you’ll see the green valley of Alpine Meadows below. The first mile of your course gains 660 feet; 430 of that in the initial half mile, then a quick gain of 200 feet up two switchbacks. The next mile mostly levels out, gaining another 370 feet to the group of lakes. Most of the hike is in open space, so bring sunscreen and proper hydration. According to Granite Chief Wilderness officials, camping at the Five Lakes Basin – 600 feet away from the lakes’ shorelines – is permitted without the need of wilderness permits. Proper food storage and only gas powered stoves are required. The Chronicle’s Tom Steinstra ranked Five Lakes in Tahoe’s No. 10 best hikes back in 2012. This column was originally printed in the Piedmont Post in September 2020. Look for this sign off of Alpine Meadows Road to start your hike.
